title: Appearance
text: Reference

title: Appearance
text:
Settings → Interface → Appearance (Ctrl+,). Everything on that page belongs to Arbor rather than to Bennu, and changing it here
changes it in every Arbor window — the same page is in Corvus's settings, Merula's, the explorer's and Tyto's, and it is the same page, not a copy.

title: The pages under Interface
text:
Appearance

The theme, the chrome and the text size — below.

Animations

How fast transitions run, or whether they run at all.

Keyboard Inputs

The overlay drawing every key and chord you press, with the action each triggered — for demos, screencasts and pairing.

Terminals

The shells the built-in terminal offers. Bennu's terminal is Arbor's: the same shells, configured once.

title: The Appearance page
text:
Colour theme
The active theme, and the editor that makes new ones. The title bar's gear has the same list as a submenu, for switching without opening settings.
Window controls
A Mac-style trio on the left, or flat Windows controls on the right. Not shown on macOS, where the system paints the real ones.
Compact title bar
A shorter title bar, for a short screen.
Minimized dialogs cap
How many dialogs may sit parked in the status bar. Past it a minimize is refused with a toast; nothing parked is ever closed for you.
Font scale
Every piece of UI text together, from 80% to 140%. The editor's own font size is separate, under Editor.

title: Rearranging the rails
text:
Customize Activity Bar… — from the command palette, the title bar's gear, or the button on the Appearance page — decides what is on the two icon rails
and in what order: one tab per rail, and in each the top cluster (the tool windows) and the bottom one (the dock toggles).

The default order of the right rail starts with the build tools the project has — Maven, Gradle, Cargo, Node — then Tests, then the rest.
A tool that appears later (a new build tool, a plugin) takes its place in that order relative to its neighbours, even if you have rearranged the rail before; your own order and hidden tools are never overwritten.

• Drag the handle to reorder within a cluster.

• The eye hides a tool. It stays reachable — every one has a shortcut and a palette entry — it just stops taking a slot.

• Project carries a lock: it is the way in, and with no file open and no tree nothing on screen could open one.

• Restore defaults puts the current tab back in natural order with everything visible, without touching the other tab. Nothing is written until Save.

A Cargo root has no Structure, Maven or Forms button, so they are not there to arrange — but the arrangement you gave them on a Maven project is remembered, and comes back with them.

title: Distraction-free mode
text:
Alt+Z (or Distraction-free mode in the palette) leaves the editor alone: the rails, the tool windows, the bottom dock and the status bar go away, and the title bar and the open tabs stay. Nothing is closed — the panels that were open come back as they were when you press the chord again.
Resting the pointer on the left or right edge of the window brings that side's rail back; picking a tool from it opens the tool window and leaves the mode.
It is not remembered between launches: it is a mode you go into to write, not one you want to find on the next start.

title: Where it is kept
text:
In the active profile's config.toml, beside the rest of the interface settings — never in the project. Two machines on one profile get the same bar; two
projects on one machine do not each get their own.

title: The welcome tour
text:
Bennu opens its first-run tour once, on the first launch. Welcome tour in the palette opens it again whenever you want, and it can be skipped from any step. It is
Bennu's own tour, with its own record of having been seen: going through Arbor's does not count, nor the reverse.

title: AssertJ
text: Build, run & test

title: AssertJ
text: The assertions that cannot fail — found in the test while you write it, rather than on the day the bug they were meant to catch reaches production with a green build.

title: The assertion that asserts nothing
text:
assertThat(x) builds an assertion object. Nothing is compared until a check such as isEqualTo is called on it, and the methods that only
configure it — as, describedAs, extracting, filteredOn, usingComparator — are not checks.

A statement that stops before a check is a warning: it compiles, runs and passes whatever the value is. The same goes for assertThatObject,
assertThatCode, the BDD then(…), and a soft-assertions object's softly.assertThat(…).
assertThatThrownBy(…) on its own is fine — it asserts that something was thrown.

title: Soft assertions nobody reports
text:
A SoftAssertions object does not throw: it collects, and throws everything at once when assertAll() is called. Forget that call and every failure
is collected into nothing.

The variable is flagged, and Alt+Enter on it offers Add softly.assertAll() as the method's last statement. The fix is offered only
where the end of the method is certainly the end of the test: no return in it, and no lambda or anonymous class using the variable.

The moment the variable goes anywhere — passed to a helper, returned, assigned — whoever receives it may call assertAll(), and nothing is said.
AutoCloseableSoftAssertions in a try-with-resources, SoftAssertions.assertSoftly(…) and the JUnit 5 extension report on their own and are never flagged.

title: Dedicated assertions
text:
A boolean assertion throws away the value it was computed from — the one thing you need when it fails in CI:

Written — Fails with — Alt+Enter rewrites to

assertThat(names.isEmpty()).isTrue() — expected true — assertThat(names).isEmpty()

assertThat(names.size()).isEqualTo(2) — expected 2 but was 3 — assertThat(names).hasSize(2)

assertThat(a.equals(b)).isTrue() — expected true — assertThat(a).isEqualTo(b)

assertThat(x == null).isFalse() — expected false — assertThat(x).isNotNull()

assertThat(x instanceof Order).isTrue() — expected true — assertThat(x).isInstanceOf(Order.class)

Also contains / doesNotContain, startsWith, endsWith, isPresent, and hasSize from a string's
length() or an array's length. The finding is a faint style note, and the rewrite is offered anywhere in the statement even when those notes are hidden.

The rewrites that depend on a type — isEmpty, hasSize, contains — are offered only when the variable's type is written
in the file as a JDK string, collection, map, Optional or array. On anything else there may be no such assertion, and the edit would not compile.

title: From JUnit to AssertJ
text:
With the caret in a JUnit 4 or JUnit 5 assertion, Alt+Enter offers Replace with AssertJ. In a file with two or more,
Replace every JUnit assertion in this file with AssertJ does them all in one edit.

JUnit — AssertJ

assertEquals / assertNotEquals — isEqualTo / isNotEqualTo

assertSame / assertNotSame — isSameAs / isNotSameAs

assertTrue / assertFalse — isTrue / isFalse

assertNull / assertNotNull — isNull / isNotNull

assertArrayEquals — containsExactly

The static import of AssertJ's assertThat is added with the edit when the file does not have it. The JUnit imports are left where they are.

A delta overload (assertEquals(1.0, ratio, 0.01)), a Supplier message (() -> "…"), a JUnit 4 assertTrue(label, flag)
whose first argument is not a literal, and assertArrayEquals over arrays whose types are not visibly the same. Nor in a file where a bare
assertThat already belongs to Hamcrest or a helper — the import would take the name away from it.

title: What it will not judge
text:
• Every call is resolved through the file's imports, never matched by name: Hamcrest's assertThat(x, is(1)), JUnit 4's, and a project's own helper are not
AssertJ's, and are left alone. A class implementing WithAssertions is recognised.

• assertThat(x instanceof T).isFalse() is not rewritten: isNotInstanceOf fails on null, where the original holds.

• A chain configured further than Bennu knows — usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields(…) with nothing after — is read as a check. That misses one, and
never reports a real assertion as broken.

• A test class extending JUnit 3's TestCase inherits its own assertEquals, so nothing in it is converted.

title: Bean Validation
text: Java & JSP

title: Bean Validation
text:
A constraint's message is resolved against a bundle the validator chooses — almost never the bundle the rest of the application reads, and sometimes
named in a @Bean. Bennu finds it, and checks the keys against it.

title: The assumption that is wrong
text:
")
private String name;`, 'java')}

The application has messages.properties, the field has that message, and it is entirely natural to assume the two go together. They do not.

Bean Validation resolves a message key against ValidationMessages — that exact base name, at the classpath root — plus the provider's own
bundle inside its jar, where the defaults of @NotNull and friends live.

A key that exists in messages_it.properties and nowhere else is one the validator cannot find, and it renders the key itself — braces included — into the field
the user is looking at.

That is why constraint messages are checked apart from the other message bundles. The bundle tooling answers does any bundle declare this key — true, and the wrong
question. Here the question is whether the validator can find it.

title: Where the bundle is named
text:
The specification's

ValidationMessages.properties

On a resource root, in every locale written. Nothing declares it — being called that is the declaration, which is also why it wears an icon of its own in the project tree, locale variants included: it is the one .properties among dozens that decides what a person filling in a form reads.

Named in code

A resource bundle locator

A base name in a string literal in a method body — in no configuration file, nothing to grep for — redirecting every custom message. An AggregateResourceBundleLocator naming several is read the same way.

Spring's

setValidationMessageSource(…)

Points the validator at the application's own MessageSource — the one wiring that makes the natural assumption true. Recorded as such, and checked against those bundles.

`, 'java')}

A bundle the code names and no file provides is flagged on the line naming it, rather than on the hundred messages it breaks: every custom message resolved through it
renders as its own key, all at once, and nothing else in the project looks wrong.

title: What counts as a key
text:
A message is interpolated, and only one of the things that can appear in it is a bundle key:

Written — Is

{min} on a @Size — The constraint's own attribute, resolved before any bundle

{order.name.length} — A bundle key

${validatedValue} — An expression, evaluated at interpolation — never looked up

\{ — An escaped brace, printed as written

Not cosmetic: reading every brace as a key would report min and max missing on every custom @Size message. Bennu knows each
constraint's attributes, so it reports the one genuinely unresolvable. Keys in the provider's own bundle —
jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull.message, and its javax spelling — are resolvable though nothing in your project declares them: they are in the jar.

title: In the editor
text:
Completion
Inside a message's braces, the keys the validator can resolve, with their text — deliberately not every key in the project: offering one from messages.properties would teach the mistake.
Hover
On a key, what the message will say and which bundle it comes from; on the annotation, what the constraint checks and which attributes its message may interpolate.
Go to declaration
On a key, the bundle line defining it, one target per locale.

An error

No validator for the type

@NotBlank on an int, @Size on a long: Hibernate Validator refuses it at startup — not a wrong message, an application that does not come up.

A warning

A constraint that can never fail

@NotNull on a primitive reads as a rule and enforces nothing.

A project type, a type variable, or a JDK class beyond those Bean Validation names produce no diagnostic: a custom ConstraintValidator is invisible from here,
and Bennu will not contradict one it cannot see. On a project with no validation bundle nothing is said about keys at all — the messages are literals or defaults.

title: The Constraints panel
text:
Every constraint the project declares, in one list: the member it is on, the message it will show, and its type as a tag. Group by constraint to answer "where do we use
@Email".

The tag to look for is missing: — a row whose message names a key no validation bundle declares. On screen, a constraint whose message does not resolve
looks exactly like one whose message does, until a user trips it.

title: Bevy ECS
text: Rust

title: Bevy ECS
text:
In an ECS the architecture is the data: a component and the systems that read and write it say more about how a game works than any file layout. Bennu reads
that out of the source — the declarations, the system signatures, and the pairs of systems whose accesses cannot run at the same time. No build, no running game.

title: When it turns on
text:
On a project whose Cargo manifest declares bevy or any bevy_* crate, corroborated by the sources — a #[derive(Component)], an
add_systems call. Which signal convinced Bennu is listed under Projects. A Maven project never carries this tooling.

title: Components
text:
Alt+Shift+B, or the rail button. One row per declared Component, Resource, Message,
Event, Bundle and States, badged. Expand a row for the systems touching it — each naming the system, whether it reads or writes,
and the parameter it was read from:

{`Health Component read by 2 · written by 1
damage write mut q: Query Update
draw_health read q: Query> Update
PlayerBundle in bundle carries Health`}

This is find usages asked properly: who writes Health is a question about signatures, and a text search answers it with every comment mentioning the word.

A marker
A component nothing reads, whose whole job is With<Player>, is counted apart, as filtered on by. A filter is not an access — two systems filtering on one marker do not contend — but a marker twenty queries depend on is not unused either.
Messages and events
Two roles, not two names: a message is buffered — written with a MessageWriter, drained by whoever reads it — an event is triggered and delivered to observers. A message is found through the queue it is posted to, an observer event through the On<…> parameter handling it.

title: Systems
text:
One row per system, badged by the schedule it was registered in, so grouping by badge groups by schedule. The row summarises what it touches; expanding lists each access
with its query filters. A system with no add_systems call found is tagged so rather than hidden — on a project registering through a helper, that tag is the
honest answer.

title: Access conflicts
text:
Two systems in one schedule wanting the same data, one of them mutably, can never run in parallel. Bevy derives that from the signatures when it builds the schedule, and so
does this panel:

{`damage ⇄ tick Update contend over Score unordered
Score write/write — mut score: ResMut
tick mut score: ResMut`}

Working as intended

ordered

Two conflicting systems explicitly ordered — what .before, .after and .chain are for.

Worth a look

unordered

Serialised in whichever order the schedule picks: a frame-order dependency nobody wrote down.

An exclusive system — one taking &mut World — contends with everything in its schedule, and gets one row saying so rather than one per component.

Only an unordered pair is also mentioned in the editor, as a single informational note on the name of each system that lists its peers (contends with 3 unordered
systems (a, b, c) over Score). Contention without a declared order is the normal state of most Bevy projects, so it is never a warning. Ordering is followed transitively —
a.before(b) plus b.before(c) orders a against c — and .after and .chain() count the same way.
Sets count too: configure_sets(Update, (Input, Logic).chain()), Input.before(Logic), Logic.after(Input) and a set nested
with .in_set(…) order every system in them, and sys.after(Input) orders a system against a whole set. Only what this project writes is read, so
a pair that only a plugin's configure_sets could order is shown as unordered in the panel, never as a guess in either direction.
The note is left out when Bennu cannot stand behind it: a system in a set (the set may be ordered by a plugin Bennu never reads), an exclusive one,
a system registered with a .run_if(…) — its own, or its set's — and a pair that only meets through a message buffer, one side writing and the other
reading. All of them still appear in the panel.

title: In the editor
text:
Mark — Beside

◈ — A component

▣ — A resource

✉ — A message

✳ — An observer event

▦ — A bundle

Clicking one opens the systems that touch it — one jumps, several ask.

title: Engines built on Bevy
text:
A project on an engine of its own may never write Res or MessageReader: it declares #[derive(DomainResource)] and takes a
DomainResMutParam<Board>, and the engine's parameter does the Res underneath. Bennu reads the wrapper as what it wraps, so the declaration still
lists its systems and a contending pair still pairs.

The wrappers known are fulcrum's per-domain layer — DomainResParam, DomainResMutParam, DomainStateParam,
DomainStateMutParam, DomainMessageReader, DomainMessageWriter, DomainQuery — and its derives DomainResource,
DomainMessage, DomainState. A #[derive(SystemParam)] the project itself declares is read from its own fields and needs no table.

title: Where a component is created
text:
A signature says who reads a component; nothing in one says who makes it — so a type six systems read has, by its parameters alone, no origin. Under
every declaration is a row per site putting it into the world: a spawn, an insert on an existing entity, an insert_resource, an
add_message, an init_state — each naming its function and the argument given.

Read from call sites, so spawn((Health(100.0), Player)) is a row under Health and one under Player — what a bundle-as-tuple means. A value
whose type cannot be named from the expression is skipped, and the call names are a closed list: an insert method on your own type contributes nothing.

title: Materials and shaders
text:
A #[derive(Asset)] type is a row in the components list like any other — "who touches SpiralHoverMaterial" is answered by the same signatures. An asset
is reached through the Assets<T> resource storing it, which is how it is looked up here. A material carries its shaders as the first rows under it, and the
relationship is described in Shaders (WGSL).

title: What it does not claim
text:
Bennu reads this project's own sources and nothing else — not the engine's plugins, not a dependency's systems — which decides what is safe to say:

A conflict stays true
Two systems contending over Score contend however many systems a plugin adds — so the report is short of pairs rather than full of invented ones.
Disjoint queries are not conflicts

With and Without on the same component keep two queries apart, and so does a plain &T / &mut T / Mut<T> /
Ref<T> in the query data, which requires T just as With<T> does — Query<(&mut A, &mut B)> never overlaps
Query<&mut B, Without<A>>. An Or<…> filter makes no claim at all.

Run conditions and tests are not read as a schedule
Whether a .run_if(…) is true cannot be known from the source, so a conditional system is never accused. Code under #[cfg(test)], #[test] functions and mod tests is skipped, so an App built inside a test does not invent pairs.
Parallelism is never claimed
"These two run at the same time" cannot be shown from part of a schedule: one unseen system writing the same component would refute it.
No ordering graph
Most of an app's ordering lives in plugins, so a picture from this project's add_systems calls would be a fragment presented as a whole. Ordering appears only as the tag on a conflict row. Systems are matched to the open file by name and position, so a same-named function in another module, or a method called like a system, does not collect another system's note.
Names are not resolved
Health is matched by name, so two Health types in two modules look like one — though generic arguments are kept, so NextState<GameState> and NextState<MenuPage> stay apart. Every row shows its parameter, so a wrong one can be recognised.
Registration is read literally
A system added behind a cfg, in a loop or by a macro is not seen as registered — it appears with no schedule.

title: Bevy Remote
text: Rust

title: Bevy Remote
text:
Look at a running Bevy game from the editor: its entities and how they nest, every component with its current value, its resources, and the types it registered —
and change them while it plays.

title: Connecting
text:
The game has to serve the Bevy Remote Protocol. Add both plugins to its App:

app.add_plugins((RemotePlugin::default(), RemoteHttpPlugin::default()));

Then open the Bevy Remote sidebar — Ctrl+Shift+A, the radar button in the right activity bar, or the command palette — and press
Enter on the endpoint (http://127.0.0.1:15702 unless the game changed it). It is offered on projects that depend on Bevy.

Bennu asks the game what it can do rather than guessing from a Bevy version: the verbs it offers are the ones the game lists, so an older game that cannot spawn or
watch simply does not show those controls.

Mutating, spawning and despawning act on the game at the endpoint. A game on another machine is flagged in the panel's header.

Saved games:

The bookmark button beside the endpoint saves it; saved games are listed on the connect page, in the server menu of the panel header and in the command palette
(Bevy Remote: connect to …). The inspector holds one connection at a time, so choosing another game replaces the current one.

Driving the game: the companion crate:

The stock protocol inspects and edits the world. To let Bennu (and Imber) also drive the game — screenshots, keyboard, mouse and gamepad input, named actions, frame statistics and an on-screen
indicator that someone is attached — add the arbor-bevy-remote plugin, which registers extra arbor.* methods on the same server (Bevy 0.18):

app.add_plugins((
DefaultPlugins,
with_arbor_methods(RemotePlugin::default()), // instead of RemotePlugin::default()
RemoteHttpPlugin::default(),
ArborRemotePlugin::default(), // ::without_indicator() hides the border
))
.register_remote_action("restart", "Start a new game", |world, _arg| Ok(serde_json::json!("ok")));

The methods can be called from the Console view (arbor.info lists them all), and three views of the bottom panel are built on them.

• Screen — the game's window as a picture. Live re-captures every second; with Click through on, a click on the picture is a click in the game at the matching spot.

• Input — a virtual keyboard (with Ctrl / Shift / Alt), text, mouse and gamepad, the game's registered actions, and the indicator switch. Record keeps everything you send as a script with its timing; Replay sends it again, and the script can be copied as JSON or loaded back.

• Stats — frame-time percentiles (p50, p95, p99, worst), a graph of the last frames against a 60 fps budget, and every diagnostic the game registered.

While a client is attached the game draws a soft coloured border and a small label: blue when connected, orange while input is being sent, grey when paused. The Input view and the command palette switch it off; ArborRemotePlugin::without_indicator() removes it from the game.

title: When the game restarts
text:
Rebuilding and running the game drops the connection. Bennu notices, retries quietly in the background and picks the new process up by itself, re-reading its
types: the old registry described a binary that no longer exists. A banner shows the retries; a notification appears only if the game stays away after the first retry,
once when it is lost and once when it is back, or once more if Bennu eventually gives up.

title: The tree
text:
The sidebar is one tree with three roots, all closed until you open them: Entities (the hierarchy), Resources and States. Selecting a leaf shows its
detail in the bottom panel, where it can be edited; the buttons in that panel's header switch to the game-wide views — statistics, screen, input, console and the type registry —
and back to the detail. Expand all / collapse all are in the sidebar's toolbar; ← and → close and open a node, / or just typing a letter starts the filter,
Esc clears it.

Entities:

An entity's icon says what it is when a marker component does: a camera, a light, a mesh, a UI node, a sprite, text or a window; any other is a cube, with a branch when it has children. A node opens one level at a time, so a parent with thousands of children costs one page. The world is re-read only while the sidebar or the panel is open, once a second while it is
changing and progressively less often while it is quiet.

The search box takes plain text — a name, or digits for an id — and two filters, which can be combined:

Write — Shows

goblin — Entities whose Name contains it

has:Health — Entities with that component (short name or full path)

no:Dead — Entities without it

The filter applies to all three roots: an entity that matches stays under the parents it hangs from (names match loosely from three letters — gbch finds Goblin Chief), and resources and states match by name; a root with nothing to show disappears. Reveal in hierarchy, in the right-click menu, takes a hit back to its place. Delete on a row despawns it, after a
confirmation. Ids are written the way Bevy prints them: 3v1 is slot 3, generation 1.

The bookmark button beside the search box keeps a search under its own text and runs a saved one again; the command palette lists them too (Bevy Remote: search …).

title: Components
text:
Select an entity and the panel shows its components as flat, collapsible lines — a closed one summarises its value, a lone number, text or flag is edited on the line itself. The values are pushed by the game rather than polled — the Live badge says the
stream is on — so a field that moves in the game moves here.

• Numbers, booleans, text, enums and nested structs have their own controls; short number lists such as positions are on one line, labelled by axis. Drag an axis letter to change the value (Shift finer, Ctrl coarser), double-click it to reset.

• Transform shows position, rotation as angles in degrees (a toggle shows the quaternion) and scale with a lock that scales the three axes together. Colours show a swatch, a picker, a hex field and alpha. A Duration is seconds; a handle is a small chip; an entity reference jumps to that entity.

• A type's #[derive(RemoteInspect)] hints (below) turn a number into a slider, an angle in degrees or a date, and a list into a colour.

• Edit as JSON, on each card, edits the value exactly as it is sent. It is always right, where a typed control can only be as good as what the game's type registry says.

• Add component searches the registered types and starts from a well-formed placeholder value; Ctrl+Enter inserts it.

• A component the game could not serialise is shown with the game's own message instead of a value.

title: Resources, states and types
text:
The panel's detail is deliberately narrow: a few lines of values need a few hundred pixels, not the dock's whole width.

A resource opens in the detail view and is edited with the same lines. States are the game's Bevy state machines, found in the type registry as State<T> beside NextState<T>: the detail shows the current variant and the others, and Switch to asks the game to move there (it applies it on its next state transition). A variant whose name says it ends the session — a menu, a quit, a reset — asks first. A state without a registered NextState can be read but not changed. The type registry view is the registry itself: every component and resource the game
registered, with its exact path — the string the protocol wants — one click from the clipboard, and a shortcut to add the type.

The copy button in an entity's or a resource's header copies it as JSON, as the game sent it, or as RON: the same data in RON syntax,
fields named, lists in brackets. The RON follows the shape of the JSON, not the Rust type, so a position stays [x, y, z]. The palette has both for the selected entity.

Telling the inspector how to draw a field:

A bare number says nothing about being a volume, an angle or a date. #[derive(RemoteInspect)] (re-exported by arbor-bevy-remote) attaches that to a field:

#[derive(Component, Reflect, RemoteInspect)]
struct Lamp {
#[inspect(color)] tint: [f32; 3],
#[inspect(range = 0.0..=1.0, step = 0.01)] intensity: f32,
#[inspect(angle)] beam: f32, // radians, edited in degrees
#[inspect(date)] installed: f64,
#[inspect(label = "speed", unit = "m/s", readonly)] measured: f32,
}

app.register_inspect::<Lamp>();

A /// doc comment on a field is its description — shown on hover and as a quiet line under the field's name — and one on the struct describes the type under its name (description = "…" overrides either). Hints are sent through arbor.inspect_hints and read once per connection. color, range, angle and date each say how to draw the field, so a field takes one; step, readonly,
label and unit combine with them.

title: Console
text:
The Console view calls any method the game lists, with raw JSON params: the game's own remote methods, and anything newer than the inspector. Type a
method — the suggestions are the game's own rpc.discover — press Tab to take one, then Ctrl+Enter to run it. The answer is shown as
JSON and can be copied; calls are kept in the list on the left for this session, and picking one loads it back. A call is sent as written: a method that spawns or
despawns does so.

The game sends each value through the type's own serialisation, which sometimes differs from the type's description: a position is described as a struct of
x, y, z but arrives as [x, y, z]. The editors follow the value and use the description only to refine it, so an unusual type
can fall back to the JSON editor, never to a wrong control.

title: Limits
text:
• The protocol has no method for systems, schedules or the game's diagnostics, so there is nothing to show for them; a game that adds its own method for them can be called from the console.

• The protocol cannot filter or page on the game's side, so each refresh reads every entity's name and parent. A world of hundreds of thousands of entities is read
less often, not more cheaply.

• Entity ids are exact up to 253; a slot recycled millions of times is shown by its raw digits.

title: Rust & Cargo
text: Rust

title: Rust & Cargo
text:
What a Cargo workspace is, what you can run on it, and what is wrong with its manifests — all of it read from the files rather than asked of
cargo.

title: The Cargo tool window
text:
Alt+8 opens it on a Rust project. Its rail button is there whenever the active project has a Cargo crate — at its root
or in a subfolder, as in a Tauri app — and sits beside Maven's when it also has a Java one.

title: Several Cargo projects
text:
The window lists the Cargo projects of the whole workspace, not only the project on screen: a Rust crate in a
subfolder of a Node project (a Tauri app's src-tauri) is a Cargo project like any other, and so is one in
another project of the workspace. With more than one, a small tree at the top — grouped by project when the workspace has
several — picks the one the commands act on. Pick a row with Enter or a click; pick it again to let go. With
nothing picked the window follows the file you are editing; with a single Cargo project there is no tree at all.

The same rule applies to the palette: a command that acts on one Cargo project runs straight away when a row is picked or the
open file belongs to one, and otherwise asks which, in a list you can filter by typing.

The first group is the whole workspace — every command aimed at every crate, --workspace. Under it, one group per crate,
each holding three things:

Click to run, with -p

Commands

check, build, test, run, clippy, fmt, doc — output in the Run console.

Discovered, not only read

Targets

The binaries, examples, integration tests, benchmarks and the library. src/main.rs and src/bin/*.rs are Cargo's conventions, not the manifest's, and each row says which it was. A binary or example runs when clicked; anything else opens its source.

What the crate declares

Features

The ones default reaches, transitively, are marked, with what each turns on. An optional dependency's implicit feature is listed — unless something refers to it as dep:…, Cargo's own rule for suppressing it.

The crate header answers what the three groups cannot — where the crate is. Its locate button, or Focus in
Project from a right-click on the header, opens the Project tree on the crate's folder, expanded, selected and holding the keyboard focus. The
same menu opens its Cargo.toml and copies its path.

The common commands are in the command palette too — "Cargo: …", aimed at the whole workspace — since a row can only be clicked with the
panel open.

title: Two things it tells you unprompted
text:
A directory under the root with a Cargo.toml no members pattern covers. Otherwise silent: it compiles when built directly and is
invisible to --workspace. The panel names it and offers to open the manifest missing it. A crate inside another crate's tree is not flagged —
that is how a fixture crate is written.

cargo clippy without the component fails with an unknown-subcommand error, which reads as a broken button. The row says needs clippy
instead, and rustup component add clippy then ⟳ fixes it. Without rustup at all nothing is greyed: not knowing is not knowing it
is absent.

title: Cargo.toml
text:
A manifest gets completion and diagnostics of its own, both from one description of what a manifest may contain — which is why a key that completes can
never underline itself as unknown.

Completion:

Ctrl+Shift+Space, or just type. What is offered depends on the caret:

The caret — Offered

In a [header] — The tables, minus those already there — except [[bin]] and friends, where a second is the point

On a key — The table's keys not yet set, each with a line saying what it does

After a dot — workspace, on the keys Cargo lets a member inherit — nothing on name, which it does not

In a dependency table — Crate names from this workspace, Cargo.lock and the crates already downloaded; accepting writes the whole assignment with the newest known version

On a version — The versions this machine has, newest first — a pre-release never above its release

Inside a spec — version, path, git, features, optional, workspace, …

A value with a closed set — Editions, crate types, lint levels — with quotes when the caret is not in a string

In [features] — The other features, the optional dependencies, and both reference forms, dep:serde and serde/

In members — The directories holding a crate, and the dir/* glob covering what is under one

The crate list is what this machine has seen, so the popup appears while you type. What crates.io answers is the two questions below, off the same cached index.

Newer versions:

A dependency that is behind gets a line above it — 1.0.219 available — and pressing it writes that version into the manifest as one undo step. It is
deliberately quiet:

• nothing about a path, git or workspace-inherited dependency, which has no version to be behind;

• nothing about a pin (=1.2.3) or a range — you already decided;

• nothing about a pre-release, either way.

Answers come from an on-disk cache refreshed at most daily per crate, and a failed lookup falls back to whatever was cached — offline, last week's list beats
silence. Settings → Rust turns it off, making Bennu entirely local again.

title: Adding a dependency
text:
• Press the ＋ in the Cargo window's toolbar, or Add dependency… in the palette.

• Type the crate name, then pick a published version and the features that version declares.

• Pick the table — dependencies, dev-, build- — and, in a workspace, the member.

It runs the real cargo add: the requirement written cargo's way, [workspace.dependencies] inheritance honoured, the features validated
against the resolved crate, the entry in the file's own style. When cargo refuses, its words are shown — they are the fix. Afterwards the manifest is read again,
the crate graph refreshed and the language server told to resolve the project.

The index Cargo uses has no search: a crate is looked up by name. An unknown name or an unreachable index still adds — leave the version empty and cargo picks it.

Diagnostics:

Silent in Cargo

A key typo

[dependancies], feature = […] — the symptom is a dependency that is not there or a feature that does nothing, in a manifest that looks fine.

Refused by Cargo

A feature referring to nothing

Usually after a rename. All four reference forms are understood, and a bare name that is a non-optional dependency gets its own wording — the fix is optional = true.

Plus:

• workspace = true with no matching entry in the root's [workspace.dependencies] or [workspace.package];

• a path or members entry with no crate behind it; a default-members entry that is not a member;

• a duplicate key; a dependency naming both a git and a path, or no source at all;

• an optional dev-dependency; a version requirement with no number in it.

Red is only for what Cargo refuses to build. An unknown key is a warning — Cargo warns on those and gains new ones every few releases. Nothing is said about a table
Bennu does not recognise, or anything under [package.metadata] and [lints.*], which belong to other tools.

title: Dependencies
text:
Alt+N opens the panel a Maven project uses, in Cargo's vocabulary: one group per crate, and per row the crate, the version,
where that version came from, its kind — normal, dev, build — and whether it is in the local registry.

• The version is the one Cargo.lock chose, not the requirement written — serde = "1" is not what you compile against. With no lockfile
the panel says so and shows the requirement, unknown rather than missing.

• A workspace = true dependency is marked as pinned by the workspace; a renamed one shows both names; a target-specific one carries its
cfg(…).

• The last group is everything in the lockfile no crate of yours declares — what your dependencies dragged in.

title: Running and debugging
text:
▶ and Shift+F10 launch the active run configuration, and a Cargo configuration is a cargo subcommand: a crate, a command, a
target, features, a profile, and two argument fields. On a workspace with exactly one binary none of it is needed — ▶ makes the configuration and runs it. With several
it opens the editor, because cargo run refuses to guess too.

Field — Goes — Reaches

Cargo arguments — Before the -- — cargo

Program arguments — After it — Your program or the test harness — --nocapture belongs here

A cargo run has no build step in front of it — the command is the build. Its output, Stop, ⟳ and the tab strip are the Run console's usual ones. Debugging a
Cargo configuration builds the binary first and launches it under a debug adapter — see Debugging.

title: Navigating
text:
Ctrl+N opens the navigator on Types rather than Classes — structs, enums, traits and type aliases — and
Ctrl+Shift+Y finds functions, methods and constants. The language server does the matching, so both start at two characters.

Both of its views read Bennu's own engines — tree-sitter grammars for Java and JSP, and Java's declaration model — so on a Rust project it could only report their
absence, which would read as Bennu not understanding a language rust-analyzer is answering everything about. The rail slot holds the Cargo window instead.

title: Generated Rust
text:
Settings → Rust → Code Style says how a code template writes Rust — read as style.rust
in a template. It is a short list, and deliberately: rustfmt owns the formatting, and a second set of
switches here would either agree with the project's own rustfmt.toml or fight it. What is left is what a
generator has to decide and a formatter never touches:

• Visibilitypub, pub(crate) or private, for a generated item and its fields

• Deriveswhat a generated struct or enum derives, in order — empty writes no #[derive(…)] line

• Documentation linesa /// on each generated item, which is what missing_docs asks for on anything public

• Errorsanyhow::Result, a crate error type, or a Result<T, E> spelled out

• Self inside implSelf rather than the type's name — Clippy's use_self

The page carries a preview of a small generated type, so each choice is read in the output rather than in its label.
Java's equivalent is Settings → Java → Code Style, and the two are separate because almost nothing
they say overlaps.

title: Code generators
text: Editor

title: Code generators
text:
Generators write the code that is the same in every project and different in the details: a Spring
Security configuration, a JPA converter, a Jackson serializer, a client for your own endpoints. Each has
its own dialog with its own options, shows the result before anything is written, and
writes it as one step — new files are created, and what goes into the open file is a single undo.

title: Opening one
text:
• The command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P): every generator the open file can take is listed as «Generate …».

• The editor's context menu › Generate: one submenu with Members… (the dialog Alt+Insert opens), From a template…, the configuration-properties flows where they apply, and then the same list.

• A folder's context menu › Generate in the project tree: the classes are written into that folder's package.

title: What the dialog does
text:
The options are on the left, the preview on the right — one tab per file, one for what is inserted into
the open class, one for the snippets meant for other files (an application.yml key, a
TypeScript wrapper). The preview follows every change. Below it Bennu lists the dependencies the code
needs and the classpath lacks, the annotations it adds to your existing code, and anything worth knowing
before you accept.

The first field has the focus when it opens; Tab walks the options, Ctrl+Enter
generates, Esc cancels. A file that already exists is never overwritten: the dialog says so and
waits for another name or package.

title: What it reads from the project
text:
Defaults come from the project: the Java level (records and pattern matching only where they compile),
jakarta.* or javax.* from the Spring Boot, servlet and persistence versions,
whether Lombok, MapStruct, AssertJ or Mockito are on the classpath, and the package of the application
class. The detected facts are shown as chips at the top of the dialog.

title: Spring Security configuration
text:
A SecurityFilterChain for an API with JWT, an API with several issuers (a fixed list, each
with its audience and roles claim — a dotted path such as realm_access.roles is walked), a
web app with form login, a stateless API with HTTP Basic, or an API and a web app together as two ordered
chains. Rules are a list of method, path and access; CORS, CSRF (optionally with the token in a cookie),
method security, a user store (in memory, JDBC, your own) and the password encoder are options.

Excluded from security lists Ant patterns (/css/**, /favicon.ico…)
that skip the filter chain altogether through a WebSecurityCustomizer bean
(configure(WebSecurity) before 5.7). Web scenarios start with the usual static resources; for a
path that still needs security headers add a rule with permitAll() instead.

The style follows the Spring Security version: the lambda DSL, the fluent .and() chain where
it still exists, requestMatchers or antMatchers, @EnableMethodSecurity
or @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity, and a WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter before 5.7.

title: JPA attribute converter
text:
Dates as ISO text, durations as milliseconds, enums by name or by a code accessor, booleans as
Y/N, lists as separated text, JSON columns through Jackson, encrypted strings
(AES-GCM, key from an environment variable) or any pair of expressions. It is registered with
autoApply or wired onto a field of the open class with @Convert.

title: Jackson serializer / deserializer
HTTP client from Spring endpoints
text:
Pick endpoints from the application's request mappings, grouped by controller, and choose the library:
RestClient, WebClient, RestTemplate, an @HttpExchange
interface, OpenFeign, java.net.http.HttpClient, OkHttp or Retrofit. Path, query and header
parameters and the body become typed method parameters; the return type loses its
ResponseEntity / Mono wrapper. The base URL is read from a property, authentication
(bearer, basic, API key) from further ones, and a configuration class builds the client with timeouts and
an error handler that throws a generated exception carrying the status and the body. The DTOs are either
imported from the server's module or generated as records or classes next to the client.

title: Web services: SOAP and CXF
text:
SOAP call — paste an envelope (and the WSDL, if you have it) and get the class that makes the
call. The Body gives the operation and its namespace, and every value in the request becomes an argument; the
WSDL gives the address, the SOAPAction and the service and port names. Variants: the JDK
HttpClient with the envelope in a text block, Spring-WS WebServiceTemplate,
WebClient, CXF Dispatch or a generated CXF port, and Apache HttpClient. SOAP 1.1 and
1.2 are told apart by the envelope namespace (content type, action header), a WS-Security
UsernameToken is optional, and the response is read by XPath, unmarshalled with JAXB, or returned
as XML; a SOAP fault is thrown as an exception.

CXF REST client → modern client — paste a JAX-RS interface or resource class
(@Path, @GET, @PathParam, @QueryParam, @HeaderParam,
@Consumes, @Produces) and get the same API as any of the HTTP client generator's Java
libraries, or as Rust reqwest / ureq. XML bodies stay XML: the Spring converters,
Jackson's XmlMapper (JAXB annotations honoured), a JAXB converter for Retrofit, or
quick-xml in Rust. Form, matrix and cookie parameters are reported, not converted.

title: Class generators
text:
• DTO and mapper — a record, Lombok or plain DTO from the entity's chosen fields, and a MapStruct interface or a hand-written mapper (static or a Spring component), both directions and lists.

• Builder — a nested fluent builder written into the class, with toBuilder() and required-field checks; or Lombok's @Builder on it.

• equals, hashCode and toString — over every field, the id alone (the default for an entity) or a chosen set; arrays and floating-point fields are compared correctly.

• Test class — a MockMvc test with a call per known endpoint for a controller, a Mockito test with the dependencies mocked for a service, a @DataJpaTest for a repository, plain JUnit otherwise; JUnit 4 or 5.

title: Rust generators
text:
• Tauri command — the #[tauri::command] function at the caret (state, app handle, window, async, Result), its generate_handler! line and a typed invoke() wrapper with camelCase arguments.

• HTTP client — from an endpoint description (method, path with {'{id}'} variables, query and header parameters, body and response types): reqwest async or blocking, or ureq; serde structs for the payloads, an error enum (thiserror or hand-written), bearer / basic / API-key authentication, a timeout, and the Cargo.toml lines it needs.

• ratatui application — terminal init and restore, the event loop with an optional tick, an App with its state, draw and key handling; ratatui::init() from 0.28, the manual crossterm set-up before.

• ratatui widget or component — a Widget (also for &T), a StatefulWidget with its state, or a component with handle_key and render.

• ratatui list or table screen — the row type, wrapping selection (next, previous, first, last), the highlighted render and the arrow, Home/End and vim keys.

• ratatui key map — an Action enum and from_key written from specs such as q, ctrl+c or shift+tab, with the labels and descriptions of a help line; a key bound twice is refused.

• ratatui popup, confirmation or input — a centred popup, a yes/no dialog that reports the answer, or a one-line text input with a cursor, drawn over Clear.

• Bevy component, system or plugin — components, resources, events (messages from 0.17), states, systems with a filtered query and resources, and plugins that register them.

The generators write sensible, ordinary code and stop there. The templates under Code templates
are the way to shape a generator's output to your own style when a project needs something different.

title: Completion
text: Editor

title: Completion
text: What the popup knows, where each suggestion comes from, and the members that exist without being written anywhere.

title: Asking for it
text:
Typing . after an expression offers the members. Ctrl+Space — or Ctrl+Shift+Space — asks explicitly, anywhere. In Java the answers come from the project index and appear once it is warm; edits are indexed
again in the background as you type, so completion and go-to follow your changes without reopening anything.

Not a style choice. macOS claims the whole Ctrl+Space family for switching input source, above
applications: those chords produce no key event in any program. Cmd+Space is Spotlight, which is what the
Shift is for.

• Typing fast does not send a question per key. Within a burst the list is asked for when you pause, and at least every few hundred
milliseconds while the burst lasts; the first letter, a . and Ctrl+Space are answered at once.

• When an explicit request finds nothing, the footer says so for a moment — No suggestions here, or No engine answered for
this file when no server or index is up. Silence would look like a shortcut that never arrived, and those two have opposite fixes.

• If a shortcut seems to do nothing at all, turn on Show keyboard inputs (Alt+Shift+K) and press it again: the overlay draws every chord the window receives. Nothing drawn means the key never arrived — a
conflict outside Bennu.

• Command languages ask on every position. A .dev scenario or a .dig line is words and
arguments rather than dotted paths, so with the caret after unlock the server — nd-dig-lsp, geode's
own — is asked too, not only after a trigger character.

title: The pages
text:
The order things are offered in
Eight signals, strongest first: what the position wants, who declares it, what you picked, and the rest.
Smart suggestions and ghost text
The learned and project-aware signals, finishing the line in grey, type names and where the import counts come from.
Matching and writing
How a name is matched, a name with nothing to its left, what accepting writes, and how to read a row.
Annotations, abbreviations and postfix
Names that expand into code.
Positions with their own rules
After a dot, method references, arguments, enums, keywords and a declaration's name.
Members that do not exist yet
The method this class calls and does not declare, missing accessors, and what Lombok and records generate.

title: Frames, values & watches
text: Build, run & test

title: Frames, values & watches
text: Where the debugger puts what it found, and how to read a value that is bigger than the row it sits in.

title: It all happens in the Run console
text:
There is no separate Debug window: debugging is the same launch with more to look at, so Run (Alt+R) grows what the moment needs. While a
session is attached, the transport controls sit on the left of the status row. While the program is stopped, two columns open left of the transcript:

What got here

Frames

Library and JDK frames are muted and open their source or a decompiled stub. A run of consecutive library frames folds into one row — a stop inside a framework is forty frames around your three; ⊟ turns folding off.

In the selected frame

Variables and watches

The frame's variables, with your watches underneath — both read again when you pick another frame.

• The editor follows the debugger. Every stop and step opens the current frame's file at its line — stepping into a method changes the tab for you — and the stopped line
is banded full width with a bar down its left edge.

• Both columns are resizable, and each collapses to a labelled strip from the ⇤ in its header, giving the transcript the rest. Where you left them is remembered.

• When the program stops, Bennu comes to the front and opens the console: a breakpoint fires because of something in another window, and the editor is where the answer
is. A step does not raise it — you did that here.

title: Stepping
text:
Key — Does

F8 — Step over

F7 — Step into

Shift+F8 — Step out

F9 — Resume

A step passes straight through the JDK, Spring's AOP machinery, Reactor and the logging façades, rather than stopping in ArrayList.add or walking
ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed a dozen times. Landing in a proxy — a Spring CGLIB or Hibernate stand-in, methods existing only at runtime — it keeps going,
so stepping into service.place(order) arrives at place.

Which packages are passed through is a judgement about whose code you are debugging: Settings → Java → Debugger lists them, and removing org.springframework.* steps
into Spring. A pattern may carry * at one end only — the VM refuses anything else, and one bad entry would stop stepping altogether — so it is checked as you type. Changes apply
to the next launch.

title: Reading a value whole
text:
The variables tree fetches a row's contents only when opened — a stopped program is a graph, and walking it eagerly would be a round trip per node nobody looked at. That is wrong for one job:
a struct of fifteen fields, four of them structs, is nineteen disclosure triangles before you can read it, and then no longer fits on screen.

So every row with something inside carries a {'{}'} button — on hover and on keyboard focus — reading the value and everything under it at once, as text you can scroll, search
with the editor's find, and copy. The tree is for looking around; this is for looking at. It works on a watch row too.

RON
The value is a Rust value, and RON keeps the three distinctions JSON throws away: a struct is not a map, a tuple (1, "x") is not a list, a variant is a name. It is RON-shaped, as the footer says — a debugger reports names, rendered values and children, not a type system — for reading, not parsing.
Literals stay literals
A value the debugger already rendered as a literal is printed, not opened. Rust's formatters render a String, PathBuf or OsString as text and offer children — a byte buffer underneath — and following those turns a path into four levels of internals and a row per character. A size=3 describes a container, so it still opens.
Bounded, and saying so
Each value is a round trip against a suspended program, so the walk stops at a depth, a node count, a container width or a time budget — and says so, at the top and where it stopped. A value containing itself is named as a cycle. The same modal works on a Java object graph.

title: Watches
text:
A watch is a path: order, order.customer.name, items[2]. On a native session it takes a leading * to follow a reference —
*head — and *self.next means what the same line means in the source, the star binding looser than the dots.

A path is read out of the variables tree, not handed to an evaluator. So v[0] in the watch box and [0] under v are the same row, mean the
same whichever adapter resolved, and know which variant an enum actually holds — which no static type can. A subscript is fetched alone, so v[400000] on a million-element
Vec is a fair question with an exact answer. Watches are saved with the breakpoints.

A watch may also be a small expression over paths, in the language Java breakpoint conditions use: i + 1, order.total * 2 > limit, items[i],
done && n % 2 == 0, -x; on Java also Status.ACTIVE and other static fields, and + joining strings. Numbers behave as the language does —
Java's int and long wrap around; on a native session every integer is a checked 64-bit number, overflow and dividing by zero are errors, integers and floats are never
mixed, a u64 above the signed range is refused rather than wrapped, and two structs are compared field by field, not with ==.
A method call is refused by name: it would run application code inside a stopped program. An expression this language understands is answered by it, and a failure is its own,
not quietly retried on the debugger; what it does not parse (x as u64, &x, Enum::Variant, closures) goes to the debugger's evaluator below.

Anything not a path or such an expression goes to the debugger's own evaluator, and Bennu says which and what it can do:

CodeLLDB prefix — Evaluator

/se — the default — Its own reader: follows the formatters, runs nothing in the program

/nat — LLDB's own parser

/py — Python, with $name from the frame

The other two adapters have one evaluator, so a prefix they lack is refused by name rather than sent back as a syntax error about a slash.

Not a debugger limitation: a debugger can only call a function that is in the binary, and a generic function nobody called was never compiled. So v.len(), a macro, a
turbofish, ?, .await and a closure each come back with one line saying why, and what to read instead.

title: Things worth knowing
text:
Objects show fields, not toString()
An object reads Order@1f3c and expands to its real fields, superclasses included. toString() would read better and would run application code in a paused program — blocking on a lock the stopped thread holds, changing state, or throwing.
Variable names need -g
Maven compiles with full debug information by default. A class compiled without it still holds breakpoints — the line table is separate — but the panel shows only this.
The launch is not frozen
The program starts and runs, so a start-up breakpoint may pass before the debugger listens. Tick Suspend the VM until the debugger has attached in the configuration, and every debug launch begins stopped, waiting for Resume.
Detach is not Stop
Detaching leaves the program running without a debugger; the console's ■ ends it. A suspended VM holds its locks and port, so a session left paused looks exactly like a hang — the rail's Debug dot turns amber to say so.

title: Debugging
text: Build, run & test

title: Debugging
text: Stop the program where you want it and read what it is actually holding — Java over JDWP, Rust through a debug adapter, with the same panel and the same gestures for both.

title: Starting
text:
Gesture — Does

Shift+F9, or 🐞 beside ▶ — Launches the active configuration with a debugger attached

A click in the left margin, outside the line numbers — Sets or clears a breakpoint

Ctrl+F8 — Sets or clears one on the caret's line

Ctrl+Shift+F8 — The breakpoint list

Breakpoints belong to the project, not to a session: they are kept in .arbor/bennu/config.toml beside the run configurations, still there tomorrow, and a
launch installs whatever is set. What happens once the program stops — frames, values, watches — is Frames, values & watches.

Attaching to a running JVM:

A run configuration of the Attach to JVM kind debugs a program Bennu did not start — an application server, a service in a container with its debug port published. Start that JVM with

-agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=*:5005

(suspend=y makes it wait for the debugger before main; the older -Xdebug -Xrunjdwp:… spelling works too), then give the configuration the same port. The host is not a
field: Bennu connects to 127.0.0.1 only, so a JVM on another machine needs an SSH tunnel to a local port.

Gesture — Does

🐞 beside the configuration chip, which reads Attach for this kind, or Shift+F9 — Attaches; ▷ is off, since there is nothing to run

Command palette › Attach to JVM… — Attaches with the active Attach configuration, else the first one; with none, creates one on port 5005 and opens the editor

The unplug button in the Run console header or in the debugger's controls, Detach the debugger in the palette or the ⋮ menu — Detaches; the program keeps running, with no debugger attached

The attach gets a console tab like a launch, and the session — starting, running, paused — is reported in the same panel with the same buttons. If nothing listens on the port, or what listens is not
a Java debug port, the reason appears as a notification and in the tab.

The program was not started by Bennu, so Stop on an Attach tab, closing the tab and closing the window only let go of the debugger. A program stopped at a breakpoint at that moment is resumed.

title: More than one at once
text:
Several programs can be under the debugger together, each in its own console tab. A session and its tab are one thing, so the panel shows the one whose tab is in front, and moving
along the strip moves the frames, variables and watches with it. What the VM made of each breakpoint is per session — two VMs on one project can disagree, one having loaded the class.

When a breakpoint fires in a program you were not reading, its tab comes forward with the window — having to hunt for which of three consoles it happened in would be the one case where
the debugger makes you work for it.

title: Rust, and the debug adapter
text:
A Cargo configuration debugs too, in the same panel with the same keys. Underneath it differs: a JVM is debugged by launching it differently — an agent argument, and the VM
connects back — while a native binary's debugger must be what starts the process. So a Rust debug launch:

• Builds the target, its errors going to the console under the same tab — a failing build reads as one.

• Reads the executable's real path from cargo's own JSON. target/debug/«name» is wrong on any project configuring anything — a named profile, a [[bin]]
named apart from its package, a target-dir, a cross target — and a test binary's name carries an unpredictable hash.

• Hands that path to a debug adapter.

Adapter, in order of preference — Why there

CodeLLDB — It has Rust data formatters: a Vec<T> shows its elements, an Option Some(3), a String its text. It ships as a VS Code extension, so the extension directory is searched as well as PATH.

lldb-dap — LLVM's own, on most Macs without installing anything — Xcode's toolchain included, which no windowed app's PATH has. Its Rust formatters come from the toolchain (below).

GDB — In DAP mode, GDB 14 or newer — the fallback on a Linux machine with no LLVM.

Settings → Java → Debugger can pin an adapter. A pinned one that is missing is reported, not quietly replaced: the three render values differently, and one you did not choose would
make the variables panel disagree with itself between machines.

Why a Vec shows its elements:

Neither LLDB nor GDB knows Rust's types. Stopped on a Vec<Order>, an unconfigured LLDB shows buf → inner → ptr →
pointer → an address — five clicks down to nothing. String is a byte buffer, HashMap a table's internals, Option a discriminant
and a union, Rc a control block. One fix per adapter, applied for you:

CodeLLDB
Ships Rust formatters, and is told the source language so it uses them.
lldb-dap
Ships none — but the Rust toolchain does. rust-lldb is, entirely, a script loading two files from lib/rustlib/etc into a plain LLDB; Bennu loads the same two at launch. Without a toolchain, the variables tree says at the top what to install.
GDB
Reads the printers the binary names and understands Rust as a language, so it is left to its own auto-loading.

Formatters cover the standard library. A struct of your own has none anywhere, and LLDB's default prints nothing on its row. On lldb-dap Bennu turns
on synthesised summaries — {'{'}id:7, total:19.9{'}'} — and where even that is unavailable the row says how many fields it holds.

A frame carries one name — geode::mine::dig — not a class and a method, since splitting it would invent nonsense on synthetic frames. And the session follows
the thread that stopped; choosing among threads is not offered yet.

title: Breakpoints
text:
Where one can go:

A Java breakpoint is a position in bytecode, so only a line compiling to some takes one. A package statement, an annotation, a class or method signature, a field with nothing to
run, a comment or a lone brace compile to nothing, and the margin does not offer a breakpoint there — the faint dot under the pointer appears only on lines that can take one.

• A field with an initializer is offered, since its initializer runs; so is any statement.

• A breakpoint already set stays clickable when an edit makes its line unqualified — otherwise you could not remove it.

• Breakpoints follow their lines as you edit above them. One landing on a line with no code binds to the statement below, and the tooltip names the line it really stops on.

• A line inside an anonymous or nested class binds in that class, including one the program loads later.

In a library's source:

A dependency opened with its downloaded sources, or a JDK class, takes breakpoints like your own code: the margin, Ctrl+F8, conditions
and pass counts. The breakpoint is remembered by its class — org.springframework.web.client.RestClient, line 118 — so it is kept with the project and
installed on every launch, hollow until the program loads that class.

• When one stops the program, the frame selected is that library line, not the nearest frame of your own code.

• The breakpoint list shows it by class and package, marked library; choosing it reopens the source.

A class with no sources opens as signatures rebuilt from bytecode, whose line numbers are Bennu's rather than the class's — so its margin offers nothing. Download sources
replaces it with the real file, and breakpoints can be set from then on. They stop on the lines of the version on the classpath: sources of another version put them on the wrong statements.

title: What the dot says
text:
Dot — Means

Solid — The VM accepted it; the program will stop there.

Hollow — The class is not loaded yet — resolves itself the moment the program touches it.

Grey outline — Disabled. Right-click a breakpoint to disable one you will want back in ten minutes.

A ring — It carries a condition or a pass count — below.

A sparkle — Set by Imber, the assistant — see Imber debugging below. Fainter while its class is not loaded, grey when disabled.

The list, exceptions and muting:

Ctrl+Shift+F8 lists every breakpoint in the project, grouped by file, with a switch to disable and a bin to remove. It is also where to add an
exception breakpoint, which stops where a throwable is thrown rather than caught — the only way to see the state that produced it, with no line to click.

The ⊘ in the debugger's controls mutes every breakpoint: they stay set and listed, and the program runs to its end at full speed. Muting lasts for the session — a
debugger silently ignoring your breakpoints tomorrow would be a trap. It works on both kinds of session: a JVM's breakpoints are uninstalled from the VM, a native session's removed from
the adapter and put back on unmute. Either way the list is untouched.

Several threads stopped at once:

A breakpoint stops the whole program by default. Turn on Suspend only this thread in the Breakpoints list and a hit stops just the thread that reached it: the others keep running and can stop too, each as a stop of its own.
The stop you are looking at is one; the others are listed under the frames and a click switches to one, after which the frames, variables, steps and resume follow it. Resume lets the current stop go and moves on to the next waiting one.
A stop that was hit while another was still open is labelled Leftover stop, so it is not taken for a new breakpoint. Removing a breakpoint resumes the threads that were parked on it, but never the stop you are looking at.
While the whole program is suspended and more stops are waiting, a step is refused until they are done, because nothing can run.

title: Why it stopped
text:
Above the frames the stop says whether it is a new breakpoint, a step or a leftover, and, when the breakpoint has a condition, the condition and what it read (total = 250), so a stop the condition should not have allowed shows at once. A condition that could not be evaluated says so and stops anyway.

Stepping:

Step into does not stop in a record's accessor (id() {'{'} return id; {'}'}): it steps out and goes on, the way it already passes through library code. A step can also read what the method it leaves returned — the last method that returned during the step — shown with the stop; it costs time on a step over heavy code, so it is asked for, not on by default, and needs a VM that supports it.

title: Conditions, and stopping every Nth time
text:
Right-click a breakpoint → Add condition…, or use the breakpoint list, where each has a condition field and a pass count. A breakpoint with either is drawn ringed — a
breakpoint that does not stop is the most expensive thing to misread in a debugger, and "it has a condition" is usually the answer.

Stop on every Nth hit counts after the condition — "the third time i > 5" — the only reading that composes. The count restarts each
launch, and the list shows how many times each breakpoint has stopped the program: also the quickest answer to "is this line even running".

The VM stops every time the line is reached, the condition is evaluated in that frame, and the program is let go when it does not hold — as in every debugger. On a line run a million
times, it is slow.

What a Java condition may say:

A boolean expression over the paths a watch takes — comparisons, arithmetic, &&, ||, !, ? : and parentheses. Strings compare by their text, other objects by identity, and a boxed Integer or Boolean reads as its primitive:

Condition — Note

i > 5, count == 0, ratio < 0.5 — —

order.customer.name == "acme", items[2].price > 0 — Fields and subscripts

items[i].price > 0, items.length > 3 — A subscript may itself be an expression; an array has length

i + 1 == n, total % 100 == 0, price * qty > 1000 — Arithmetic as Java computes it: int and long wrap around, integer division truncates, a char is a number, and dividing by zero is an error that stops the program

label + "!" == "ok!" — + joins strings; an object is not joined, because that is toString()

order != null && order.total > 100 — && and || short-circuit, so the left guards the right

done, !order.paid — A path alone must be a boolean

status == Status.ACTIVE, limit < Limits.MAX — Enum constants and static fields, named as the source file names them: its imports, its package and the classes around it are consulted, and a fully qualified name works too. The class has to be loaded and initialized — not yet, and the condition says so

status.name == "ACTIVE" — Also fine: every enum constant carries its name

A condition quietly answering something adjacent to what you typed swallows the stop, with nothing on screen. So method calls — list.size() > 3 runs
application code inside a paused program — along with casts, instanceof, new, lambdas, assignments, ++ and the bitwise operators are refused by name as you
type, not approximated. So are a condition that reads nothing from the program (true, 1 == 1) and one that is a number rather than a yes or no (i + 1).

When a condition cannot be answered at a hit — a null halfway down the path, a field missing on this subclass — the program stops anyway and the breakpoint says why. A bug in
a condition is only visible from where it happened; running on would turn a typo into a breakpoint that never fires and never explains itself.

title: On a Rust session
text:
The condition is the debug adapter's own expression language, sent untouched — it has a real evaluator and documentation, and a subset reimplemented here would be worse and
disagree with all you have read about LLDB or GDB. What it may say is CodeLLDB's, lldb-dap's or GDB's documentation; the status bar names which is driving.

• Bennu cannot check it as you type — it has no parser for a language it does not own — so a mistake shows after launch, as an unverified breakpoint with the adapter's
complaint in its tooltip.

• The pass count goes as that adapter's hit-condition expression, %3 for every third, which not all read alike: a breakpoint stopping every time is the adapter
not doing it. An adapter declaring it supports neither has the field dropped instead, because a request setting a file's breakpoints sets all of them.

title: Logpoints
text:
A breakpoint with a log message does not stop the program: each hit prints the message to the run console and the program goes on. It is how to watch a line in a loop or a
request handler without freezing it. The message is plain text with {'{'}path{'}'} placeholders — order {'{'}order.id{'}'} has {'{'}items[0].qty{'}'} lines — read from the frame the way a
watch is read (a name, .field, [0]), and {'{{'} / {'}}'} are literal braces. A placeholder that cannot be read prints the reason in its place rather than
nothing. Common JDK types print as values — a BigDecimal as 123.45, a date as ISO text, an enum as its name, a list as ArrayList(size=3) — and any other object as Type@id; use a longer path to print one of its fields. A condition and a pass count apply first, so a logpoint can say "only when total > 100". Imber can set them too (below); the breakpoint list marks them logpoint.

title: Imber debugging
text:
With the Debugger group of tools on (Settings › Imber), Imber, the assistant, can debug a Java program the way you would, on the very session this panel shows: it sets breakpoints and logpoints, launches or attaches (each asks first), waits for a stop, reads the stack and values, steps and lets go. You watch the same stop and can take over with the buttons you already have.

• Its breakpoints are yours to control. They are drawn with a sparkle in the gutter, badged Imber in the list, and you can disable or delete them like any other.

• When the program stops while Imber is not waiting, Bennu takes a snapshot itself and shows a card in the conversation with Send to Imber now.

• Changing the program is a separate switch, off by default, with no undo; every change is listed in the Debug panel as an Imber action.

The full description (what each tool does, what asks, session lifetime, snapshots, the mutate tools) is on the page Imber: Debugging with Imber.

title: Dependencies
text: Projects

title: Dependencies
text:
The libraries a project pulls in — listed, searchable and, with sources, readable in the same editor as your own code.

The panel describes one Maven, Gradle, Cargo or Node project at a time. When the workspace has several (a Rust crate in a Node project's subfolder, two
projects side by side), a tree of them tops the panel and picks which; with one there is nothing to pick.

title: Node projects
text:
A folder with a package.json is a Node project — npm, pnpm or Yarn, told apart by the lockfile beside it. The
panel lists one group per package.json: the root, and every member of a monorepo's workspace
(workspaces in the manifest, or pnpm-workspace.yaml). Each row is a declared dependency, with:

• The version you actually getfrom package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml or yarn.lock — the range in the manifest (^4.17.0) is only shown when there is no lockfile yet

• The kindruntime, dev, peer or optional — the section of the manifest it is declared in

• Where it comes froma tag for anything that is not the registry: workspace (a sibling package, shown at its own version), git, file, url, an npm: alias or a pnpm catalog

• Whether it is installeda declared package with no node_modules folder (found the way Node finds it, up through the parent folders) is called out as not installed; peer and optional ones are exempt, since they are legitimately absent. Until there is a lockfile or a node_modules, the panel says the column is unknown

• A newer releasean ↑ 5.0.1 badge, amber for a major bump, on a package whose resolved version is behind the registry's latest. It uses the same look packages up online switch and cache window as the version hints inside package.json, so turning that off removes the badges

• Vulnerabilitiesthe shield badge — see Dependency security

Resolve tree on a Node project reads the lockfile — no npm ls, no network, no package manager — and
runs as a row in the Jobs panel. It gives the Duplicate versions group (a package present at several versions, with
who asked for each), the via … line on every transitive row and the full routes down to it. Without a lockfile there is no
resolved graph to read, and the panel says to install first.

The Node tool window (right rail, Alt+Shift+9) is the other half of a
package.json: each package's scripts as rows that run in the Run console with the project's package
manager, and Install (npm install, pnpm install or yarn install). Above the scripts a
Dependencies row summarises the project — declared and transitive counts, how many packages have a newer release, how many are
vulnerable — and opens the Dependencies panel on it; the toolbar also opens the Vulnerabilities window. A project that is only a frontend gets the Dependencies panel and the Node window
but no Tests catalogue and no Alt+8 build-tool slot.

title: How the classpath is found
text:
On a Maven project Bennu resolves the dependency jars from your local repository, so completion, navigation and
validation see library types and not only the JDK and your own sources. Every module of a multi-module project adds its
own.

• The poms are read straight from disk with your local repository — parent chains, imported BOMs, the transitive
closure and the exclusions — in milliseconds and with no build tool involved.

• Only when that comes up short is Maven run — and the two answers are combined, because a mvn run that
fails halfway still wrote the entries it did resolve.

• The result is cached against your poms' timestamps, against what was missing, and against the library
files it was resolved from — a jar or pom in your local repository that is rewritten retires it.

A project whose Maven is missing, misconfigured or simply broken still resolves, from the poms and the repository alone.

The resolve is offline — it downloads nothing — so a dependency that has never been fetched cannot be
resolved, and Bennu names it rather than reporting a count. The moment one of the missing artifacts lands in your
repository the cache is stale, so installing a dependency is picked up on the next open instead of being hidden until a
pom is edited. Rebuild index resolves again unconditionally.

When Maven is needed it is looked for on PATH, then in the usual install directories, then as the
project's own mvnw wrapper.

Adding a dependency or bumping a version has the classpath resolved again and the index rebuilt behind it, a few seconds
later, with nothing pressed. It waits for the file to settle first, so a save in the middle of an edit does not start a
rebuild against half a <dependency>.

title: When a sibling module is installed
text:
In a workspace of several projects, mvn install on a module rewrites its jar and pom in your local
repository — and every project that depends on it is now resolved against a library that no longer exists. Bennu
notices when the window regains focus (and when the panel opens): the Dependencies panel shows a notice
with a Reload dependencies button, and a toast offers the same once per change. The panel itself is
always drawn from the repository as it is now, so Resolve tree and Pulled in transitively agree;
what stays old until you reload is the editor's classpath — completion, go-to and the library index.
