Reload dependencies is also in the toolbar of the panel and in the command palette.

title: Changing what is on disk
text:
The three actions that change the disk — as opposed to reading it again — live in the build tool's window: the Maven
tool window's actions menu. All three run as background jobs and report in the Jobs panel. So does the work Bennu starts by itself when a project opens: Indexing, Resolving dependencies — a failure there stays in the list, a success clears it — and Analyzing project; and, when you ask for them, Validating project (Cancel stops it) and the project-wide vulnerability check, which shows only if it takes more than a couple of seconds.

When the editor disagrees with the disk

Re-resolve dependencies & rebuild index

Drops the cached classpath, reads the local repository again and reindexes — the two halves of "make the editor agree
with the disk", since either alone leaves the other's stale answer. Rarely needed by hand: saving a pom does it.

When the pom is right and the jar is not there

Download missing dependencies Alt+Shift+U

The one action here that uses the network: dependency:go-offline for the project, then a rebuild.

When a library is a decompiled stub

Download sources

Fetches every dependency's -sources.jar, so Ctrl+B into a library lands on real
source. Artifacts that publish no sources are skipped, not reported as failures.

Editing a pom.xml covers what the same reading does inside the editor.

title: The Dependencies tool window
text:
Alt+N shows the classpath as a list, one group per module. Each row carries:

• The coordinategroup and artifact

• The version you actually getwith ${…} expanded and <dependencyManagement> applied

• The scopeand the optional tag where it applies

• Where the answer came fromdeclared here, pinned by a parent's management, or inherited whole from a parent's own <dependencies>

• The profilewhen the dependency only exists under a <profile> — shown and labelled, since whether it is active depends on the JDK, the OS and the command line

Clicking a row opens the pom that decides it — which is usually not the one you were reading.

The last group, Pulled in transitively, is every jar on the classpath that no module asked for: where
"why is this version of that library here" gets answered.

Who brings what, and version conflicts:

The list above is read from the poms and never runs Maven, so the window opens instantly. Two questions need Maven itself —
which dependency brought a jar in, and why there is more than one version of it — because Maven's choice between versions
depends on the whole reactor. The Resolve tree button (the flow icon in the toolbar, or the one in the notice
at the top) runs mvn dependency:tree in the background. It can take a while on a cold cache, so it only runs when
you ask, honours the automatic download setting (offline otherwise), and keeps its answer per project until you resolve again. While it
runs it is a row in the Jobs panel, like any other long resolve.

Once it has answered:

• Version conflictsa group at the top with every artifact the project sees at more than one version. Each lists the version Maven kept, the ones it dropped, and for each version the chain of dependencies that asked for it.

• via …every transitive row names the declared dependencies that bring it in; its chevron opens Required by, every route from what a module declared down to it (spring-boot-starter-web → spring-web → spring-core)

• Detailsa declared row opens (chevron) to show what it pulls in and, when conflicted, its versions

• Searchthe filter also finds a library by what it pulls in — typing freemarker opens the dependencies that bring it, with the match highlighted — and by the routes of a transitive row

• Vulnerability badgea shield with the count on a dependency with known CVEs — see Dependency security

On a Cargo workspace the same button runs cargo tree --workspace. Cargo never drops a version — two incompatible
versions of a crate are both built — so the group is called Duplicate versions and lists them without "kept / dropped".
Maven runs under the JDK the project is indexed with.

Every group starts closed, so opening the panel shows the modules and nothing more; a filter opens the groups it found something in.
Show only this module — on a group header's menu (right-click) or on a module of the selector tree above the list — narrows the panel to that module;
Show all brings the rest back.

Each group header has Focus in Project — its locate button, or a right-click on the header — which opens
the Project tree on that module's (or crate's) folder, expanded and selected, with the keyboard focus on it. The same menu
opens its pom.xml or Cargo.toml and copies its path.

title: A jar that is not there
text:
A Maven repository often holds a dependency's .pom without its .jar. The pom is what Maven reads
to walk the graph; the jar arrives only when something compiles against it. So a project whose tree has been resolved but
never built has the folders and none of the code.

Allow Maven to use the network, under Settings → Java, is on by default and closes that gap: when a jar
is missing, the resolve fetches it. It is the one switch for every place Bennu runs Maven — the resolve, the build before a
run, the run's classpath and the goals started from the Maven panel, whose Offline toggle flips the same setting.
Turning it off resolves from the local repository alone — worth doing on a metered connection or behind a slow corporate
repository.

A declared dependency whose jar is still missing is called out, because that is exactly what "cannot find symbol" looks
like in a file that is fine. Until the classpath has been resolved, the panel says the column is unknown rather than
marking everything missing.

title: What it will not compute
text:
Reading the list runs nothing: the poms are files, and the classpath is the one already resolved for the index. The list
itself does not work out imported BOMs, version ranges or which of two transitive versions wins — a version only they can
answer stays blank, unless the resolved classpath settles it, which is not a guess but the jar the compiler is being given.

The classpath resolve, by contrast, does apply BOMs, nearest-wins and exclusions, but it never picks a version out of a
range and never activates a profile — both are decisions about a build. Where those rules come from and what they decide is
covered in Dependency versions.

title: Versions and vulnerabilities
text:
Dependency versions explains where a version comes from, scopes, exclusions, duplicates and the
newer-version offers. Dependency security covers the known-vulnerability check and the Vulnerabilities
window.

title: The module graph
text:
The list answers what does this module need. Who needs it, what a change to it rebuilds and
whether the project has a dependency cycle are properties of the shape instead, and they have their own window —
Alt+Shift+D, or the network button in the Maven or Cargo tool window's header. See
The module graph.

title: Dependency security
text: Projects

title: Dependency security
text:
Whether a library you depend on has a published vulnerability is not something a machine can know by itself. Bennu asks
OSV.dev, tells you where in the pom the affected dependency is written, and which version fixes it.

title: What is sent, and to whom
text:
The data source is OSV.dev, the open vulnerability database that aggregates GitHub advisories and other
sources. For each dependency Bennu sends the Maven groupId:artifactId (or, on a Node project, the npm package
name) and the version, and nothing else about the project, to api.osv.dev.

The newer-version check reads a public file and says nothing about your project. This one sends your dependency
coordinates to a third party. The two have separate switches.

Settings → Java → Check dependencies for known vulnerabilities controls it, and it is on by default.
Off, nothing is sent: the pom shows no warnings, the Dependencies panel no badges, and the Vulnerabilities window explains
the check is off and offers Turn on.

title: When it is asked
text:
• Editing a pom.xml — shortly after you stop typing, in the background. A cold lookup can take a few seconds and typing never waits for it.

• The Dependencies tool window — once the dependency list has loaded, to draw the badges. Maven, Gradle and Node projects.

• The Vulnerabilities window — on opening, and again on Refresh.

Cargo projects are not checked. A Node project is checked in OSV's npm ecosystem — see below — and the Vulnerabilities window follows the project the Dependencies panel is showing.

Caching, limits and offline:

• An answer is cached on disk, one small file per dependency and version, and reused for the same freshness window as the version check (a day by default).

• A request looks up a bounded number of dependencies and advisory records. What it does not reach stays uncached, so the next pass continues: a large pom fills in over a few passes. The Vulnerabilities window checks up to 400 distinct artifacts at a time and says so when a classpath is larger.

• With no network, or when OSV cannot be reached, the check is silent — no error, no dialog. Fresh cached answers are still shown; an expired cached answer is not reused offline (unlike the newer-version check), so after a day of being offline the warnings go quiet until the next successful lookup.

• A dependency whose advisory details could only be partly fetched is shown with what is known and is not cached, so the next pass retries it.

title: Which version is checked
text:
A dependency with a literal version is checked at that version. One with no literal version — managed by a BOM or a parent, or
written as a property — is checked at the version the build resolved, which needs the classpath to be resolved and
happens as the project indexes. Coordinates containing an unexpanded property are skipped.

The pom only marks what it declares. The Vulnerabilities window and the panel badges also cover everything those
dependencies drag in, at the version actually on the classpath.

title: Node projects
text:
The same check, on the same switch, for a package.json project. What is looked up is what the lockfile
resolved (package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml or yarn.lock) — every declared package and everything it
drags in — at its exact version. A project with no lockfile has only ranges, which OSV cannot be asked about, so nothing is looked up until
the first install. Findings carry the declaring package.json and line, and the badges, the window and the "Ask Imber" question
work exactly as on Maven; answers are cached separately under the same freshness window.

title: How findings are shown
text:
In the pom

A warning on the dependency

The version is underlined (or the <dependency> tag, when there is no version text). Hover for up to
four advisories — the CVE, or the advisory id when there is none, its severity, a one-line summary and the nearest
version that fixes it — then "…and N more". The warning is drawn in the editor; the Problems panel lists only the
synchronous checks.

In the Dependencies tool window

A shield with a count

A declared or transitive dependency with known vulnerabilities carries a shield with the number, coloured by the
worst severity. It appears only while the check is on, and the tooltip points to the Vulnerabilities window.

The whole project

Vulnerabilities…

The shield button in the Dependencies panel's toolbar, or Vulnerabilities… in the Command Palette
(also reachable by asking the assistant to show them). The same window the Corvus security dashboard uses: severity
tabs with counts, worst first, one row per advisory, and a detail view with the summary, whether the dependency is declared
(and in which modules) or pulled in transitively, the fixed version, and links to osv.dev and — for a CVE — NVD.
Ask Imber in the detail's header asks the assistant whether this project is really exposed — whether the
vulnerable part of the library is used, and reachable, from your code — and what fixing it would change: the version to move to,
what that drags in, the API changes your code would have to follow. It reads the project and changes nothing.

title: Severity
text:
GitHub advisories carry a plain severity word, which is used (OSV's moderate reads as medium). Records from other
databases carry only a CVSS vector, which is not re-derived: they read as unknown and are still reported. Unknown ranks above low — unrated
is not harmless.

title: Acting on a finding
text:
The finding names the version that fixes it — the lowest fixed version above the one you have, taken from the
advisory's ranges for that artifact — or says the advisory lists none. Moving there is a manual edit of the version (or the property, parent or
BOM that decides it): see Dependency versions for where a version comes from.

The line above a dependency offers the newest release on Maven Central, not the fixed version of an advisory. It is often
the same one, but nothing ties them together.

title: What it does not do
text:
• There is no one-click "update to the fixed version", and no way to ignore or suppress a finding.

• It does not check Cargo dependencies.

• It does not say whether your code reaches the vulnerable code — only that the version is affected.

• The freshness window follows the shared metadata setting; there is no separate control for it.

title: Dependency versions
text: Projects

title: Dependency versions
text:
A dependency line rarely says which version you get. It is written in a property, inherited from a parent, pinned by a
bill of materials or decided by a conflict three levels down. Bennu follows each of those and says where the answer
lives.

title: Where a version comes from
text:
The version a pom resolves to is found the way Maven finds it, nearest first:

• A <version> written on the dependency itself.

• A ${property} in it, expanded against the properties of the pom that wrote the string, then
those of its parents.

• With no <version> at all, the <dependencyManagement> of this pom, then of each parent up the chain.

• A BOM imported there (<scope>import</scope>, <type>pom</type>) sits behind the pom
that imports it: an explicit entry beside the import wins, which is how a project pins one library away from what the
BOM says.

Reading a pom means opening several files, and every one of them is a jump from here:

Ctrl+B on — Goes to

A coordinate of one of your modules — The module that builds it

A coordinate something else pins — The parent's <dependencyManagement> entry, or the BOM's own .pom when a BOM supplies it

Any other coordinate — The artifact's own .pom in the repository — where what it drags in is written

A ${property} — The pom that defines it, on the line that does

A <module> — That module

Hover says the same without moving: what the coordinate resolves to on disk, what the version expands to and who decided it,
the scope, and every version of that artifact you have installed. Completing a <version> offers the
managed one first, naming the pom that decided it.

A version range ([1.0,2.0)) is never turned into a version — picking one is a decision about a build, and
inventing it would produce a classpath no build has. A declaration whose version only a range or an undefined property
can answer is left off the classpath rather than guessed.

title: Checked on the way
text:
Marked — What it means

Parent not found — The <parent> is neither beside the pom (through <relativePath>) nor in the local repository. An error: every managed version and inherited dependency it should have supplied is missing, which otherwise surfaces as many unrelated "no version" reports. A reactor's own parent is built from source and does not need to be installed.

Moved to other coordinates — The old coordinates publish a jarless pom that only redirects. Maven follows it, so the build works; the warning names the new coordinates, and updating removes the indirection.

A missing version, a version already managed, an undefined property, a misspelled scope and the repository checks
(artifact or version not installed) are described in Editing a pom.xml.

title: A dependency's own pom
text:
The .pom you land in from a coordinate lives in the local repository, not in your project — and it is still a
pom. The colour, the hover and the same Ctrl+B on its dependencies and its
<parent> all work there, so "what does this actually drag in" is followed as far as it goes, not one step.

The checks are written against a file you can fix. An artifact was built against dependencies your machine had no reason to
download, so there the check that finds a real problem in your own pom would underline the ordinary state of a repository,
on a line nobody can edit.

title: Scopes
text:
A <scope> that is not compile, provided, runtime, test,
system or import is marked as a warning: Maven treats it as compile without a word.
Completion offers the valid ones with what each means, and the Dependencies tool window shows every row's scope as a
coloured badge, since test changes what a dependency is for.

The classpath Bennu resolves for the index applies Maven's own rules to what a dependency drags in:

Declared as — Reached through — Ends up

compile — compile — compile

runtime — compile — runtime

anything — provided — provided

anything — test — test

anything — runtime — runtime

test, provided, system — a dependency of a dependency — not inherited

<optional>true</optional> — a dependency of a dependency — stops at the artifact that declares it

A system-scoped dependency lives at its <systemPath>, so it is never looked for in the
repository and never reported missing.

title: Exclusions
text:
<exclusions> are honoured when the classpath is resolved: an excluded artifact is held out of the whole
subtree beneath the dependency that lists it, and the wildcard form
(<groupId>*</groupId><artifactId>*</artifactId>) cuts the subtree entirely. An
<exclusion> names something that is by definition not on the classpath, so it is never marked as missing.

There is no dedicated exclusion check, hover or action, and the Dependencies tool window does not list a dependency's
exclusions. To see what an exclusion changed, compare against Resolve tree.

title: Duplicates and conflicts
text:
• Declared twicethe same artifact twice in one <dependencies> block (or one
<dependencyManagement>) is a warning on the second, because Maven keeps the last silently. The same artifact in management
and in the dependencies, or in two profiles, is the normal way to write a pom and is left alone.

• Two versions on the classpaththe nearest declaration wins: the version the project declares beats the one a
dependency asks for, and a later, deeper sighting of the same artifact contributes nothing.

• Management overrides transitivesa version pinned in the reactor's <dependencyManagement>
(including an imported BOM) applies to the whole graph, not only to what the project declares — so the BOM decides which Jackson you
get, whoever asked for it. Where two modules pin the same artifact differently, the first module's is used, as one classpath serves the project.

The classpath is one answer for the whole project, so it cannot show why a version won. The Resolve
tree button in the Dependencies tool window runs mvn dependency:tree and lists every artifact seen at more than
one version — the one Maven kept, the ones it dropped, and the chain that asked for each. See Dependencies.

A dependency written under a <profile> in your own poms is used when its jar is in the repository, and its
absence is never reported — whether a profile is on is a fact about a build. In a library's pom, a profile is ignored: no
downstream build can switch it on.

title: When a newer version exists
text:
Two different things say a dependency is behind, and they answer different questions.

Hint, local

A newer version, already here

A hint on the version when a newer release is already in your local repository, so switching costs nothing.
Only the same numbering scheme counts (2025.1 is not newer than 6.1.3), and a pre-release is never
suggested over a release.

Offer, network

A line above the dependency

The version Maven Central has, in the accent colour above the dependency; pressing it writes that version in place.

The local repository holds only what somebody here has already asked for, so by its measure a dependency nobody updated is
permanently current. Turn the Central check off in Settings → Java → Check Maven Central for newer versions;
the Java side is then entirely local again.

• Only what this pom pins. A version inherited from a parent or a BOM, or written as a ${property},
is left alone: the line the hint would sit above is not the line that would have to change. Entries in
<dependencyManagement> get none either — the parent's own offers appear when the parent is open.

• Answers are cached on disk for a day per artifact, and a failed lookup falls back to whatever is cached, however old — on a
train, last week's answer is the right one.

• A milestone or a release candidate is never offered as the newer version.

• One pass fetches a bounded number of artifacts; a pom with many dependencies and a cold cache fills in over a few passes
while typing never waits.

• One dependency is updated at a time: there is no update-all, and no action that edits a parent or a BOM.

Whether the version you have is safe is a separate question, answered in Dependency security.

title: DTO Lab
text: Java & JSP

title: DTO Lab
text:
What a class makes of a payload, and what its constraints make of the result — answered by the project's own Jackson and Bean Validation, running on the project's own
JDK. And, from the same answers, the tests that pin it down, written the way you write tests.

title: Opening it
text:
From — Opens on

Alt+Shift+J — The innermost class around the caret — a nested DTO too

Open in DTO Lab, in the editor's right-click menu — The class under the pointer

The command palette — DTO Lab: try the class at the caret, DTO Lab: generate validation tests for the class at the caret — The class at the caret

The flask button in the right activity bar — The lab

It is offered on projects using Bean Validation, Jackson, or both. The lab reads the class as it opens, and the refresh button in its header reads it again after you change it.

title: Payload
text:
The left column is the JSON, starting from a sketch of every property the class exposes under the name Jackson gives it — with a test value where one answers the field.
Use the project's JSON replaces the sketch with what the project's own ObjectMapper writes for a new instance: its modules, its naming, its date
format. Ctrl+Enter, or Run, sends it, and two answers come back:

Jackson

What it binds to

The object built, field by field, and the JSON it writes back. A property sent and not written back is lost on the way back — the field with no accessor, the @JsonIgnore that also stops it coming in. A payload that does not bind shows Jackson's error.

Bean Validation

What the validator says

Every violation: its path, the message a user reads, its template and its constraint. Messages are interpolated in the locale typed beside the list, with the bundle the project really configures — one named in a @Bean included — so an unresolved key shows as itself, as a user would see it.

On a Spring Boot project an unknown property is ignored and dates are written as text — what Boot changes from Jackson's defaults. A project without Jackson has its payload
bound by field name, with no JSON written back.

title: How it runs
text:
The answers come from the project itself, so it is compiled first when anything changed since its last compile, and its classes are loaded and run — static initialisers
included.

The JVM
The one the project declares, started the first time the lab needs it and stopped after a while without questions — ten minutes by default, under Settings ▸ Java ▸ DTO Lab. A rebuild is picked up without a restart.
The classpath
Classes under src/test are not on it, and an unsaved class has not been compiled yet.
A class that hangs
One whose static initialiser waits on a database or a network service gets no answer within a minute; the lab says so and starts a fresh JVM for the next question.

title: Tests
text:
The Tests tab turns the class's constraints into test cases — one per way each constraint can fail, plus one checking that a valid instance really is valid:

Constraint — Cases

@Size(min = 2, max = 40) — too short, too long

@NotBlank — null, blank

• Choose the fields, the template, and where the tests go.

• Generate. Every case is checked on the JVM first: the valid instance is validated, then each case — the valid instance with one field changed — and
what the validator reports is what the test expects, including constraints the source does not show, like a custom or composed @Constraint.

• Read the preview. It lists what needs a look: a valid instance that is not valid, or a value that did not violate the constraint it was chosen for. When the JVM could
not answer, expectations are predicted from the source and the preview says so.

• Apply. Nothing is written before.

A new test goes beside the class's tests — src/test/java, same package, ClassValidationTest. When that file exists, or you choose another,
the tests are added to it, and the preview lets you pick the class inside, nested ones included. Added to a file open in a tab, they arrive in the buffer as one undo step,
with the imports they need.

title: Test values
text:
A constraint says what a value must not be, and rarely what it is. So wherever a rule answers a field — for its name or for a constraint it
carries — the field gets that rule's value, in the valid instance every test starts from and in the payload sketch. Every other field keeps the value computed from its constraints.

Field — Gets

email, billingEmail — mario.rossi@example.com

codiceFiscale, codice_fiscale, CODICE_FISCALE — A real tax code

One carrying @Iban — A real IBAN

• Names match ignoring case, _ and -, and a * at either end matches any prefix or suffix: *email is also
billingEmail. Constraints match by simple name.

• A rule answering a constraint comes before one answering a name; otherwise the first rule wins, and yours come before the built-ins.

• A value that does not fit the field is passed over — text for a number, too long for its @Size, outside its @Min / @Max. What cannot be
read from source, a @Pattern or a custom validator, the JVM check of the valid instance reports.

• Values are fixed, so a test comes out the same every time. A rule can give a Java expression to write instead — your own factory — while its value is
still what the JVM checks.

• A rule naming a constraint can give an invalid value too: the case written for a constraint Bennu does not know, instead of a TODO.

Rules ship for the common Italian and English fields: email and PEC, phone, fax, tax code, VAT number, IBAN, BIC, card number, postcode, URL, UUID, IP address, ISBN, username,
password, first, last and full name, company, address, city, province, country, currency, language, gender, age and number plate. Each can be switched off in
Settings › Test Values, where your own are added, edited and ordered; one named like a built-in replaces it. They live in your profile, so every project uses them.

title: Templates
What a template is rendered with
text:
• mode"file" for a new test class, "members" for what goes inside an existing one — which has its own imports, so spell types in full or put them through imported

• classname, package, fqn, binary, record; test_class is the new test class's name

• java, junit, assertjthe language level; 4 or 5; whether AssertJ is there

• validation, verifiedjakarta.validation or javax.validation; whether the expectations came from the JVM

• validone entry per field: field, setter, setter_chains (the setter returns the object), wither (its withName, when there is one), constrained, type_simple, value, value_java

• fieldsthe constrained fields: index, name, json_name, type_name, type_simple, setter, setter_chains, getter, wither, cases

• caseindex, name (size_max), constraint, constraint_fqn, violated (the attribute crossed), attributes, value, value_java, expected, verified

• expectedeach violation: path, template, message, constraint, attributes, constant

value is the value as data. Its kind is one of null, empty, blank, string_of_length (with
length), integer / decimal (with value), bool, empty_collection, collection_of_size (with
size), past_date, future_date, email (with valid), text, non_matching (with
regexp), named (a test value, with name, value and java) and unknown — the kind a constraint Bennu does
not know gets, for the template to fill in by constraint name. value_java is the same value already spelled in Java.

Opened in the editor, a template is coloured as Java with its Jinja tags on top, and it completes inside them: the data above — following the template's own loops, so inside
{'{%'} for case in field.cases {'%}'} typing case. offers a case's fields — the filters after |, the tests after is, the tag
names after {'{%'}, and the kinds a value can have after value.kind == ". Hovering any of them says what it is. The eye button in its toolbar previews
the tests it writes for a class, beside the source, as you type.

A comment line bennu.constants: com.example.Messages asks Bennu to look through those classes for the public static final string holding each expected
template or message, and hand it over as expected.constant — how a template writes Messages.REQUIRED instead of the text the constant holds.

title: For an AI client
text:
The same check is offered to an AI client connected to Arbor as bennu_validate_payload: a payload and a class in, the binding and every violation back. It compiles
and runs project code, so it asks for permission like any tool that changes something.

title: The editor
text: Editor

title: The editor
text:
What a file looks like and does once it is open — highlighting, folding, guides, the overview ruler, and what
happens when you save it or when something else changes it underneath you. Moving around the code is
Navigation; what the editor offers as you type is Completion.

title: Languages
text:
How much the editor knows about a file depends on the language, in four tiers:

Tier — Languages — What you get

A real grammar — Java, JSP, .dig — Semantic highlighting and folding. Java and JSP add navigation and index-backed completion; .dig completes from its own vocabulary.

Highlight and fold — HTML, JSON — Colour and folding.

Ready for a server — Rust, C, C++, Python, Lua, Go — A colouring mode of their own, so a .py build script, a plugin's main.lua or a .cpp beside a JNI library reads as code with no server at all — and gains completion, hover and semantic colour the moment clangd, pyright, lua-language-server or gopls is installed.

Colour only — TOML, RON, XML, YAML, .properties, CSS/SCSS/LESS, JavaScript/TypeScript, shell, Windows batch (.bat, .cmd), Dockerfile, SQL — Highlighting. Navigation and completion want a language server, and until one is wired those actions are hidden rather than offered and silent.

Markdown is a case of its own — below. A few languages have details worth knowing:

Dockerfile

Matched by name, so Dockerfile, the Dockerfile.dev a project gains once it builds more
than one image, api.dockerfile and Podman's Containerfile all read the same.

DTD

.dtd, and the .ent and .mod fragments a large one is split into, have a mode of
their own. A DTD is not XML — <!ELEMENT is a malformed tag to an XML highlighter — and it is what the
struts.xmls and .tlds of a legacy project are written against. The declarations, the name
each one declares and the parameter entities (%common;) a real DTD is mostly made of each read apart.

SQL

Highlighted per dialect, because the engines disagree about quoting: Oracle's q'[…]' and
PostgreSQL's $$ … $$ are each a broken string under the other's rules, and getting it wrong paints the rest
of the file as one literal. Nothing in a .sql file says which engine it targets, so it is a setting —
Settings → Editor → SQL → Dialect. The default, Portable, uses the rules valid on both.

title: Tabs
text:
• A file opened from the Project tree or a Find in project hit joins the tab strip.

• A click switches tabs; the × closes one, and a neighbour takes the focus.

• A tab keeps its cursor, its scroll position and its undo history while it is open, so coming back to
a file lands you where you left it and Ctrl/Cmd+Z still takes back what you typed there. That holds
across switching to another project of the workspace and across closing Arbor: the cursor and scroll are part of the saved session, and the undo history is
kept on disk — but only while the file is the same text it was, so a file changed outside Arbor in the meantime reopens without it. Closing the tab lets
them go.

• Drag a tab to reorder it: the tab you hold follows the pointer while the ones it passes slide aside, so
what you see is the order you will get. Esc cancels.

title: Two editors side by side
text:
The editor splits in two, each side with its own tab strip. Drag a tab out of its strip: over a lone editor a
Split right zone appears at its right edge, and over a split the other pane lights up — release to move the tab there.
The same moves are in the command palette (Editor: move tab to the other pane, focus the other pane,
close split). Drag the divider to resize it, or focus it and use ← / →; double-click puts it back in the middle.

• A file is open on one side at a time, so moving a tab moves the file, and opening a file that is already open on the other
side takes you to it — two views of one buffer would each keep their own undo history.

• The side with the caret is the one Shift+F6, Alt+Enter, the status bar and the palette commands act on.

• Closing the last tab of a side, or close split, gives you one editor again. The split — which tabs are on which side, and each side's active tab — is remembered across a restart; the divider's position is not.

title: Markdown
text:
A .md opens rendered, in the same live-preview editor Garrulus's notes use: headings are
sized, links read as their titles, tables are tables, images and video appear, and fenced code is highlighted by language —
including the ones this app is built around and no Markdown renderer has heard of: dig, merula,
wgsl, ron.

It is still the file and still an editor: put the caret on a line and that line shows its markup, so a typo is fixed where
you found it. The button in the toolbar — or Markdown: edit the source in the command palette — switches to the
code editor for when the markup itself is the work, and the choice is remembered.

The source view colours its fences from the same vocabulary: a bash, sh,
zsh or console block reads as shell in either view, a bat, cmd or
batch one as Windows batch, and so do java, xml, yaml,
dockerfile and the rest of what a README quotes.

Alerts:

An alert renders as a callout — a coloured band with an icon and a title:

GitHub's five (NOTE, TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING, CAUTION)
and the Obsidian words that mean the same things (info, hint, success,
attention, danger, question, example, quote) are
recognised, in any case. Anything written after the marker becomes the callout's title.

Formatting:

In the live preview a thin strip above the text formats what the caret is in: bold, italic, strikethrough, highlight,
inline code, a heading level, quote, bulleted / numbered / task list, link and code block. The buttons are
toggles that follow the caret — bold is drawn pressed when the caret is inside bold text, and pressing it
again takes the bold off. The same actions have chords: Alt+B bold, Alt+I italic,
Alt+S strikethrough, Alt+H highlight, Alt+C code,
Alt+L link, Alt+Q quote (again: callout, again: plain) and
Alt+T task.

title: Tables
text:
A table stays a table. Click a cell and you edit that cell — only the cell you are in shows its markdown,
everything around it stays rendered. The strip under the table adds and removes rows and columns and sets a column's
alignment; Tab and Enter walk the grid and Esc leaves it. The toolbar's
⊞ inserts a new one — point at the grid to say how big.

Editing a table rewrites its markdown with one space each side of every cell, so a hand-aligned table loses its padding the
first time it is edited here.

Links:

Following one

Ctrl / Cmd+click — the gesture that follows a symbol in code. An http link opens in
the browser; a path opens the file in a tab, resolved against the document's own folder, so ./notes/api.md
means the one beside it; a #anchor jumps to that heading, in this file or the one it opens. Bare URLs count,
both <https://…> and one written on its own. A plain click puts the caret where you clicked, and the hand
cursor appears only while the key is held, so it never promises a jump a click alone won't make.

Writing one

Typing ]( offers every file in the project, written relative to this document, and every heading in it —
from the list the jump reads, so an id that is offered lands. Typing # first narrows it to the headings,
each showing its title beside its id.

A heading needs no id: its text is one. Lower-cased, punctuation dropped, spaces turned into dashes —
GitHub's rule, character for character, so an anchor copied from a table of contents generated there lands:

Heading — Answers to

## Perché il CST — #perché-il-cst, and #perche-il-cst — accents may be left out

## Titolo, twice — #titolo and #titolo-1

## Pipelines — CI / CD — #pipelines--ci--cd, and #pipelines-ci-cd without the doubled dashes

An underlined heading has an id like any other, a path.md#anchor works the same way in the file it opens, and a
# comment inside a fenced code block is never mistaken for a heading.

title: Diagrams
text:
A mermaid fence is drawn — flowcharts, sequence diagrams, state machines — in the theme's own
colours. The caret inside it brings the source back, highlighted: the arrows, the node labels and the
diagram type each read apart. A .mmd file opens with the same colouring, and a diagram that does not parse says
so where the picture would have been, in mermaid's words, naming the line.

title: Find and replace
text:
Ctrl+F opens a slim bar in the editor's top-right corner, over the code rather than above it. The word under a selection fills the field, every change
re-runs the search and the editor jumps to the first match from the caret, and the counter inside the field says which match you are on (3/8).
The three keys at the end of the field switch match case, whole word and regular expression.

• Enter / Shift+Enter — next / previous match. Esc closes the bar and returns to the code.

• Alt+C, Alt+W, Alt+X — match case, whole word, regular expression.

• Alt+P — shows the replace row (Ctrl+H is the type hierarchy). There, Enter replaces the current match and Ctrl+Enter replaces all.

• The magnifier hands the query to Find in files (Ctrl+Shift+F).

The other occurrences of a selected word are outlined too, so a variable's uses read at a glance without opening the bar.

title: The editor's context menu
text:
Every entry carries the colour of what it does — navigation, refactoring, generation, history. Refactor is one submenu with
everything that can reshape the code at the caret or the selection: rename, the extract, inline and move refactorings, add parameter and
convert case. A refactoring that cannot be done where the caret is stays in the list, greyed, with the reason — the same rows
Alt+Enter shows. Generate is one submenu with every way to write code.

title: Folding
text:
Braced blocks — classes, methods, blocks — and block comments fold from the gutter chevrons, keeping the head line visible.
In an indentation-delimited language like .dig the body folds from the end of its header line instead. Folding is
computed live from the syntax tree, with no indexing needed.

Settings → Editor → Folding can fold a file's block comments on opening — the licence header and the
documentation above every method, which on a legacy file can be most of the screen. It is an opening state, not a rule:
nothing folds again what you unfold. The same section turns the gutter off entirely.

The import block folds as one region — collapsed it reads import … on the line of the first import — and
starts collapsed when a file opens (Settings → Editor → Folding → Fold imports by default). Whatever you fold or
unfold stays exactly so, per tab, until the tab is closed. Opening a region animates the lines it uncovers, and the chevrons
turn; both follow the application's animation setting.

title: What the surface shows
text:
Settings → Editor → Appearance

Appearance

The font size, the line-number gutter, the tint on the caret's line, word wrap, and spaces and tabs drawn as glyphs — each applied to the file already in front of you.

Palette → Convert Case · Ctrl+Shift+W

Convert case

Rewrite the selection, or the name at the caret (each cursor of a multi-cursor selection), as camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, kebab-case, lowercase, UPPERCASE or Title Case — from the palette, the editor's context menu (Refactor › Convert Case), or the shortcut, which moves it one step round the first five. Words break at separators, humps and the end of an acronym (HTTPServer → http_server); digits stay with their word. The result stays selected, so pressing again goes on. It is a text change, not a rename: use Rename to change a declared name everywhere.

Settings → Editor → Caret

The caret

A two-pixel line in the theme's caret colour, with a hairline halo so it stands out from the tinted current line and the selection. You can make it a block or an underline, thin or thick, blink smoothly or not at all, and take the accent or a #rrggbb colour. Every cursor of a multi-cursor selection looks the same. The shared code editors elsewhere in the app use the default look.

Always on

Rainbow brackets

Every (), [] and {} is tinted by nesting depth, a matching pair sharing a colour. Brackets inside strings and comments are left alone.

Settings → Editor → Indentation guides

Indentation guides

A line per indent level, in the colour of the bracket that opens the block; the block the caret is in is fully highlighted.

Settings → Editor → Sticky scroll

Sticky scroll

Scrolling into a long body pins the enclosing declarations — the class, then the method — to the top. Click a pinned line to jump back to it.

Settings → Editor → Scrollbar overview

Scrollbar overview

Every error and warning is a bar at its place in the file. Hover to preview that spot, drag to scroll, click a mark to put the caret there ready for a quick fix.

The top-right corner

File health

The file's error and warning counts — a green check when it is clean — mirroring the marks on the overview strip.

The overview marks include the compiler's errors and warnings, not only the live analysis: after a build,
whatever javac, Maven or cargo reported for the open file is a mark on the strip and a squiggle on the
line. A rebuild replaces them, so a fixed error clears its mark.

title: Indentation
text:
The footer shows the active indentation as Spaces: N or Tab Size: N. Click it — or focus it and press
↑/↓ — to switch between spaces and tabs and pick the tab width
(2, 4 or 8). The change applies to the open editor at once.

Enter in Java:

Enter starts the new line where the code's structure puts it, in that same indentation, and drops the whitespace
left around the break:

After — The new line

{ — One level in. Between { and } the brace moves to a line of its own at the outer level.

A finished statement, }, an annotation — The same level as that statement.

An unfinished statement — an operator, =, ->, a call chain — Two levels in from where the statement starts, until its ;.

An open ( — Two levels in from the line of the parenthesis.

if (…), for (…), while (…), else with no brace — One level in; after that single statement, back out.

case X:, case X -> — One level in from the label.

A blank line is indented for where it is, not copied from the line above. Typing }, ) or a
case label at the start of a line moves it to its level — labels outdented from their statements or not, as
Settings → Java → Code Style → Formatter says.

In a comment, Enter after /** writes the closing */ below the caret, and inside a Javadoc
or /* */ each new line starts with an aligned *. Splitting a // comment starts the rest
with // too. Inside a string or a text block, the line keeps its indentation.

title: Reformat
text:
Alt+Shift+F reformats the open file. A language with a language server is
formatted by it — Rust by rustfmt, reading the project's own rustfmt.toml or .prettierrc,
where the team and the CI read it from. Java is formatted by Bennu:

• every line re-indented to its nesting;

• trailing whitespace stripped;

• runs of blank lines collapsed.

That is all it does until you ask for more: Settings → Java → Formatter has every option — braces, spacing,
wrapping, imports, annotations, comments — with a live preview, a style per project, and detection from the code already there.
With text selected the same key formats just the selection, and a file can be formatted when it is saved. The Formatter
page of this documentation describes it all.

Out of the box it never rewraps a long line, reorders anything, adds or removes braces, or changes the spacing inside an
expression. Those are the rules that can be wrong — a < b and Map<K, V> differ by context,
-1 and a - 1 by parse — so each one is a choice you make. Comments and text blocks are left exactly as
written, and a file that does not parse still formats.

title: Optimize imports
text:
Ctrl+Shift+O on a Java file drops the imports the file does not use and puts the rest in
order: everything else first, then javax and java, then the static imports — alphabetical inside each
group, a blank line between groups, duplicates collapsed, as one undo step.

What counts as unused is the judgement the unused-import warning makes, so the command and the squiggle can never
disagree — and it inherits that caution: an import named only in a Javadoc counts as used, and a static or wildcard
import is never removed, only moved. It will not fold imports of one package into a wildcard, which can change what a simple name
resolves to, and it will not add a missing import — that is Alt+Enter's.

A comment sits above the import it was written for, and reordering would strand it above another — so such a file is left alone.

Over a whole project or module:

Optimize imports in project… in the command palette, or Optimize imports… in the right-click menu of a folder in
the project tree (or of the tree's empty space, for the whole project), applies the same rule to every Java file under a folder.
The dialog lists the files that would change and how many imports each loses; Change… narrows it to a module or any other
folder. Nothing is written until Ctrl+Enter, a file that changed on disk since the list was built is
skipped, and files with unsaved edits are left out and named. Build output and dependency folders are never entered.

title: Parameter and inlay hints
text:
Ctrl+P inside a call's argument list (or Parameter info in the command palette) shows a tooltip
above the line with the signature and the argument you are on picked out, following the commas as you type.
It never opens by itself; Esc closes it, and so does moving the caret out of the call. Bennu answers it for Java,
the language server for everything else.

It describes the call, not the declaration: the receiver's type arguments are filled in, so
Optional<PathPattern>.orElseThrow(…) reads : PathPattern rather than : T. A type
variable the receiver does not bind — one the call's own arguments decide — stays as written.

Inlay hints (Settings → Editor) draw what the code does not say:

• Parameter namestransfer(source: from, target: to, amount: 500) — in front of each argument that does not already carry the name

• Inferred typeswhat a var or a Lombok val was inferred as

• Lambda parametersrows.forEach(row: String -> …) — for one written without a type

They are not part of the file: the caret cannot land in one, they are not copied with a selection, and no offset shifts. An
argument that already says the name, a lambda or a long expression is left alone. Rest the pointer on a parameter
name and it shows the type the parameter is declared with.

The type hint includes the primitives, which are the hardest to work out from the line:
var n = path.indexOf('/') is an int, var half = a / 2 an int and not a
double, var c = chars[i] a char. A type the engine cannot work out gets no hint rather
than a guess — a hint reads as though the compiler had said it.

An overloaded method still gets its names when the arguments settle which overload it is:
addAllowedMethod("*") against (HttpMethod) and (String) is decided by the literal. When
they do not — an argument whose type does not resolve, a null that fits both — the call gets no names, because a
name from the wrong overload is a claim about the code that is not true.

They appear once the sources are on disk — the JDK's own, and any dependency whose sources you fetched with the decompiled
view's Download sources. A class file carries no parameter names unless compiled with -parameters, which
almost no published jar is, and a decompiled stub's arg0 is the decompiler's placeholder. Sources fetched while
you work take effect at once, in every file that calls that library.

title: Emmet
text:
In JSP and HTML files, type an Emmet abbreviation and press Tab to expand it into markup. When the
caret is not on a valid abbreviation, Tab indents as usual.

Typed — Becomes

ul>li.item*3 — a list of three items

div#app — a div with an id

a[href] — a link

title: Brackets and quotes
text:
(, [ and { insert their closing half when the caret is followed by whitespace, the end
of the line or another closer; typing the closer over one steps past it, and Backspace between an empty pair
removes both. The bracket matching the one at the caret is underlined.

With a selection, typing an opener wraps it instead of replacing it — and in Java that includes <:

Selected — Typed — Becomes

String — < — <String>

a + b — ( — (a + b)

name — " — "name"

Without a selection < is just typed: the same character opens a type argument list and a comparison, so there is
no right closer to guess.

In Java, " and ' pair only where a literal can start:

• in code — never inside a string, a character literal or a comment, where a quote is text;

• not straight after a letter, a digit or another quote, and only when what follows is whitespace, the end of the line, or
) ] } , ;.

Typing the quote that closes the literal you are in steps over it, and Backspace inside an empty "" or
'' removes both quotes. A third " after an empty "" opens a text block,
with the caret on its own indented line and the closing delimiter below it:

title: Pasting into a string
text:
Paste inside a Java "…" and the text is escaped as it lands: quotes and backslashes are escaped,
tabs become \t. Something that spans several lines becomes concatenated literals, one per line,
aligned under the opening quote and joined with + — the shape you would have typed, since a "…"
cannot span lines in Java:

• In a text block (""") newlines stay newlines, pasted lines are indented to match the block, and
only the quotes that would close it early are escaped.

• In a '…' character literal the text is escaped and never split.

• Everywhere else — in code, in a comment, just past the closing quote — a paste arrives exactly as it left.

Past 500 lines
Still escaped, no longer split: the newlines stay inline in one literal. A concatenation of thousands of pieces nests thousands of levels deep, more than the tools that read it can walk.
Past 64 KB
Refused, with a note at the caret. That is the most a compiled string constant can hold however it is written — the compiler joins the pieces back into one constant — so no arrangement of that text would build.

title: Git
text:
The editor's right-click menu has a Git submenu — Corvus answers all three, by file path, so the repository does not have to
be open there. They are also in the Command Palette.

• Show History lists the commits that touched the file, newest first; the diff of the selected one is beside it. ↑ /
↓ walk the list.

• Show History for Selection does the same for the lines you highlighted — git follows those lines through moves and
renames, and each commit shows only what it did to them. It is greyed out until something is selected.

• Annotate with Git Blame draws a slim colour bar per commit in the left margin, so a run of lines reads as one change. At the start of each run, the author and the age follow the code — and on the line the caret is on, whatever run it belongs
to. Hover the bar for the whole commit; Editor → Commit message in Git Blame in the settings adds the subject to the text. Close Annotations
removes it.

All three read the committed file. Lines typed since the last commit have no author yet, and a selection is read by line number, so save and
commit first if you have been editing. After committing, close and reopen the annotations to refresh them.

Problem markers:

A line with a problem is underlined, and hovering the underline says what is wrong. A marker in the gutter beside the line is optional
(Settings › Editor › Show problem markers in the gutter, off by default): without it the gutter keeps the same width while errors come and
go, and the line numbers reserve room for four digits so the text does not shift when a file crosses 100 or 1,000 lines.

title: TODO and FIXME in comments
text:
The words TODO, FIXME, HACK, XXX, NOTE, BUG, OPTIMIZE and
DEPRECATED are bold and tinted in their own colour where they are written in a comment — in Java, JavaScript / TypeScript, Rust, XML / HTML /
JSP, YAML, SQL, shell, properties and the other languages whose comments Bennu can read, and never inside a string. TODO(name): counts too.
Each spot is also marked on the scrollbar overview, and optionally by a dot in the gutter.

Settings › Editor › Comment markers switches this off, edits the list of words, decides whether case matters and turns the gutter dot on.
The TODO tool window scans for the same words, so what is coloured is what it lists.

Change markers:

A thin bar beside the line numbers marks what differs from the last commit: green for lines you added, blue for lines you changed, a red
wedge where lines were removed. Click one to see the block as it was against what is there now, Revert block to put the
old text back (an added block is removed) or Copy old text. The buffer is only edited — save when you are happy.
Alt+F3 and Ctrl+Shift+F3 jump to the next and previous change, also in the Command
Palette (Git: next change, Git: previous change).

The diff is asked of Corvus a moment after you stop typing, and not at all outside a repository, for an untracked file or one over 2 MB.
Editor → Change markers in the gutter in the settings turns the markers off; the editor then makes no such calls.

Changes panel:

Inside a repository the activity bar has a Changes button (Alt+Shift+C, or Git: show
changes in the Command Palette); a dot on it means there is something to commit. The panel is Corvus's staging list: Unstaged and Staged
sections as a flat list or a folder tree, stage / unstage / discard per file, folder or all, and a commit box with Amend last.
Click a file to see its change in the diff beside the list — Corvus's diff viewer: unified or split, full-file context, change-to-change navigation
(F3 / Shift+F3), and staging or unstaging single lines or hunks. Switching branches, pushing and resolving merge conflicts stay in Corvus — the
Corvus button opens the project there.

Inside a git repository the status bar names the current branch, with ↑ the commits you have not pushed and ↓ those you
have not pulled. It is read-only — hover for the staged, modified and untracked counts, click to open the project in Corvus, where branches
are switched. The names of changed files are coloured in the editor tabs and in the Problems panel as in the project tree: amber modified,
green staged, blue untracked, red in conflict.

title: Saving
text:
Autosave is on by default: a changed file is written a short moment after you stop typing, when you switch tab,
and when the window loses the focus. Ctrl+S still saves on demand, in the project's encoding — and a
rename applies and saves its edits the same way. Turn autosave off in Settings → Editor → Autosave to save only
on Ctrl+S; the choice persists.

title: Files changed outside Bennu
text:
Bennu watches the files you have open — another editor, a git checkout, a code generator, a build — and never
writes over a change it did not make.

No unsaved edits in the tab

Picked up silently

There is nothing to lose and nothing to decide.

Unsaved edits in the tab

Bennu asks

Keep my edits overwrites the disk; Reload from disk discards yours; Not now defers the choice.

While a file waits on that decision its tab is badged disk and autosave is paused for it, so an
unattended timer cannot pick a side for you. Every other tab keeps autosaving.

A write whose file moved underneath is refused rather than applied, and the toast says so — for
Ctrl+S, autosave, save on tab switch, and the writes a Rename makes across files.

A file deleted under an edited buffer is not a conflict: your buffer is the last copy, and saving recreates the file.

title: Encodings
text: Projects

title: Encodings
text:
Legacy Java sources are very often not UTF-8, and reading one as if it were quietly corrupts every accented
character in it. Bennu reads each file as what it is — and can tell you which files were damaged before you ever
opened them.

title: Which encoding a file is read with
text:
A legacy project usually says so in its pom.xml:

Bennu decodes every file with the encoding the pom declares, and the footer shows which one won — so mojibake never
slips in silently. When more than one answer exists, the most specific wins:

• An override for that one file.

• The sourceEncoding the project's pom declares.

• Settings → Java → Default source encoding — only ever a fallback, for a project that declares
nothing.

Rust source is UTF-8 by the language's own definition, so the default configured for a legacy Java tree never
reaches it.

title: Finding text that is already broken
text:
Check file for mojibake, in the command palette, scans the open file for text that was UTF-8 but was
once read as Windows-1252 and saved that way:

In the file — Was

Ã© — é

â€™ — ’

Each hit is squiggled with a one-click Replace with «…» quick fix, and a summary says how many were
found.

The other kind: a byte that could not be read at all:

A file written in Cp1252 and decoded as UTF-8 loses the byte rather than garbling it: the editor shows a replacement
glyph — one character standing where è was written. There is no quick fix and there cannot be one, because
the byte that would say what it was is gone before the text reaches the editor. Reload the file in the encoding it is
actually written in — Project Configuration → Encoding, or the footer's encoding picker for one file
(see Reinterpret below).
Typing over the glyph saves a file the original byte has already been thrown away from.

They ride the ordinary validation, so a message bundle, a code template, a .sql or a README is checked the
same way a .java is — which is where a legacy tree keeps almost all of its accented text.

The palette command and the project-wide scan are still there for asking on purpose. What the command adds is the
answer out loud — how many of each kind, or “no broken characters found”, which is the one thing a squiggle
cannot say. It draws squiggles of its own only in a file that validation does not reach.

Detection is exact — a table of real corruption sequences, not a guess about which characters look odd — so correct
accented text stays unmarked.

title: Reinterpret: read it differently, change nothing
text:
The encoding pill in the editor's footer — or Reinterpret file as encoding… in the palette — makes Bennu
read the open file as another encoding. The file on disk is not touched; the choice is remembered for that file in
your profile, and As the project reads it takes it back. Use it when accents show as Ã© or a
replacement glyph: the bytes are fine, they were just read with the wrong rule.

title: Convert: rewrite the file
text:
Convert file encoding… (palette, the footer pill's last entry) rewrites the bytes in another encoding.
Convert project encoding… and the tree's Convert encoding… on a folder or module do the same for
a whole subtree. The dialog previews as you change options, and nothing is written until you press the button
(Ctrl+Enter):

• From is, by default, each file's own encoding as Bennu reads it. Set it explicitly when the preview marks
files Not valid — it then suggests what they look like.

• Byte-order mark (UTF-8 and UTF-16 targets): keep what the file had, add one, or remove it.

• A character that does not fit — the euro sign has no Latin-1 byte, an emoji has no Cp1252 one: stop (nothing is
written, and the preview lists every character and where it is), replace it with ?, or write an escape
(\uXXXX in Java and properties files, &#xXXXX; in XML and JSP).

• Line endings are never changed, and binary files and files that are not valid in their source encoding are
skipped and listed rather than damaged.

• A file that declares its own encoding — an XML prolog, a JSP pageEncoding — has it updated, unless you turn that off.

• Declare it in the pom (whole-project conversions): sets project.build.sourceEncoding so the build
and Bennu agree with the files.

Many files run as a Job with progress, and can be cancelled from the Jobs panel. Before a file is rewritten it
is copied to a backup folder in your profile and recorded in Local History, grouped as one change. Undo
conversion (in the dialog afterwards, or Undo last encoding conversion in the palette) puts back every file
that has not been edited since, and the way Bennu reads them with it.

Converting part of a project pins each converted file to its new encoding (so the editor keeps showing it correctly);
converting the whole project changes the project's encoding instead. Local History keeps older revisions as they were
written, so a revision from before the conversion is read with the new rule.

title: Other file types
text: Editor

title: Other file types
text:
A project is not only code. These open in the editor as themselves rather than as bytes — the documents as viewers, not editors: Bennu shows
them, it does not claim to author them.

Source, with a preview beside it

HTML pages

The rendered page next to the buffer.

Read-only viewers

Images, Word, spreadsheets, fonts

The file as itself, in a tab.

Coloured and understood

RON, package.json, merula, dig, Jinja

Languages with their own modes.

title: HTML pages
text:
An .html opens as source, with a Preview button in the toolbar. It puts the rendered page beside the source, in a
pane you can drag wider — a page is edited and looked at in the same breath, and a preview replacing the buffer would make every fix a round trip.
⤢ grows it to nearly the whole window and back.

It shows the buffer, not the file on disk, so an edit and ⟳ is the loop, and the page's stylesheets and images load from beside it.

The frame is sandboxed and has no origin of its own: it cannot read Arbor's window, its storage, or anything the application holds, whatever the page
contains. A dialog in front of every preview would be one nobody reads.

Its own scripts are the only question — that is what lets a page act: run its code and reach the network. The pill on the preview's bar
says which of the two you are in, and is the switch:

• Press the pill to allow scripts.

• Choose this once, or always for this file — a report opened every morning should not ask every morning.

• Press it again to block.

The files remembered are kept in your profile, never inside the repository.

title: Images
text:
.png, .jpg, .gif, .bmp, .webp, .ico, .avif, .tiff and
.svg open as a preview in a tab of their own — so checking the asset a .ron or a stylesheet names is a click.

Control — What it does

Fit F — The default. It never magnifies: a 16 × 16 icon blown up to fill the panel answers "what is this" worse than a 16 × 16 icon.

Actual size 0 — 1:1.

+ / −, Ctrl+scroll — Steps through a zoom ladder. Above 1:1 pixels are drawn with hard edges — zooming into an icon is how you count its pixels.

The status line gives the format, the pixel dimensions and the file size. A chequerboard behind the image tells a transparent background from a black one.

An image tab has no buffer, so Ctrl+S on one does nothing rather than writing an empty file over your artwork. Formats a browser cannot
decode — .psd, .xcf, .svgz — are declined: a broken-image glyph is worse than a clear refusal.

title: Word documents
text:
A .docx opens as a rendered page — pages, styles, tables and images as Word laid them out, not a converted approximation. You open one
from a project to check the document — a spec, a hand-off, a table somebody sent — and a version with the layout thrown away cannot be checked against the
one the sender is looking at.

It is read-only, and its bar says so with a badge. The same bar opens the file in whatever application owns it, and it is the only bar: a viewer has
nothing for the editor's toolbar to act on. The document never becomes a buffer, so no stray Ctrl+S can write back over it. The old binary
.doc is not supported — Bennu says so rather than rendering it wrong.

title: Spreadsheets
text:
A workbook opens as a grid: the values, the sheet tabs, the column letters and row numbers pinned, and numbers aligned right so one that does not
belong in a column shows itself.

Format — Files

Office Open XML — .xlsx, .xlsm

Binary — .xlsb

Excel 97-2003 — .xls

OpenDocument — .ods

The bytes decide, not the name
A file saved as OOXML under an .xls name — every export tool has shipped one — opens as what it is, and the bar above the grid says which format that turned out to be.
A grid, not a rendering
The opposite call from Word, deliberately: nobody opens a spreadsheet from a source tree for its borders and fills, but for the column mapping an import expects, the codes, the translations.
What the file records
A formula shows its last computed value, saved with the workbook, never recalculated; a cell whose value was never stored is empty rather than guessed. A date is a number in a spreadsheet, shown as a date only where the cell's own format says so.
Read-only
Nothing for a stray Ctrl+S to write over. A long or wide sheet shows its beginning and says so; Open externally hands the file to the spreadsheet application.

title: Fonts
text:
A .ttf, .otf, .woff or .woff2 opens as a specimen: a field you type into, with size, weight,
tracking and italic beside it; a waterfall of the line at eight sizes; and a coverage column. Every question about a font in a project is visual — how it looks,
whether it has this project's accents, how it holds up at eleven pixels.

A code point counts when it draws as something other than the replacement box — the judgement your eye makes — so it reports blocks rather than glyph names, and works
on any font the browser can load. .eot is not among them: no engine loads it any more, so Bennu says it cannot open one.

title: .ron files
text:
RON borrows Rust's syntax and none of its vocabulary, so it has a mode of its own. A field reasonably called type:, mod: or
ref: is a field, not a keyword, and what a RON file is mostly made of — the field names — has its colour:

• the left-hand column reads as the left-hand column;

• struct and variant names are told apart from plain values — a constructor (Sequence(, Single() and a bare
unit variant (blend: Additive) both read as the type names they are;

• #![enable(…)] reads as the header it is.

Checking a .ron as you type:

Every .ron is checked for brackets and syntax: an unclosed ( is marked on the bracket that was never closed, not at the end of the file,
and a closer that closes the wrong kind says which opener it met. Brackets inside strings, chars and comments do not count.

To check the contents against a Rust type, say which type on the first line — the same comment Studio reads:

{`// ron-studio: schema = "src/settings.rs", root = "crate::Settings"
#![enable(implicit_some)]
(window_title: "Game", vsync: true)`}

The path is relative to the .ron; a .arbor/studio.toml with a default and per-glob overrides works instead. Bennu then marks:

• a field the type does not have (with did you mean), and an unknown variant — warnings;

• a required field the document leaves out — an info on the struct, since a type that is #[serde(default)] as a whole makes them all optional;

• a string where a number goes, and the like — a warning.

Serde's rename, rename_all, alias, default and flatten on fields are honoured; Option accepts Some(…),
None or a bare value. The check runs after you pause typing, reads the crate once and remembers it for a minute (and again when the .rs named by the directive is saved).
A directive that cannot be followed — no crate, no such type — is marked on the directive line. Bevy scene files (.scn.ron) name types by path rather than being one type,
so they get the syntax check only.

title: package.json
text:
Recognised by name, so a tsconfig.json stays ordinary JSON and a manifest under node_modules is left alone. On top of the
JSON colouring it gets what the syntax cannot say:

Sections as headings
scripts, the four dependency sections, engines, exports — landmarks instead of four hundred identical strings. A script's command, the one string that is code, is coloured as code.
How pinned a version is
Three colours and no more: a range that floats on install (^5.0.0, ~2.1, a comparator), one pinned (5.0.0), and one not from the registry (workspace:*, file:../lib, a git URL).
Run a script from its line
Each scripts entry has a ▶ naming the command it runs — pnpm dev, not Run. The package manager is read off the lockfile (bun.lockb, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock, else npm). Output goes to the Run console, and a workspace member's script runs in its directory.
A dependency that is behind
An ↑ 6.0.0 available offer, as in a Cargo.toml, writing the version in place — only for ^, ~ and exact versions, never a comparator range, an alternation, a dist-tag or a workspace:, file: or git dependency. The lookups share the Look crates up online setting and its cache.

title: merula .merula patterns
text:
A piece of music for Merula, highlighted with the grammar Merula's own editor uses, so a file looks the same in both windows, mini-notation
included: notes and chords share the pitch colour, sound names the other, the island brackets and a $splice mark where a pattern meets host code, and
~ / _ stay muted so a dense pattern reads as its sounds.

Folding collapses a call's arguments — so a whole track inside tracks(…) folds away — a meta { … } block, and a
block comment. Ctrl+/ toggles a // comment.

They come from the DSL catalogue the audio backend serves, which Bennu does not start. Open the file in Merula for those; edit it here beside the rest of the project.

title: geode .dig scripts
text:
A mole program for geode — indentation-delimited, with a fixed set of host builtins — parsed with geode's own grammar. Highlighting and
folding — a fn, if, while, for, match or struct body, multi-line lists and
maps — work from the tree, and Ctrl+/ toggles a # comment.

The vocabulary is closed, so completion and hover are answered locally, with no index and no waiting:

• Completion offers the builtins, reserved words, namespaces, and the fn, struct and let names of the file.
After Crystal., Tool., Tick., Speed. or Item., that namespace's members and nothing
else; after a dot on anything else, the collection methods of both lists and maps, each labelled — without type inference both are true.
An import line is not completed: a module is a library unlocked in the shop, not a file.

• Hover shows the signature and the full explanation with its examples — the game's own help text, so ripe_left() explains the enormous
number and block_size() warns that above 1 also means a wall. A member is looked up with its namespace, so Speed.MAX_VALUE and
Tick.MAX_VALUE never swap texts. Over a name the language does not own, hover is silent.

title: Jinja templates
text:
A .jinja, .jinja2 or .j2 file is coloured as the language it generates, with its tags on top: OrderTest.java.jinja
is Java, page.html.jinja HTML. The name says which — Java, Kotlin, Rust, SQL, Go, Lua, XML, HTML and JSP, YAML, properties, TOML, JSON, CSS, Python,
JavaScript, shell — and one whose name does not say is text with coloured tags. Each tag sits on a faint ground of its own, so the output and the logic writing it read as two layers, and the file wears the Jinja
mark in the tree.

• Inside a tag, completion offers the statement names after {'{%'}, the filters after |, the tests after is, and the names the
template binds with set and for — plus loop inside a loop. Hovering any of them says what it is.

• A code template also completes and explains the data its kind is rendered with, and the eye button previews what it renders beside the source — see
Code templates.

• Ctrl+/ comments a line out with {''}.

• In Markdown, a fence marked jinja is coloured as a template, and one marked with the language it writes — java.jinja,
yml.jinja — as a template that writes it.

title: Form analysis
text: Java & JSP

title: Form analysis
text: For a page with forms on it, the Forms panel reads what each one submits and where — the fields, what they post, and the action on the other end.

title: The Forms panel
text:
In the bottom dock, toggled from the right rail with Alt+3 — offered only on a project that has JSP pages. It analyses the open JSP and
lists every <form> relevant to it, each with the complete set of parameters it posts.

Where it goes
The action the form targets — the mapped action class, and the struts.xml fragment declaring it — even when written as an Entando <wp:action path=…>. The config button opens that fragment.
What it posts
Every input, hidden ones included, with the value each posts — a fixed value or a ${…} / %{…} expression.
When it posts it
A field inside <c:if> or <s:if> is marked if — hover for the condition — since it is submitted only when that holds.

Clicking a form or a field jumps the editor to it. Two badges mark each field:

bound

The field name is a writable property of the action class.

valid

The field carries a Struts validation rule.

It reads as muted — the signal that the name is a typo, or a request parameter nothing maps.

title: Forms split across includes
text:
A JSP form is often split across <jsp:include>s: the page opens the <form>, and the hidden tokens, the wizard-step inputs
and the button bar come from fragments. The panel follows both directions:

• On a parent page, each form gathers the fields its includes contribute, each tagged with the fragment it comes from.

• On an included fragment, the parent form it feeds surfaces — a chip names the page it lives on — with its whole parameter set, and the fields
this fragment contributes highlighted.

The walk is recursive and cycle-safe, and a very large include graph shows a "…more" hint rather than silently dropping pages.

title: Formatter
text: Editor

title: Formatter
text:
Bennu formats Java itself, so it works on code that does not compile and on a file halfway through an edit. Out of the box it
only re-indents; every rewrite of an expression, a brace or an import is a choice you make in
Settings → Java → Formatter, where a live preview shows what each one does.

title: What it does, and what it does not
text:
The formatter reads the file the way the editor does — as a tree that tolerates errors — and rewrites only whitespace and, where
you ask for it, line breaks, braces and the order of imports. It never changes what the code means: names, literals and the
contents of comments and text blocks are left as written, and a file that does not parse still formats.

With nothing changed it re-indents every line to its nesting, strips trailing whitespace, collapses runs of blank lines and ends the
file with a line break. Spacing normalisation is off, and every wrapping, brace and annotation policy is keep as written.
Nothing is rewritten that you did not opt into.

title: Where the style comes from
text:
A file is formatted with the style that results from laying these layers over one another, later ones winning:

• Defaults — the cautious style above.

• Global — what you set on the page with Global selected. It applies to every project.

• Detected — what the project's existing code does nearly always, when Detect from existing code is on.

• .editorconfig — indent style and width, line width, line ending and final newline from the project's
.editorconfig, when Read .editorconfig is on (it is by default).

• Project — the override saved for this project alone.

Each row on the page says where its value comes from: a small project, editorconfig or detected badge
marks a value that a layer other than your own style decides, and the reset button on a row undoes what the scope you are editing
has set.

title: A style for one project
text:
Switch the page to This project and every change is saved as an override of that project only, in
.arbor/bennu/config.toml under the [format] table:

Only what differs from the layers below is written: setting an option back to what the global style, .editorconfig or
detection already say removes it from the file. That file is meant to be committed, so the team formats alike. Reset in
this scope removes the override altogether.

title: Detecting a project's style
text:
Detect from project… — or Detect code style… in the command palette — measures the project's Java files and
lists what it found: the indent, where braces go, how long lines get, how chains are wrapped, and how consistently the code
follows each (91% of 1380). Apply as project style stores the
result as the project's override, which you can then adjust; Dismiss throws it away. Alternatively, turn on
Detect from existing code and the measurement is used live, under .editorconfig and the project's override.

title: The options
text:
Indentation
The width of a level (also a tab's display width), tabs instead of spaces, the extra indent of a wrapped line, whether
case bodies are indented, and whether a wrapped argument list aligns under the character after its parenthesis.
Blank lines
The most consecutive blank lines kept (0 removes them all), and blank lines forced after the package line and
the imports and before a member. 0 leaves what is written.
Braces
For type declarations, methods, blocks and else / catch / finally: keep the brace where
it is, put it on the same line, or on the next. Always use braces adds them around a one-statement
if, else, for or while body.
Spacing
One master switch, Normalize spacing, and fourteen rules under it: before parentheses and braces, around binary
operators, assignment, ternaries, arrows and the for-each colon, after commas and casts, and inside parentheses, brackets,
array braces and angle brackets. The rules are inert while the switch is off, and the page shows them dimmed.
Wrapping
