The right margin, and a policy for parameters, arguments, call chains, binary expressions, ternaries,
extends / implements / throws lists and array initialisers. A policy is one of: keep the
author's breaks; never wrap (join onto one line); wrap if needed (fill each line); chop if needed (one element per line when it
does not fit); always one per line. A chain wraps only from a minimum number of calls, can keep its first call with the receiver,
and a wrapped operator can start the new line. A chopped list can put its closing parenthesis on a line of its own and break
straight after the opening one.
Imports
Sorting and grouping as part of formatting: an ordered list of groups (a package prefix such as java or
org.springframework, * for everything else, static for the static block), a blank line
between groups, whether static imports come first, last or mixed in, and the wildcard thresholds.
Annotations
For types, methods and fields: keep, each annotation on its own line, or marker annotations (no arguments) on the declaration's
line.
Comments
Re-aligning the * of block comments and Javadoc, a space after //, and re-flowing Javadoc prose to the
right margin.
File
Whether the file ends with a line break, and the line ending written — LF, CRLF, or whatever the file already uses.
Behaviour
Format on save, reading .editorconfig, and detecting from existing code.

Collapsing a package's imports into package.* changes which names are in scope: two wildcards that both contain a
List make the simple name ambiguous, and a class added to the package later can shadow another. The thresholds are 0 by
default — never collapse — and the unused-import check and Optimize imports never create a wildcard. Turn them on only for
a codebase that already uses them.

title: Formatting
text:
• The file — Alt+Shift+F, or Format file in the command palette.

• The selection — with text selected, the same key formats just that range; Format selection in the
palette does it by name. Only the selected lines change, whatever the file around them looks like.

• On save — with Format on save on, a Java file is formatted when you save it (Ctrl+S, or when the window is left with auto-save on). Other languages are never touched, the formatting is one undo step,
and a formatter that fails never prevents the save. The idle auto-save does not format, so half-typed code under your caret is
left alone.

A language with a language server — Rust, for example — is formatted by that server, reading the project's own
rustfmt.toml or .prettierrc; nothing on this page applies to those files.

title: Getting Started
text: Welcome

title: Getting Started
text:
Bennu is a code intelligence engine with an editor around it, aimed at the projects where the
behaviour is not in the code: Struts, Spring XML, MyBatis, JSP. It also opens a Cargo workspace
as a first-class Rust editor. Everything it knows, it knows from an index it builds itself —
which is why it answers about files you have never opened.

Maven

Java projects

Cargo

Rust workspaces

LSP

Every other language

Rust

Its own engine

The first-run walkthrough is re-openable any time —
bennuOnboardingStore.show()}>launch the welcome tour
— or find it in the Command Palette under Welcome tour.

Ctrl+O, pick the folder holding the root pom.xml or
Cargo.toml, and the tree, the index and the footer fill in on their own.

title: Opening a project
text:
• Press Ctrl+O and choose the folder with the root manifest in it

• Bennu reads the build model — modules or workspace crates, the JDK level, the frameworks

• The index builds in the background; the footer says how far along it is

The title-bar switcher keeps recent projects one click away, and the hamburger
menu carries the same list. On macOS those entries live in the system menu bar instead.

Load demo project in the hamburger menu opens a realistic sample — a Struts +
Entando portal — with a populated tree, a highlighted Java file, and the footer showing the JDK
and the encoding. Everything in this manual can be tried on it.

title: The window
text:
Left rail

Project files, the Structure of the open file, and Dependencies. Each button toggles its tool window; Alt+1 … Alt+N.

Editor

Tabs, folding, sticky scroll, rainbow brackets, and an overview ruler that marks every problem in the file rather than only the ones on screen.

Right rail

Maven and Cargo — each there when any project of the workspace has one, whatever the open file — the test catalogue, the parse and model Trees, and — on a translation bundle — the i18n panel.

Bottom dock

Build and Problems (two views of one run), Run (the launched program's console, and the debugger when it is one), TODO, Forms and the Terminal.

Footer

The JDK, the detected capabilities, the index state, the open file's encoding and the caret. On a Cargo project it reads the toolchain and the crate count.

Activity bar

Both rails can be rearranged — Customize Activity Bar…, in the Command Palette and under the title bar's gear. Drag to reorder, and hide the tools you never use.

title: Everything from the keyboard
text:
Ctrl+K opens the Command Palette —
every action Bennu has, by name. If you can do it, you can find it there, and it will tell you
the shortcut on the way past.

Action — Shortcut

Go to class — Ctrl+N

Go to file — Ctrl+Shift+N

Go to declaration — Ctrl+B

Go to implementation — Ctrl+Shift+B

Find usages — Alt+F7

Find in project — Ctrl+Shift+F

Local history — Alt+Shift+H

Build — Ctrl+F9

The full reference is under Keyboard shortcuts, and every binding is remappable there.

title: Where to go next
text:
• Projects — what Bennu resolves when it opens a folder, and what a capability is.

• Navigation — the jumps that make a legacy codebase readable.

• Validation & problems — the squiggles that appear before anything is compiled.

• Language servers — how every non-Java language is served, and how to install one.

• Git — a file's history, the history of a selection, and blame in the margin, from the editor's right-click menu.

• Local history — the record of a file's own past, including the files that are gone.

• Imber, the assistant — an AI chat and agent panel (Alt+A) that reads, edits, builds and debugs through Bennu's own tools, and asks before anything that matters.

title: Go to class, file, symbol
text: Editor

title: Go to class, file, symbol
text: Reaching something by its name — including the names that are not in your source tree at all.

title: One navigator, three lists
text:
Tab — Opens with — Lists

Classes — Ctrl+N — Every class

Files — Ctrl+Shift+N — Every file

Symbols — Ctrl+Shift+Y — Every method and field the project declares

All — Tab to it — The three together, each one's best few under its own heading

Tab moves between the tabs without reopening; they sit above the field because they decide what it searches. The field
has the caret the moment it opens, and nothing is read until you type — listing every class of a reactor would be a
wait paid on every use, for an answer nobody scrolls.

The selected entry is shown in context on the right — the declaration with the lines around it, or a file's head —
coloured. A list of names says where there is an OrderDao; it does not say whether it is the one you meant, and
on a legacy tree with four classes of that name that is the only question left. ↑/↓ read as you go; nothing
opens until Enter, which jumps a class or a symbol straight to its declaration line. A word selected in the editor pre-fills
the field.

Files work in any project; Classes and Symbols read the Java index, so a Cargo project gets its types from a language server instead —
see below.

Projects a language server answers for:

The first tab is Types rather than Classes, and its rows come from the server: a struct, a trait, an enum, a TypeScript
interface. Where a repository is several languages at once, every server rooted there is asked and the answers merged — a Rust
workspace with a Svelte app inside lists both.

A server starts when you open a file it serves. Search a repository whose .svelte files you have not opened yet and
Svelte contributes nothing, because nothing Svelte is running.

A Svelte component has no declaration inside it to point at — the file is the component — so its server
reports a generated name, BennuSidebar__SvelteComponent_. Bennu shows it under the name you wrote, among the types, where
somebody looking for a component goes. The functions and stores in its <script> are ordinary symbols, under Symbols.

title: Narrowing
text:
Module

On a multi-module project, a dropdown on the header row of Classes and Files. It lists only modules that have something in them, and
a nested module wins over the parent listing it — a class under modules/core is filed there, not under
modules. Switching tab clears it. Every row also says where it came from: the module for something this
build compiles, the project for a sibling, the artifact for something it only depends on.

Workspace
The toggle beside the field — the one Find in project has — makes Classes and Files read every project of the workspace. A project's class index is built the first time you search it, and reused.

How a name is matched:

By subsequence, not substring — the letters appear in order — and the characters that matched are lit in the row, so a
loose match is legible rather than mysterious:

Typed — Finds

agpo — AGGIORNAMENTO/POS

agg pos — The same, each term matched on its own — for a path that separates them

Results rank on where the hit lands: the start of a word beats the middle, a run beats a scattered match, a short name beats a long one.

Directives:

Directive — Keeps

in:dao — Paths containing dao

ext:java — That extension

sort:new — Everything, most recently modified first

title: Reaching what is inside the dependencies
text:
The Source picker on the header row decides whose code Classes and Files are about: Project, the
outside, or both, ranked into one list rather than two tabs for one question. It is how you reach what is on the
classpath and nowhere in the tree — the framework annotation whose package you cannot remember, the struts-default.xml
declaring the interceptor stack, the schema an XML file is validated against.

The outside, for Classes

Dependencies & JDK

Half of what anyone looks up is in the JDK — List, Optional, Path — and it opens on the real .java from the JDK's src.zip.

The outside, for Files

The dependency jars

From Java 9 the JDK is a single image file, with nothing in it a reader would recognise as a file to open.

A dependency row is tinted and names its artifact — a classpath is where four versions of one name live,
and what you can read is not what you can change. The same picker is on Find in project, where Dependencies
alone is often what you want.

Search the dependencies too (Settings → Java) moves the default to Project & dependencies. It no
longer decides whether the classpath is reachable — that is one pick away.

• A library class opens like a stack-trace frame does: the real .java when the JDK ships sources or a
-sources.jar has been downloaded, otherwise the decompiled stub.

• A library file is extracted from the jar and opened read-only, keeping its extension — so an XML still reads as XML.

• Classpath rows are searched as you type rather than listed: hundreds of thousands of entries, nothing fetched without a query. The
first search after opening a project spends a moment reading the jars, and is instant after that.

title: The Gradle tool window
text: Projects

title: The Gradle tool window
text:
The build's own scripts, as things to run. Alt+8 opens it. Its rail button is there whenever the
workspace has a Gradle build, in the slot Maven's takes on a Maven project. A project with a
settings.gradle[.kts] or a build.gradle[.kts] at its root opens as a Java project, with the same
symbol index, completion and validation a Maven one gets.

title: One section per project
text:
A Gradle build is a root plus the projects settings.gradle includes — include ':api', ':web:client',
with project(':x').projectDir honoured. The window has one section per project, the root first, and each holds
two groups:

What the project offers

Tasks

The tasks the applied plugins are known to add (build, test, run,
bootRun, war…) plus the ones the script declares itself with
tasks.register or task. clean build is there as one row.

What the script applies

Plugins

From plugins {'{'} … {'}'} and apply plugin:. A row opens the build script at the line that
applies it; apply false is labelled.

A Version catalogs section lists gradle/libs.versions.toml and any catalog the settings declare;
a row opens the file. Which sections are open is remembered for each project.

title: What a press runs
text:
A task row runs that task in that project — test on :orders runs
:orders:test from the build root. The root row runs the bare task name, which Gradle applies to every project that
has it: the whole build. The output goes to the Run console, in a tab named for the task and the project, and ⟳ on the tab
repeats exactly that run.

The launcher is the project's own gradlew when it has one — a build is only guaranteed to work with the Gradle
version it pins — else a gradle on the PATH or in the usual install directories.

title: The switches
text:
Control — What it does

Skip tests (flask) — Adds -x test to every task run from the window, until turned off.

Offline (actions menu) — --offline on every task and on the classpath resolve. The same setting as Settings → Java.

Re-resolve dependencies — Under the actions menu: these change what is on disk, as background jobs that report in the Jobs panel.

Download missing dependencies Alt+Shift+U

Module graph Alt+Shift+D — This window lists the projects; the graph shows how project(':x') dependencies wire them together.

title: Dependencies
text:
The Dependencies window reads a Gradle build the way it reads a pom: one group per project, each row with the
scope its configuration folds into (implementation and api are compile,
compileOnly is provided, anything with test in it is test), the version, who decided
that version — the script, a variable (ext, gradle.properties), a version-catalog alias, a
BOM, or an allprojects {'{'} {'}'} / subprojects {'{'} {'}'} block of a parent — and whether the jar is in the
Gradle cache. Every row jumps to the line of the build script that declares it. Resolve tree runs
gradle dependencies in the background and adds who brings each dependency in, and the versions Gradle replaced
(1.0 -> 1.2) as conflicts.

title: What it reads, and what it does not
text:
Building the window costs a read of the settings and every build script — no Gradle, no network — so it draws at once on a
build that was never run, and the refresh is cheap enough to press freely. Gradle starts only when you press a task, resolve
the tree, or when the symbol index asks it for the classpath (a few seconds on a warm daemon; the result is cached until a
script, libs.versions.toml or gradle.properties changes).

Groovy and Kotlin build scripts are programs. Bennu reads the declarative subset every real build is made of — plugins,
dependency blocks, variables, sourceCompatibility, java {'{'} toolchain {'}'}, options.encoding — and
nothing else. A dependency added in a loop, by a function or by a convention plugin does not appear in the Dependencies list
(the resolved tree and the index classpath, which ask Gradle, do include it), and a convention plugin's tasks are not in the
task list: run gradle tasks in a terminal for the authoritative one.

The ▷ button next to a main method launches a JVM on a classpath assembled from a Maven reactor, which a Gradle
build does not have. For now, run the application from the window — run, bootRun — and use
the Build button (gradle classes) for diagnostics.

When no Gradle can be found — no gradlew in the project and no gradle on the PATH this
app inherits — the window says so once at the top. The index then falls back to the jars the build files declare, read straight
from the Gradle cache, and says that its classpath is partial.

title: i18n labels
text: Java & JSP

title: i18n labels
text:
A fulcrum project keeps its user-visible text out of the code: content declares a label, and the strings live in per-language TOML beside it. Bennu reads
both sides, so a label nothing declares, one a language has forgotten, and one nothing reads any more are all visible.

title: The layout
text:
Bennu recognises the convention by its shape — an i18n/ directory with a languages.toml in it:

{`i18n/
languages.toml the declared languages; the first enabled one is the fallback
styles.toml one table per style — what $red.bold{…} may name
glossary.toml one table per entry — what @potion{…} may name
it/
menu.toml the file name IS the category
tree.toml
en/
…`}

A label is category:dotted.key: menu:items.new_game is new_game under [items] in menu.toml. The same label in
it/ and in en/ is one label with two declarations.

More than one tree is normal — the base project's and each mod's. They merge, later trees winning, exactly as the engine merges them, and a language declared in one tree can be
translated in another.

The tooling is useful on a project that only authors content — a .ron tree with its bundles and the engine nowhere in its manifest — and the layout is what
the engine itself keys on. Which signal convinced Bennu is listed under Projects.

title: The markup
text:
Written — Means

{'{amount}'} — A placeholder, interpolated when rendered

{'$red.bold{…}'} — A style span — chainable, and $mod:red{…} for a namespaced one

{'@potion{…}'} — A glossary reference — @rpg:hp{…} namespaced, @status.protect{…} dotted

{'~sleep(0.8)'}, {'~slow{…}'} — A control, pacing or effect; arguments and body both optional

\ escapes any of $ @ ~ { } \.

A literal $ is written \$ — in a literal TOML string, since "\$" is not a valid TOML escape. And Bennu can point at a problem
inside a literal string, while inside a double-quoted one carrying escapes it can only point at the whole value.

title: What Bennu tells you
text:
In a .ron or a .rs

On a string that is a label

Hover: what it says in every language, who has not translated it, which placeholders it expects. Go to declaration: one target per language.
Completion: the labels continuing what you type, with their text. And a warning when no bundle declares it.

In a bundle

On the markup

Markup problems — an unclosed {'$bold{'}, a $ with no style name, unbalanced parentheses. A style or glossary entry that does not
exist, on the name. Missing in the fallback language, which makes the fallback itself fail.

A mistyped label is invisible to the compiler and to every test, and the engine renders the label itself when it cannot resolve one — so it survives QA until somebody notices
tree:nodes.drill.name written on screen.

• A missing style or glossary name is checked only when the project has a styles.toml — one that does not has not written a wrong name.

• Missing in the other languages is a tag in the Labels panel, not a warning: mid-translation that would be a warning per label, burying the mistyped ones under the unfinished.

title: The i18n panel
text:
A bundle is a file where TOML sees a string, and the markup inside it is invisible to every tool that reads TOML. The panel is the other half of that file:
Alt+Shift+I, or the i18n button on the toolbar of a translation file. It opens beside the editor — the markup on the left, what it
comes out as on the right, both changing as you type.

It follows the caret. There is no label to pick: the line you are on is the translation.

The preview:

The sentence with its constructs resolved: styles painted from styles.toml, glossary terms marked, each placeholder shown as its name until you give it a sample.

It shows the distinctions the stylesheet draws — that $warning is not the colour of $hint, that a title is bigger than the text around it —
not the engine's output. Sizes are relative: the smallest declared renders at the panel's own size, the rest in proportion, since a faithful 48-point heading in a side panel would
push everything off screen.

A control is a chip, not an animation — ~shake is motion, and a still of it would lie. A style or glossary name the project does not
declare is underlined rather than recoloured, because the real consequence is that the span has lost its styling.

Parameters:

Every parameter of the label — not only the ones this language uses. That union is the point: en passing {'{amount}'} while the Italian never
mentions it is a real defect, invisible to compilers and tests because both files are valid, and invisible in any view showing one language at a time. The row says which languages
use it, and its button writes it in at the caret.

A sample value is substituted into the preview — "the sentence, as somebody will read it" — and long ones are the reason to bother: {'{name}'} reads fine
until it is Bartolomeo della Fortezza and the line wraps into three. Samples are scratch, never saved.

title: Writing markup
text:
Four buttons in the header wrap the editor's selection — or open an empty construct with the caret inside when nothing is selected. The words stay selected afterwards, so
$red.bold{…} is two presses on the same words.

Style, glossary
Offer only what the project declares: a name not in styles.toml is a defect.
Control, placeholder
Accept anything — a control is whatever the engine implements, and i18n knows its form, not its meaning. The controls the project uses come first, most-used first. sleep(0.8) and sleep 0.8 both write ~sleep(0.8).

Such a string's content is shorter than its source, so no offset inside it can be trusted, and Bennu will not write to a byte it cannot locate. The panel says why — and rewriting the
value with single quotes fixes the toolbar, the colouring and the problem markers at once.

Switching language:

The picker beside the label lists every declared language, and the ones with no translation yet are what it is for: picking one opens the file the translation would go
in, even when it does not exist yet. Languages declared but switched off stay listed, marked. Below the parameters, the languages that do have the label show what they say.

title: Markup colouring in the editor
text:
In the bundle, the parts of a value that are structure rather than prose are coloured — placeholder names, style names, glossary keys, controls — with a tint over each construct so
nesting reads as nesting. A name the project does not declare is coloured as a warning as you type; the diagnostic follows with the next scan, and the failure it prevents is
silent, since a style that does not exist renders as the default.

title: The Labels panel
text:
From the command palette, i18n labels. One row per label — the label, its text, its category as a badge — with tags saying how many places read it and which languages lack it.
Expanding a row gives two kinds of child:

• one per language — what it says there; clicking jumps to the declaration;

• one per reading — which file and line; clicking jumps to the use.

So find usages, find unused and which languages are missing are one list with a filter, the way they are really used. Filter for unused to find
labels content deleted and left behind, for missing to find what a translator still owes. Group by category or key prefix. A label read from hundreds of files shows the
first fifty readings; the count on the row is the real one.

title: Jakarta EE
text: Java & JSP

title: Jakarta EE
text:
@Inject OrderService orders; says what it wants and nothing about what it gets. The container decides at deployment — and when the answer is
none, or two, the application does not start. Bennu reads what the container reads and puts the answer beside the field.

It switches on for a project that uses CDI, EJB or annotated servlets, in either the javax or the jakarta namespace. When the
same project also wires beans with Spring, Spring answers @Inject and this page's injection features step aside; the EJB, proxy and servlet
checks still run.

title: Beans and injection
text:
Icon — Beside — Click to

I — A bean class or a @Produces method or field — See the injection points it satisfies

B — An @Inject field, constructor or initializer parameter, or an @EJB field — See the beans that may satisfy it

Go to
Ctrl+B on an injection point's name opens its bean, or asks when several may answer.
Hover
On an injection point, the bean it gets or the candidates; on @ApplicationScoped, @Stateless and the rest, what that scope or bean kind means in one line.
Completion
Inside @Named("…") on an injection point, the names of the project's beans.

A bean is matched by type through the project's own hierarchy and by qualifier: @Named, the project's annotations marked
@Qualifier, @Default and @Any. @Singleton from javax.inject and from
javax.ejb are told apart, and a JAX-RS @Produces is never mistaken for a producer.

An arrow lists every bean that could satisfy a point, including one whose qualifiers Bennu cannot fully read — you choose. A warning appears only when
the source leaves no doubt.

title: The CDI beans panel
text:
Open Jakarta EE beans from the Command Palette. Every bean class and producer, badged by scope or EJB kind
(@ApplicationScoped, @Stateless, @Produces, …), tagged with its @Named name, qualifiers and
alternative, and grouped by scope or package. Expand a row to see the injection points it satisfies; each one opens its field.

title: Servlets in the Endpoints panel
text:
Every @WebServlet and @WebFilter URL pattern, and every <servlet-mapping> and
<filter-mapping> in web.xml, is a row of the Endpoints panel — badged SERVLET or
FILTER, beside the routes of every other framework the project uses.

title: The checks
What it will not judge
text:
• Portable extensions add and veto beans at will: a project that implements one gets no injection warnings at all.

• Library bean archives and producers of types Bennu cannot read may hold the missing bean, so a point of a library type is never
reported unsatisfied.

• Alternatives enabled at deployment are not in the source: any @Alternative, @Priority,
@Specializes or @Typed bean of a type silences both injection warnings for it.

• Generic injection types, @EJB points, points of classes the container does not manage, and any qualifier or scope Bennu cannot
classify (@ViewScoped, a library's own) are left alone.

• A beans.xml with bean-discovery-mode="none", or modules that disagree, make which classes are beans unknowable — nothing
about injection is claimed.

• JSF managed beans and EL names in pages are not modelled.

title: JAX-RS resources
text: Java & JSP

title: JAX-RS resources
text:
Every route a project's @Path resources answer — the application path, the class path and the method path joined into the URL a request actually hits —
and the mistakes the runtime only reports when that request arrives, or by refusing to deploy.

title: Routes in the Endpoints panel
How the application path is found
text:
Source — Read as

@ApplicationPath("api") on the Application subclass — The prefix /api, when it is the only value in the project

web.xml servlet mapping to /rest/* — The prefix /rest, when nothing is annotated — for the Jersey or RESTEasy servlet, or a servlet named after an Application subclass

Several distinct values, or a constant — No prefix, and every row tagged application path unknown rather than guessed

title: The checks
Completion and go-to on @PathParam
text:
Inside @PathParam("…") the completion list offers the variables of that method's route — application path, class path and method path — replacing the
whole string. Ctrl+click on the string jumps to the {id} it binds, in the method's @Path or the class's.

Whether a parameter names a variable depends on the class path, possibly inherited from an interface, and on every sub-resource locator in the project; whether a route is
claimed twice depends on another file. Neither is reported before the project has been indexed. The other three are about one method and are reported immediately.

title: What it will not judge
text:
• A @Path that is not one plain string literal — a constant, a concatenation. The route is still listed, with … for the part that cannot be read.

• A path parameter on a class with no class-level @Path, or one whose name any sub-resource locator's route declares: it may be bound through that
locator.

• An interface implemented by more than one class, or re-annotated by its implementation — which annotations are in effect is not in the source.

• A parameter carrying an annotation Bennu does not know — Jersey's @FormDataParam, RESTEasy's @MultipartForm — is never counted as the
entity.

• Clashes involving a route declared on an interface (usually a REST client mirroring the server), across build modules, between several applications, when the
application lists its classes by hand, or when the regexes of two variables are written differently.

title: The JDK
text: Projects

title: The JDK
text: Which Java a project is read with, where that answer comes from, and what changes when it is wrong.

title: The language level
text:
The footer shows the Java language level Bennu resolved and where it came from. When it cannot be inferred the footer
reads JDK —. The places it is read from:

• maven.compiler.sourcethe usual one

• maven.compiler.releasethe newer spelling of the same thing

• <java.version>the Spring Boot property

• The compiler pluginits own <configuration>

• Toolchainswhen the build uses them

• A manual overridewhen you have set one

title: A multi-module project
text:
The whole reactor is read, not only its root. An aggregator pom usually declares no level at all — it exists to list
<modules> — so the highest level any module declares becomes the project's.

The index has one language level, and the choice is not symmetric: too low invents errors in the module that
legitimately uses newer syntax, while too high can only stay silent about an older one.

And the level in force follows the module you are in. A reactor part-way through a migration has one
module on 21 and another still on 8, which is an ordinary state: the validator's version checks and the postfix
templates ask the open file's own module, and the footer names it beside the level.

Only that question is answered per module. The index and the dependency classpath are one JDK by construction, since
an index holds one standard library.

The project tree says the same on every module and crate row — JDK 21, JDK 21 · war,
Rust 2024 · bin — and its tooltip carries the artifact id, the packaging and the key that declared the
level.

title: The installation
text:
The standard library is resolved against an installed JDK. Bennu looks for one in this order:

• The extra JDK directories in Settings → Java → JDK locations.

• JAVA_HOME.

• Each platform's usual places: the JavaVirtualMachines bundles on macOS, the Program Files vendor
directories on Windows, /usr/lib/jvm on Linux, the Homebrew openjdk formula, and the
directories a version manager or an IDE installs JDKs into.

The one whose level matches the project wins; failing that, the newest installed.

When none is found the title bar carries a No JDK warning, because without one nothing — not even
String — resolves.

title: Builds and tests use the same one
text:
The installation Bennu found is handed to Maven as JAVA_HOME, so the level your code is analysed at is
the level it is compiled at.

If no JDK of that level is installed, the build inherits whatever JAVA_HOME your environment already sets
instead of being pointed at a different one.

A compiler of the wrong version fails with a message about the target release, which says nothing about the JDK that
caused it.

title: JPA
text: Java & JSP

title: JPA
text:
Entities, their mapping and the queries written against them — resolved together, so a field name in a query is a reference rather than a string.

On a project with JPA or Spring Data on its classpath — and only there, like every framework tool here.

title: Generated sources are part of the project
text:
The static metamodel Criteria queries are written against — Order_, Customer_ — is written by an annotation processor into
target/generated-sources, and so are MapStruct's *MapperImpl, QueryDSL's QOrder and jOOQ's output. None of it is under
src/, all of it is referenced from there, so Bennu indexes those generated roots.

Nothing else under target/ is indexed — it holds build output, and sometimes an unpacked copy of somebody else's sources.

title: Derived query names are checked
text:
That is not a name but a query Spring Data compiles at application start. A typo in one is invisible to the compiler and to every test not touching that
repository — and then it takes the context down on deploy. So every segment is resolved against the entity:

Segment — Resolved as

CustomerName — customer.name — relations are followed

TotalGreaterThan — total, compared with one argument

• A segment addressing nothing is flagged where you wrote it.

• The argument count is checked too: Between wants two, IsNull none, and a Pageable is Spring's, not yours.

An entity whose @MappedSuperclass chain leaves the project, a relation whose target was never scanned, a repository over a type Bennu does not have —
each turns the check off for that method. Nothing about the database is checked: whether a column exists needs a connection, which is Picus's business.

title: A @Query stops being a string
text:
• It is coloured with the same SQL lexer as the Picus editor: keywords, types, function calls, parameters, literals, numbers, comments, and a name after a dot as a column or attribute. The same colours apply in a text block and under // language=sql.

• Completion works inside it, in a one-line string and across the lines of a text block: entities after FROM/JOIN, attributes after alias., the method's parameters after :. In a native query it offers the tables and columns the entities map (@Table, @Column, @JoinColumn, or the derived upper-snake name) — a table the code does not map is not offered; connect Picus to complete from the live schema.

• JPQL and native SQL are tinted apart, being different risks: JPQL is resolved against the entity model, native SQL sent to the database as written.

• A :name no parameter binds is an error on the placeholder, with the fix named.

• Ctrl+B inside a query opens the entity it selects from.

title: The gutter links the two ends
text:
Icon — Beside — Opens

R — An entity — The repositories managing it

E — A repository — Its entity

Hovering a repository method says what it asks for — a derived name rendered as the sentence it compiles to.

title: The toolbar follows the file
text:
Standing on — The toolbar offers

An entity — Add attribute, Add lifecycle callback, Add named query, Repository, Projection

A @MappedSuperclass — The attribute and callback buttons — it has no table, so none of the repository ones

A repository — Add query method, Add modify method

Anything else — Nothing — the buttons present are the answer to what kind of file this is

Every generator previews live, Ctrl+Enter commits, and nothing is written before that. Each is also in the command palette by name.

Adding an attribute:

It writes the field, how it is stored — a plain column, @Enumerated(STRING), @Embedded, @Lob — its constraints, the Bean
Validation you ask for, and optionally its accessors. A second preview tab shows the alter table the column implies, because field and column are one
decision usually made in two places, the second from memory later.

No dialect, and no back-fill for a not null added to a table that already has rows.

Choose a relation and it writes the pair people get backwards by hand: the owning side gets the @JoinColumn, and filling in
mapped by makes it the inverse side, owning no column.

• A to-many is a Set unless you say otherwise — a List of children makes Hibernate delete and re-insert the whole collection on any change.

• It is always initialized: the omission that becomes a NullPointerException the first time anything adds to a new entity.

• Cascade and orphan removal are there; the helper methods keeping both sides of a bidirectional relation in step are still yours to write.

title: Query methods
text:
Built from the entity's own properties — the point: a name assembled from properties that exist cannot be misspelled, and the parameter list follows from the keywords.
Leave method name empty and the derived name is used; write one and the method arrives with its @Query spelled out, since a name Spring Data
cannot parse is no longer a derived query.

The operation — find, count, exists or a derived delete — is chosen where the dialog is opened
(the repository's Add query method menu, the palette, Alt+Enter); the small switch at the top of the dialog can still change it.
The dialog is one screen: the method name (empty: built from the conditions, shown live), then the switches Distinct, @Query, Sort, the result type and a limit,
then one line per condition — property, operator, value, case — where an empty value is a method parameter and a typed one is written into the query.
Alt+Ins adds a condition, Alt+↑/↓ moves the row (Spring Data reads them left to right),
Ctrl+Enter adds the method; Order by and Projection are folded until needed.

Returns — Worth knowing

Optional, the bare entity, List, Stream — —

Page — Takes a Pageable, and also runs a count(*) for the total

Slice — Takes a Pageable, skips the count and only says whether more rows follow — the one behind infinite scrolling

A finder can take a Sort so the caller decides the order — except a paged one, whose Pageable carries one already; taking both would not
compile, and the dialog says so. The button you pressed decides where the form opens, not what it produces: the verb, the return shape, the ordering, a limit
and distinct are all editable. Add and continue writes one and clears the form for the next, keeping the repository.

title: Modify methods
text:
Always @Modifying with the JPQL written out — Spring Data has no naming scheme for an update.

It goes straight to the database: rows are not loaded, so @PreUpdate and @PreRemove do not fire and the persistence context does not see it.
The dialog says so, and warns when there are no conditions at all.

Repositories and projections:

Repositories land in the package the project already keeps them in, read off the ones that exist. A projection can be its own file
or an interface nested in the repository that returns it — both idiomatic, both offered.

title: Checking against a database
text:
With Picus installed, the Database tool window (Alt+D, right rail) checks the persistence layer against a live schema. Pick one of the connections defined in Picus — connections are created and edited there — and connect.

• Entities compares each @Entity with its table: a missing table, a field with no column, a Java type that cannot be stored in the column's type. Names are compared loosely (firstName, first_name and FIRST_NAME are one column), so the project's naming strategy does not matter. Columns no field maps are listed dimmed — a legacy table has columns an entity never needed. A finding jumps to the field.

• Queries prepares every @Query(nativeQuery = true) on the server without running it; the server's own rejection is the finding. :name and ?1 placeholders are rewritten for the engine first.

• MyBatis (shown when the project has mappers) prepares every mapper statement the same way, so a missing table or column, or a join on a column that is not there, comes back as the server's message. Dynamic tags are flattened first — every <if> kept, the first <when> of a <choose>, <where>/<set>/<trim> applied, <foreach> written once — and #{…} becomes NULL. A statement using ${…} or a fragment from another mapper cannot be rendered and is reported as not checked, with the reason.

• The window shows only what the project has: Entities and Queries need JPA or Hibernate, MyBatis needs mappers. Lists are filterable, every verdict can be checked again, and a field stored through an AttributeConverter (@Convert, or an auto-applied one) or an embedded object is not judged by its Java type. A column no field maps is listed as unmapped; it is left unsaid when an embedded object or a foreign key of an unknown name might own it. A statement that splices ${name} can be given a value in the MyBatis tab, per project, and is then checked too.

• The first connection is chosen by hand. The project is then paired with it: coming back to the project reconnects that database, and a project with no pairing is checked against nothing (the unlink button forgets it).

• A native query is also checked as you type: what the server rejects is a red squiggle at the place it names, in a repository's @Query and countQuery, createNativeQuery, @NamedNativeQuery, and any string under // language=sql (or @Language("SQL")), which is also coloured and completed as SQL. A query written as "…" + "…" is left unchecked. A MyBatis statement the database rejects is red on its opening tag in the mapper, and is checked again as you edit it (not when it uses a ${…} with no value, or a fragment from another mapper). A field that a JPQL / HQL query names and its entity does not have is an error where it is written, without a connection.

• Generate entity (the wand in the window's header, a dialog) writes an entity from a table: package and source root default to where the existing entities live, and the file is never overwritten if it exists. The preview is syntax-highlighted, and two switches choose Lombok accessors (@Getter/@Setter) and fluent accessors (name()/name(v) returning this); the last choice is kept and becomes the next default. A single-column foreign key becomes a @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) with its @JoinColumn (pointing at the project's entity for that table when there is one), a serial or sequence-default key gets @GeneratedValue, and a composite key gets an @IdClass with a nested key class — each with its own switch. A composite foreign key stays plain columns.

The same connection feeds completion in .sql files, inside native queries (createNativeQuery("…"), @NamedNativeQuery, @Query(…, nativeQuery = true)) and in the text of a MyBatis mapper's statements (<select>, <insert>, <update>, <delete>, <sql>; not inside a tag or a #{…}): tables after FROM/JOIN, the columns of a table or alias after alias., and the columns of the tables the statement already names elsewhere. In a .sql file Picus's SQL abbreviations work too (s#orders(id)[id=1] expands to the full statement, with the column types deciding the quotes and the foreign keys the joins). It works once a connection is chosen and open in the Database window; without one, completion in those places is unchanged.

Without Picus, the tool window and its commands are not offered.

title: JSON types
text: Java & JSP

title: JSON types
text: What a DTO will and will not put in its JSON, read from the class — instead of discovered from a payload that came out wrong, on the other side of an HTTP call, days later.

title: Jackson fails quietly
text:
Almost nothing here throws where you can see it:

• A field with no accessor is simply absent from the payload.

• A property two members both claim throws only when that object is serialised — in practice, in front of a customer.

• A @JsonIgnore meant as "not on the way out" takes the property off the way in as well.

None of it shows in the class: you see a field, spelled correctly, with an annotation on it, and the first person to notice has no reason to suspect the DTO.

title: What is checked
text:
Check — Why

Two members claiming one JSON name — an error — Jackson refuses to serialise the type at all. A field and its own getter are one property; what conflicts is two fields, or two members both naming themselves with @JsonProperty.

A field nothing can reach — Not public, no accessor: it will not appear in the JSON.

@JsonIgnore and @JsonProperty on one element — Jackson drops the property, which is unlikely to be what the @JsonProperty was for.

Hover on a field or an accessor says what it will be called in the JSON, and why — named by @JsonProperty, named after the member, or not serialised at all.

title: A creator whose arguments have no names
The gate that keeps it usable
text:
Jackson's visibility rules are configurable globally at run time, per class with @JsonAutoDetect, and through mix-ins registered somewhere else entirely. So
the reachability check runs only where the class says plainly what it is: it carries Jackson annotations, sets no visibility of its own, and generates no
accessors through Lombok.

Without it the check fires on every Lombok DTO in the project — all of them — and a check wrong about all of them is turned off before it is ever right about one.

title: JSP pages
text: Java & JSP

title: JSP pages
text:
A JSP is not HTML with noise in it. The taglib tags, the scriptlets and the EL and OGNL expressions are each parsed as what they are — which is what makes a name
inside ${…} something you can navigate.

title: The grammar
text:
A dedicated grammar colours namespaced taglib tags (<s:iterator>, <c:if>), scriptlets, EL ${…} and
OGNL %{…}. Navigating a Struts application from its pages is Struts navigation.

title: Expressions are parsed
text:
An EL or OGNL expression is not one block. A path — a name and what is read off it, #session.currentUser, items[0].price — is a
construct of its own, with identifiers, property accesses, strings, numbers, operators and keywords each coloured.

• The # of an OGNL context reference is marked apart from the name after it: #session is precisely not a property of the action.

• The syntax tree shows that structure, and a structural search can put a hole inside an expression — %{#session.$prop$}.

An expression that does not parse — every line while it is being typed — is left plain and stops at the next tag: an unclosed
${ never swallows the rest of the page.

title: Script blocks
text:
A <script> body is read as real JavaScript: object keys, member accesses and call sites each have a colour; numbers in every form — hex, binary,
exponents, separators — are numbers; template literals colour their ${…} holes as code; this stands out; and a regular
expression is told from a division, which keeps one / from painting the rest of the line as a literal.

Completion and hover work inside it too, answered by Bennu itself — no language server will ever serve a JSP, a template that prints JavaScript:

What the block declares

Its own names

var, function, the foo: function (…) form a jQuery-era page is mostly written in, and their parameters — each hovering with the line it was declared on.

By reflection

The platform

After document., location. or Math., the members the object really has, read in the engine the page runs in — a list that cannot be stale.

$ is offered as a name, but there is no loaded library to read $(…). off.

title: JSP inside the JavaScript
text:
The script body is a template that produces JavaScript, and it is read as one. A scriptlet, a <%= … %>, an EL or OGNL expression
and a whole namespaced taglib tag are recognised as what they are — inside a string too, which is where it matters:

errore = "<wp:i18n key="LABEL_REQUIRED_COMUNE" />";

Read as plain JavaScript, the tag's own quote closes the string and the rest of the line is coloured as something it is not. The marker wins instead — which is what
the server does, since substitution happens before there is any JavaScript to quote, and the rule the page grammar applies to attribute values.

The marker is painted over the JavaScript the way it is in the page: a tag wears its taglib's colour, its attribute names and values are coloured, and an EL or OGNL
expression inside it (test="${skin == 'text'}") is read as one. A scriptlet takes the JSP meta colour. The JavaScript around it is read
with the markers taken out, so a <c:if> wrapping a block of script never turns the statements inside into a comparison. A marker spanning several
lines is followed across them.

A tag that closes inside the script — </c:if> after a <c:if> that opened in it — does not end the script: only
</script> does, so the markup after the block keeps its own colours.

title: A colour per taglib
text:
Each taglib gets its own colour, and its <%@ taglib %> line wears the same one — so the declarations at the top of the page are the
legend for everything below them, and Struts, JSTL and Entando tags are told apart at a glance.

• A prefix keeps its colour across every file that declares it; two prefixes in one page never share one.

• A prefix the page never declared stays the plain tag colour — the quickest way to notice a missing directive, since the server will not render it either.

title: Language servers
text: Reference

title: Language servers
text:
Bennu's Java intelligence is its own engine. Every other language is served by an external language server, and the editor treats both the same way. This page is what a
server gives you; getting one running is Installing a language server.

title: What you get
text:
For a file a server owns, the whole editing surface is live — the gestures of a Java file, answered by the server:

Feature — How

Completion — As you type and after the language's punctuation — for Rust . and ::. An item needing an import brings the use line.

Go to declaration — Ctrl+B or Ctrl-click; on the declaration itself it flips to find usages, as in Java.

Find usages — Alt+F7

Hover — The signature, where the item lives, its documentation.

Diagnostics — In the editor and the Problems panel — below.

Rename — Shift+F6, with the same preview.

Quick fixes and refactorings — Alt+Enter — the server's whole list: fixes first, then refactorings; one it offers but cannot apply here is shown last with its reason.

Format — Alt+Shift+F, with the language's formatter and the project's configuration.

Semantic colouring — Below.

Signature help — The parameters of the call the caret is inside.

Go to type / symbol — Ctrl+N, Ctrl+Shift+Y, across the workspace — below.

Structure — The Structure panel and the Ctrl+F12 popup, in the language's vocabulary — structs, traits, impls, functions.

Occurrences — Every other place the symbol under the caret appears in the file, a write tinted apart from a read.

Folding — By item: a use block, a doc comment, a #[cfg]-gated module, a match arm.

Expand / shrink selection — Alt+Shift+→ / ←, one syntactic step at a time.

Placeholders — Tab through an accepted completion's holes — below.

Code lenses — Clickable counts above an item — below.

Call and type hierarchy — Ctrl+Shift+H, Ctrl+H — below.

Extracting a variable or a function has to be told what, so at a bare caret the server's list is short by design. And "selection crosses a block" on a disabled row tells you what to change —
an absent row would not.

title: Go to type, go to symbol
text:
With no Java index, Ctrl+N asks the server. The tab is Types — structs, enums, traits, unions, aliases — and Ctrl+Shift+Y, Symbols, finds the rest: functions, methods, constants, statics, fields. The server does the matching, which is why it needs two characters: a workspace is too
large to hand over, and one character discriminates nothing.

Each row is named and marked in the language's vocabulary. The protocol has 26 fixed kinds and every language squeezes in — rust-analyzer reports a trait as an
interface, an impl as an object, an alias as a type parameter — so they are translated back. In Types every row is a type, so the mark is a lettered ring:

Mark — Is

S — struct

T — trait

E — enum

A — type alias

In Symbols the mark is a shape, the distinction worth drawing being function against constant against field. A union arrives as a struct and a static as a constant,
indistinguishable downstream, so both keep the protocol's word rather than a guess.

title: Code lenses
text:
A line above an item counting implementations of a trait, or references to a type or trait, and taking you to them — one result jumps, several open the
Alt+F7 popover. It costs nothing extra: the server found those places to count them and sends the list along. Reference counts are asked on types and traits only —
each is a query per item, and methods are by far the most numerous.

title: Call and type hierarchy
text:
Ctrl+Shift+H on a function opens its callers; Ctrl+H on a type its implementors — in the
Hierarchy panel, whose direction chip walks the other way. On a file the server owns it answers; on a .java Bennu's own index does, into the same panel.

Expanding a call graph eagerly does not terminate: mutual recursion, a trait implemented by a type using it, or a widely-called helper turn "expand everything" into a sweep of the workspace.
A recursive chain is walked as far as you care to.

A caller row jumps to the call, not the head of its function, and says 3× for several calls inside one. The panel takes the keyboard as it opens: arrows walk and expand,
Enter jumps.

title: Placeholders in a completion
text:
Accepting a completion with holes puts the caret in the first and Tab moves on — println! lands between its parentheses, a function on its first argument.
Shift+Tab goes back, Esc leaves the run, and moving elsewhere ends it. Two placeholders the server marks as the same value are two ordinary stops,
not one mirroring the other.

title: Expanding a macro
text:
Alt+Shift+M on a macro call shows what it generates, in a dialog to read, copy and re-expand from. It is also under Alt+Enter,
named after the macro — Expand vec! — only when the caret really is inside a macro call.

• The expansion is recursive, all the way down: the server has no single-step form.

• It is text, not a file the server knows — no go-to, hover or completion inside. To expand a nested macro, point at it in the real source and expand again.

• Re-expand asks about the caret as it is now: move it in the file behind the dialog and press it.

title: Semantic colouring
text:
A file is coloured twice:

Local and instant

First pass

Keywords, strings, comments, numbers — what you see the moment a tab opens, and when no server is running.

From the server

Second pass

A struct told from a trait, a macro from a function, a mut binding from an immutable one, a parameter from a local — facts rather than guesses.

title: Diagnostics arrive on save
text:
For Rust the real errors — types, borrows, unreachable code — come from cargo check, which the server runs when a file is saved. They appear a moment after a save;
while typing, you see what the parser alone can tell. Autosave counts as a save, so with it on — the default — the loop is: stop typing, wait a beat, read the compiler's answer.

Settings → Rust chooses the command: cargo check, or cargo clippy — every check error plus several hundred lints, at the cost of a
slower build per save. The server reads it when it starts, so it applies on the next start.

title: Live
text: Run

title: Live
text:
Live is the tool window for the services a project runs: start a stack in one go, read what each process prints, send requests to it, follow one request through
every service's log, and replay the same checks as a scenario — by hand, or through Imber, the assistant. Ctrl+Shift+F11, or the rail button
beside the Profiler.

title: Processes
text:
A managed process is a long-running command (a Spring service, npm run dev, a Cargo binary) started on behalf of the project. It is not a Run
configuration: it has no console to type into. Its output is kept in a bounded buffer with timestamps (stdout and stderr, colours removed), it can be asked whether it is
ready, and stopping it ends the whole process tree — on Windows through taskkill /T, elsewhere through the process group — not
only the launcher.

Ready
Any combination of: a port that accepts connections, a log line matching a regular expression, a http://localhost health URL (any 2xx, or an exact status), a delay. All of them must hold, within a timeout. If the process exits first, the wait fails with its last output.
Caps
At most 8 processes running at once, 24 finished ones kept for their logs, 5 000 log lines and 2 MiB per process, and a lifetime of 30 minutes unless a recipe says otherwise. A declared port that is already taken refuses the start before anything runs.
Cleaning up
Closing a project stops what it started; so does closing Bennu. A backend that dies without cleaning up is covered by the same exit watchdog as Run and Test.

In the list, ↑ ↓ choose a process and Delete stops it.

title: Recipes
text:
A recipe is a named stack in .arbor/bennu/live/recipes.toml. Services start in dependency order, each after the previous one is ready. Create recipes
file in the Recipes tab writes a starter.

{`[[recipe]]
name = "shop"
description = "Gateway plus the orders service"
stop_order = ["gateway", "orders"] # optional; default: reverse of the start order

[[recipe.service]]
name = "orders"
command = "mvn -q spring-boot:run"
cwd = "orders" # relative to the project; may not leave it
env = { SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE = "dev" }
ports = [8081]
ready = { port = 8081, log = "Started .*Application", timeout_s = 120 }

[[recipe.service]]
name = "gateway"
command = "npm run dev"
depends_on = ["orders"]
ready = { http = "http://localhost:3000/health", status = 200 }`}

The file is validated as a whole: names, dependency cycles, regular expressions, loopback-only health URLs, ports declared twice, a working directory outside the project. Every
problem is listed at once. max_minutes overrides the lifetime cap of a service.

The first run of a recipes file shows every command and asks. The approval is bound to the content of the file: change a command and it asks again. It is kept
for the session only — nothing in the repository can approve itself.

title: HTTP to localhost
text:
Imber's http_request reaches services on this machine and nothing else: localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1] over plain
HTTP. Every request carries an X-Correlation-Id header (unless it names one). Secret headers (Authorization, Cookie,
Set-Cookie, X-Api-Key) are redacted in what is recorded and shown to the model. A POST, PUT, PATCH or
DELETE to a port none of the started processes declared asks first.

title: The timeline and correlation ids
text:
The Timeline tab merges what every process printed, each request and its answer, and the start / ready / exit of every process into one chronological stream. Filter by text or
kind, or paste a correlation id to see everything that request touched: the request, the response, and every log line of every process that mentions the
id, with the stack-trace lines that follow. For that to reach the services' logs they must log the header — typically a request filter that puts it in the logging
context.

title: Scenarios
text:
A scenario is an ordered list of steps with assertions, in .arbor/bennu/live/scenarios/<name>.toml. It runs without Imber: select it in the
Scenarios tab and press Enter. Each step reports pass or fail; a failing step shows the failed assertions and the timeline slice while it ran, and its
request's correlation id opens the timeline on that request. Execution stops at the first failing step unless the step sets continue_on_fail.

{`name = "order-flow"
description = "Log in, list orders, expect no errors in the log"

[[step]]
type = "start_recipe"
recipe = "shop"

[[step]]
type = "http"
name = "login" # saved: later steps can use it
method = "POST"
url = "http://localhost:8080/api/login"
headers = { "Content-Type" = "application/json" }
body = '{"user":"demo"}'
expect_status = 200
max_ms = 800
[[step.expect_json]]
path = "$.token"
exists = true

[[step]]
type = "http"
url = "http://localhost:8080/api/orders"
headers = { Authorization = "Bearer \${login:$.token}" }
expect_status = 200
expect_body = "orders"

[[step]]
type = "assert_log"
pattern = "ERROR"
present = false
timeout_ms = 500

[[step]]
type = "stop_all"`}

Step types
start_recipe / stop_recipe (recipe), stop_all, http, wait (ms), assert_log, assert_running (process, running).
HTTP checks
expect_status, expect_body (a regular expression), max_ms, and any number of [[step.expect_json]] with a path ($.a.b[0], $['key'], [-1]) and one or more of exists, equals, matches, gt, lt.
Log checks
assert_log looks at lines written since the scenario began, or in the last window_ms. With present = true it waits up to timeout_ms for the line; with present = false it waits that long first and then requires its absence.
Saved values
A named http step is saved. Later steps may write {'${name:$.json.path}'}, {'${name:status}'} or {'${name:body}'} in the URL, a header or the body. A reference to something that is not there fails the step instead of sending a blank.

The model — a scenario is a suite, a step a test case, an assertion a check with its own pass or fail — is the one JUnit XML and Playwright specs share, so a scenario
can later be exported to either. The file format does not change for that.

title: Who owns a process
text: Every process records who started it: you (from this panel) or a particular Imber conversation, and the list shows the owner. Stopping from this panel always works, whoever started it. An Imber conversation stops only its own processes; a name or port that another owner holds is refused instead of duplicated or killed, a stack another conversation already runs is attached read-only (status, logs, requests), and a recipes file approved in one conversation is not approved in another. Scenarios run one at a time per project, and a scenario's stop_all stops only the processes of whoever runs it.

title: The build queue
text: Builds, test runs and whole-project checks of a project take a numbered ticket and run one at a time, in the order they were asked for, whoever asks — the Build button or any Imber conversation. When anything is queued the panel shows a Build queue section: the run in progress and each waiting ticket ("#2 · waiting behind build of …") with the conversation it belongs to. A waiting ticket can be cancelled with its ✕; the run in progress is stopped from the tool that started it. Requests for the same thing queued before a build starts share that one build.

title: Imber's live tools
text:
Settings › Imber › Tools it may use has a Live services switch. When it is on the model can run_start, run_status,
run_logs, run_stop, wait_ready, list_recipes, run_recipe, http_request,
trace_request, timeline, list_scenarios, run_scenario, save_scenario and the log readers described below. Reading and inspecting never asks.
Starting a process asks every time; running a recipe or a scenario asks once per content of its file; stopping what the run started does not ask. The processes are the same
ones the Live panel lists.

A run that used these tools ends with a Live run card: what it started and stopped, what is still running, the requests it sent (each opens the timeline on
that request), the scenarios and assertions, the files it changed, and what the run cost.

title: Reading logs without reading them
text:
A log is read as records: a line together with its stack trace, the Caused by chain, a Rust backtrace or a multi-line statement. The levels, timestamps and exceptions are read by the same interpreter that colours the Run console, from logback / log4j / Spring lines, Rust env_logger and tracing, logfmt and JSON logs. The same readers work on a managed process, on the output of the Run console and on a log file.

• run_logs — a process's records, newest 80 by default. summary gives the counts per level, the first distinct errors (with first time and count) and the last error; level (at least that severity), pattern (a regex over the whole record), last (30s, 5m), after / before (ISO-8601 or epoch milliseconds; no offset means UTC), context (records around each match, merged, gaps shown as --) and frames (stack lines per record; the last Caused by is always kept) narrow it. Identical consecutive records are folded (x12). next_since returns only what is new.

• wait_log — waits for a new line matching a regex (default 30 s, at most 300) and returns it with three records of context on each side; it returns early, with the last output, if the process exits.

• console_logs — what the Run console printed for the Run button: lists the recent runs (r3, configuration, start, status) and reads one with the same filters. The backend keeps the last six runs of a project, up to 5,000 lines or 2 MB each, and forgets them when the project closes.

• tail_file — the end of a log file (512 KB by default, at most 4 MB), whole records only. It returns next_offset; passing it back as since_offset gives only what was appended, and a file that shrank (rotated or truncated) is read again from its end, and says so. The encoding is detected. It is a read of that file under the access rules.

• log_facets — a compact digest instead of lines, for a process, console or file:<path>. Exceptions are grouped by class, root cause and the first frame inside the project (shown as file:line); queries (Hibernate, p6spy, JdbcTemplate, MyBatis, sqlx) have their literals replaced and come slowest first when the log carries times; requests (access logs, tower / axum traces) are grouped by endpoint with their statuses, failing endpoints first; warnings are grouped by message template. Each group has a count, first and last time and a sample record id. facet shows one facet in depth, limit raises the groups listed, and where filters its occurrences (status >= 500, duration > 200ms and sql contains orders, class contains Order).

• log_record — one record in full, by the id a digest printed, optionally with the records around it.

Every answer lists what it left out (older records, hidden stack lines, records without a level or a timestamp, lines the process's buffer dropped) and how to ask for it.

title: Command palette
text: Toggle Live, Live: recipes, Live: scenarios, Live: timeline and Live: stop all processes.

title: Local history
text: Editor

title: Local history
text: Every version of a file Bennu has seen, whether or not it was ever committed — including the files that are no longer there.

title: Why it exists
Opening it
text:
Alt+Shift+H, Local History in the editor's or the project tree's right-click menu,
or the command palette. The dialog has four scopes:

This file

Every revision of the file in front of you.

The folder

Deleted files stay visible here, struck through where you left them, with a Restore beside them.

The project

Everything, across every file.

Deleted

The files the project no longer has. A deleted file has no row to right-click, so a list that does not depend on the filesystem is the only way back to it.

title: History of a selection
text:
Highlight some lines and choose Local History → Show History for Selection (editor menu or palette). The list then holds only the
revisions that changed those lines — each is the text the lines had before somebody changed them — and the diff shows only the hunks that touch
them, against what is on disk. The most recent 120 revisions are examined; the footer says so when there are more. Restoring is off in this mode,
because it would put back the whole file, not the lines.

title: When a revision is recorded
text:
When — The row says

You save — A save — you

A tool writes — a refactor, a generate, a format — Which tool; a refactor's row shows every file it touched, marked in the folder column

A file changes or vanishes outside Bennu — An outside change

You rename or create a file — The rename or the creation

Not on every keystroke: the editor's own undo covers that scale.

title: Comparing
text:
The right-hand pane compares the revision you picked with what is on disk now. It opens side by side — the old text on
the left, the current on the right, each changed line opposite the line that replaced it, and a hatched band where one side has nothing.

The button in that pane's header, or Alt+D, switches to the unified patch — one column with
+ and − — for reading the change as a change. Whichever you leave it on is the one it opens with next time.

title: Labels and how long it keeps
text:
Put Label… pins a name on a moment — before the atlas refactor — and a labelled revision never expires.
Everything else is kept for the number of days set in Settings → Editor → Local history, within a size budget per
project, and each file's newest revision always survives both.

Files git ignores are not recorded: build output is regenerated, not recovered. And nothing is written inside the project — the store
lives in Arbor's data folder, so it is never something you could commit by accident.

title: Installing a language server
text: Reference

title: Installing a language server
text: Which servers Bennu knows about, how to install one from inside the app, where it looks for the binary, and why the project root decides what a server can see.

title: Supported out of the box
text:
Language — Server — Files — Project marker

Rust — rust-analyzer — .rs — Cargo.toml

Go — gopls — .go — go.mod

Python — Pyright — .py — pyproject.toml, setup.py

C / C++ — clangd — .c, .cpp, .h, … — compile_commands.json, CMakeLists.txt

TypeScript / JavaScript — typescript-language-server — .ts, .tsx, .js, … — tsconfig.json, package.json

Svelte — svelteserver — .svelte — svelte.config.js, package.json

Angular (templates) — ngserver — .html — angular.json

Lua — lua-language-server — .lua — .luarc.json, plugin.toml

WGSL — wgsl-analyzer — .wgsl — Cargo.toml, .git

title: Installing one
text:
Settings → Language Servers lists each one with the path it resolved to, or — when it found nothing — how to install it. For the ones distributed through a
package manager you already have (rustup, cargo, go, npm) an Install button beside the hint runs exactly that
command, streaming into the Build panel: cargo install --git builds a server from source and takes minutes, so it is worth watching rather than waiting on.

Not a download

A command, on purpose

The server lands where the rest of your toolchain lives, so it keeps working after Arbor is updated or removed, and wgsl-analyzer --version says the same thing in your own terminal.

No button

System packages

clangd is LLVM, lua-language-server is Homebrew. Bennu installs language servers, not toolchains.

A shader gets diagnostics, completion and find usages whether or not wgsl-analyzer is installed — see Shaders (WGSL), under Rust. The server, when present,
serves the file instead, which is worth knowing before installing it on a Bevy project: its module system is WESL rather than naga_oil, so it does not understand
#import, and it replaces Bennu's deliberate silence on a composed shader with its own reading of those lines.

title: Svelte and Angular
text:
A .svelte file is coloured as markup with <script> and <style> in it, immediately and with no server. What that cannot know — that a name
is a component, a prop, a store — arrives from svelteserver as semantic tokens layered on top, along with completion, hover, diagnostics, go-to, find usages and rename. The
template syntax itself ({#each}, {expr}) stays uncoloured: no HTML grammar can be told it is Svelte, and pretending otherwise would colour it
wrongly rather than not at all.

Angular serves templates, not .ts:

Its server also speaks TypeScript, but one server serves a file here and the first match wins for every project — so claiming .ts would take every TypeScript file on
the machine away from typescript-language-server, Angular project or not. Templates are the half that otherwise has nothing, so this is the trade that only adds. A
.ts file keeps the server it has always had, which means a rename started in a component's class does not follow the name into its template.

Wanting the other trade is a [[lsp.servers]] entry with id = "angular": a custom entry shadows the built-in completely, so its extensions and its
args are the ones used. Spell out the probe locations if you do — ngserver is a front end for the TypeScript and Angular language services and locates them from
the command line; without them it starts, handshakes, and answers nothing.

A server is selected by extension, so .html joins the language-server set for every project, including one with no angular.json anywhere — where
nothing starts, and go-to or rename on a plain page simply finds nothing. Turning Angular off in Settings → Language Servers takes .html back out.

title: Who watches the files
text:
A language server either watches the project for outside changes itself, or trusts the editor to tell it. Most watch for themselves, which is what Bennu wants — it does not deliver those
notifications, so a server that stopped watching would quietly stop noticing a file cargo build regenerated.

It is told the editor watches: left to itself it walks the entire workspace root, which in a repository that is a Svelte app and something much larger means tens of thousands of
directories and a server that dies on too many open files before answering anything. The cost is that it learns about a change only when the file is opened or saved here — which looks
like a Bennu bug when it bites.

title: A server you have not installed
text:
Not in the running list
That list answers "what is serving this project", and a server whose binary was never there is not failing at that — the table above already says so, with an Install button. Repeating it per open project would fill the list with rows offering a Restart that can only fail again.
Looked for once
Bennu remembers that it looked, so it does not search your PATH on every keystroke, and forgets the moment something could change the answer: installing a server, or saving the settings — which is how an executable path gets pinned by hand. Nothing to restart, nothing to clear.
It does not claim the language
A server starting up still owns its files — the correct answer while it warms up is "nothing yet", not an answer from another engine. A binary that is not installed is never going to answer, so the file falls through to whatever Bennu can do by itself. That is what keeps a .wgsl shader's go-to, find usages, hover and compiler diagnostics working on a machine that never installed wgsl-analyzer.

title: Where the binary is looked for
text:
• An explicit path you set.

• The language's own install location.

• PATH.

• The places these tools generally install themselves.

The last step matters more than it sounds: a windowed application does not inherit your shell's PATH, so ~/.cargo/bin, ~/go/bin, Homebrew's directory
and npm's global prefix are all invisible to a plain PATH lookup even though your terminal finds them instantly. For rust-analyzer it also includes the rustup
toolchains and the VS Code extension's copy.

Rust: the file that exists and does not work:

~/.cargo/bin/rust-analyzer is usually not the server. It is a rustup proxy — a link to rustup itself — there whether or not the component is
installed. Run without the component, it exits immediately with Unknown binary 'rust-analyzer' in official toolchain.

So Bennu looks in the rustup toolchains before PATH — the real binary should win from wherever it is — and when the only candidate left is a proxy for a
component nobody installed, it reports not installed rather than a resolved path and then a server that dies. The fix is the one the panel prints:

A cargo installed copy lives in the same directory and is a real binary — that one is used normally.

title: Starting, and what the footer says
text:
A server starts when a project is opened, not when you first ask it something: a cold Rust workspace takes rust-analyzer tens of seconds to index, and a go-to that answers nothing during that
time is indistinguishable from a go-to that does not work.

Footer — Means

A spinner with progress — The server for the open file is loading

Its name — Ready

A warning triangle — Not running

Clicking it opens Settings → Language Servers.

Deliberately, so a server that is not installed is reported once instead of respawned on every keystroke. Restart language server in the command palette, or the button in
Settings, is the way back — and what to press after installing one.

title: The project root decides everything
text:
A server is started for a workspace root — the highest directory above the file carrying the language's project marker. In a Cargo workspace that is the top
Cargo.toml, not each member's: one server over the whole graph is what makes cross-crate go-to work at all.

It is also the gate that keeps things quiet. A stray .py in a Java repository has no pyproject.toml above it, so no Python server starts. Nothing runs unless there is
a real project for it to analyse.

What it analyses: the whole workspace:

Not the open file. The server is handed the root, reads the project's manifest, resolves the entire dependency graph, runs build scripts, expands procedural macros and indexes every crate —
what the footer's progress line is doing, and why it takes tens of seconds on a cold workspace. Cross-crate Ctrl+B and Ctrl+N would be
impossible otherwise.

• The only per-file thing is the unsaved buffer: the file you are editing is sent as you type, every other file the server reads from disk.

• Diagnostics are workspace-wide too — the cargo check run on save checks everything, so a problem can appear in a file you never opened.

That check and your own builds share target/, and cargo locks it. On a large workspace a cargo build started from the Cargo tool window right after a save can sit
waiting for the server's check to finish.

A dependency's source is not a workspace:

Following Ctrl+B into a library opens a file under ~/.cargo/registry/src, and that unpacked crate has a Cargo.toml of its own — so by the rule
above it would look like a root and get a server of its own, one per library you looked into. It does not: those locations are known, and a file in one borrows the session
that already has it. Your project's server has every dependency's source open already, because that is what resolving the crate graph means — and it is the only one that can answer about
your code as well.

With two projects of the same language open, a file inside a shared dependency gets no intelligence rather than an arbitrary one of the two: which server answered would depend on ordering,
and a feature that works intermittently is worse than one that is honestly absent.

title: Renaming a file, and reloading the project
text:
F2 in the Project tree
Renames a file and the code referring to it by name: for Rust, the mod declaration naming it and every use path through the module it declares. The server is asked what the rename implies before anything moves, so the dialog says how many files it will touch — and a rename that cannot be performed changes nothing. The edits go through the editor, one undo step like any other change.
Reload workspace
In the command palette: the server re-reads the manifests and resolves the crate graph again, keeping what it has indexed — which a restart would throw away. rust-analyzer notices a Cargo.toml it knows about changing on its own; this is for what it cannot see — a .cargo/config.toml edit, a patched or vendored dependency changing underneath, a cargo add run in a terminal.

title: Adding a language
text:
Any server speaking LSP over stdio can be added in bennu/config.toml — the same fields the built-in entries carry, so it gets the same features with no new release:
