• extensions and root_markers are both required: without an extension the entry can never be selected, without a marker it can never start.

• An entry whose id matches a built-in replaces it — how a server is reconfigured (other arguments, other options), as opposed to re-pointed at another binary.

title: Limits worth knowing
text:
No files created or deleted for a server
Bennu edits buffers through the editor so every change is undoable, and performs a file rename itself (above). A refactoring wanting a new or deleted file says so instead of being half-applied.
Only lenses that do something
rust-analyzer's ▶ Run and Debug lenses above fn main and every test are asked for because the Run console launches exactly what they carry — see Building & running. A lens whose press would do nothing is not requested: a control that does nothing teaches that the feature is broken.
Inlay hints
Inferred types shown inline are not rendered for a language-server file.
Macro expansions
Cannot be navigated — see Language servers.

title: MapStruct mappers
text: Java & JSP

title: MapStruct mappers
text:
A mapper is an interface full of methods nobody writes. Bennu reads it the way the annotation processor will — and says what is wrong in the file where the mapping is
written, instead of in a compiler message about generated code on the next build.

title: What is checked
text:
`, 'java')}

Build fails

A property that does not exist

A target or source path segment that names nothing on its type. Nested paths like address.street are followed
property by property; with several source parameters, a path that starts with a parameter's name.

Build fails

Mapped twice, or refused together

The same target on two @Mappings of one method, and elements MapStruct will not combine — source with
constant or expression, constant with expression, a default value with a default expression.

Build passes

A target property nothing maps

Shown on the method name: every writable property that is neither targeted nor filled from a same-named source property or parameter. A
warning, or an error when the mapper's unmappedTargetPolicy is ERROR.

MapStruct only warns about it, in a build log. The generated method compiles, leaves the field unset, and the first person to notice sees a null three
services away.

title: Alt+Enter
text:
On — Offers

An unmapped target — Ignore N unmapped target properties — one @Mapping(target = "…", ignore = true) per property above the method, importing Mapping when the file does not.

An unknown property — Change to … — when exactly one property is a likely typo of what was written.

title: Inside the strings
text:
A mapping path is code written as a string, and it behaves like code: completion offers the properties of whatever the path so far leads to (writable ones for a
target, readable ones and parameter names for a source), replacing only the segment under the caret. Ctrl+B on a segment
opens the property's field — or its getter or setter when there is no field — and hover shows its type and where it comes from: a field, an accessor, a constructor, a
record component, or Lombok.

A mapping method whose generated implementation exists under generated-sources gets a gutter mark that jumps into it.

title: The Mappers panel
text:
Command Palette → MapStruct mappers lists every mapper with its component model, and under it each mapping method with its source and target types,
whether it maps, updates a @MappingTarget or iterates a collection — and the properties it leaves unmapped, tagged, so the question "which mappers drop a
field" has an answer without opening them one by one.

title: What it will not judge
text:
• Types it cannot see completely. A class from a dependency, a DTO whose superclass comes from a jar, one with accessors renamed by Lombok
@Accessors, fluent setters, a hand-written builder, or several constructors: nothing is said about their properties either way.

• A policy it cannot read. A config class it cannot find, an inheritance strategy, or a build without a pom.xml — processor
options set in Gradle are not visible, so unmapped targets are reported there only on mappers that set their policy themselves.

• Mappings that come from elsewhere: @InheritConfiguration, @InheritInverseConfiguration,
@BeanMapping(ignoreByDefault = true), a "." wildcard, a target written as a constant — and any annotation on the method it does
not recognise, since MapStruct lets a project compose its own mapping annotations.

• Collection, array, map, Optional and generic methods, which MapStruct maps element by element through other methods.

• A property Lombok's constructor or builder only may take is never reported as unmapped, and a name is unknown only when nothing on the type carries it.

title: The Maven tool window
text: Projects

title: The Maven tool window
text:
The project's own poms, as things to run. Alt+8 opens it. Its rail button is there whenever the
workspace has a Maven project, and sits beside Cargo's when it also has a Rust one — the key opens the tool of the
open project's own kind.

title: Several Maven projects
text:
The window lists the Maven projects of the whole workspace, not only the project on screen: a Rust crate in a
subfolder of a Node project (a Tauri app's src-tauri) is a Maven project like any other, and so is one in
another project of the workspace. With more than one, a small tree at the top — grouped by project when the workspace has
several — picks the one the commands act on. Pick a row with Enter or a click; pick it again to let go. With
nothing picked the window follows the file you are editing; with a single Maven project there is no tree at all.

The same rule applies to the palette: a command that acts on one Maven project runs straight away when a row is picked or the
open file belongs to one, and otherwise asks which, in a list you can filter by typing.

title: One section per module
text:
A Maven project is a reactor, so the window has one section per module, the root first, and each holds two groups:

What every pom can run

Lifecycle

clean, validate, compile, test, package,
verify, install, site, deploy — plus clean install,
the one combination nobody types out because it is the one everybody runs.

What that pom configures

Plugins

A plugin that binds goals lists them, and each one runs. A plugin that only carries
<configuration> has nothing to press — a lifecycle phase calls it — so its row opens the pom that
declares it instead. That is most plugins, and the row says which kind it is.

Which modules, groups, plugins and the Profiles section are open is remembered for each project: closing the window,
switching project or restarting brings it back as you left it. A module or plugin that leaves the poms is forgotten.

title: What a press runs
text:
A phase runs in its module's directory. Pressing install on orders installs
orders; pressing it on the root row runs the whole reactor, because that is what the root pom's build is.

No -am, no -pl: what runs is what running mvn in that folder would have run.

Every run row carries Maven's own mark. When a phase that compiles (compile, test, package,
install, …) finishes well, the symbol index reads the sources again, so what the annotation processors generated —
the JPA metamodel (Order_), MapStruct's implementations, QueryDSL's QOrder — resolves without a manual rebuild.

The module header answers what the two groups cannot — where the module is. Its
locate button, or Focus in Project from a right-click on the header, opens the Project
tree on the module's folder. The same menu opens its pom.xml and copies its path.

title: Profiles, and skipping tests
text:
These belong to the window rather than to one press: you set them once, then run several goals.

Profiles

Above the modules, because a profile changes what every press below it does. They are passed as -P. The
ones the poms mark activeByDefault start ticked — that is what mvn with no -P
does, and starting with none ticked would quietly run a different build from the terminal's. Every other kind of
activation Maven supports is a fact about the machine or the command line, so the panel does not claim to know
whether it holds.

Skip tests
The flask in the header. While it is on, every goal run from this window carries -DskipTests.
Offline
In the actions menu, and off by default: a goal you pressed on purpose may need to fetch the plugin that performs it.

A console tab's ⟳ repeats the build that happened, with the profiles it had — not the ones the window
is set to by the time you press it.

title: Where the output goes
text:
Into the Run console (Alt+R), as its own tab beside the tabs a
java launch and a cargo command make. The tab is the run:

• Stop kills the process tree.

• The log is annotated like any other — levels, paths and stack frames picked out, and a frame clicks through to the file.

• Two runs of the same phase are two transcripts to compare, not one that overwrote the other.

The tab is named for what ran and where — install · orders. Two modules running the same phase are two
different builds, and a strip that called both "install" would be unreadable from the second one on.

title: The header's actions
text:
Action — What it does

Refresh — Reads the poms again — for this window and the Dependencies panel, because they read the same files and a pom that gained a module changed what both should say.

Re-resolve dependencies — Under the actions menu: these change what is on disk, as background jobs that report in the Jobs panel. Dependencies says what each one fixes.

Download missing dependencies Alt+Shift+U

Download sources

Module graph Alt+Shift+D — This window lists the modules; the graph shows how they are wired to each other.

title: What it reads, and what it does not
text:
Building the window costs a parse of every pom in the reactor — no Maven, no network — so it draws at once on a project
that has never been built, and the refresh is cheap enough to press freely. Maven starts only when you press something.

A plugin publishes its full list of goals inside its own jar, and reading that would mean resolving the plugin first —
so a goal nobody has bound is not listed. Any goal at all can still be run from a run configuration, or by typing it.

When no mvn can be found on the PATH this app inherits and the project has no
mvnw, the window says so once at the top, rather than letting every press fail to start.

title: Message bundles
text: Java & JSP

title: Message bundles
text: .properties bundles are resolved rather than read as text: a key used in code or in a page points at the line that defines it, in every language it is defined in.

title: Why they need a model
text:
Half of what a web application puts on screen is not in its source. It is in a .properties file, reached by a string — a string normally checked by
nothing: not the compiler, not the tests, and, because Struts renders an unresolved key as the key itself, often not by anyone looking at the page either.

title: What counts as a key
text:
By shape rather than by a list of tags, because every framework in a legacy page spells it differently:

Where — Example

An attribute called key — <bean:message key="label.user"/>

An attribute whose name ends in Key — titleKey, messageKey

The name of an <s:text> — the one tag where name is a key — <s:text name="label.user"/>

The first string argument, in Java — getText("…"), getMessage("…"), getString("…")

%{keyName}, ${row.label} or a scriptlet usually is one at run time, but nothing can say which, and guessing would flag every
dynamic label in the project.

<wp:i18n key="…"> reads the platform's label table in the database, edited from its admin console — no .properties
declares it, and treating it as one would underline every label on every page. That one tag, by name, and no attempt at the rest of Entando's vocabulary.

title: On a key
text:
Ctrl+B
Opens the line declaring it — one entry per translation, each showing what that language says, so choosing is reading.
Hover
The same without leaving the page, naming the locales that do not have the key yet.
Completion
Inside a key attribute, from the bundles, with each key's text beside it.
A missing key
A key no bundle declares is underlined where it is written.

title: The Messages panel
text:
From the command palette. Every key with its default text and its bundle, and two things you cannot see any other way:

How many places read it

unused

When the answer is none.

Which locales lack it

missing

Counted per bundle — two bundles with different locale sets is normal, and comparing across them would invent a debt nobody has.

Expanding a key shows every translation, each row opening its own file at its own line. Group by bundle or by key prefix.

title: Mockito
text: Build, run & test

title: Mockito
text: Mockito used wrongly, caught in the test that is wrong — instead of in the stack trace of the test that ran after it.

title: Why the exception points at the wrong line
text:
Mockito remembers a half-built stubbing or verification between calls, and notices it only when it is next used — by the next Mockito call. That call is often the
first line of another test, so the stack trace names a line that is fine. The broken line compiles and reads naturally; it is only found by reading it.

title: What is checked
text:
Error · UnfinishedStubbingException

A stubbing never finished

when(…) or given(…) as a statement of its own, with no thenReturn; a doReturn(…).when(mock) that never names the method.

Error · UnfinishedVerificationException

A verification never finished

verify(mock) or then(mock).should() with no method called on it. The line verifies nothing.

Error · InvalidUseOfMatchersException

Matchers beside plain values

When one argument of a stubbed or verified call is a matcher, all of them must be. Each plain value is marked.

Warning · NullPointerException

@Mock fields nothing initialises

No MockitoExtension, no MockitoJUnitRunner, no openMocks(this): the fields stay null, and the first stubbing fails as if the code under test were broken.

title: Alt+Enter
text:
On — Offers

A plain value beside matchers — Wrap plain arguments in eq(…) — every one in the call, not just the one under the caret. eq is written the way the file already reaches it: bare, qualified like the call's own matchers (ArgumentMatchers.eq), or bare with import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.eq added.

An uninitialised @Mock — Add @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) on JUnit 5, Add @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class) on JUnit 4 — on the class, at its indentation, with the imports.

No fix is offered for null beside a matcher: isNull() is what is usually meant, and that is a choice rather than a rewrite. Nor when eq cannot be spelled
so that it certainly compiles — a file declaring an eq of its own, for one.

title: How it stays quiet
What it will not judge
text:
• Stubbing a void or final method, a matcher used outside a stubbing, and Mockito's other run-time complaints.

• A stubbing whose result is kept — var s = when(…) may be finished elsewhere — deep stubs, lenient().when(…) and willReturn(…).given(…).

• Initialisation inherited from a superclass, or registered globally through JUnit's extension auto-detection.

• TestNG, and files that mix JUnit 4 and JUnit 5.

• A when inherited from a test base class: imports cannot see it.

title: The module graph
text: Projects

title: The module graph
text:
The Dependencies panel answers what does this module need. The questions it cannot answer are properties of the
project's shape rather than of any one row — and in a workspace of twenty crates they are the ones you arrive
with. Alt+Shift+D, or the network button on the Dependencies and Cargo windows, draws them.

Who uses this

And therefore whether anything still does.

What breaks if I touch it

How many modules rebuild, transitively.

What is foundational

What sits at the bottom, and is worth being careful with.

Is there a cycle

Which cargo refuses to build and Maven refuses to order.

It works on a Maven reactor as well as a Cargo workspace, from the same reading of the manifests. Nothing runs cargo or
Maven, so it opens on a project that has never been built. The window says crates or modules depending on
which it is looking at.

title: Reading it
text:
Layers run left to right: dependents first, the foundation last, so a chain reads like the sentence that
describes it:

app → core → util

An arrow points from the module that declares the dependency to the one it depends on, so every arrow in a healthy
project points rightwards.

That is why the layout runs this way round: a cycle is visible as a shape, without counting anything or consulting a colour.

Each column is labelled with its layer — how far above the foundation it sits. Layer 0 depends on nothing
else in the project; a module is one layer above the deepest thing it depends on. Every module of a cycle shares a layer,
because there is no order between them.

title: What the lines mean
text:
The legend button in the footer draws each mark beside its meaning. It is open the first time you arrive, and
stays closed once you close it.

Line — Means

solid — An ordinary dependency — a Cargo dependencies or build-dependencies entry, a Maven compile, provided or runtime scope. It orders the build.

dashed — A Cargo dev-dependency or a Maven test scope. Real, and it does not order the build. Under cargo it may legally close a cycle: a crate's tests compile as a separate unit, so a library whose tests use something that depends on it is normal. Maven refuses such a cycle anyway, because it orders the whole reactor as one graph. Either way it counts towards what rebuilds — changing the library does rebuild the tests that use it.

dotted — Optional — on the graph only when a feature turns it on. Whether one has is not a fact about the manifest, so it is drawn and labelled rather than guessed at.

red — Part of a cycle: the build tool refuses this.

blue — Touching the selected module — or the one under the pointer. Resting on a box lights its own lines: the quickest way to answer "which of these is mine".

Solid dependencies decide the order things are built in; dashed ones do not. That is exactly why the cycle
check ignores dashed lines under cargo and not under Maven.

The bar on a box
What the module builds: a library, a program, both, a proc-macro; a jar, a war, or an aggregator pom that builds nothing.
The number
How many modules rebuild when it changes.
The border
Red when it is in a cycle, blue when it is selected.

An edge that crosses several layers is routed between the boxes of the columns it passes rather than straight
across them — a long dependency you can follow, instead of a line disappearing under three other modules.

title: The list, and the numbers
text:
Beside the drawing every module is a row, and it is not a lesser view: finding a half-remembered crate in a picture of forty
boxes is a scan, and here it is three keystrokes. It is also the keyboard surface — ↑ ↓
walk it, Enter opens the manifest — so the whole window works without touching the graph.

• Most rebuilt onhow many modules a change here reaches — the number to know before touching something, and why a leaf with a high one is not really a leaf

• Layerdeepest first, in the drawing's order

• Most third-partywhich module pulls in the most outside code

• Name

Selecting is one act across all three views: the list moves the drawing, the drawing moves the list, and either fills the detail
panel underneath — the module's numbers, and its direct dependencies and dependents as rows you can walk into.

A fact, not a verdict. A library published to a registry and a deployable war both legitimately have nothing in the project
depending on them; in a private workspace a library in that state is usually dead code. Only you know which.

title: Solo, and searching
text:
Alt+S — a filter

Solo

Draws only the selected module's world. The columns are recomputed from what is left and empty ones collapse, so in a workspace
of sixty crates the other fifty stop taking room. Three scopes: everything connected, only what it is built on,
or only what it would break.

A dimming

Search

The matches stay lit and everything else recedes without moving. Both can be on at once — the search then dims inside the soloed world.

Solo follows the selection, so picking another module isolates around that one: that is how you walk a dependency chain a crate at
a time without leaving the mode. The header counts what is on screen — 4 of 22 crates — because the project's totals would
describe a picture you are not looking at.

title: Cycles
text:
The header counts the cycles, and pressing the count goes to one. The whole ring is named, not the single pair the
build tool mentions when it refuses: five crates that all reach each other usually contain several rings, and naming one would
suggest the others are fine.

What counts as a cycle is the build tool's own answer — see the dashed row above — and the drawing agrees with the count by
construction: the members share a layer, so their arrows are the ones pointing the wrong way.

title: Taking it elsewhere
text:
The export button beside the window's ✕ copies the graph or writes it to a file. There is no import: the manifests
are the truth, and this is a description of them.

For a language model, or a person

Markdown

Each module with what it depends on and what depends on it, then the three lists worth having: most expensive to change, nothing
depends on them, the cycles. It says what each number means — fewer tokens than a schema the reader has to infer.

For a script

JSON

Every field exactly as computed, keyed by module name rather than by array index.

For a spreadsheet

CSV

One row per edge, with a column saying whether it orders the build.

Solo and the dashed-edge filter included, and the file's own header says which filters were on. An export that silently described
the whole project while the window showed one crate's neighbourhood would mislead whoever — or whatever — read it.

RON is deliberately not offered: it would be a second spelling of the JSON with nothing that prefers to read it.

title: What it will not tell you
text:
Everything here is read from the manifests, which is what makes it instant and makes it work on a project that has never compiled.
The cost is stated rather than hidden: nothing is resolved. Feature unification across the workspace, which
dependencies a cfg(…) actually admits, and whether a Maven profile is active are cargo's and Maven's answers, not the
manifests' — so conditional and optional edges are drawn and labelled.

A project with more than 400 modules says truncated in the header rather than quietly drawing less than it has.

title: MyBatis mappers
text: MyBatis

title: MyBatis mappers
text: A mapper is an interface with no implementation and an XML file with no compiler checking it. Bennu links the two, so each half is one jump from the other.

title: What Bennu treats as a mapper
text:
An .xml file whose root is <mapper namespace="…">, anywhere in the project. The namespace is the fully-qualified
name of the mapper interface; every <select>, <insert>, <update> and <delete> whose
id equals a method name is that method's SQL. A mybatis-config.xml also contains <mapper> elements, but its root is
not one, so it is left alone.

MyBatis support turns on when the project has mapper interfaces or mapper XML. The mappers are collected with the rest of the project index, so
cross-file jumps and checks wait for it, while everything that stays inside one file works at once.

title: A mapper, both halves
text:
`, 'markup')}
`, 'java')}

title: Colouring
text:
A mapper .xml is coloured for what it is, not only as markup: the SQL of each statement (keywords, functions, strings,
numbers, comments), #{name} bindings, and ${name} in the warning colour — it is spliced into the
statement rather than bound, so it is the one that can be an injection. The dynamic tags (if, where,
foreach, …) and their test conditions stand apart from the SQL they control; statement ids, references
(refid, resultMap) and the Java types a mapper names each have their own colour. The details are on
Statements, parameters and result maps and Dynamic SQL.

title: Following a piece
text:
In a mapper .xml, Ctrl+B — or Ctrl+click — follows the piece under the caret. The caret only has to be
inside the attribute value:

The caret on — Goes to

A statement's id="findById" — The matching method on the mapper interface

The mapper's namespace="…" (also on <cache-ref>) — That interface

<include refid="columns"> — The <sql> fragment it pulls in

resultMap="orderMap" on a statement, <association>, <collection> or <case>; extends="…" on a <resultMap> — The <resultMap> it uses

An <association select="…"> or <collection select="…"> — The statement it runs

type, resultType, parameterType, javaType, ofType, typeHandler — The Java class — by qualified name, or by simple name when the project has exactly one class so named

A result property="name" — The field on the mapped class, else its setter or getter; the class itself when neither is written out (a Lombok property)

A reference written com.acme.other.OtherMapper.columns, or a bare one that this file does not declare, is looked up in the other mapper files of
that namespace. A built-in alias such as long or map names no project class and goes nowhere. A value written as an expression
(${…}) names nothing yet and is not followed.

The other way, on the mapper .java interface: Ctrl+B on a method's name opens its
<select|insert|update|delete> statement in the XML — on the declaration, and on a call made through a mapper too. If the method has no
statement, the ordinary go-to applies. Go to implementation
(Ctrl+Shift+B) lists that statement together with any Java override.

A fragment or result map referenced from the same file resolves at once, with no index needed.

title: Find usages
text:
Alt+F7 in a mapper .xml:

The caret on — Lists

The id of a <sql> or <resultMap>, or a reference to one — Every reference to it across the project's mappers, the unsaved text of the open file included

A statement id — The Java usages of the interface method — what calls the statement

title: Where to go next
text:
• Statements, parameters and result maps — what each statement and mapping element is, and how a statement is checked against a database.

• Dynamic SQL — if, where, foreach and the rest, and how they are read.

• Mapper checks — every problem Bennu reports in a mapper or its interface.

title: Mapper checks
text: MyBatis

title: Mapper checks
text:
MyBatis reads a mapper at start-up, or at the first call, and refuses it with a stack trace. Bennu reports the same mistakes while you type — in the mapper
XML, on the interface, and, when a database is open, in the SQL itself.

title: The checks
text:
Code — Level — Where — Reported when

mybatis-property-unknown — Error — Mapper XML — A result property is no field, getter or setter of the class the map describes

mybatis-ref-unresolved — Error — Mapper XML — An <include refid>, a resultMap, an extends or an association's select names a declaration its namespace does not have

mybatis-duplicate-id — Error — Mapper XML — A statement, <resultMap> or <sql> id is declared twice in one mapper

mybatis-type-missing — Warning — Mapper XML — A fully-qualified type names no class, in a package the project does have

mybatis-statement-missing — Error — Java interface — An abstract method of a mapper interface has no statement with its name in the mapper XML

mybatis-statement-unmapped — Weak — Mapper XML — A statement has no method of that name on its interface

Database: … — Error — Mapper XML — The server rejects a statement when asked to prepare it — a connection must be open

The first six run in the full validation pass, a moment after you stop typing; the fast pass that paints syntax errors does not run them. They are judged
against the text in the editor, so unsaved edits count. Like every check, they appear as squiggles and in the Problems panel.

title: Under-reporting on purpose
text:
Every check here prefers silence to a guess. A hierarchy that leaves the project, a name that two classes share, a namespace nobody in the project declares —
each is skipped, because a false error on working code costs more than a missed one.

Unknown property:

• The owner must be a project class: a qualified type, or a bare name that only one project class carries (usually an alias).

• The class and all of its superclasses must be in the project. A library base class may hold any property, so a chain that leaves the project proves nothing and is not checked. Enums, records, annotations and interfaces are not checked.

• A property is a property if a field, a getter or a setter has that name. For address.city or items[0] only the first segment is checked.

• An <association> without a javaType, a <collection> without an ofType, and anything under a <discriminator> or <case> are not checked: the class cannot be named for certain.

• A value written as an expression (#{…} or ${…}) is not checked.

Unresolved reference:

A bare value is looked for in this mapper first. A qualified one (com.acme.OtherMapper.columns) is looked for in the mapper files of that namespace.
The check stays quiet when the project has not yet indexed its mappers, when the namespace is declared by no indexed mapper (another module, a generated
file), and when a sibling file of the namespace cannot be read.

Duplicate id:

The second declaration is the one marked. Two statements with the same id are legitimate when their databaseId differs — one per
vendor — so the databaseId is part of the identity.

title: Missing class
text:
Only a qualified name is judged, in type, resultType, parameterType, javaType and ofType.
An alias (Order), a built-in (long, map), a library class, a typeHandler and a <cache type> are not.
Nested classes written with $ or . are accepted when the enclosing class exists.

Statement missing — on the interface:

// default and static methods are not mapped
@Select("SELECT 1")
int ping(); // the annotation is the statement
}`, 'java')}

MyBatis fails the first call of such a method with Invalid bound statement (not found). The error is drawn on the method name. A method is
answered by a statement of that id, or by one of @Select, @Insert, @Update, @Delete, their
*Provider forms, or @Flush. It applies only to an interface that

• some indexed mapper XML declares as its namespace — an interface with no XML may be annotation-only, or have its XML in a module the project has not opened;

• extends and implements nothing — a parent interface, or a generic base mapper supplied at run time, may bring methods and statements from elsewhere.

Statement unmapped — the reverse:

A statement no method maps is only a faint hint, because a legacy codebase calls statements by name (sqlSession.selectList("ns.findAll")), and a
statement reached that way is still reached. It is also what a renamed method leaves behind, which is why it is worth a quiet line. The same two conditions
apply: the namespace is a project interface, and that interface stands alone.

Database errors:

With a connection open in the Database panel, each statement is rendered to plain SQL and prepared on the server; a rejection is drawn on the
statement's opening tag as Database: …, because a position inside rendered SQL has no place in the XML. A statement that cannot be rendered into
something preparable — a ${…} with no value, a fragment of another mapper — is left alone rather than reported. Editing one statement
asks the server again about that one only. See Statements, parameters and result maps.

title: Silencing a check
text:
•
By kind: the project's inspection policy re-levels or turns off a check by its code, for every diagnostic alike — the six codes above included.

•
By place, in Java: a comment on the method's line or the line above it, or @SuppressWarnings on the declaration.

•
By place, in the mapper XML: there is no comment form. Fix the declaration, or turn the check down by kind.

• Database errors are asked only while a connection is open; they are the server's verdict on the SQL, not a Bennu inspection.

Bennu draws ${} in the warning colour, and a statement that uses one is unchecked against the database until you say what it stands for — but
no diagnostic is raised for the splice itself. It is often right, so the decision stays visible rather than flagged.

title: Dynamic SQL
text: MyBatis

title: Dynamic SQL
text:
The tags of a statement decide which pieces of the SQL exist at run time. Bennu draws them apart from the SQL they control, and — for the database check —
reads them as one possible expansion.

title: A dynamic statement
Colouring
text:
Piece — Drawn as

The name of if, choose, when, otherwise, where, set, trim, foreach, bind, include — A dynamic-tag colour, on the opening and the closing tag

test="…" on any of them — An expression (italic) — the OGNL condition

<bind value="…"> and <foreach collection="…"> — An expression, like a test

The SQL inside the tags, however deeply nested, and inside CDATA — SQL: keywords, functions, strings, numbers, comments

#{…} / ${…} inside them — A bound parameter / a splice, as anywhere else

The tags and their conditions therefore read as a layer over the statement, and the statement still reads as SQL. A test is only drawn:
its expression is not evaluated, completed or checked.

A word right after FROM, JOIN, INTO, UPDATE or TABLE, or after a ., is a name and
never a keyword — user, value and index are columns somewhere, and a perfectly good query must not read as broken.

title: How the database check reads them
text:
To check a dynamic statement against the database (see Statements, parameters and result maps), Bennu flattens the tags into a single
statement. The result is one expansion among many, which is why a rejected dynamic statement says Checked with every dynamic branch included.

Tag — Rendered as

<if> — Its body, always kept

<choose> — The body of the first <when>; the <otherwise> only if there is no <when> — the other branches would repeat the same clause

<where> — WHERE plus the body, with a leading AND or OR dropped (whole word only: android_id keeps its letters). Nothing at all if the body is empty

<set> — SET plus the body, with the trailing comma dropped. Nothing if empty

<trim> — The body with its prefixOverrides and suffixOverrides (separated by |) removed, wrapped in its prefix and suffix. Nothing if empty

<foreach> — Its body once, between open and close

<bind>, <selectKey> — Nothing

<include> — The fragment of this mapper, with the include's <property> values substituted for ${name} in it; a fragment of another mapper, or a missing one, leaves the statement unchecked

An include that includes itself is cut off after a few levels rather than looping. A ${name} that an include property filled in is
not a splice any more; one that stays is, and needs a value to be checked.

title: Not covered
text:
• No test condition, <bind> expression or foreach collection is validated — a misspelled parameter name in OGNL is not reported.

• <foreach> attributes (item, index) are not cross-checked against the #{} inside.

• Only the first <when> reaches the database, so a mistake confined to a later branch is not seen by the server check.

title: Statements, parameters and result maps
text: MyBatis

title: Statements, parameters and result maps
text:
A statement is SQL with holes in it. Bennu draws the holes apart from the SQL, links every name in a mapper to its declaration, and — with a database open —
asks the server whether the SQL is valid.

title: Parameters: #{} and ${}
text:
WHERE status = #{status}
AND customer LIKE '%\${customer}%'
`, 'markup')}

Written — Meaning — Drawn

#{status} — A bound parameter: the value travels separately from the SQL — As a parameter

${table} — Text pasted into the statement before it is prepared — In the warning colour, bold — also inside a string literal such as '%${customer}%'

Anything reaching ${} from outside becomes part of the SQL itself. It is the right tool for a table or a column chosen by the caller and
the wrong one for a value. Bennu draws it loudly for that reason; it does not report it as a problem — see Mapper checks.

title: Result maps
text:
The property is the Java side and is coloured as a member; the column stays plain. The class a property belongs to is the
nearest enclosing container: the <resultMap type>, an <association javaType>, or a
<collection ofType>. Ctrl+B on a property lands on the field, else the setter or getter.

A property path such as address.city is judged by its first segment. A <discriminator> or <case> has a result
type of its own, and an <association> without a javaType infers it from the owner — so the properties nested in them are never
judged against the outer class.

title: Fragments
text:
.id, \${alias}.customer

SELECT
FROM orders o
`, 'markup')}

<sql id> and <resultMap id> are declarations, drawn in bold; refid, resultMap, select and
extends are references — what Ctrl+B follows. Alt+F7 on either lists every reference
across the project's mappers. A reference with a dot is read as namespace.id; a bare one belongs to this mapper's namespace, and may be declared in
a sibling file of the same namespace.

The attributes that name a Java type — parameterType, resultType, type, javaType, ofType,
typeHandler and the mapper namespace — are coloured as types and followed to the class, including the class of a type handler.

title: Completion in a mapper
text:
Inside the text of a statement — between its tags, not in an attribute, not inside a #{…} or ${…} — the
editor completes tables after FROM, JOIN, INTO, UPDATE and TABLE,
and columns after alias. or, elsewhere, those of the tables the statement already names. Dynamic tags are looked through: what
they wrap is still SQL, and the statement is the nearest enclosing select, insert, update, delete or
sql.

The names come from the database connection chosen in the Database panel, so this works only while that connection is open. Without one — or
anywhere outside a statement's text — the caret gets the ordinary XML completion.

title: Checking statements against the database
text:
With a connection open, the Database panel has a MyBatis tab (it appears only when the project has mapper statements) listing every statement.
Each is rendered to plain SQL and prepared on the server, so a missing table or column, or a join on nothing, comes back as the server's own message.
Validate all runs the lot; the check button on a row runs one, and the row name opens the statement.

The same check runs in the mapper editor while you type: the server's message is a red squiggle on the statement's opening tag, prefixed Database:.

How a statement is rendered:

A database understands none of MyBatis's templating, so the rendering is one possible expansion of the statement — an approximation, and the panel says so:

In the mapper — Becomes

#{…} — NULL — any type accepts it when a statement is only being prepared

Dynamic tags — Expanded with every branch kept; see Dynamic SQL. A rejected dynamic statement is annotated Checked with every dynamic branch included

<include> of a fragment of the same mapper — The fragment, with the include's <property> values filled in

${name} with a value you gave — That value, as text

${name} with no value — The statement is unchecked, naming the splice that needs a value

<include> of a fragment of another mapper, or of a fragment that does not exist — The statement is unchecked

An unchecked statement says why instead of showing a clean result it did not earn, and the editor shows nothing for it. A statement with a
databaseId is checked only against a connection of the matching engine.

title: Giving ${} a value
text:
Above the list, the tab collects every ${name} the mappers splice, once each, with a field to say what it stands for — a table name,
a column list. A value is stored per project and every statement using that name is rendered again with it.

The server is asked to prepare the rendered SQL, which parses and resolves its names. The statement is not executed.

title: Navigation
text: Editor

title: Navigation
text:
Getting to the thing you are thinking of, from wherever you are. Everything here works from the keyboard, and everything
answers from the index rather than from the open tabs — so it finds what you have never opened.

title: Find
text:
Ctrl+F searches the current file. Ctrl+Shift+F opens
Find in project: a search across the whole project, with Match case, Whole
word and Regex beside the field — and on a workspace a fourth toggle reaching every project of it.
Hits are grouped by file with the match highlighted, and stream in as the scan finds them, so a large project fills the list
rather than making you wait.

The selected hit is shown in context beside the list — the lines around it, match highlighted — which is what
tells four identical-looking lines apart without opening four files. ↑/↓ move and the preview follows;
Enter opens. A word selected in the editor pre-fills the field, here and in find-in-file.

The header row decides what is searched:

Source
Project, Project & dependencies or Dependencies — whose text is read.
Module
On a multi-module build, one module.
File mask
*.java, or several at once as *.jsp, *.tag.

Module and mask filter what came back rather than what is scanned, so changing either re-lists instantly without searching again,
and both are remembered per project. The count between them says how many matches survived.

Reading the jars' XML, schemas, tag libraries and property files is how you find which artifact declares the interceptor or the
bean you are looking at. Those hits are tinted, named by their artifact, arrive after the
project's own, and open read-only. It is chosen per search rather than as a setting, because every candidate entry has to be
decompressed to be read — a cost you take for the question you are asking now.

title: Back, forward, and where you have been
text:
Shortcut — Goes

Ctrl+Alt+← — Back to where you jumped from

Ctrl+Alt+→ — Forward again

Ctrl+Shift+Backspace — Back to where you were typing; again for the edit before

Ctrl+Shift+E — Recent locations, as a list

A stop is recorded when an action navigates — a go-to, a usage, a structure or find hit, a diagnostic, a file
opened from the tree or the palette, a switch to another tab — and never when the caret merely moves. Arrow keys, a click,
page-down and scrolling are reading. What a navigation records is where you were when it started, down to the
column, so Back lands exactly where you left; Forward returns to where you were when you pressed Back, including anywhere you
read on to after arriving. Opening a file and landing on a line in it is one step, two places on the same line are one stop,
and navigating after a Back starts a new branch the way a browser does.

It belongs to the window, not to one project: switching to another project of the workspace keeps it, and Back (or Forward,
or a row of Recent locations) into a file of a project you left switches to that project first. It is not saved — closing
Arbor starts a new one — and the stops of a project that is no longer open are dropped.

Typing above a remembered place moves it with the text, so Back still lands on the same code after lines are added or removed
above it. A file that can no longer be opened is dropped from the history instead of stopping it.

Typing has its own history, because "where was I reading" and "where was I editing" are different questions.

Recent locations shows the history most recent first, each row with the line you were on. Type to filter by file
name or by the text of the line, ↑/↓ to move, Enter to go. Edited only keeps the
places you changed — how you find the file you were working on before the interruption, instead of pressing Back five times.

title: Go to line
text: Ctrl+G — type 42, or 42:8 for line and column, and press Enter.

title: Go to declaration
text:
Ctrl+B, Ctrl+click, or the right-click menu. Where it lands depends on what the caret is on:

The caret on — Lands on

A Java class, method, field or local — Its declaration

helper in Reports::helper, run in this::run — The method — a method reference is a use of it

Reports in Reports::helper — The type

A call to an overloaded method — uri(b -> …), uri(someUri) — The overload the call binds to, in project code and in a library view alike: a lambda or method reference picks the one taking a matching functional interface, and null, literals and typed arguments pick by type. The hover card describes the same overload, with that overload's own Javadoc — from project source or a library's downloaded sources. When the arguments cannot settle it, the first declaration

A declaration itself — a signature, a variable, class or record declaration — Its usages, since jumping there would go nowhere

A JSP action reference — action="…", /do/Category/viewTree — Where the action is declared: the Struts config fragment, or its view JSP; for one that only resolves to a class, the class name is shown

A Struts <result> JSP path, /WEB-INF/x.jsp — That JSP

A Struts OGNL or EL result, ${urlErrori} — The action's property

A library or JDK method — list.add(…), LOGGER.info(…), String::valueOf — That library's source view, on the method itself

A library or JDK type with no source — A decompiled stub

It answers from the project index and the configuration graph, so it works once the index is warm and stays quiet when a symbol
cannot be resolved. In a Struts config, a JSP path that does not exist under the web app, or an OGNL root that is not a property of
the action, is flagged with a warning.

A library method's receiver is typed against the project's classpath, so it works on anything your dependencies resolve to, and it
chains: from inside one library view you can go on to the next — including a view you opened by hand (Go to Class, the hierarchy, a tab restored
from the last session), a bare call or field of the class you are reading, and a member the receiver inherits, which lands where it is declared
(list.stream() opens Collection.stream).

Generated from the bytecode: the type declaration and every field and method signature, with a header saying it is decompiled —
method bodies are not stored in a class file. It is cached, read-only, and not validated, since without bodies validation would
only report noise.

title: Go to implementation
text:
Ctrl+Shift+B on an interface or abstract class lists every type built on it, at any depth; on a
method it lists the subtypes that declare it themselves. One result jumps straight there, several open a popover. On a MyBatis
mapper method the XML statement is listed too.

title: Find usages
text:
Alt+F7 on a class, method or field lists every place it is used across the project, in a popover — pick one to
jump there. It answers once the index is warm.

A field counts every read of it, with or without a receiver:

void setCount(int count) { // the parameter, not the field
this.count = count; // a use of the field
}
}`, 'java')}

this.count, other.count, Config.MAX and the bare count meaning
this.count are the same field — and that bare shape is the usual one, often the only one for a
static final constant. A local or parameter of the same name is that variable, not the field it hides. A declaration
is never a use of itself.

In a .svelte file, Alt+Shift+F7 lists the usages of the component
itself — its imports and <Foo /> tags. The file is the component, so there is no name inside it to put
a caret on.

title: Usage counts, and what nothing reaches
text:
Above a class, method or field, a line says how many places use it. It reads the same whole-project index as find usages, so it
counts uses in files you have never opened, and pressing the line opens the list it counted. Turn it off in
Settings → Editor → Usage counts.

A declaration nothing reaches has its name drawn faint — a claim deliberately harder to earn than a count of zero,
because a name faded wrongly invites deleting working code. Zero uses is a fact about the index; unused is a fact about the program.
So a declaration is one of three things:

Count shown · faded at zero

Nothing outside the code reaches it

The count is the whole story. This is the case the feature exists for.

Count shown · never faded

Something might

It carries an annotation the engine does not recognise — @Deprecated, one of your own — so no claim is safe. A deprecated method nobody calls is exactly what you were looking for.

Nothing drawn at zero

Something does, by design

A @Test run by JUnit, a @Bean built by Spring, a @GetMapping the dispatcher calls, a @PrePersist, main, an override. A row saying "no usages" above every test method is true and useless.

The last kind still shows a count when there is one: a @Bean method called from another @Bean
method is an ordinary call, and the number is worth having. Silence is only ever for a zero.

A type whose members a framework calls is one itself — which is how a test class goes quiet without anybody guessing
from its name. A class holding @Test methods is one JUnit instantiates; the same covers a configuration full of
@Bean factories and a controller full of mappings. A TestUtils with no test in it is an ordinary class.

A constructor gets no count at all: its callers are new expressions, which the index keys by the type.

What is faded — a plain declaration, no annotation, no supertype, nothing calling it — is exactly what Safe delete would
agree to remove. One question, asked once, so the colour and the refactoring cannot disagree.

title: Call and type hierarchy
text:
Shortcut — Opens

Ctrl+Shift+H — The callers of the method at the caret

Ctrl+H — The type hierarchy of the class you are in, the caret anywhere inside it

Both land in the Hierarchy panel at the bottom, whose direction chip walks the other way — callees, or what a type is built on. The
tree expands a level at a time, so a recursive chain is walked as far as you care to.

It is the index find usages reads, which is why the two agree — and why the callers of a method declared on an
interface include the ones written against an implementation, and the other way round: the family a rename carries.
A caller row jumps to the call, not to the head of the method containing it, and says 2× when there is more than
one. A call in a field initialiser or a static block is filed under its class, as a leaf.

Calls into a dependency are not there: the index records an edge only when the callee is the project's own code.
And overloads collapse — process(String) and process(int) are one row, because the index
keys a method by name. A supertype from a jar does appear in a type hierarchy and can be expanded upward, but has no source to jump to.

title: Hover
text:
Rest the pointer on a class, method or field for a card saying what it is — a tag: class, interface, enum, method, field, variable — its
signature, and the type that declares it, which is the supertype for an inherited member. It answers from the index, once warm.

The top

The signature, the package, and for a type out of a jar the dependency as groupId:artifactId:version.
The package says which type; the coordinate says whose — on a long classpath the question actually asked. These stay
put while a long card scrolls; move the pointer onto the card to scroll it.

The documentation
From your own source, or from the library's -sources.jar or the JDK's src.zip when on disk. A dependency without downloaded sources shows the signature alone — a .class carries no comments — until Download sources on its decompiled view.
The signature
Written as Java and coloured like it, generics and throws included: <X extends Throwable> T orElseThrow(Supplier<? extends X>) throws X.
A long one breaks after each parameter, one per line. In the line of the package, the package itself is muted and the type name is the
part that stands out.

A Javadoc is rendered, not printed:

A doc comment is HTML — that is what the language says it is — so its headings are headings, its <pre> examples
are code blocks that scroll sideways rather than wrap, its lists are lists, and @ is an @.

• {@link …} reads as the member it points at, {@code …} as code.

• @param, @return and @throws are lifted into a labelled list; @deprecated is
highlighted, since it changes what you do next. An @Override inside an example stays in the example.

• Angle brackets that are not markup are left alone: Vec<T> and Map<K, V> are type parameters.

• Code blocks are coloured with the grammars a fenced block in a rendered .md gets: Java for a Javadoc,
the file's language for what a language server documents.

title: Variables, and JSP
text:
Hovering a variable — a local, a parameter, a loop variable, a catch parameter, a pattern variable —
is tagged variable and names its type and the fully-qualified type under it (which of the four
Orders this one is). A var or a Lombok val never shows as
var: the card shows the type the compiler deduced, including the element type in for (val row : rows).

In a JSP, hovering a form field, an OGNL reference or a *-validation.xml <field> shows the
type of the matching property on the bound action class, with the action it belongs to.

title: New Project
text: Projects

title: New Project
text:
The New Project wizard creates a project on disk from a generator: you pick a project type,
give it a name and a folder, adjust its options, and Bennu opens the result. It is reached from the palette
(New Project…), from Ctrl+Shift+P, from the main menu, and from
the empty Project panel when nothing is open.

title: The common case
text:
• Pick a project type on the left — the arrow keys move through the list and the form follows.

• Type a Name. The Location is the one you used last time.

• Press Ctrl+Enter.

Everything else — the Java level, the group, the edition, Git — starts at a sensible default, and the
choices you make are remembered for the next project.

title: Project types
text:
Java

Spring, Quarkus, Maven, Gradle, web apps

Spring Initializr and Quarkus are downloaded from their own services, with
the Boot version, language, packaging and a searchable list of dependencies or extensions.
Maven and Gradle (Kotlin or Groovy DSL) are written locally with source
folders, an optional sample class and JUnit 5. Servlet + JSP writes a WAR with a
web.xml, a JSP using JSTL and a servlet, for javax (Tomcat 9) or
jakarta (Tomcat 10.1+); Struts 1 writes the legacy Struts 1.3 layout.

Rust

Binary, library, workspace, Bevy, CLI, web, WASM

All written locally, so Cargo is not needed to create them. Bevy offers the releases
crates.io knows, with a camera, a sprite, a component, a system and a plugin, the dev profile Bevy
projects use, an assets/ folder, an optional dev feature for dynamic linking
and an optional RON settings file. CLI uses clap, Web service axum and
tokio, WASM wasm-bindgen with a page that loads it.

Node

Vite, Angular, SvelteKit, Vue, Next.js, plain package

The framework generators run the official scaffolding tool (create-vite, the Angular CLI,
sv create, create-vue, create-next-app) with the options you chose
as flags, choosing npm, pnpm or Yarn. The tool's output streams into the wizard. A plain
package is written locally, JavaScript or TypeScript, ES modules or CommonJS.

title: Name, location and the destination
text:
The line under the two fields always says what will happen: that the folder will be created (and which
parent folders with it), that an existing empty folder will be used, or why the location can't be
used. The name is checked against the rules of the project type — a Cargo package name, a Maven artifact id,
an npm package name.

If the folder exists and has anything in it, the wizard asks for a different name. There is no override.

title: Git
text:
Create Git repository runs git init in the new project and adds a .gitignore
suited to the project type. It is disabled when git isn't on the PATH.

title: Tools that must be installed
text:
The footer shows which of git, Node, npm, Cargo, Java and Maven were found. A generator that needs a tool
that is missing — the Node scaffolders need node, npm and npx — is shown
dimmed with the reason, and can't be created until it is installed and Bennu is restarted. Locally written
projects never need a tool to be created, only to be built.

title: What leaves your machine
text:
Only four kinds of request exist, to fixed hosts: the Spring options and download from
start.spring.io, the Quarkus extension list and download from code.quarkus.io, the Bevy
release list from the crates.io index (the same switch as the other Cargo tools), and
whatever the Node scaffolders themselves fetch from the npm registry. If a service can't be reached the form
says so and offers Try again; the option lists last seen are shown meanwhile, marked as such.

title: Creating, cancelling, failing
text:
The project is built in a scratch folder next to the destination and moved into place in one step when it is
complete. A downloaded archive is unpacked with limits on the number and size of the files and is rejected if
any entry would land outside the project. If anything fails — or you cancel, which also stops the scaffolding
tool and everything it started — the scratch folder and any parent folders the run created are removed, and
the wizard returns to the form with everything you typed.

When it succeeds the project opens (added to the current workspace, or instead of it — your choice when a
project is already open) with its README or main file. A step that is allowed to fail without undoing the
project, such as installing dependencies, is reported as a warning.

title: Keyboard
text:
Shortcut — Does

Ctrl+Shift+P — Opens the wizard

↑ / ↓ in the type list — Selects the previous / next project type; Enter or → moves into the form

Ctrl+↑ / ↓ — Switches the project type from anywhere in the form

Enter in Name or Location — Creates the project

Ctrl+Enter — Creates the project from anywhere

In a dependency or extension list — Type to filter; ↑ / ↓ move, Enter ticks, Backspace on an empty filter removes the last choice, Esc clears the filter

Esc — Closes the wizard; during a run it cancels it

title: Patina (Voriz mods)
text: Rust

title: Patina (Voriz mods)
text:
.ptn files are mod scripts for Voriz, written in Patina. Bennu colours them itself; everything that needs to understand the
language — completion, hover, go-to, find usages, rename, diagnostics — comes from a language extension, a wasm package
that implements the language-intel interface.

title: What you get
text:
Highlighting
Local and instant, from the shape of the text: calls and method calls, fields, associated functions (BlockPos::new, in
italic like a static), variants and constants (Mood::Calm, Some, POWER), declarations, module
paths, primitive types (int, fx, f32, bool, str) in a colour of their own, apart from keywords and other types, named arguments, #[attributes], block!(…) forms, labels, numbers with their suffixes and durations.
Brackets are coloured by depth and blocks fold by their braces. It never claims to know which names exist, so it cannot go out of
date — telling a parameter from a local, or a mut binding, would need the backend. In Markdown, a fenced block tagged
ptn or patina (any case, extra words after the tag allowed) is coloured the same way, in both the rendered and the source view.
Completion and hover
After a dot, the fields and methods of the receiver's type, with its generics filled in; after ::, variants and associated items;
inside a call, the parameters by name. A name the file does not import yet is offered with the use line it needs. Hover shows the
declaration as written, with the attributes that matter (#[context(server)], #[capability("world.write")]), and the
inferred type of a local.
Go-to, find usages, rename
Across the whole mod. A rename lists every edit with the text it expects to find, and refuses names from a library.
Diagnostics
Syntax, names, types, contexts (#[server], #[client], #[worldgen]), the capabilities the mod's
manifest.ron declares, exhaustive match, writes to what is not mut.

title: What a request carries
text:
Every request carries the mod, so the answer never depends on what the extension remembers. The Patina package is
persistent: Arbor keeps one instance of it alive, and it keeps the mod's index between questions, re-reading only the
files whose text changed — about a millisecond per question instead of rebuilding the mod. A request carries the
nearest folder above the file with a manifest.ron whose script/ holds the file, that manifest, and every
.ptn under script/ as it is on disk — with the editor's buffer standing in for the file you are typing in. Without a
manifest, the file's own folder is the mod.

Only the file you are asking about travels with its unsaved text. A change in another open .ptn that is not saved yet is not seen by
the question until you save it.

title: UI ids and translations
text:
Inside ui!("barra", "matassa-1") and t!("ui:avvio.solo") Patina checks the id or the key, offers the known ones as you type,
and gives the UI nodes as typed constants (ui::barra::MATASSA_1). What it checks against is read by the package itself, in two layers:

The base game
The UI node catalog and the translations of the base Voriz project, embedded in the package: each version of the plugin knows the game it
was built for, and does not need to find it on your disk.
The open mod
Its own documents (presentazione/hud/**/*.ron) and translations (presentazione/i18n/«lang»/**/*.toml and .md), read through
Arbor's read-only fs interface. A mod's node scopes begin with the mod's id (ui!("my_mod/hud", "kills")). On a collision the
mod wins. Only changed files are re-read.

The package declares fs = "read", so Arbor asks for it when you install or update it, and the mod has to be inside the repository open in Arbor. If the
permission is declined — or the mod is somewhere else — Patina keeps working and checks no ids and no text keys, instead of reporting every
one as unknown. The mods this one depends on are found the same way (see Dependencies below), so what they export is known too.

title: Dependencies
text:
The manifest says what the mod needs (dependencies: [(id: "marmo")]), not where it is. The package finds each one by id,
with the same read-only fs interface: it looks in the folders next to the mod and in a dlc/ or plugins/ folder next to
the project (and, for a mod that lives inside such a folder, one level up). A folder is a mod if it has a manifest.ron, and its id is the manifest's — the folder's name does not matter.
It reads that mod's script/**/*.ptn, and its own dependencies in turn. The libraries built into the package (voriz, patina) are not searched for.

The same lookup feeds the editor: with a dependency found, use marmo::Gem resolves, diagnostics see the dependency's lib.ptn, and go-to-definition lands in its file.
The lookup happens when the session for the mod is built (opening the mod, changing its manifest), not on every keystroke, so a change to a dependency's files shows up the next time the session is rebuilt.

The host lets the package read only the repository open in Arbor and the paths in fs_scope. A dependency that lives outside is reported as
cannot be read by the plugin, not as missing — open the folder that contains both, or add it to fs_scope.

title: Build
text:
Build runs the real Patina compiler on the whole mod and shows what it says. Nothing is written: a mod is compiled from its sources at every load,
and there is no bytecode cache, so a build is a full compile whose result is the report. Dependencies are needed at run time and are not embedded.

Where
With a .ptn file active: Ctrl+F9, the title bar's Build button (it reads Build Patina mod), or Build Patina mod in the command palette. Opening the mod
folder itself as the project makes the ordinary Build do the same. The output goes to the Build panel, whose problems are clickable and marked in the editor.
What it reports
The checker's diagnostics (errors and warnings) and the compiler's, each with file, line and column; the counts (files, functions, entries, schemas) and the time; the
#[state], #[event] and #[intent] schemas; the capabilities the mod really uses and the host functions it imports; the dependencies that were found.
Full compile
A construct the compiler cannot lower yet is an error named after the construct (compile.unsupported), because that is what the game would do with it.
If the checker finds errors the compiler does not run (the game refuses a mod that does not check), and the report says so.
Missing dependency
A dependency that is not found is an error entry (dependency `marmo` not found) and the build stops there.

Like a question to the language extension, a build sees other files as they are saved. Save before building.

The package has to export build (an optional function of language-intel). With an older one the build answers This Patina backend has no build and
everything else keeps working; rebuild and reinstall the package.

title: Installing the extension
text:
The package declares [[provides]] interface = "language-intel" with id = "ptn": the id is the extension
it serves. A debug build of Arbor finds packages in the repository's plugins/ folder; an installed one in the profile's plugin folder.

No completion, no hover, no diagnostics — and no errors either. A .ptn is never handed to the Java engine, which would read it as Java and
answer confidently about the wrong language.

title: Editing a pom.xml
text: Projects

title: Editing a pom.xml
text:
A pom is the one file in a Java project whose correctness is a fact about your machine. Bennu reads your local
repository and answers from it — completing coordinates that are actually there, and marking the ones that are not.

title: Colour
text:
An XML mode has one colour for tag names and none for the text between them, and a pom is almost nothing but text
between tags. Here it is coloured by what each thing is:

• Namesan artifactId, a module

• Literalsa version

• Fixed wordsa scope, a packaging, a lifecycle phase

• Propertiesone colour where a property is declared and where it is used

Nothing is ever dimmed. The tags of each top-level block take that block's own hue, so the file can be scrolled by its
shape: <dependencies>, <dependencyManagement>, <build>,
<properties>, <profiles>, the repositories, and the other projects
(<parent>, <modules>) are each a different colour, and the closing tag matches its opening
one. The project's own coordinates keep the ordinary tag colour.

`, 'markup')}

${spring.version} is tinted as a substitution, its name in the colour a property has everywhere
else. The only mistake possible there is the two ends not matching, and one colour is what makes that visible.

title: The local repository
text:
Every answer on this page comes from the repository your build would use — not ~/.m2/repository assumed, but
found the way Maven finds it:

• -Dmaven.repo.local in MAVEN_OPTS.

• <localRepository> in your settings.xml.

• The default.

Dependencies reports which repository is in use — the first thing to check on a machine that builds fine
from a terminal.

It is walked once into a list of coordinates and cached, so completion is instant. The walk runs in the background the first
time a Maven project is opened; until it lands, completion is thinner and nothing is marked as missing — an empty
answer means "not read yet", never "you do not have it".

title: Completion
text:
Coordinates

<groupId> and <artifactId>

Every coordinate in your repository, each with its newest installed version, then a built-in table of the libraries a Java
project usually reaches for, marked not installed. Completing an artifactId while the groupId above it is empty
fills both in one edit.

Versions

<version>

The versions you have, newest first. One a <dependencyManagement> entry supplies comes first and says
which pom decided it; a ${…} property already holding a version of that library is offered too —
usually what the line should have said.

Anywhere a ${ is typed

${properties}

Every property in scope — this pom's, its parents', the implicit project.* ones — each with the value it expands
to and, when decided elsewhere, the pom that decided it. This pom's first, then the inherited, then the implicit ones.

Fixed vocabularies

Scopes, types, phases, modules

<scope>, <type>, <packaging>, <optional> and an
execution's <phase>, each with what it means. <module> completes the directories beside
the pom that hold one and are not listed yet.

title: What gets marked
text:
A dependency whose jar is not in the repository is underlined where it is written. That is the point of the
whole feature: an artifact that was never downloaded makes every type in it unresolvable at once, in files that are perfectly
correct — and without this, the pom says nothing about it.

Marked — What it means

Not in the local repository — Nothing has ever downloaded this coordinate. When a near-identical artifactId is installed, it is suggested.

Version not installed — The artifact is there at other versions — which are listed, so a mistyped version is obvious.

Undefined ${property} — Nothing in this pom or its parents defines it. In a coordinate that is an error — Maven resolves it to the literal text and then finds no artifact by that name. Elsewhere it is a warning, because a plugin may supply the value during the build; inside a <configuration>, where those live, nothing is reported.

No version — Declared with no version, and nothing in management supplies one.

Version already managed — Identical to what a parent's <dependencyManagement> says — harmless, but it will not follow when the parent moves.

Declared twice — The same artifact twice in one block. Maven keeps the last, silently.

Not a Maven scope — A misspelled <scope> is treated as compile without a word.

Missing module — A <module> with no pom.xml — the reactor drops it, and every type in it stops resolving everywhere else.

Nothing is marked before the repository has been read. A module of your own project is built from source and never looked
for in a repository. A <dependencyManagement> entry names a version for something this module may not
even use, so its absence is not a problem. And a plugin, or a dependency that only exists under a <profile>,
is a warning rather than an error — neither is necessarily fetched on a machine that has not run it.

title: Versions, navigation and vulnerabilities
text:
Ctrl+B and hover on a coordinate or a ${property}, a dependency's own pom,
scopes, exclusions and the newer-version offers are covered in Dependency versions. The one check that
sends your coordinates to a third party, the known-vulnerability warning, is covered in Dependency security.

title: When something is missing
text:
Nothing on this page downloads anything — that is what makes it instant, and what makes it work with no network.
Download dependencies is the deliberate action that does: it runs Maven's dependency:go-offline
for the project as a background job, and rebuilds the index when it finishes so library types resolve. It is the fix for a pom
that is right on a machine that simply does not have the jar yet.

title: Profiler
text: Build, run & test

title: Profiler
text:
Where does the time go, and what allocates? The profiler records a run, folds the samples into a call tree and shows it as a flame graph, a table of hot methods,
allocations, garbage-collection pauses and lock waits. The same numbers are written in the editor, on the method they belong to.

title: Opening it
text:
Ctrl+Shift+F9, the flame button on the right rail, or Toggle Profiler in the command palette (a finished recording opens it by itself). Recordings are kept per
project, newest first (the last twenty), and survive restarting Bennu.

title: Recording
text:
The gauge button beside the bug (Shift+F11, Profile in the palette and the ⋮ menu) records the run configuration selected in the title bar: an Application or Spring Boot one under
JDK Flight Recorder, a Cargo one that runs a binary (cargo run) under samply. While it records, the button is Stop. A script, a JUnit run or a cargo check configuration has no
program to look inside, so the button is dimmed — still clickable, because its tooltip and a toast say why. Profile a command or running JVM… (the ⋮ menu, the palette, or Profile… in
the panel) opens a dialog for everything else: a Node or native command, a JVM that is already running, and the samply tool. The panel itself only reads recordings and shows a recording in progress.

Java

Recording the application or Spring Boot configuration selected in the title bar runs it under JDK Flight Recorder, in the Run console like any other run, and reads
the recording when the program exits. Stop and read takes the recording from the live JVM and then ends the run. Attach (in the Profile… dialog) records inside a JVM that is
already running (listed from jcmd); it needs a JDK with jcmd, and the target must run as you.

Node

In the Profile… dialog, give a command (node server.js, npm run dev, an Angular or Vite dev server). It runs with NODE_OPTIONS=--cpu-prof, so every Node process it
starts writes a .cpuprofile when it exits — stop a dev server with its own shutdown (Ctrl+C in the console). Killing it leaves no profile. Frames are reported at
the file V8 ran; source maps are not applied, so a bundled application shows its bundle.

Rust

A Cargo run configuration is built first and its binary — not cargo — is what samply records. A command can also be given in the Profile… dialog. Uses samply. Bennu picks the first one it finds, in this order: the executable you chose in the panel,
the copy Bennu downloaded, then samply on PATH. The panel shows which one is in use and its version. The command is wrapped in
samply record --save-only. Build with debug info ([profile.release] debug = true); without it frames are raw addresses and the recording says so.

Getting samply

On the Rust tab of the Profile… dialog, Choose… picks an executable you already have; Bennu runs samply --version on it and shows the version it found. Download samply fetches the latest official release
(github.com/mstange/samply) for your operating system and CPU, after showing the version, file, size and source. The download is checked against the SHA-256 published with the release; if none can be
obtained, Bennu says so and installs only if you tick the explicit confirmation. The copy goes into Bennu's data folder and can be updated or removed from the same row. On macOS and Linux unpacking the
.tar.xz uses the system tar (with xz support); on Windows the .zip is unpacked by Bennu. A path you chose always wins over the downloaded copy, and a chosen path that no longer exists is reported rather than skipped.

Import
The upload button reads a .jfr, a .cpuprofile or a samply profile (.json or gzip-compressed .json.gz) made elsewhere. Compressed files are recognised by content, and a profile that
expands past 512 MB is refused.

title: Which JDKs can be recorded
text:
Bennu checks the project's JDK before recording and, when it cannot, says why and what to do — it never fails silently.

JDK — Recording — Reading the file

12 and newer — yes — the JDK's own jfr tool

11 — yes — jfr of another installed JDK 12+, otherwise a built-in reader run with java

8u262 and newer — yes — a built-in reader compiled with javac (a JRE alone cannot)

8 before 8u262 — no — Oracle's older builds need a commercial license flag, which Bennu does not enable; update the JDK

9, 10 — no — Flight Recorder was open-sourced in 11

OpenJ9, IBM Semeru — no — they have no Flight Recorder; use a HotSpot JDK (Temurin, Corretto, Zulu, Oracle)

jlink image without jdk.jfr — no — rebuild it with --add-modules jdk.jfr

title: Reading a recording
text:
Flame graph

Width is share of the weight. Click a box to open its source; double-click or Enter zooms; Backspace zooms out; arrows move between boxes; the search dims what does not
match; the thread picker narrows to one thread. Hover a box for its tooltip — it follows the pointer when the graph is scrolled. What the boxes weigh is a choice:
CPU (where Java code is running), Waiting (time blocked off the CPU — a query waiting for the database is here, and nowhere in the CPU graph) or
Allocations (bytes, by who asked for them). With Heat on, a CPU box is coloured by the share of the run it spent itself and everything unremarkable is grey; off, boxes take a colour
per package. The class filter takes the other frames out of every stack, so with it.acme.* the graph is your code only; the root keeps the whole recording and says how much the filter hides.

Hot methods
Self time (in the method itself) and total time (with its callees), the hottest source lines of each, and the method's package. Self time is drawn as a bar and coloured by its level; the bars are scaled to the hottest
method on screen. Enter opens the source. A recursive method is counted once per call path.
Memory

From your code answers which of your methods allocates: JFR reports an allocation at the code that performed it (Arrays.copyOf), so the allocation's whole stack is walked up to the
nearest frame of the project and the bytes are credited there — Service.load allocated 30 MB, mostly byte[]. A click opens the method. Allocated types and
Allocation sites are the raw views, each row with its share of everything allocated; GC pauses shows each collector with the share of the run it stopped the program. These are samples, not
an exact count — a large number of small allocations is under-represented. A recording made before allocation stacks were kept can show types and sites only.

Waits

I/O and parks is time blocked off the CPU: waiting on a socket (the database), a file, a pooled connection. Each row names what was waited on (db.internal:5432), the method that waited longest and the
total, coloured by its level. Lock contention is the monitors threads queued for. JFR reports socket, file and park waits of 10 ms or more (1 ms or more with a shorter sampling interval on JDK 17+) and lock waits over 20 ms.

Compare
Against an earlier recording of the same language, by change in each method's share of the run (percentage points), so recordings of different lengths compare fairly.

title: Filtering and colours
text:
Every tab starts with a search over its names, a Packages field and a My code switch. My code hides the JDK and the libraries, using the classes the project index knows.
The field is typed by hand, like a search: it.acme.*, !*.generated.*. A name without a wildcard covers everything inside it (it.acme covers it.acme.web but not it.acmeco); * matches
any run of characters and ? one, so *.service.* is any class in a service package and *Dao any class ending in Dao; a leading ! hides instead of keeps. Separate patterns
with commas or spaces. While you type, the grey text after the caret is the longest package every candidate agrees on — taken from the project's own packages, never guessed — and Tab (or →) takes it. The filter applies as you
type. In the tables the rows are hidden and shares stay relative to the whole recording. The filter is remembered per project; the search is not.
