Yellow, orange and red mark readings that deserve a look: a method's self time, a type's share of allocations, a collector's pause share, time blocked on a target, and an increase in Compare.
A key beside each table says where each colour starts. The sliders button in the panel header edits those values — one scale per kind of reading, since their units differ. They are saved with the project in
.arbor/bennu/config.toml ([profiler]), together with the class filter, so a team shares one idea of "hot".

Ctrl+F inside the panel focuses the search. From the command palette: Profiler: filter by name, Profiler: only this project's classes (and show all classes),
Profiler: clear the class filter, Profiler: colour thresholds… and Profiler: show / hide the numbers in the editor.

title: Numbers in the editor
text:
After a recording, every method carries a mark after its signature: what it earned — 38% CPU · 120 ms self · 4.2 MB alloc (byte[]) · 1.2 s waiting on db.internal:5432 — or not sampled in grey when the
recording never caught it. That is not the same as fast: the CPU sampler takes a stack every ~10 ms of the threads that are running, so a method shorter than that, one that did not run in the recording, or one whose whole cost is waiting
for the database leaves no CPU sample. Its wait shows up as waiting (and in the Waits tab) when it lasted 10 ms or more.

A line that stands out — on CPU, on allocation or on waiting — is labelled in place, on the line that causes it (12% CPU · 4.2 MB alloc · 1.2 s wait; allocation and wait include what the line calls), and a gutter bar
marks the others. Both are coloured on the same yellow / orange / red scale as the tables, by the worst of the three, and grey while nothing stands out; changing the thresholds redraws them. An allocation is credited to the nearest
method of your project, not to the JDK code that performed it. Hover for the details. Matching is by qualified name from the current text of the file, so the marks follow the code while you edit; if the file changed after the recording they
are drawn dimmed and labelled stale. The eye button in the panel header, Profiler: show / hide the numbers in the editor in the palette, or Settings › Editor › Profiler hints turns them on and off.

title: Sampling interval
text:
The Profile… dialog sets the CPU sampler's interval for the next Java recording: 10 ms (the default), 5, 2 or 1 ms. A shorter interval catches shorter methods and also reports shorter waits on sockets and files, at the cost of
more overhead. It needs JDK 17 or newer; on an older one the recording keeps 10 ms. A launched JVM also records stacks up to 256 frames deep (JFR's default is 64, which a Spring request outgrows, leaving the allocation or the wait with no project
frame to be credited to); attaching to a running JVM cannot change that depth.

Samples are statistical: a method that ran for a few milliseconds may not appear, and a short recording is noisy. Record a representative scenario for at least a few seconds.

title: For Imber
text: Imber, the assistant, can read the newest recording (hottest methods, allocation sites, lock waits, GC) to propose a change. It only reads; it never starts a recording. See the page Imber: Bevy games and the profiler.

title: What is not claimed
text:
• Bennu downloads samply on request, but does not install Node or a JDK for you.

• Native frames inside the JVM (garbage collector threads, JIT) are not sampled by Flight Recorder's Java sampler.

• Source maps (Node) and inlined frames (Rust) are shown as the runtime reports them.

title: The project tree
text: Projects

title: The project tree
text:
The left rail's file tree: what its icons and its dimming are telling you, and everything you can do to a file without
leaving it.

title: Reading the tree
text:
A folder holding pom.xml or Cargo.toml

A package icon

That is where a build target is declared, so it is drawn as a package rather than a folder.

Main, test, resources, webapp

Tinted source roots

Each source root is tinted by what it holds.

A leading dot, or .gitignore

Dimmed rows

Hidden entries are dimmed and ignored ones most of all — but still listed: a stale ignored artifact you cannot see is one you cannot explain.

Ignoring is honoured the way git honours it: a nested .gitignore, a !negation and
.git/info/exclude all count. Build output (target, node_modules) and
.git are the exception — those are skipped outright, because listing them costs more than the rest of the tree.

Changed files:

A file that differs from what is committed — what a push would carry — shows it in the tree, in the colours the file explorer uses:

Name — Mark — Meaning

Amber — ● — Modified

Green — + — New and staged

Blue — ? — New and untracked (everything inside an untracked folder too)

Theme accent — » — Renamed

Red — ! — In conflict

A folder keeps its name and gets a dot in the strongest colour beneath it, so you can see where the changes are without the whole tree turning
coloured. The marks refresh when a save settles, when the tree reloads and when the window regains focus. They come from Corvus, by path — the
repository does not have to be open there.

Packages:

Inside a source root — src/main/java, src/test/java and the matching
resources — directories are shown as packages. A chain with nothing in it but the next
directory collapses into one dotted row with a package icon:

src/main/java
it.comune.gestionale_atti
AttoService.java

The three levels of indentation it replaces were spelling one name. A folder that holds files, or more than one
subfolder, ends the chain and keeps its own row. Everywhere else the tree stays a plain folder tree — including
src/main/webapp, whose directories are paths and not packages, because they are what a URL is made of.

title: New files
text:
New › — from a right-click, from the Project header's ＋, or from the tool-window menu —
offers the same entries wherever you open it: a typed file, a plain file, an HTTP File, and a directory. A file is created in the
chosen directory, opened and revealed in the tree; an existing file is never overwritten.

New › HTTP File asks for a name (requests is offered; the .http extension is added when you leave it out) and creates a
.http file with a starter request and a ### separator, ready to run from the editor. .http and .rest files wear their own icon in the tree and on tabs.

Right-click the empty space below the last row: that targets the project root, rather
than whatever folder happens to be selected.

The kinds follow the project:

A Maven project

Java, JSP, XML

A class, interface, enum, record, annotation or exception, with the
package inferred from the directory — following src/main/java and friends —
a JSP or XML file with the right header, or a plain file.

A Cargo project

Rust

An empty file, a struct, enum, trait, module or
test module.

The two ask for different things, and the field says which. A Java file is named after the type it declares. A
Rust file names its own module, in snake_case, and the type is derived from it:
atlas_player gives atlas_player.rs holding AtlasPlayer.

Module creates atlas_player/mod.rs, because foo.rs and foo/mod.rs
are two different decisions about how the module will grow.

Code templates of your own are listed in the same dialog, under Your templates — see Code templates.

title: New modules
text:
New › Module in the tree's right-click menu, or New module… in the command palette. Maven
projects only.

A module is not a folder: it is a folder its parent knows about. So creating one goes like this:

• Choose which pom of the reactor will list it — preselected to the one nearest the row you opened the menu on.

• Name it, and choose its packaging.

• Leave group and version as they are, unless you mean otherwise (see below).

• Create: the folder, the pom and the source roots are written, and the parent gets its <module>
line. A parent that was not an aggregator becomes one (<packaging>pom</packaging>) — the
dialog says so before you press Create.

What is greyed out is what the parent gives, and leaving it alone writes nothing into the new pom — the right pom almost
every time. A module that repeats its parent's version is how a release ends up needing eleven files edited. Type over
the placeholder to say you meant otherwise.

Packaging — Folders created

jar — src/main/java … src/test/resources

war — The same, and src/main/webapp/WEB-INF

pom — None — sources in an aggregator would never be compiled

Nothing is written until every refusal has been checked: an occupied directory, a name that is not a folder name, or a
parent that builds sources of its own and so cannot also aggregate.

title: New folders and packages
text:
New › Directory — from a row's right-click menu, the header's ＋, the tool-window menu,
or New folder or package… in the command palette — creates a directory in the chosen folder and reveals it.

The name is a path, so there is no need to open the dialog once per level. Inside a
source root the entry is called Package, and a dot separates too — the
package written the way the package itself is written. Everywhere else a dot is just a character of a name.

Typed — Where — Creates

assets/icons — Anywhere — assets, and icons inside it

it.acme.web — A source root — Three folders, it/acme/web

.github, my.config — Outside a source root — One folder each

src/main/resources — Where src/main exists — Only resources — levels already there are stepped through

The line under the field shows what will exist before you press Enter, and the confirmation says exactly what
was created.

In package territory the field opens already filled with the package you were on, every part of it editable, and the
folders are created from the source root. A child is Enter after one word; a sibling, or a
package one level up, is a few Backspaces. Outside a source root the field starts empty and folders are created
inside the one you picked, because there a chain of directories really is a place.

title: Copying a class
text:
• Ctrl+C on a file in the tree — or Copy from its right-click menu.

• Ctrl+V on the package or folder it should land in — or Paste.

• The dialog opens with the name selected and the extension left out of the selection: renaming is one word and
Enter.

For a .java file the copy is not a file copy. Copying OrderService from
it.acme.orders into it.acme.billing as InvoiceService:

}`, 'java')}

}`, 'java')}

• The package declaration is rewritten to where the copy lands.

• The type is renamed with the file — its declaration, its constructors and every mention of it as a type. A field that
happens to share the name is left alone: the rename walks what the parser calls type names, not the text.

• The classes it used by simple name — its old neighbours, which needed no import while they shared a
package — become imports. That is the part that silently breaks when a class is duplicated by hand.

If the old and the new package both declare the same simple name, no import is written: the copy resolves to its new
neighbour, and picking the other one for you would be a guess.

Nothing is ever overwritten: a paste that would land on an existing file says so and waits for another name. Folders are
not pasted — every file inside one would need its own package rewrite and its own collision check, and half of that would
be worse than none.

title: Renaming a file
text:
F2 on a file in the tree, or Rename… from its right-click menu. It refuses to overwrite an
existing file, and a rename that only changes letter case is a rename, not a collision.

For a language with a language server behind it, the rename also fixes the code that names the file.
Renaming a Rust parser.rs rewrites the mod parser; that declares it and every
use crate::parser::… that goes through it. The dialog says how many files that touches before you
commit, if the rename itself cannot be performed nothing changes at all, and the edits go through the editor as one undo step.

For a Rust project that moves a whole module path, and offering it here would mean offering half of it.

title: Moving a file
text:
Drag it onto a folder in the tree, or use Move to folder… from its right-click menu when
the destination is nowhere near it on screen. A move is a rename with a different destination, so it has the same
guarantees: the buffer is saved first, an open tab follows the file, the destination is never overwritten, and a language
server's edits — that mod line, those use paths — are applied with it.

It asks first when the move sets off a refactor, and only then: dragging an image into
assets/ just moves it. The confirmation names the files that will be edited before anything moves.

The file moves and its package line stays as it was. Bennu flags the mismatch on that line, and
Alt+Enter sets it to the new package — but whatever imports the class still names the old one, so a
package move is not yet a one-gesture refactor.

title: Deleting, and getting it back
text:
Delete — Del or ⌫ on the focused row, or from the context menu — asks first and says
what it is about to remove.

It does not use the system trash: the files go into Bennu's own local history. That is why
Ctrl/Cmd+Z with the tree focused puts them back — identically on every platform — why the
toast that follows carries the same Undo, and why days later they are still in Local History › Deleted.

Ctrl/Cmd+Z in the editor means "un-type that"; in the tree it means "un-delete that".
Whichever has the focus answers.

title: The header and the menus
text:
The Project header carries a New menu, locating the open file in the tree, collapsing or
expanding the whole tree, and an options menu.

Which folders are open is remembered for each project — closing the panel, switching project or restarting brings the
tree back as you left it, including what Expand all, Collapse all and locating a file
opened or closed. A folder that no longer exists is forgotten.

Right-clicking a file or folder opens: New · Open · Rename · Delete · Local History · Copy path · Reveal in Project · Reveal
in File Explorer. Shift+F10 — or the Menu key — opens the same menu on the focused row, so every entry
is reachable without the mouse.

Reveal in File Explorer

Shows the row on disk: a folder as its listing, a file selected inside its folder. It follows Settings → File Explorer →
Open in the built-in explorer — Arbor's own explorer window when that is on, the system file manager when it is not.

Focus in Project

Sends the tree somewhere from outside it — on a crate in the Cargo panel or a module in Dependencies — opening it on
that folder, expanded, selected and with the keyboard focus on it, so the arrows carry on from there. Clicking any row, or
opening any file, hands the selection back to whatever the editor shows.

title: It follows the disk
text:
A git checkout, a cargo new, an npm install, another editor saving a file — all of them
show up on their own, with nothing to press and nothing to reopen. Changes arrive in bursts, so a checkout touching four
hundred files is one reload, not four hundred — and a burst is never held for more than a few seconds, even while a build
keeps writing.

What the tree follows is its shape: files and folders created, deleted or renamed. Editing a file does not
reload it. The exceptions are pom.xml and Cargo.toml, which update the project's name and modules
in place, and .gitignore, which changes what is dimmed. A folder renamed while open stays open under its new
name.

When the structure changes

A folder added or removed directly under the project, a top-level folder renamed, or a module added or renamed anywhere,
raises one notice naming what changed — a bulk rename is one notice, not dozens. When a module or a pom.xml is
involved the notice offers Rebuild index. Files never raise one.

When the window comes back

Returning to Bennu re-lists the project folder and every open folder, one level deep, and reloads the tree if anything
disagrees — the safety net for a change the watcher missed, such as the tail of a very large rename.

By hand

Reload project tree in the command palette re-reads the project from disk on the spot.

target, node_modules, .git, .svelte-kit, coverage and their
kind are not filtered afterwards but unwatched. A build writing into target would otherwise be a burst
that never goes quiet — the tree refusing to settle at exactly the moment the machine is busiest. Such a folder
appearing at the top of the project — .idea, .vscode — still shows up.

title: Projects
text: Projects

title: Projects
text:
A Bennu project is a folder holding a root manifest — a Maven pom.xml or a
Cargo Cargo.toml. Opening it reads the build model: what the project is called,
its modules or workspace crates, and — for Maven — the JDK language level and the frameworks the code relies on.

A folder with neither opens too, as a plain project named after the folder: a set of SQL scripts, a Node or
Angular tree, anything else you want to edit. It gets the editor and the shared surface — the file tree, go-to file, find in files,
TODOs, the terminal, highlighting — and, where a language server serves the files, that server's answers. There is no build model, so no
JDK, no capabilities and no module list, and the Java tool windows stay hidden for the same reason they are on a Cargo project. Files are
read in the default encoding from the settings.

title: What opening a folder does
text:
• Bennu reads the root manifest: the display name, and the modules or the workspace crates.

• On a Maven project it resolves the JDK language level and detects the
capabilities — the domain frameworks the code uses.

• The footer says which kind of project is open: the JDK and the capability count for Maven, the toolchain
and the crate count for Cargo.

title: The model follows the manifest
text:
Saving a pom.xml or a Cargo.toml reads it again. Rename an
<artifactId> and the project is renamed everywhere it is shown — the window title, the
workspace switcher, the Canopy recents — without closing anything.

The index is not rebuilt and no language server is restarted.

title: Maven and Cargo
text:
The two kinds of project get different tools, because different engines answer about them.

pom.xml

Maven — all of Bennu

The symbol index, completion, go-to declaration, find usages, rename, capability detection, JDK resolution,
validation, Generate, the Structure, Maven, Dependencies and Forms tool windows, and Tomcat hot-swap.

Cargo.toml

Cargo — the editor and rust-analyzer

Everything rust-analyzer supplies: completion, go-to declaration, find
usages, hover, rename, quick fixes, rustfmt, semantic colouring and the compiler's own diagnostics
on save.

A Cargo project also gets the shared surface — the file tree, go-to file, find in files, TODOs, the terminal,
TOML highlighting — and Check project, which runs cargo check over the workspace and
puts its errors in the Problems panel like any other build.

Its intelligence comes from the language server, so it depends on rust-analyzer being installed; the footer says
which server is serving the open file and whether it is ready. What stays hidden on a Cargo project is the
Java-specific machinery — the JDK footer, the capability count, the Structure, Maven, Dependencies and Forms tool
windows — so the window never shows a panel that could only ever be empty. Language servers has
the whole picture.

It opens as the Maven project: that is the model with more to say.

title: Workspaces
text:
A workspace is a named, coloured group of projects you switch between as a unit. One workspace
holds several projects, several workspaces sit side by side, and the same project may belong to more than one.

Each workspace remembers its open tabs — and the line each of them was on — so switching, or opening Bennu again
tomorrow, puts you back where you were rather than at the top of every file.

A default workspace called Scratch exists from the start, so a project has somewhere to land without you
creating anything first; deleting the last workspace leaves it rather than leaving nothing. A workspace you create
without naming takes the name of the first project you add to it.

The switcher

In the title bar, as a tree: every workspace is a row with its projects nested underneath. Click a
workspace to switch to it, or a project to jump straight into it — switching
workspace first if needed. Add project… adds one to the workspace you are in, whether or not it already
holds any. From the command palette, Switch project and Switch workspace do the
same from the keyboard; Ctrl+Tab (hold Ctrl, press Tab until the project you want, release) toggles between the
projects you were in last. A project you come back to has its open files, tabs in both editors, active file, caret and scroll exactly
as you left them — and so does the whole session after a restart.

The workspace manager

Ctrl+Shift+W, or Manage workspaces… in the dropdown. Every workspace is a
column and every project a card in it.

• Move a project to another workspace by dragging its card into that column, at the spot where it
should go; or select it and press Alt+←/→. A project moved into the workspace you
are in opens in the background — it does not take over the screen — and one moved out of it is closed.

• Reorder projects by dragging within a column, or Alt+↑/↓.
The order is the one the title-bar tree shows.

• Reorder workspaces by dragging a column's header, or Alt+←/→ on it.

• Enter (or a double-click) opens a project, Del removes it from its workspace,
Esc cancels a drag.

• The panel on the right holds the selected workspace's name, colour, and the switch / delete actions.

Moving a project carries its open tabs with it. If the same folder is already in the destination workspace, it is just
taken out of the source.

Open project

Ctrl+O resets the active workspace to a single project. The whole set is remembered and
opened again on the next launch — closing the window writes the last of it before it goes.

Across its projects

Find in project and Go to both have a toggle beside their field that reaches into
every project of the workspace at once, and a row from another project says which.

Every project of the workspace keeps its tabs and tree. Its index, framework models and language servers start
when you switch to it, not when the workspace opens, and a project you have not looked at or searched for ten minutes gives
them back — Settings › Language Servers › Release projects you are not using after sets how long, or never.
Switching back sooner is instant; later, the index is read back from disk and the server starts again. The project on
screen is never released. A project that leaves the workspace — removed, replaced with Ctrl+O,
or left behind when you switch workspace — is released about twenty seconds later, without waiting for the rest.
A file opened from another project of the workspace stays in the current tab strip,
badged with the project it belongs to.

title: When a project or a module goes missing
text:
A workspace remembers projects by their folder, and folders get renamed, moved and deleted outside Bennu.

A project folder that is gone

Whether it disappears before Bennu starts or while the project is open, a notification says
Project … no longer exists at … and offers Locate… — a folder picker opened at the nearest
folder that still exists, which adds the project from its new place — or Remove from workspace. Both
stay in the command palette as Locate missing project … and Remove missing project … from workspace
after the notification fades. A project whose folder vanished while open has its index released at once.

A module that is gone

When a pom.xml lists a <module> whose folder or pom.xml is not there — the
usual result of renaming a module's folder — Bennu says Module … declared in … was not found once, with
Open pom.xml, and names a folder beside it that has a pom.xml no
<modules> lists, which is usually the renamed one. The <module> entry is
underlined as an error in the pom, and the dependency warning names it too: every type in the lost module stays
unresolved until the pom and the folder agree again.

title: Which profile, and where it is kept
text:
A profile is an isolated Arbor environment — its own settings, plugins and, for Bennu, its own
workspaces. The gear menu's Profile submenu names the active one and switches between them;
Manage profiles… creates, clones, renames and deletes them. Switching is live: the window reloads onto the
new profile, and Bennu's backend restarts so it reads and writes the new profile's files instead of the old one's.

Bennu keeps two files, both inside the active profile:

bennu/config.toml
The settings — editor toggles, JDK paths, language servers.
bennu/workspace.toml
The workspaces, their projects and their open tabs.

System — The profile folder

macOS — ~/Library/Application Support/arbor/profiles/<profile>/

Windows — %APPDATA%\arbor\profiles\<profile>\

Linux — ~/.config/arbor/profiles/<profile>/

The symbol indices and the cached decompiled sources are deliberately outside the profile, under
arbor/data/bennu/, so an index built once serves every profile instead of being built again for each.

A development build runs on the dev profile by default and an installed one on default,
each remembering its own choice, so running from source never touches an installed Arbor's data.

title: Capabilities
text:
Bennu detects the domain frameworks a project uses and shows how many in the footer. Each capability rests on
evidence, at one of three tiers:

Tier — Evidence — Weight

A — A dependency: a coordinate in any pom.xml of the reactor, one the build resolves to transitively, or a crate in a Cargo.toml. — The strongest

B — A configuration file — a struts.xml, a TLD — in any module. — Strong

C — A pattern in the source. — Corroborating; a capability with only this is provisional

The resolved dependency tree matters more than it sounds, because an API is rarely what a pom declares.
jakarta.validation-api arrives through a Spring starter or a parent pom, so Bean Validation is
recognised from the tree once Maven has resolved it — and the tooling that depends on it switches on then, without
opening the project again.

The detected set decides which features light up — JSP taglib awareness only when a taglib is actually in use, for
instance. The demo project shows Struts (convention and XML), JSP taglibs, the OGNL value stack, a JDBC DAO and
Entando.

Project Configuration — the title bar's gear, Ctrl+Shift+,, or
the command palette — holds everything that is true of this project rather than of you, as four sections with
a sidebar: Project (the JDK level it targets, its encoding, its modules), Frameworks
(every capability Bennu knows, grouped by kind: the ones found, each with the evidence that convinced it and a
provisional mark when only a pattern in the source supports it, and the ones not found, each with what Bennu
looks for — so "why is that feature not here" has an answer; filter the list or hide the missing ones), and the two that override your profile —
Naming and Spelling. Settings holds what belongs to you and to the machine instead,
which is why the two are different dialogs; they share a layout so the boundary is the only thing you have to learn.

A bevy or bevy_* dependency

Bevy ECS

A Cargo project is detected the same way, from the same evidence in its own manifest.

i18n/languages.toml beside a .ron tree

i18n labels

Recognised by layout rather than by dependency, because it is useful on a project that only authors content.

title: Refactoring & intentions
text: Editor

title: Refactoring & intentions
text:
The edits Bennu makes for you. All of them go through the reference index navigation uses, which is what separates a rename from a
search-and-replace: the index knows which getName is this one.

title: Where they are
text:
The right-click menu
Cut · Copy · Paste, and the semantic actions — Go to declaration, Find usages, Rename, Generate, Save — on the symbol under the pointer: right-clicking moves the caret there first.
Alt+Enter
The intentions popup at the caret — everything available there, ↑/↓ to move, Enter to apply, Esc to dismiss. The entry to the generators, the refactorings and the quick fixes.

title: Intentions
text:
The popup is read in sections, each with its colour: Quick fixes (red) repair the problem under the caret,
Intentions (yellow) change code that is already right, Refactor (blue) reshapes it, and
Generate (green) opens a generator. A row that cannot be done here stays at the bottom of its section, greyed, with the reason.

The generators — Generate constructor, getters and setters, Implement / override methods — are offered where a member
is written: in a class body, on a field, on the class header. Not inside a method, and not while a quick fix is on offer: on an
unimported type, the import is what the key was pressed for. Alt+Insert opens them anywhere.

On a type that is not imported, Import '…' adds the import — after the package, sorted among the
others. When several classes share the name each is its own entry, so you pick the package; a type in the same package, in
java.lang, or covered by a wildcard is not offered, needing none. The entries are ordered the way completion ranks the same
names — what the file already imports, its package, what the project imports everywhere — so java.util.List comes before
java.awt.List; the JDK's internal packages go last. When one candidate is ahead by those rules rather than by the alphabet, it is
marked suggested. A class written as a receiver — Limits.MAX, Filter.builder(), Factory::create — is
imported the same way.

A static member written without its class — MAX_RETRIES, assertThat(…), an enum constant outside a
switch — is reported as unresolved until it is imported, and there Import static '…' adds
import static pkg.Owner.NAME; after the other static imports. Every class declaring a public static field (for a name) or method
(for a call) of that name is an entry, ordered like the class imports; a member the file already imports by name or by
import static Owner.*; needs nothing. The classes are read in the background the first time it is asked — your own types first, then
the JDK, then the libraries — so on a large classpath the first Alt+Enter may list fewer owners than the next.

Offered on — Becomes

logger.info("user " + id + " logged in") — logger.info("user {} logged in", id) — parameterized logging; a trailing exception stays last

x.equals("literal") — "literal".equals(x) — never throws when x is null

list.size() == 0 — list.isEmpty()

flag == true — flag

!(a == b) — a != b

Foo.java holding public class Bar does not compile, and it happens both ways — a class renamed in a text editor, or a
file copied and the class inside renamed. So the popup offers both ways out: rename the type to match the file, or the file to
match the type. Picking one for you would be wrong half the time, in the direction that loses the name you meant to keep. Renaming the type goes
through the rename preview, so every use follows.

title: Extract and inline
text:
One Alt+Enter list, offered from what is selected: a run of statements means extract method, a caret in an expression
extract variable, a caret on a name one of the inlines, a caret on a member's header one of the moves. Every one arrives as a single undo.

Extract method:

The selected statements become a method and a call. The locals it reads become parameters, typed as declared; a local it produces that
outlives the selection, and that the code after reads, becomes the return value — a name declared inside a loop or a branch of the selection
dies with it, whatever the later code calls its own variables.

• A static method extracts a static one; a generic one carries the type parameters its signature needs, with their bounds —
the throws clause counts.

• The checked exceptions the moved body can raise are declared on it, and the body is re-indented rather than pasted.

• A name caught as A | B has no single type to write in a signature, so a selection reading one is refused.

Extract variable · extract constant:

The expression gets a name: a local above its statement, or a private static final beside the class's fields when it is constant to read.
The type is resolved, so the declaration says List<String> rather than var, and its import comes along.

• The name steps aside from anything in scope — a field the method reads keeps its name, and the new local becomes value2 rather than
quietly taking over every later mention.

• A constant is refused in the type's own header, where @SuppressWarnings sits before the { and a field would not be in scope.

• Where the surrounding code decides the type — an argument, a return, an arm of a conditional — a type it works out but cannot write is a
refusal: var there would have nothing to infer from.

• A captured wildcard — a.annotationType() gives Class<? extends Annotation> — is refused at a field and
keeps var at a local: a capture has no name anyone can type. An expression it cannot type at all gets var, as javac would infer.

title: Invert if · merge nested if
text:
The condition is negated the way a person would: a comparison flips its operator, a ! comes off rather than doubling, and
&& becomes || over negated halves. A shape with no exact opposite is wrapped, not guessed at. Two ifs with
nothing between them join into one — refused when either has an else, which would run in a case the merged test no longer tells apart.

Split · join · var:

A declaration separates from its assignment and joins back, and a written type swaps with var both ways — going back asks the project what
the initialiser's type is, and declines rather than leaving var. Splitting a final local is refused: Java allows that shape only
where it can prove the variable unset. The four things var cannot read — a lambda, a method reference, a bare {…},
null — each say so by name.

Introduce field:

A local becomes a field of its class, and its initialisation stays where it ran:

Initialising the field at its declaration would run the expression at construction time — a different program whenever it reads a parameter, throws,
or costs anything. The field joins the other fields, except for a local in an initialiser block, where it goes above the block, since a
field may only be read by initialisers declared after it.

• A local of a static method makes a static field; a var local still gets a written type.

• Refused: a name the class already declares; a local typed with its method's own type parameter; an interface, whose fields must be initialised at
their declaration; a record, which may not have instance fields; a local inside an anonymous class, whose field would land on the class around it.

title: Replace if chain with switch
text:
An if / else if ladder testing one value against constants becomes a switch, with the breaks the compiler
accepts — none after an arm that already returns or throws, where it would be unreachable. Enum constants lose their type, as a switch writes them.

The subject must be something re-reading cannot change, so a chain testing kind() stays — it ran the call once per rung. So does
"a".equals(s), null-safe where switch (s) throws. An arm ending in a try or a nested switch, where a
break's reachability cannot be read off the text, refuses the whole conversion. And a switch over a String is
Java 7: below that, it is said rather than written.

Pull up · push down · move member:

A member changes the type it belongs to; the three differ only in which type, and the menu is where you choose. Every target written in this file — each
extends and implements, each subtype declared here — is its own row, so the common move is one keystroke. The rows ending in
… open a filterable list of every candidate the project index knows: a superclass in another file, a subtype elsewhere, any type
for a sideways move. A target in another file is edited too, with the imports the member reads carried over.

First it checks who still needs the member where it is, across the whole project: one something calls, or a subclass overrides, does not go
down or sideways. Then what it takes from the type it leaves — and each refusal names what keeps the member there:

• a field it reads that the target does not have — a method reading count will not go where there is no count;

• the class's type parameter, where the target never declared it;

• its own class by name — a factory returning it, a new of it — which would mean the same class wherever it lands;

• a super call, meaning another method once moved; an @Override, a promise about the type it is in; no body, a contract rather than code;

• a name the target already declares;

• a call to one of its own overloads, which reads as recursion and is not;

• a pull up into a generic supertype whose type arguments this class fixes, where the member would meet a type variable in place of its concrete type.

Another package
A type the member reached through its own package resolves to nothing there and has no import to carry, so only what is self-contained moves, widened to protected if it was package-private.
Sideways
For static members needing nothing from where they were: an instance member would find this pointing elsewhere.
Into an interface
A method becomes default and drops the modifiers it may not carry; a private static helper does not stay private. default and static interface methods are Java 8 — below it, you are told. A static method called from anywhere is refused: static interface methods are not inherited (JLS §8.4.8).
Back into a class
It loses that default and keeps the public the interface gave it; an enum whose constants had no ; gets one.
A private member pulled up
Widened to protected where the class it leaves still reads it — the row says so. One nothing reads goes up as written.

It and its serialization neighbours are read by name at run time, so no source mentioning them proves anything.

title: Move class
text:
A type written inside another gets its own file beside it — the same folder, which is "the same package", so every unqualified mention in the package still
resolves. It takes the package line and the imports it reads, and drops the modifiers a top-level type may not carry: static,
private, protected. It stays nested when:

• it is inner — a nested class without static holds a reference to its outer instance, which a top-level type has nowhere to keep;

• it reads the outer class's own members, or names a sibling nested type, which would resolve to nothing from outside;

• this file spells it Outer.Inner anywhere, or any other file mentions it at all;

• the outer class reads its private members — a private constructor included.

Inline variable · inline method:

The value goes back where the name was, parenthesised wherever the surrounding expression binds tighter. Which occurrences count is a question of scope:
the ones in the declaration's own scope, after it, that read the variable — not Math.max, not a selector after a dot, not a lambda parameter,
not a same-named variable in the next block.

It declines where the declaration did work the expression alone cannot: final byte n = 5; narrows a constant only an assignment may, and a value
moved into a lambda becomes a capture that may only read unchanging locals. A one-expression method goes back into its call with its arguments substituted
structurally, so a local sharing a parameter's name is untouched and a non-simple argument is parenthesised.

title: Creating what is missing, and deleting safely
text:
On a call to a method that does not exist

Create method

Written just below the calling method. The call site is the specification: argument types and names become the signature, how the result is used the return type — nothing means void, a condition boolean, an assignment the type of what it assigns to — and a static caller gets a static method. A declared type is copied as written; for what the text cannot declare — a method call or chain, an expression, a var local — the type is the one the call resolves to, with the imports it needs. Only what cannot be resolved stays Object. The completion popup writes the same signature. The body throws, so it compiles and fails loudly rather than returning a plausible null.

On .map(this::toIdentity)

Create method from a method reference

A reference has no arguments, so the signature comes from the functional interface it is passed as: Optional<Jwt>.map wants a Function<Jwt, U>, so toIdentity(Jwt jwt). A return type nothing around it decides is Object. this::name writes an instance method, ClassName::name a static one, with the imports the signature needs. Declined when the callee is overloaded or the interface cannot be read.

On order.total(label)

Create method in the receiver's class

Written at the end of that class's file, public, with the imports its types need, and the file opens. Declined for a receiver from a jar, a class that already declares the name at any arity, or a receiver whose type does not resolve.

On a type that does not resolve

Create class

The file is created beside the one naming it and opened. The use decides the kind: an implements clause makes an interface, after @ an annotation, anything else a class. A name that already has a file is refused.

On a member

Safe delete

Removes it and its doc comment — or refuses and lists every use with file, line and text, because "it is used" is not an answer. Works from a declaration or a call, on members of nested types too; among overloads it is the one under the caret, or the one the call binds to. Declined outright on an override of something from a jar, a method declared at several levels of one hierarchy, one something implements, and anything annotated, which a framework may reach by name.

It stays in the list, greyed, with the reason: "the selection produces total and count, and a method can only return
one" tells you what to change. So do a return leaving the selection, a variable assigned again later, a value with a side effect read
twice, an overloaded call its arguments cannot resolve, a var local whose type cannot go in a signature.

On a file a language server serves — Rust, TypeScript, Python — the same list carries the server's own refactorings, with its full type
knowledge and its disabled ones with their reasons. The gesture is the same.

title: Quick fixes
text:
With the caret on a diagnostic, Alt+Enter offers the repair, not only the sentence:

Diagnostic — Fix

Unused, duplicate or redundant import — Remove it, with its line

Unhandled checked exception — Add throws — extending a clause already there — or surround the statement with try/catch

Non-exhaustive enum switch — Write the missing cases, in the form the switch uses — arrows or colons, never a mix

Strings compared with == — equals, the literal on the receiver side; != keeps its negation

Switch fall-through — Add the break;, indented with its group

A stray ; — Remove it

A missing import — Add it, one entry per candidate package

A final field nothing initialises — Add it as a constructor parameter — a constructor is written when there is none, and one calling this(…) is left alone — or all such fields at once; initialise it in the constructor or on the declaration; or drop final. With Lombok, @RequiredArgsConstructor, listed first when the project already uses it. Offered anywhere on the declaration, before validation has run.

A fix is keyed to the kind of diagnostic and reads the source itself, never guessing from the wording. The two that need types are recomputed from
the analysis that raised the diagnostic, so a fix that appears is one that clears the squiggle.

The frameworks a project uses add their own to the same list — ignoring the target properties a MapStruct mapper leaves unmapped, wrapping Mockito arguments in
eq(…), rewriting a JUnit assertion as AssertJ. A fix that touches more than one place, a rewrite and the import it needs, is still one
Ctrl+Z.

title: Rename
text:
• Put the caret on a symbol and press Shift+F6. A small field opens at the caret.

• Enter applies — or Shift+Enter first opens a preview of every edit, grouped by file.

• Either way it goes through the editor, so one Ctrl+Z undoes it all — and either way the file moves when the rename requires it.

The caret on — What is rewritten

A local or parameter — Scope-exact: that method only — never a same-named variable elsewhere, or a field.

A method or field — Its declaration and every use in the project, including through a library generic — a lambda parameter off list.stream().map(…). A method carries its whole override family and all its overloads: to a caller they are one. A member of a nested type — static, inner, enum or record — is matched inside its own outer type, never a same-named nested type elsewhere in the file.

A record component, or a field Lombok writes accessors for — The field and the calls to accessors nobody wrote — failure.sourcePath(), order.getCustomerName() — getters, setters and @With copies. A hand-written accessor is its own declaration and stays.

A class or interface — Declaration, references, imports and Spring <bean class="…"> entries — a Struts <action class="…"> names a bean id and is left. A public top-level type's file is renamed with it; a nested type's file is its outer type's.

A member reached through import static carries the import and its bare calls, and a method reference —
Failure::sourcePath — moves with its method. Edits that cannot be pinned exactly, like an overloaded method's call sites, are marked for review
in the preview rather than applied silently. It answers once the index is warm; OGNL and JSP references are not rewritten yet.

A method implementing an interface from a dependency has its name fixed by that dependency; renaming only your side leaves a class that no longer implements
what it declares. The preview still shows what it would have done and names the library type, but will not apply it.

title: Add parameter
text:
• Put the caret anywhere in a method's signature — its modifiers, return type, name or parameter list — or on a call of it, and press Ctrl+F6, or choose Add parameter… from Alt+Enter.

• Write the parameter's type and name, the value every existing call passes (empty passes 0, false or null for the type), and where it goes — last, first, or before any existing parameter. With the caret inside the parameter list, the position starts at before that parameter.

• The preview lists the declaration, every override and every call, grouped by file. Ctrl+Enter applies it all as one bulk edit, with the imports the type needs.

A call is edited only when it passes as many arguments as the declaration being changed takes, so the calls of another overload are left alone. When two overloads
take the same number of parameters their calls cannot be told apart by counting: from a call Bennu lists the signatures that could be meant and asks which overload,
and from the declaration the call edits are marked inferred for review.

The method's Javadoc follows: a @param line for the new parameter is added where the parameter now sits, in the declaration and in every override that has Javadoc of its own.

It is also a quick fix. A call that passes one argument too many — No overload of total takes 2 arguments — offers
Add parameter 'Type name' to 'total': the extra argument becomes the parameter, taking its type and its name from what is written, and every other call passes the type's default.

A method reference (this::total) has no argument list to add a value to — the preview names the first one, so it can be changed to a lambda first — a varargs method has no single place for a new parameter, a method
overriding a library type cannot have its signature changed, and a name the method already uses for a parameter or a local would collide. So does a call whose
receiver the engine could not resolve. The preview names the reason and does not apply.

title: Generate
text:
Alt+Insert builds a constructor, getters, setters or both from the class's fields: pick a mode, tick the fields, choose fluent or
plain setters and camelCase or snake_case accessors, watch the live preview, and Ctrl+Enter inserts it at the caret.
From a template… there writes with a code template of yours instead — see Code templates.

title: Implement / override methods
text:
With the caret in a class, Alt+Enter → Implement / override methods… — or the command palette — lists what the class
inherits and may override, grouped by the declaring type. Tick them — a group's box takes all — and Ctrl+Enter writes
them inside the closing brace, as one undo step.

• Abstract methods start ticked, and nothing else: those the compiler demands. Their body throws UnsupportedOperationException —
a stub returning null would compile, run and lie. A concrete one's body starts with super.….

• Only what Java lets you override: never a static, final or private method, a constructor, a package-private method
from another package, or one this class declares — matched on parameter types, so unwritten overloads remain.

• The types they mention are imported in the same step: generated code that does not compile is not generated code.

title: Spelling
text:
Opt-in per project, in Project Configuration → Spelling. After the English and Italian dictionaries download —
Settings → Editor → Spelling, once per machine — Bennu checks your declared names, split by camelCase, snake_case and
kebab-case, and your comments. A misspelled word is a hint; Alt+Enter replaces it with a suggestion or adds it to a
dictionary. Common programming abbreviations are allowed, so it stays quiet on jargon.

There are two dictionaries, and both are lists you can read and edit rather than one-way doors. The one in
Settings → Editor → Spelling holds the spellings that are correct in any project of yours; the one in
Project Configuration → Spelling holds this codebase's own vocabulary — a domain term, a legacy abbreviation, a table name — and lives in the
repository, so everyone who clones it gets the same answer. Removing a word from either starts flagging it again on the next keystroke, which is the way back
from a word accepted by mistake.

title: Regex & languages in strings
text: Editor

title: Regex & languages in strings
text:
A string literal is often another language written inside Java. Bennu colours it as that language — a regex above all —
and the Regex Tester lets you try a pattern against real text and write it back into the literal with the
right escaping.

title: Languages in strings
text:
Mark a literal the way IntelliJ does and it is coloured as the language you name, with the Java escapes
(\n, \", \\, text-block indentation) undone first — so what is coloured is the text
the program actually sees, drawn over the characters that wrote it.

";`, 'java')}

Name after language= — Coloured as

regex, RegExp — Regular expression (see below)

lua — Lua

html — HTML

js, javascript — JavaScript

css — CSS

json — JSON

xml — XML

yaml — YAML

sh, shell, bash — Shell

The marker applies to the first literal after it, and a "a" + "b" concatenation counts as one. The same
comments work in JavaScript, TypeScript and Rust files. SQL is handled by the JPA support, which also
completes and checks it, so it is not part of this list.

title: Regex, recognised without a marker
text:
A regex needs no comment when the code already says what it is. These are coloured as patterns on their own:

• Java: the pattern argument of Pattern.compile, Pattern.matches, String.matches,
replaceAll, replaceFirst and split (when it contains a regex character),
Scanner.useDelimiter, findInLine, and the regexp attribute of
@Pattern and @Email.

• JavaScript / TypeScript: new RegExp("…"). Rust: Regex::new(…) and
RegexBuilder::new(…), including raw strings.

A replacement (matcher.replaceAll("$1")) and the input of a splitter are deliberately left alone.
Settings › Editor › Languages in strings chooses how eager this is:

• By context (default) — the list above.

• By context and variable names — also a literal assigned to a variable named like a pattern
(emailRegex, PHONE_PATTERN). A guess, so opt-in; date formats such as
"dd/MM/yyyy" are excluded.

• Only when marked — nothing but // language=regex.

title: How a regex is coloured and checked
text:
Groups and look-arounds read as keywords, quantifiers and | as operators, \d-style classes and
. as types, anchors as constants, back-references and group names as fields, escapes in the escape colour.
The pattern is read under the rules of its language — Java in Java files, JavaScript and Rust in theirs — so
a*+ is fine in Java and wavy-underlined in a new RegExp.

A mistake is underlined where it is, with the message Java itself would give: an unclosed group or class, an unmatched
), a dangling *, an illegal range, an unknown \p{…} property, a look-behind
without a maximum length, a back-reference to a group that does not exist. A pattern built with + from
something Bennu cannot see is not checked for balance, since half a pattern proves nothing.

title: The Regex Tester
text:
Ctrl+Shift+X, Regex Tester… in the command palette, or
Open in Regex Tester… in the context menu of a string literal. With the caret in a literal the tester opens
on its value; with a selection outside one it opens on the selected text; otherwise it opens empty.

Pattern

Flavour and flags

Java, JavaScript or Rust / PCRE syntax; the flags of that flavour as keys; find-all, whole-text
or start-only matching.

Test text

Live matches

Every match is painted in the text, with the innermost group underlined; the Matches tab lists
them with indexes, names and spans.

Substitution

Replace and split

The result of replaceAll with your template ($1, ${name}
for Java and Rust, $<name> for JavaScript) and of String.split.

Explain · Insert · Saved

Reading and keeping

The pattern explained token by token (hover a row and its token lights up in the field), an Insert menu with the syntax reference, and named and recent patterns kept
with the text they were tried on.

Copy as… gives the pattern as a Java string, a Pattern.compile call with its flags, a
JavaScript literal or a Rust Regex::new. When the tester was opened from a literal,
Apply to source (Ctrl+Enter) writes the edited pattern back with that literal's own
escaping: doubled backslashes in a string, the indentation kept in a text block, no escaping in a Rust raw string, and a
concatenation collapsed into one literal.

Every run happens in a separate worker with a two-second limit. A catastrophic pattern such as
(a+)+$ against a long run of as is stopped and reported as Timed out; typing
again starts a fresh run.

Java and Rust / PCRE patterns run on Arbor's own matcher, written to follow java.util.regex — greedy, lazy and
possessive quantifiers, atomic groups, look-around, back-references, inline flags, Java's line-terminator rules. No JVM is
started. JavaScript patterns run on the browser engine itself. For the Rust / PCRE flavour the syntax rules are the
flavour's, but the matching is the same backtracking engine, so a corner where the Rust engine differs (Unicode
classes, for one) is not reproduced.

title: Building & running
text: Build, run & test

title: Building & running
text: Compile the project, launch its main, and watch — and answer — its output without leaving the window.

title: Building
text:
Project — Ctrl+F9 runs

Maven — mvn compile, under the JDK the project declares

Cargo — cargo check — the button is for diagnostics, and check reaches them without linking

The split button beside it offers Validate (no compile): the editor's own analysis over every file, seconds instead of a full build, answering only what an editor
can answer — see Validation & problems.

Output lands in the Build panel (Alt+0): the parsed errors first, each clickable to its line, then the log — interpreted as the Run console's
is, so Maven's [ERROR]s stand out and paths and stack frames are links. A clean Java build indexes target/classes again, so completion sees what you just
compiled.

title: The ▶ in the gutter
text:
File — Where the ▶ is — What it runs

Java — Beside a main, in the framework marks' column — Run, Debug or Edit configurations… — running launches the class with no arguments, no VM flags, the runtime classpath

Rust — A code lens above every fn main and #[test], from rust-analyzer — Exactly what the server says — the package, the binary, or one test with --exact; Debug builds and launches the binary under the debugger

Scripts — .sh, .bat/.cmd, .ps1 — On the first line — The script, after saving the buffer — you just fixed the line, and the copy on disk would not have it

• Nothing is saved behind your back: pressing ▶ eleven times leaves no configurations. A run that needs arguments or flags wants a configuration — the third entry.

• The Java ▶ appears only for a class the project's entry-point scan knows, so what launches is a class the compiler agrees exists. Its line is read from the buffer,
so a main just typed gets its arrow at once.

The refusal says so instead of the arrow going grey. A .bat is cmd.exe syntax, Windows only. A .sh on Windows needs Git Bash,
looked for under Program Files and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git — not the bash.exe in System32, the WSL launcher, whose scripts see another
filesystem. A .ps1 outside Windows needs PowerShell 7, pwsh.

title: Run configurations
text:
A run configuration is a named launch target, kept in <project>/.arbor/bennu/config.toml — per project, surviving a restart, and yours to commit or ignore.

The selector in the title bar, left of ▷, says which one those buttons start, and opens the list, grouped by category. Picking one makes it
active — it does not launch it. Choosing what ▷ means and pressing ▷ are separate acts.

Categories:

Java

Application

A module, a main class, program and VM arguments, a working directory, environment variables. Choose lists the module's classes with public static void main(String[]), and filling one fills the module.

Java, with Spring

Spring Boot

The same launch plus active profiles, as -Dspring.profiles.active=…; Detected lists the project's application-«profile» files, and the field stays free text. The main class is optional: a Boot module has one @SpringBootApplication.

Java

JUnit

A test scope — the project, a module or a class — run through the test runner, into its own tab with the test tree beside the output.

Rust

Cargo

A subcommand: crate, command, target, features, profile — pickers, since the workspace knows them — and Cargo arguments before the --, Program arguments after.

Every project

Script

A .sh, .bat/.cmd or .ps1, picked not typed, with arguments, a working directory and environment variables. Run with chooses the shell from those that can interpret the file — Git Bash, zsh, sh for a .sh; PowerShell 7 or Windows PowerShell for a .ps1 — and Auto picks by extension. A shell this machine lacks is listed, greyed, with the reason. Whether the script runs here is answered at launch. No Debug: a shell script's debugger is set -x.

Java

Attach to JVM

Launches nothing: connects the debugger to a JVM that is already running with -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=*:«port». One field, the port (1–65535, 5005 to start with); the host is always this machine. ▷ is off for it and 🐞 reads Attach. See Debugging.

title: Environment
text:
Every category has an Environment section, folded while it is empty. Variables are edited as a table or as text — one KEY=value per line, so a block pasted
from a README fills the list. A value whose name suggests a credential (PASSWORD, TOKEN, SECRET…) is hidden until you press the eye.

The .env file field points at a file that is read every time the configuration runs — nothing is copied into the configuration, so editing the file is enough and a secret kept in an ignored
.env never reaches the committed run configuration. The variables typed in the section win over the file's. A relative path is taken from the project root; an unreadable file stops the launch with a message in the Run console.

In the Spring Boot form the less used parts — launch arguments, classpath and debugger — are folded sections too; a folded header shows what is in it.

Each category is offered only where it applies — JVM ones on a Java project, Cargo on a Cargo one, Spring Boot where there is Spring. On a project with exactly one entry point you need
none of this: ▷ finds it, makes a configuration — a Spring Boot one for a Boot application, a Cargo one for a workspace's single binary — and runs it. With several, it asks.

A Cargo configuration has no build step in front of it: the command is the build, and prefixing one would compile the workspace twice. Its debugger is a
debug adapter rather than JDWP — see Debugging.

Multi-module projects:

The module is a configuration's first field because it decides the classpath — a reactor's root usually compiles nothing, and a run without a module launches against
a directory that does not exist. The classpath is the module's target/classes, then the target/classes of the modules it depends on, then the
dependencies: your inner loop is compile-and-run without mvn install or package, so a call across modules finds the sibling's classes where they are.

• Resolved from inside the reactor. The dependencies are asked of Maven as -pl «module» -am at the project root, so a sibling module arrives as its
target/classes — never as a jar a past mvn install left in ~/.m2, and a sibling that was never installed does not break the resolve.
A sibling jar that still turns up is replaced by that module's classes.

• Only the modules it depends on. A sibling nothing depends on stays off the classpath, with its application.yml, its beans and its
META-INF files.

• Refreshed when any pom changes — the module's, a parent's or a sibling's, since a sibling's new dependency is this module's too — and when an entry has
disappeared from disk.

• A resolve that fails stops the launch, with Maven's reason in the console. Jars Maven named and could not find offline are listed at the top of the run.

Dependencies are resolved at the runtime scope — what mvn spring-boot:run and a packaged application see — narrower than the editor, which resolves every
scope to edit tests. Launching with the wider one hands the JVM libraries Maven never supplies: a @ConditionalOnClass on a test-scoped library then fires here and nowhere
else, and the application refuses to start in the IDE while Maven is happy.

Classpath in the configuration changes it — Compile, Test, or every scope — because a launcher wanting a test-scoped H2 or a provided servlet API is legitimate. The
first launch of a configuration resolves its classpath through Maven; later ones are instant until a pom changes. The resolve starts offline, from ~/.m2. A jar Maven refuses offline although it is on disk — "has not been downloaded from it before", as after IntelliJ filled the repository — is accepted on a second offline try that ignores where it came from. If a jar is
still missing and Settings → Java → Allow Maven to use the network (the Maven panel's Offline toggle) is on, the launch goes online once to fetch it — the console says so — instead of starting a JVM that dies
on a missing class. With that switch off the launch stays offline and says which entries are absent. The working directory defaults to the module's, and both the
editor's list and the title-bar selector show a configuration's module.

Entirely from the keyboard: Edit run configuration… in the palette opens the editor with the list focused; ↑/↓ move, ● makes one active,
Enter runs it, Ctrl+Enter closes. Every edit is written as you type.

title: The Run console
text:
Shift+F10 builds and launches, and Run (Alt+R) opens on the program's own output — a separate window from Build,
because a build log is finished when you read it while a program's output is live: watched, typed into, stopped.

The run itself:

Its state
A coloured pill at the left of the status row says what the run is doing: green Running, red Debugging while a debugger is attached, amber Paused at a breakpoint, and once it is over a green Finished or a red
Exited with code …, with its duration. The same state is the glyph on the run's tab, so a strip of several runs shows which is going, which is under the debugger and which failed without opening any of them.
The command that ran
On the same row, after the state: one line, cut at the end of the panel, with the whole of it in the tooltip and a copy button — selectable too. the resolved java, VM arguments and class, quoted to paste into a terminal, the classpath summarised as a count. A real classpath does not fit a command line (Windows caps one at 32 767 characters), so it goes in a JDK argument file, @«module»/target/bennu-run.args — still exactly what you can paste. A Java 8, with no argument files, gets it through CLASSPATH.
Typing back
While a program runs, > Send input opens a line writing to its standard input, so a prompt can be answered rather than look like a hang; what you send is echoed with >, and Esc puts it away. It starts closed on every run — Bennu cannot tell from outside whether a program is waiting.
Stop
Stops the whole process tree, not just the launched process.
The verdict
The exit code and how long the run took.

title: Reading the output
text:
• Every line is interpreted — level, timestamp, thread, logger, exception, URL, path — and coloured, so the line that matters is findable. Levels count in upper case
(ERROR, [WARN], SEVERE): painting the word Error in a sentence red would empty the colours of meaning.

• What a line says beats where it came from. rustc, cargo, javac and gcc write warnings to standard error, so a
warning: is amber, an error: red, rustc's note: and help: quiet, and the source excerpt under a diagnostic stays part of it.

• Red means the line said error. A line nobody interprets is neutral whichever pipe it came down — cargo writes its whole log to standard error. The two
failures with no level word are recognised anyway: Rust's thread '…' panicked at, and the JVM's Error: Could not find or load main class.

• A stack trace stays part of its error: frames under an ERROR inherit it, across Caused by:, until an ordinary line. So an
INFO Tomcat or java.util.logging wrote to standard error is no longer red.

• Colours are honoured: a program's ANSI colours win over inferred ones. Cursor movement and erase-line are discarded — this is a transcript. The real terminal is
Alt+F12.

Links:

• A frame in a class this project declares — at com.acme.Order.total(Order.java:118) — opens that file at that line.

• A frame in the JDK or a dependency opens its source view: the real .java from src.zip or a -sources.jar, otherwise the
decompiled stub, where the tab offers Download sources. Those frames are muted — a Spring trace is forty framework lines around three of yours.

• A frame of something made at runtime — a lambda carrier, a CGLIB or JDK proxy, a generated accessor — is marked but not a link: no source exists anywhere.

• URLs open in the browser, and paths, with the :42 a compiler appends, in the editor.

• A class named in a message — com.acme.order.OrderService, an exception, a logger — opens its file when this project declares it. Write the
method too and the editor lands on it: com.acme.Order#total, Order::total or com.acme.Order.total. A name no class of the project answers to is
coloured but not a link, so a click never opens the wrong class.

title: Log files
text:
The select at the left of the console bar switches what it shows: the program's Output, or a log file the project has on disk — the logs folder of each Tomcat
configuration (catalina, localhost, the access log), any *.log or logs/ folder of the project, and the files its Logback or Log4j configuration writes to.
Open a log file… takes any other. The end of the file is shown and new lines follow as they are written; a file that is truncated or rotated starts again.

A line from a file is read exactly like one from a run: levels and colours, links that open the source, stack traces with their framework frames folded, copy for SQL, Fix with Imber, the filter, the clean view
and its rules. Output brings the run back.

Tomcat's own lines (catalina, localhost, manager) are read too: the timestamp, the level, the thread and the class.method that logged are marked, and
the level is understood in the JVM's language — GRAVE, AVVERTENZA and INFORMAZIONI on an Italian machine colour the line like SEVERE, WARNING and INFO. The date
of an access-log line is marked as well. The format is recognised by its shape, so a changed timeFormat in Tomcat's logging.properties does not matter.

A log opened in an editor tab (any .log file) is coloured the same way: each line takes the colour of its level, the stack trace under an error keeps it, and the
timestamp, thread and logger are drawn as the console draws them.

The project's log format:

When the project says how its logs are written, the console reads it instead of guessing. Bennu looks in logback-spring.xml, logback.xml,
log4j2-spring.xml, log4j2.xml, log4j2.properties, log4j.xml, log4j.properties and the logging.pattern.console of
application.properties / .yml, in the project and its modules' src/main/resources and WEB-INF. Properties the file defines
(<Property> in Log4j2, <property> in Logback) are substituted, and colour wrappers such as %highlight{…} are looked through. The Columns tab of the clean view
says which file the layout came from, or that none was found — in which case Logger and Thread have nothing to work on. For a pattern like

{'%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} | %-5level | %logger{1} | MDC:[tenant=%X{tenant.id},trace_id=%X{Trace-Id}] | %msg%n'}

the date, the level and the thread are known by position, the logger column is the class (a bare OrderService, or abbreviated like
c.a.o.OrderService, opens its file when exactly one class fits), and every MDC entry is marked — the key quiet, the value it names in colour. An MDC:[tenant=acme,trace_id=…] block is recognised by its shape even when no
configuration is found, as is any bracketed group of two or more key=value pairs. The message after the prefix is read as before, so a URL or a class name
inside it is still a link. Lines that are not in the layout — stack frames, other libraries' output — keep the ordinary rules.

A pattern the console cannot model (%replace, an unresolved {'${property}'}, Spring Boot's built-in default) is not used, and the output is read by shape alone.
The configuration is read when a run starts.

title: The clean view
text:
A log says a lot that is not what you are looking for. The eye at the top of the console (Ctrl+Shift+L) draws it without that,
and only draws it: the text the program wrote is untouched, so copy, select-all, search and Fix with Imber all work on the original.

• Columns — the time, the level word (or its letter), the thread (hidden, shortened to exec-3, or full) and the logger (abbreviated, class name only, full or
hidden) are each chosen from the panel button at the right of the toolbar. The logger shows on lines whose layout Bennu read from the project's logging configuration.

• Rules hide, dim or highlight the lines of a logger, a thread, a level or a message — by prefix, text, exact value or regular expression. The quick way is to
right-click a line: hide, dim or highlight its logger, hide everything from its package, hide its thread. A toast offers Undo; the settings list every rule to edit or remove.
A run of hidden lines is one row, ▸ 14 hidden lines, that opens in place.

• Stack traces keep the exception, every Caused by: and the frames of your code, and fold the rest into ▸ 14 framework frames (press to open).
Your code is the packages Bennu finds in the project's sources; Also mine adds more. With no package known nothing folds.

• MDC — the key=value entries a layout prints can be hidden all at once (MDC: Hidden) or one key at a time: right-click a line and pick Hide MDC “trace_id” for any of its keys, or
list the keys in Hidden MDC keys. The entry goes with its comma, so what remains still reads [tenant=acme]; when every entry is gone the empty MDC:[] wrapper goes too.

• Repeats — identical lines in a row (a pool's heartbeat) become one with ×12.

• The level menu and the filter box narrow the console by severity and by text, with the eye on or off.

• The command palette has Console: toggle clean view, show all levels and show only warnings and errors; Ctrl+Shift+L works from anywhere in Bennu.

The settings are kept in your Bennu profile and apply to every project's console.

title: Tabs
text:
• Each tab says which project it came from in a workspace with more than one — a chip after the label, since run
configurations are named after what they launch and three projects with a Main produce three tabs called Main. The tab's
tooltip names the project whatever the workspace holds.

• Tabs can be dragged to put them in the order you want, like the editor's; the Tests tab, when there is one, stays first. They keep their full width up to the buttons at the right of the header.

• One tab per run, so this run can be compared with the last. The eight most recent are kept; ⟳ repeats the tab you are looking at, into a new tab; 🗑 closes
the finished ones. Past the width of the strip the rest are in the ⌄ menu at its end. Closing a tab whose program is still going stops it —
and says so first, naming what is about to stop.

• The console follows new output only while you are at the bottom; scroll up and it stays put.

• Long lines scroll sideways, one line one row. Past four thousand characters a line is cut and says how much; ten thousand lines are kept per tab.

• Several programs run at once — a server and its client — each with its tab, stdin and Stop, and a ▷ in the strip on live tabs. Stop and the input line act on the tab in
front; looking at a finished one with several running, Stop waits for you to pick.

title: Which Java runs it
text:
The one the project is analysed with — the level from maven.compiler.release, source/target, <java.version> or the compiler
plugin, resolved to an installed JDK and handed to Maven as JAVA_HOME. With no JDK of that level installed, the build inherits your environment's JAVA_HOME.
See The JDK.

title: Things worth knowing
text:
A launch builds first
And stops if the compile fails — the console says so, the Build panel has details. That build is mvn compile -pl «module» -am: the run's module and the modules it is built from, and no package — the run starts from target/classes and the jars. Resources are copied, so an edited application.yml is picked up, and a deleted one is removed from target/classes. Without Maven there is no launch: the javac fallback only reports errors, and does not rebuild the classes a run uses.
Nothing changed, nothing runs
Before Maven, Bennu compares each module in the build — its src/main and its poms, sizes and times, no file opened — with how it looked at its last successful compile. Unchanged, it says Up to date and launches at once: Maven's floor is seconds with nothing to do. A build of one module never counts for a module outside it, and a module whose target/classes is missing is compiled however quiet the rest has been. The record is kept between sessions, so the first launch after a restart is as fast as the next one — but it is never taken on faith: the files are compared again, and a module's record is used only while its target/classes still holds the newest class that compile left. A mvn clean, or a build run from a terminal, makes it void and the launch compiles. The resolved run classpath is kept the same way, and used only while the poms are unchanged and every entry is still on disk. Rebuild index drops both.
Projects build independently
Two different projects share no target/ and no index, so one compiling does not hold up the other: launch a second project while the first is still compiling and it starts at once. Two builds of the same project do line up — a launch pressed while that project is compiling or being validated waits for it (the console says so) instead of being dropped.
No mvn clean needed
Maven's incremental compile leaves three kinds of stale output, and Bennu removes them before compiling, rebuilding that module from scratch — its .class files, target/generated-sources/annotations and the compiler's status — and saying why in the Build log:

• A module it depends on changed since it was compiled — including when another launch has already recompiled that module, which Maven cannot see, and which otherwise ends in NoSuchMethodError. With no record from this session, a module whose classes are older than a dependency's counts too.

• A source was deleted or renamed, whose class would otherwise stay behind for Spring to scan.

• Its pom or a parent pom changed.

A module rebuilt this way takes the modules built from it along. And a compile that fails inside target/generated-sources, or on duplicate class — MapStruct or Lombok output left from an earlier compile — is rebuilt from scratch and compiled once more on its own.
Spring Boot runs the class directly
As an IDE does, not through spring-boot:run — so devtools and the plugin's resource handling are not in play.
One build at a time
A build, a validation or a test run: they all touch target/, and two Maven processes on one tree fight over it. Launched programs are not part of that lock — a launch is refused only while something compiles.

title: Scheduled jobs
text: Java & JSP

title: Scheduled jobs
text: Every @Scheduled method the project declares, what its cron expression says in words, and the ways a job never runs without anything failing.

title: Nobody reads cron
text:
0 0 2 * * ? is four seconds of counting fields every time — and the counting is where the mistake happens, because the field that moved is the one you did
not count. Hovering a cron expression says it in words, and the Scheduled panel shows the words rather than the expression in its second column.

Expression — Hover says

0 0 2 * * ? — every day at 02:00

An expression Bennu cannot phrase confidently says nothing at all, rather than something almost right.

title: The silent failures
text:
Refused at startup

The expression is not one

A five-field Unix crontab line pasted into @Scheduled(cron = …) — what people paste — an hour of 25, a misspelled @dayly. Spring and Quartz refuse it in a stack trace nobody reads until the report has not arrived for a week. The five-field case is named for what it is: it needs a leading seconds field.

Never called

Scheduling was never switched on

@Scheduled in a project with no @EnableScheduling is an annotation with nothing behind it. Nothing fails, nothing logs, and the class looks completely correct.

Refused by Spring

No "when" at all

Exactly one of cron, fixedRate or fixedDelay is required.

Refused at startup

A job that takes parameters

The scheduler calls a job with no arguments, and Spring refuses a @Scheduled method that declares any.

`, 'java')}

That is the trap: Boot's autoconfiguration needs @EnableScheduling to be somewhere. The warning is shown on every @Scheduled in the
file rather than once somewhere central — there is no central place to look, and the person who needs to know is the one reading the method that is not being called.

title: What it will not judge
text:
• A cron written as a placeholder — ${report.cron} — or as a constant is resolved from something Bennu cannot see, so nothing is claimed about it
