either way; the alternative reports every externalised schedule as broken.

• Spring's - marker, meaning "declared and switched off", is left alone.

• Nothing is said about scheduling being off until the project has actually been scanned: reporting a cold start as the project's defect is the worst kind of noise.

title: Shaders (WGSL)
text: Rust

title: Shaders (WGSL)
text:
.wgsl files get their own highlighting, completion, go-to, find usages, hover and compiler diagnostics — from Bennu itself, with no language server. The one thing
it will not pretend to do is resolve a Bevy composition, and it says so rather than guessing.

title: The file on its own
text:
Highlighting is built for WGSL rather than borrowed from a C-family language: the @group, @binding and @vertex attributes read as the
interface they are, vec4<f32> and texture_2d<f32> as types, and the standard library — textureSample, mix,
dot — apart from your functions.

Go-to, find usages, hover
Within the file, with nothing installed. A hover on your declaration shows its signature and the // block above it — WGSL has no doc comments, so those lines are the documentation. On a built-in it says what the language says; on an attribute it answers about the attribute — @fragment and the fn fragment under it are different things.
Imports complete
On an #import line — plain or braced, bevy_pbr::{…}, across its lines — your project's #define_import_path modules come first, then Bevy's. Inside braces only the tail is offered. Once the path names a module, the names inside it complete: bevy_pbr::forward_io:: lists its structs and functions.

title: What an import brings with it
text:
A Bevy shader is a fragment of something larger, and most of its names — VertexOutput, globals, apply_pbr_lighting — are declared
elsewhere. Bennu reads those modules: your own .wgsl, and the shader sources of the bevy_* crates the project resolved, at the versions in
Cargo.lock. Everything an #import names then behaves like your own declaration:

• Completion offers it, with its module beside the name;

• hover shows its real signature and the comment above it;

• go-to opens the file declaring it.

Importing a struct brings its fields — mesh.uv is why VertexOutput gets imported. A name your file declares always wins over an
imported one of the same name: the local declaration is what runs.

A name resolving only because another shader imports it is not in scope here. Without the bevy_* sources on the machine — never built, or a git or path dependency —
the module list falls back to a catalogue of the common paths, and imported names do not resolve.

title: It compiles the shader
text:
With no language server installed, Bennu validates a .wgsl through naga — the front end wgpu and Bevy compile with — so a squiggle is an error the
shader would hit at pipeline creation, types and binding rules included. Completion offers the file's bindings, structs and functions first, then the language's vocabulary.

A shader with an #import or an #ifdef — most of a Bevy project's — has half its identifiers in the modules it imports, so checking it alone would
report a hundred problems on a correct shader. It keeps highlighting, completion and find usages, and gets no compiler errors.

A language server does not fix that yet. wgsl-analyzer is in the catalogue and installs with one button, but its module system is
WESL (import foo;), not naga_oil's #import — its parser has no preprocessor directives. Installed, it takes the file over, so on a
Bevy shader it replaces the silence above with its own reading of those lines; on a standalone shader — a compute pass, a material with no imports — it adds
cross-file navigation and rename. Until installed nothing changes: see Installing a language server.

title: The material on the other side
text:
A shader is half of something. The other half is a Rust #[derive(AsBindGroup)] struct saying what the pipeline supplies, and an impl Material naming the
file — and nothing in the toolchain checks the two agree. Write f32 where the shader says vec4<f32>, or swap two fields, and it
all compiles: the uniform is read with a different layout than written, and the colour is not the one you asked for. Bennu reads both files:

Checked — How

The layout — Field by field — names, order, types, with Vec4 ↔ vec4<f32>, Mat4 ↔ mat4x4<f32> and the rest. An unrecognised type on either side ends the comparison for that field.

The bindings — Every #[uniform(0)], #[texture(1)] and #[sampler(2)] must exist in the shader's material bind group — one in another group is told apart from one that is absent.

The entry point — A material naming a fragment shader wants a @fragment in it.

The file — A path resolving to no asset.

title: Getting from one to the other
text:
Ctrl+B follows whichever join the caret is on, both ways — a declaration split over two files has no primary half:

The caret on — Goes to

The path in fragment_shader() — a const too — The .wgsl

A #[uniform(0)] field — The shader's @binding(0)

A ShaderType struct or field — The shader's struct, or that member

A shader struct or member — The Rust layout, or that field

A shader binding variable — The Rust field supplying it

Anywhere else in a .wgsl — The materials that run it — a fallback, since several may

A gutter mark beside every material names its shaders, and the Shaders panel in the palette is the list the other way round: one row per shader, the materials
running it underneath, and whatever the two disagree about.

shaders/x.wgsl, relative to the project's assets/, and embedded://crate_name/shaders/x.wgsl, how a library crate ships shaders under its own
src/.

title: Naming the lanes of a vec4
text:
A Bevy material extension binds a vec4<f32> and packs four unrelated things into it — a frequency, two amounts, another frequency. WGSL gives them one name,
so whatever drives the material has X Y Z W and a guessed range. A comment fixes it:

) @binding(100)
var rock_params: vec4;`, 'wgsl')}

naga fails with unknown attribute on anything outside the spec, so a custom @range(…) would stop the shader compiling — in the game as well as
the preview.

The form is // @preview «label» [«min»..«max»] [= «default»] [: «hint»], one line per lane in declaration order, everything after the label optional. On a struct
member it works the same, the label a nicer name for one that has one. The lines are highlighted apart from ordinary comments, because a load-bearing comment that looks like
prose gets deleted while tidying. Attribute lines between comment and declaration are stepped over; a blank line detaches it. A shader without any is read as before.

A colour
A hex default — // @preview hot = #ff6b14 : the centre of a crack. Otherwise whether a vec4 is a colour is guessed from its name, which works for sand_color and fails for hot, deep and foam; and even a right guess opens on a palette entry rather than your colour.
A texture
The line names what it is: // @preview normal, diffuse, pbr, ao, height — any word. It picks the picture the preview generates (a flat normal, white, a chequer) and decides what shares a slot: top_normal and side_normal would get byte-identical images, so one slot; write normal.top and normal.side to have them apart.

title: Materials with textures
text:
A preview cannot ask for a bind-group layout matching whatever binding indices a shader uses: AsBindGroup fixes a material's layout when it is compiled.
Widening covers a binding missing or too small, never one of the wrong kind — index 101 is a buffer in one material and a sampler in the next.

So the shader is renumbered. Bennu rewrites a copy — only the numbers inside @binding(…) — onto slots the viewer has: eight uniform blocks, twelve 2D textures,
three samplers, and a pair each of array and cube textures. Names, offsets and // @preview lines are untouched, and nothing is written back. A material with ten
textures and a shared sampler renders with generated images in place of the atlas, and the panel lists one row per kind.

wgpu's GL backend gives a texture unit to every layout entry of every bind group, used or not, and WebGL2 has sixteen: the view and mesh groups spend seven, a material
extending StandardMaterial six more. So the panel's viewport has two slots for an extension and four for a material owning its bind group, while the headless
renderer behind bennu_shader_render has twelve for both. A material with more kinds says so on the row that lost out. And because the layout is static, a shader
sampling no textures is charged for its type's slots anyway — which is why the counts stay tight.

What no renumbering reaches is named, not attempted: a storage buffer, a storage texture, a comparison sampler, a depth texture — things a pass fills, and the preview runs none —
and anything past the slot counts.

Meshes carry a second UV channel and tangents, so a material branching on VERTEX_UVS_B or VERTEX_TANGENTS runs the
branch it runs in the game. The values are derived from the geometry — the second channel reads as depth, 1 in the middle and 0 at the rim — a guess in the right range that
exercises the real path instead of the #else.

title: What it will not claim
text:
• A project shipping no shaders of a given form is told nothing about missing ones: an engine crate declares materials and the game depending on it ships the
assets/, so an unresolved path there belongs to another project.

• A shader struct arriving through an #import can be navigated and its fields shown, but a Rust layout is not checked against it: that needs the composed
module, #ifdef branches resolved and #{SHADER_DEF} values substituted — and reading a file is not composing one.

title: Keyboard shortcuts
text: Reference

title: Keyboard shortcuts
text:
Bennu is keyboard-first: every action below is reachable without the mouse, and Ctrl+K finds any of them by name.

Chromium drops those chords on Italian, German, French and Spanish layouts to keep AltGr working — so where IntelliJ uses one, Bennu uses Alt+Shift or another key,
and the table says which.

title: Tool windows
text:
Shortcut — Toggles

Alt+1 — Project — files

Alt+2 — Structure — symbols

Alt+N — Dependencies — by module, by crate on a Cargo project, by package on a Node one

Alt+Shift+9 — The Node window, right rail — each package.json's scripts, and install; only when the workspace has a package.json

Alt+8 — The build tool window, right rail — Maven's goals or Gradle's tasks on Java, Cargo's crates and commands on Rust; the open project's own kind when the workspace has both

Alt+5 — Tests — the catalogue, right rail

Alt+9 — Trees — the parse and the declaration model, right rail; Java and JSP, since both views read Bennu's own engines

Alt+Shift+I — i18n — the fulcrum translation under the caret, rendered. Only on a translation bundle, so there is no rail button

Alt+0 — Build, bottom dock

Alt+R — Run — the launched program's console, and the debugger when it is one

Alt+A — Imber — the assistant, a chat and agent panel on the right rail. Its other keys (expand, next mode, apply the isolated copy) are listed on the page Imber: Keyboard and palette

Alt+6 — Problems

Alt+7 — TODO

Alt+3 — Forms — JSP form analysis

Alt+F12 — Terminal

Alt+Shift+D — The module graph window; inside it Alt+S isolates the selected module's world. Ctrl+Shift+G is Switch window, bound everywhere

Alt+Shift+U — Download dependencies the build needs and the local repository lacks (the poms' for Maven, every classpath for Gradle), then rebuild the index — a background job, Java projects only

Ctrl+Shift+M — Structural search & replace

Ctrl+Shift+P — New Project — the wizard that creates a Maven, Gradle, Spring, Quarkus, web, Cargo or Node project. Inside it Ctrl+Enter creates and Ctrl+↑ / ↓ switch the project type

title: Navigate
text:
Shortcut — Goes to

Ctrl+N — A class by name, project-wide — Types on a Rust project, answered by the language server

Ctrl+Shift+N — A file by name

Ctrl+Shift+Y — A symbol — methods and fields; functions and constants on Rust

Tab, in the navigator — The next of All · Classes · Files · Symbols

Ctrl+Alt+← / → — Back / forward through the places you navigated from. Actions make a stop; moving the caret does not

Ctrl+Shift+Backspace — The last place you edited; again for the one before

Ctrl+Shift+E — Recent locations, filterable, with the line you were on and a toggle for edited places

Ctrl+Tab — Switch project, Alt+Tab style: a strip of the projects that are loaded — the one on screen, those you have been in this session and those whose index is in memory, across workspaces; a workspace member that was only restored in the background is left out. Opens on the previous one; keep pressing Tab (or Shift+Tab, or the arrows) to walk it, release Ctrl to switch, Esc to cancel

Ctrl+Shift+D — Go to project: type to find any project — every workspace, plus the projects you have opened before — and press Enter. Picking one in another workspace switches workspace

Ctrl+Shift+B — Go to implementation — subtypes and overrides; on a mapper method, its XML statement

Ctrl+F12 — File structure — a searchable outline; from the server on a language-server file

Ctrl+H — The type hierarchy of the type at the caret — anywhere inside it

Ctrl+Shift+H — The call hierarchy of the method at the caret — one level at a time

Ctrl+G — A line, or line:column

Ctrl+B, Ctrl+click — The declaration of the symbol under the caret — its usages when already on it

Alt+F7 — Its usages, across the project

Alt+Shift+F7 — The usages of this component, in a .svelte file

Ctrl+F / Ctrl+Shift+F — Find in the file / in the project

title: Edit
text:
Shortcut — Does

Ctrl+Space, Ctrl+Shift+Space — on macOS Cmd+Shift+Space — Completions at the caret; member access also opens on ., and a command language like .dev after a space. When nothing is found the footer says so. macOS takes the whole Control + Space family above the application

Alt+Enter — Option+Enter on a Mac — Intentions at the caret — Bennu's quick fixes on Java, the server's code actions on a file it owns

Ctrl / Cmd+Enter — A blank line below, caret on it — not intentions, one modifier away on a Mac

Shift+F6 — Rename the symbol under the caret, with a preview

Alt+click — Add a cursor where you click — type, delete and move at all of them, and one Ctrl+Z undoes it

Alt+Shift+drag — Select a column: one cursor per line

Alt+J — Add the next occurrence of the selected text as another cursor

Ctrl+Shift+L — Select every occurrence of the selected text; Esc returns to one cursor. Completion and Emmet stand down while there are several

Ctrl+F6 — Add parameter to the method under the caret — its declaration, overrides and every call, with a preview

Ctrl+Shift+X — Regex Tester — opens the string literal under the caret as a pattern (or the selection, or empty); Ctrl+Enter writes the edit back

Alt+Delete — Safe delete the member under the caret — only when nothing uses it; otherwise every use is listed

Alt+Insert — Generate a constructor, getters or setters

Ctrl / Cmd+I — Implement / override methods, grouped by declaring type, abstract ones ticked

Alt+Shift+F — Format the file — by its server (rustfmt for Rust), or Bennu's formatter for Java

Ctrl+Shift+O — Optimize imports in a Java file — Eclipse's key, since IntelliJ's Ctrl+Alt+O is dropped on those layouts

Alt+Shift+→ / ← — Expand / shrink the selection by one syntactic step — VS Code's keys, since Ctrl+W may close a WebView

Tab / Shift+Tab — Walk a completion's placeholders; Esc leaves

Ctrl+→ (Cmd+→ on macOS) — With a ghost text of several lines on screen — a constructor written from the fields — write the next line only and keep the rest drawn; Tab writes all of it

Alt+Shift+M — Expand the macro at the caret — recursive, and text rather than a file

Ctrl+/ — Toggle a comment — Java //, JSP <%-- --%>, XML <!-- -->

Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z — Undo / redo — the history is the buffer's, so undo never reaches past the file in front of you

Ctrl+Y — on a Mac also Cmd+⌫ — Delete the current line, wherever the caret is in it

Ctrl+S — Save the current file

Alt+Shift+H — Local history of the open file; inside it Alt+D switches side by side and unified

Brackets and quotes close themselves — typing ( [ { " ' inserts the closer, and Backspace on an empty pair removes both.

title: Files
text:
Shortcut — In the Project tree

Ctrl+V — Paste it into the folder or package you are on — a Java copy gets its package, type and imports rewritten

title: Build, run & debug
text:
Shortcut — Does

Ctrl+Shift+F8 — The breakpoint list — disable, remove, add an exception breakpoint

F8 / F7 / Shift+F8 — Step over / into / out

F9 is build with Ctrl and resume without it, and they never collide: resume only exists while the program is stopped. The Build split button's choice —
Maven build or Validate (no compile) — is remembered and becomes what Ctrl+F9 runs; see Building & running.

Shortcut — Runs

Ctrl+Shift+F5 — Every test

Ctrl+F5 — Exactly what ran last

Command palette — Rerun failed tests, Stop the test run

In a test run's tree: ↑ ↓ move, → ← expand and collapse, Enter jumps to the source, Ctrl+Enter runs what the

A service with no routes gets no Endpoints button, shortcut or palette entry, rather than a door onto an empty panel. Endpoints and Bevy components have a rail button because you keep them open
while working; the rest open from the palette, so the rail does not grow a row per framework.

title: Window
text:
Shortcut — Does

Ctrl+K — Command palette

Ctrl+O — Open project

Ctrl+Shift+W — Manage workspaces

Ctrl+, — Settings — yours, and this machine's

Ctrl+Shift+, — Project Configuration — what belongs to the open project: its JDK level, encoding and modules, the frameworks detected in it, and the naming and spelling it states differently from your profile

F1 — Documentation

The palette also carries the plugin host: Plugin Manager, Plugin Marketplace, Toggle Plugin Logs and Reload plugins — which
reads the plugin directories again without restarting Bennu, the loop you are in while writing one. What a plugin registers with arbor.command.register appears under
Plugin Commands, and each view a plugin contributes gets an Open View: … entry.

title: Spring
text: Spring

title: Spring
text:
In a Spring application a large part of the behaviour is declared rather than written — in annotations, in XML, in
application.yml. Bennu reads that as part of the program, and puts it where you are already looking.

It switches on for a project that uses Spring, detected like every other capability from the pom and the sources. Nothing in this section appears on a
project without Spring.

Page — Covers

Spring (this page) — Beans and injection in the gutter, bean XML, how annotations are recognised, the bean panels

Spring configuration — Keys inside annotation strings, @ConfigurationProperties, conditional beans, the YAML side, writing a property file

Spring web — The Endpoints panel, Struts actions beside Spring routes, endpoints checked against each other

Spring proxies and declarations — Annotations that do nothing, bean declarations Spring refuses or ignores, a transaction held across a network call

Neighbouring subjects live with their own tool: Spring Data derived queries and repositories under JPA, @Scheduled under
Scheduled jobs, @SpringBootTest next to the Mockito checks, Spring Boot launch configurations and active profiles under
Running.

title: In the gutter
text:
Icon — Beside — Click to

I — A bean declaration (green badge) — See where it is injected

B — An injection point (blue badge) — See the beans that can satisfy it

B — An injection only a dependency can satisfy (dashed teal badge) — See what may provide it — an allowlisted artifact, or Spring Boot's auto-configuration, read from each jar's AutoConfiguration.imports or spring.factories. The tooltip says whose bean it is and on what condition: a library bean is what Spring may register, never a fact. A bean a method returns as a subtype (a HikariDataSource for a DataSource) is matched by the type it returns.

» — A request handler — See its route

Injection points include the ones with no constructor in sight: a single constructor needs no @Autowired, and Lombok's generated one makes
the final fields themselves the injection points.

A bean injected in six places, a key read from three — Bennu asks instead of picking. The menu opens at the pointer for a gutter icon and at the caret
for Ctrl+B, and each entry says what kind of site it is, which tells two injections of one bean apart.

title: A bean named as a string
Bean XML
text:
<bean class=>, ref= and <property name=> navigate and complete, and a <property> naming
nothing writable on the bean's class is flagged. Every check here speaks only when it is sure:

• the property check stays quiet on a class extending something outside the project, or carrying a Lombok annotation whose accessors Bennu does not model;

• a missing class= is reported only when its package is one the project declares;

• an unknown ref= only when it looks like a typo of a bean that exists — a bean can legitimately come from a jar;

• an unresolved ${key} only when it has no default and the project already configures other keys in that namespace.

title: An annotation is checked by origin, not by name
text:
@Service is not a reserved word; a project can declare its own, and several do. Each annotation is resolved through the file's imports as the
compiler would: a qualified use decides outright, then an explicit import, then a wildcard import of the expected package — and a bare name with
no import can only be a class of the same package, so it is not Spring's. Your com.acme.Service declares no bean, gets no gutter icon and is
counted in no panel.

The same rule gates every check on the other Spring pages: an annotation of the same name that is not Spring's is never judged by Spring's rules.

Your own @MyService, itself annotated @Service, is a real stereotype and is missed — which loses a bean rather than inventing one.

title: The panels
text:
Panel — Lists

Spring beans Ctrl+Shift+F12 — Every bean, with its stereotype, scope and profile

Spring configuration — Every property key, with its value and source file

Spring bound properties — What each @ConfigurationProperties field binds

Spring property reference — Everything the dependencies accept, set or not

Spring beans from libraries — The beans declared inside the dependencies you name under Settings → Spring — by group id, artifact id or a prefix — read from bytecode, one row per artifact

All but Endpoints open from the command palette, and each row opens its declaration. Endpoints has its own button and shortcut — see Spring web.

Boot's auto-configuration is gated — @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnProperty — so a bean in a
jar is what Spring may register. Each is shown with its conditions, and none takes part in autowiring, completion or any diagnostic: your own beans stay the
only answer to what this application has.

Each panel is offered only where it has something to say: Spring on the classpath turns the tooling on, and what the model found decides which panels exist. A batch
job with no request mappings gets no Endpoints button, no Alt+4 and no palette entry. Panels appear as the index finishes, and again after a
rebuild finds the first route.

title: Where the pieces are checked
Spring configuration
text: Spring

title: Spring configuration
text:
Configuration is a second program: keys written as strings in the Java, values written in YAML, and a binding between them that only Spring knows. Bennu follows
it in both directions — from the code to the line that sets a key, and from a key to everything that reads it.

title: Keys and names inside annotation strings
Which application.yml answers
text:
A project has several — a base file, one per profile, one per module — and which runs is a launch argument, not something the sources say. Hover, go-to and
the value shown for a key are all answered by one chosen file.

Open Spring configuration from the palette and pick one under Resolve against; it is remembered per project. With none set, the
profile-less files answer — what Spring always loads.

The launch side of profiles — the -Dspring.profiles.active a Spring Boot run configuration passes, and the application-«profile» files it
detects — is described under Running. Settings → Spring names the dependencies that contribute beans and shows the file pinned for
the project.

title: Configuration properties
text:
Hovering a field of a @ConfigurationProperties class shows the full key it binds — the string that appears nowhere in the source, assembled
from the prefix, the chain of field names above it, and Spring's relaxed binding:

Field — Binds

readTimeout, three levels down — app.http.client.read-timeout — with its current value; Ctrl+B opens the line setting it

A Map — …«key»…

A List — …[0]…

A field with @Name — The name it gives

A class reached from two roots shows both keys. A class can also be written from the keys — see Code templates. The
Spring bound properties panel lists the same bindings for the whole project.

title: Conditional beans
text:
A bean behind a @ConditionalOn… is a different thing from a bean, so it says which condition gates it — in the Beans panel and on hover.
@ConditionalOnProperty, OnBean, OnMissingBean, OnClass, OnExpression and the rest are read, and the
property one goes further: its key is real, so hover shows its value now and Ctrl+B opens the line setting it.

The Beans panel shows the profile a bean is declared for beside its stereotype and scope. The same conditions are shown on the beans a library may register, which is
why those never take part in autowiring — see Spring.

title: From the YAML side
text:
In an application*.yml, each key something reads carries a count in the gutter — 2 means two places read it, and clicking asks which.
A key with no mark is the useful signal: nothing in this project reads it.

• The count includes @Value, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConfigurationProperties fields and XML
value="${…}", and both spellings of a relaxed key — readTimeout and read-timeout — count as one.

• A key whose value is a list counts like any other: allowed-origins: with entries under it is what a List<String>
binds. The items are not keys — servers[0].url is not servers.url.

• The counts follow the code: a save that changes what reads a key refreshes them shortly after, and a rename touching hundreds of files refreshes them once.

title: Writing a property file
text:
Completion
Every key Spring and the project's libraries document, and the project's own @ConfigurationProperties paths — the half that matters on a legacy tree, where nobody documented your own namespace. Under a nested mapping candidates are relative: u under spring: datasource: completes to url. Values complete where the set is closed: an enum, a boolean, a log level.
Where the vocabulary comes from
Every Spring starter packages a description of the properties it accepts inside its jar, so the list is version-exact, covers third-party and in-house starters, and needs no network. A curated table stands in until dependencies have resolved once. Spring property reference in the palette browses it all, marking the keys this project sets.
Ghost text
Only where the answer is single: a documented default for an empty key — server.port: proposes 8080 — or a prefix one known key continues. Tab accepts. Never in the middle of a finished key or before an existing value.
Hover
The type, the default, the library's description, and who reads it. The type comes from the declaration, or from the readers — 30 against a Duration means thirty seconds. Two readers disagreeing about the type are reported, since that is usually a bug. A ${…} in a value is coloured as inside a @Value.

As an environment variable:

Right-click a property line → Show as environment variable. Nothing is written; you get the name and a ready-to-paste line for a .env, a shell,
docker run and a compose file.

Property — Variable

spring.jpa.show-sql — SPRING_JPA_SHOWSQL

The one rule everybody forgets — which is why it is worth computing rather than typing.

A key written with quotes in the yaml — service."name".uri, how a map key with a special character is spelled — gives
SERVICE_NAME_URI: the quotes belong to the file, not to the name.

title: Writing a .env
text:
.env, .env.local, .env.production and *.env files complete the other way round: type the start of a
variable and the names Spring binds are offered — the framework's own and your @ConfigurationProperties — each with the property it overrides.
After the =, a closed set of values (a boolean, a documented list) completes too, and hovering a name shows the property, its type, default and
description. A name Spring does not know is left alone: a .env carries plenty of variables that are not Spring's.

title: Spring proxies and declarations
text: Spring

title: Spring proxies and declarations
text:
The mistakes that cost most in Spring compile, start and look right. A transaction that never opens, a bean that is never created, a field that stays
null: each is one line, and the line gives no sign. Bennu marks them as you type.

Every check on this page resolves an annotation through the file's imports, so only Spring's own are judged — see An annotation is checked by origin
on the Spring page. Alt+Enter offers the fix wherever the repair is mechanical.

title: When an annotation on a method does nothing
Bean declarations Spring refuses or ignores
A transaction held open across a network call
text:
A @Transactional method borrows a connection from the pool for its whole duration. A RestTemplate call inside one keeps that connection for as
long as the other server takes to answer:

`, 'java')}

On a quiet afternoon this is fine. Under load, ten concurrent calls to a four-second endpoint hold every connection while doing no database work: connection wait up,
queries queueing, pool saturated, database idle — and the cause is one line that looks like an ordinary call to a collaborator.

• A remote call is recognised by the declared type of the receiver, never by the method name — execute, send and
get are on everything — so your own repositories, mappers and services are never mistaken for one, and a Feign client or a generated stub is left alone
rather than guessed at.

• The receiver types known to talk to another process are RestTemplate, TestRestTemplate, RestClient, WebClient,
OkHttpClient, CloseableHttpClient, HttpClient, HttpURLConnection, URLConnection, WebTarget,
Jedis and MongoClient. A name merely ending in Client is not enough: that would sweep in the project's own gateway classes.

• Thread.sleep inside a transaction is the same defect without a server at the other end.

• A propagation that suspends the transaction — NOT_SUPPORTED, NEVER — holds nothing, and is left alone: it is the fix.

title: Spring web
text: Spring

title: Spring web
text:
A web application is, among other things, a list of URLs — and in Spring that list exists nowhere as text. It is assembled at startup from annotations spread over
every controller. Bennu assembles it while you edit, shows it as one list, and checks it against itself.

title: The Endpoints panel
text:
On the right activity bar, Alt+4: every URL the application answers, whoever routes it. A Spring route arrives with its class and
method mappings joined; a Struts action as its URL — the package namespace joined to the action name — with the bean id resolved to the class that
runs. An application mid-migration has both, in one list.

• Group by path, by handler or by method; filter across paths, handlers, return types and parameter names, with a count of what survived.

• Each route expands to what it takes: which values come from the path, the query string or the body, which are optional, and what each is called when renamed.

• Verbs are coloured as an API console colours them, and the {'{'}variables{'}'} in a path lit apart, so the list is skimmable.

• Media types are shown by short names — JSON, SSE, XML, form — rather than
MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE; an unfamiliar one keeps its spelling, being the one worth seeing.

A request handler also carries a » in the gutter of its own file, which shows its route. The panel is offered only where the project has routes: a batch
job gets no Endpoints button, no Alt+4 and no palette entry, and the button appears as soon as a rebuild finds the first one.

An action expands into the whole request:

Under a Struts row are the action's own <interceptor-ref>s, then one row per <result>: its name, its type, the target the config
names and — when different — the page it finally reaches:

tiles admin.Cat.tree → /WEB-INF/jsp/tree.jsp

The definition name alone says nothing about which file you will open, and following it by hand means the action fragment, then tiles.xml, then the
parent definition. Clicking opens the page. A chain or a redirect names another action and says so. An action with no interceptor rows does not override
its package's default stack — it does have interceptors.

title: A type is a door
text:
A chip naming a composite type — a route's return type, a parameter's — expands into that class's fields, and each composite field expands in turn,
as deep as you click. An interface or a class from a jar is listed by the properties its getters expose, and says so. Wrappers are seen through:
ResponseEntity<OrderDto> opens on OrderDto. Nothing is resolved until you ask.

Export:

Export — the ⭳ in the header — takes the list out as CSV, JSON or a Markdown table, to the clipboard or a file: what is on screen, filter and grouping
applied, with each route's parameters flattened onto its row.

title: Endpoints checked against each other
text:
Does this handler's @PathVariable match its path? fits in a file. Does another controller already claim this route? does not — that one is
in another package, maybe written three years ago.

")
public Order get(@PathVariable String id) { … } // no {id} in the path: a 500 on every call`, 'java')}

A startup failure

A route two handlers claim

Spring refuses to start — "Ambiguous mapping … there is already … mapped" — found by running the application, a build plus a deploy plus a wait, with no word on which class is new. Both sites are marked. A mapping with no HTTP method collides with every verb: a legacy @RequestMapping beside a new @GetMapping. Two handlers separated by produces are a deliberate pair.

A 500 on every call

A @PathVariable the path lacks

MissingPathVariableException, found by the first user. Invisible to the compiler and to a test that mocks the controller, with the two halves fifteen characters apart. The annotation's name wins: @PathVariable("orderId") String id against /{orderId} is correct.

A misspelling's shape

A path variable nothing binds

Reported only on a handler binding some of the others. One binding none is a deliberate "I do not need it" — reporting it would fire on every /{version}/ prefix.

One value, twice

Two parameters binding one variable

Both receive the same value.

A path built from a property — @GetMapping("${api.base}/{id}") — has a template Bennu cannot resolve, so nothing is claimed either way.
And the open file is always read from the buffer, not the last scan: a squiggle placed at an offset from three edits ago lands on the wrong line.

title: Structural search
text: Structural search

title: Structural search
text: Find code by its shape rather than by its text — then count it, or rewrite it. Ctrl+Shift+M. This page is the query language; running one is Searching & replacing.

title: Why it is not a better regex
text:
A text search knows nothing about Java, so these are two different strings:

— and one construct. A structural search compares nodes, so whitespace, line breaks and comments in the middle take no part in
the match. And because each hole is captured, a replacement can move the parts around, which no textual find and replace can do:

assertEquals($msg$, $a$, $b$) → assertEquals($a$, $b$, $msg$)

title: The pattern is the language it searches
text:
There is no second syntax. A pattern is the code you are looking for, with $holes$ where it may differ, parsed with the same
grammar as the file — which is exactly what makes the match structural. If you can write the statement, you can write its pattern.

The picker beside the query field says which language that is: Java searches .java; JSP
searches .jsp, .jspf, .jspx and .tag; Java in JSP searches the Java inside
pages — see Searching pages.

A pattern compiled against the wrong grammar does not fail loudly: it matches nothing, which reads as "the project contains none of this" — the one
wrong answer a search must never give quietly.

Two kinds of hole:

Hole — Matches

$x$ — One node, captured under that name.

$xs...$ — A run of consecutive siblings, possibly none — an argument list, a class body, a chain of statements. It captures the original bytes, separators and all, so a captured 1, 2, 3 comes back as written.

Where a hole can go:

A hole is read from where it stands, so it can be the thing that belongs there — not only a name:

Where the hole stands — It is…

a receiver, a method, a type, an argument — that node. f($args...$) is a run of arguments.

alone in a block — { $body...$ }, if ($c$) { $stmts...$ } — a statement, or a run of them (...). Loops, if, try, lambdas.

alone in a class body — class $c$ extends $b$ { $members...$ } — a member (method, field, nested type), or a run of them. Classes, interfaces, records; for an enum, after the constants and a ;.

alone in a parameter list — void $m$($params...$) — a parameter, whole with its type, or a run of them.

$mods...$ in front of a declaration — $mods...$ final $t$ $n$ = $v$; — zero or more modifiers and annotations, none included: the declaration need not have any. Captured, so a replacement can put them back.

A declaration pattern is exact about its modifiers: final $t$ $n$ = $v$; matches a local that is final and nothing else.
Write $mods...$ first to accept any, or $pre...$ final $post...$ to require final among others. The same
goes for a class: $mods...$ class $c$ extends $b$ { $members...$ } is any class extending $b$, public or not;
a class with an implements the pattern does not mention is a different shape, so add it or use or.

title: Declarations
text:
Classes, interfaces, enums and records (with extends, implements, generics, annotations), methods, constructors, fields, locals,
parameters, catch parameters and lambda parameters can all be written as patterns:

@Autowired private $t$ $n$;
catch ($t$ $e$) { }
for (int $i$ = 0; $i$ < $l$.size(); $i$++) { $body...$ }
$mods...$ $r$ $m$($params...$) throws $e$ { $body...$ }

as — how the text is to be read:

final $t$ $n$ = $v$; is legal Java as a field and as a local variable, and nothing in the text says which. Without help the compiler took the
first reading that parsed — a field — so there was no way to ask for a local. as says which, on a line of its own, and applies to the
alternative it follows:

Line — The pattern is…

as local — a local variable declaration

as param — a method or constructor parameter (one)

as field — a field

as member — a method, field or nested type of a class body

as statement, as expression — a statement, an expression

as class — a class, interface, enum or record

as catch — a catch clause

With as the pattern is read in that one way and no other, so a match is never found twice and a field never answers for a local.

inside — where the match lives:

g()
inside method, lambda

The match must be in the nearest enclosing declaration of one of the kinds listed: method, constructor,
initializer, lambda, class, interface, enum, record,
anonymous — or body for the first four and type for the last five. A field is inside class; a
local or a parameter of a method is inside method; the same code in a lambda in that method is inside lambda. (in
is already a path, which is why this is not spelled that way.)

title: Removing final from locals and parameters, not fields
text:
Two queries, each with its replacement — run them one after the other:

$pre...$ final $post...$ $t$ $n$ = $v$;
as local
→ $pre$ $post$ $t$ $n$ = $v$;

$pre...$ final $post...$ $t$ $n$
as param
→ $pre$ $post$ $t$ $n$

Other modifiers and annotations stay (@Deprecated final int k becomes @Deprecated int k); a hole that matched nothing takes
the space after it, so nothing is left indented. Fields are not locals, so they are untouched. Both are in the Templates column.

Questions about the model:

Asking about the structure of the code — which classes, relations, beans, endpoints — is a declaration pattern with a constraint, answered with the
project's index:

Question — Query

Every use of a member — use of $m$ on com.acme.Type

Subclasses of a type — $mods...$ class $c$ extends $b: com.acme.Base+$ { $members...$ }

Classes by superclass or interface — $mods...$ class $c$ implements $i$ { $members...$ } then group $i$

JPA entities — @Entity $mods...$ class $c$ { $members...$ }

Their relations — @ManyToOne $mods...$ $t$ $n$; with as field, and an or with @ManyToOne($args...$)

Injected fields — @Autowired $mods...$ $t$ $n$; with as field

Methods taking a type — $mods...$ $r$ $m$($pre...$, $p: Order$ $n$, $post...$) { $body...$ }

These are patterns, so what a class says is found and what it inherits is not; a constraint the index cannot decide is kept and marked
undecided. This is the minimal set — use of is the only form with a query kind of its own.

title: Constraining a hole
text:
A colon after the name narrows what the hole accepts:

Written — Means

$x: com.acme.Order$ — its static type is that

$x: Order$ — the same, matched on the simple name

$x: Order+$ — …or a subtype — the + walks the hierarchy

$x: *Dao$ — a glob on the type name

$x: #string_literal$ — a node of the grammar's kind, not a type

$x: ~get*$ — a glob on the node's own text

$x: @type$ — it names a class — a static access

$x: @value$ — it names a variable, parameter or field — an instance access

$x: !equals$ — the negation of any of the above

$x: @type & Files$ — all of them at once

• The # keeps two vocabularies apart: a type is a word from Java, a kind a word from the grammar —
string_literal, method_invocation, lambda_expression. The Trees panel
(Alt+9) says what a construct is called: click a node on its Syntax tab.

• ~ and the type globs are globs, not regexes: * is any run, | separates alternatives,
everything else is literal, and the whole is anchored — ~place|cancel, ~get*, *Service.

• & binds looser than !, so !~get* & @value reads "not a getter, and a value".
There are no parentheses: a constraint needing them is better written as two alternatives.

Static or instance: @type and @value:

orders.total() and Orders.total() are the same shape — a call whose receiver is an identifier — so no
pattern separates them. The difference is in what the name denotes, a question for the resolver, and @type and
@value are how you ask it:

Query — Finds

$o: @type$.$m$($a...$) — every static call, anywhere

$o: @type & java.nio.file.Files$.$m$($a...$)group $m$ — which Files statics this project uses, and how often each

$o: @value & Connection$.$m$($a...$) — calls on a JDBC connection, never on the class

A plain type constraint stays blind to the distinction on purpose: $o: Order$ admits order.f() and
Order.f(), since the type in play is Order in both. Add @value or @type when you mean one.

A receiver the classpath cannot reach comes back undecided, not "not a type" — turning an unknown into a no is how an incomplete
classpath starts inventing answers.

title: The clauses
text:
A query is a pattern, optionally followed by lines beginning with or, in, group, as or
inside (the last two are described under the holes above). No Java construct begins with those words, so such a line is never mistaken
for code — orders.total() is still a pattern.

or — the same question, another shape:

$o$.$m$($args...$)
or $o$::$m$
group $m$
Java spells a method use several ways, and a count seeing only one is simply wrong. Two rules keep it safe:

• A capture used to group must be bound by every alternative. Otherwise the table would have rows with an empty column, and a
hole in an aggregate reads as "none" rather than "this branch cannot answer". The query is refused as you write it, naming the branch missing it.

• One place in a file is one hit. $o$.$m$() and $o$.close() both match stream.close(), and
counting that twice gives a plausible, wrong number. Hits are de-duplicated by range.

in — where to look:

in modules/core, modules/web
Project-relative path prefixes, comma-separated. Without it, everywhere.

group — the statistics:

With a group, the answer stops being a list of places and becomes a table: the key, how many, in how many files. Four
keys, and deliberately no more — each is a question people arrive with:

Key — Answers

group $m$ — which methods, and how often each

group file — which files, and how many per file

group module — which module is full of this

group enclosing — which of my methods do this

enclosing cannot be written any other way: the method a match sits in is not part of the pattern, so there is nothing to capture — yet
"who in my code calls this" is the question asked most.

title: use of — every shape at once
text:
use of $m$ on com.acme.OrderService+
group $m$

Which methods of a class are used, where, and how often — without enumerating the ways Java spells a use. It is a shortcut for a set of
patterns, and the panel shows the expansion, so it teaches rather than hides: copy it out, edit it, run it as an ordinary query.

Name a member — use of place on … — to pin it, or leave $m$ to count them all. The + includes uses through a subtype.

Uses through a reference to the type: a call on a receiver, and both forms of method reference. Not a class calling its own member —
this.place(o), a bare place(o), super.place(o) — which needs the enclosing hierarchy a pattern cannot express.
That is usually what you want anyway: "who uses OrderService" is about its consumers, and its own internals would inflate every answer.

title: Searching pages
text: Structural search

title: Searching pages
text: The same query language pointed at JSP rather than at Java — the markup, and the Java embedded in it, which are two different searches over one file.

title: Markup
text:
A legacy Struts codebase keeps as much logic in JSPs as in classes, and text search is even weaker there: the same tag is written across four lines as
often as one, so grepping <s:property value= finds a fraction of them. Switch the picker to JSP and the pattern is markup:

<s:property $pre...$ value="$x$" $post...$/>
group $x$

That counts every property the pages print, one row per name. A pattern needs no wrapper — any run of tags and text is already a legal page — so what you
type is what is parsed.

A tag's attributes are matched in order and in full, because the engine compares children and has no notion of a set. So
<s:property value="$x$"/> alone finds only tags whose one and only attribute is value; $pre...$ and
$post...$ let the others be there, in any order, as real pages are written. Every JSP template in the Templates menu is
written that way.

title: Inside an expression
text:
An EL or OGNL body is not one blob: a path — a name and what is read off it — is a subtree, and operators, literals and spacing are its siblings.
So a hole can sit inside one — but the pattern must still match the whole expression:

Pattern — Finds

%{#session.$prop$} — Only expressions that are exactly that — not %{#session.user != null}, which has three more parts

%{$pre...$ #session.$prop$ $post...$} — All of them — the same idiom as for attributes, giving what you do not name somewhere to go

${ in a pattern is EL, not a hole: a placeholder name cannot begin with a brace, so the $ is literal and needs no escaping.
$$ is still a literal $ anywhere else.

title: Worth knowing before you discover it
text:
Self-closing is another shape
<s:property …/> does not match <s:property …></s:property>; write the one the page uses.
Scriptlets are single tokens

${…}, #{…} and %{…} have structure inside; the <% … %> family —
scriptlets, directives, declarations — is one token each. <%@ taglib prefix="$p$" %> compiles and matches nothing, because the hole
is characters inside a leaf. For that Java there is a language of its own — below.

Java-only features
use of is refused with a message in a page, and @type / @value have no resolver behind them, so they report undecided rather than filter.

title: The Java inside the pages
text:
The third setting of the picker, Java in JSP, answers that limit: the query is Java, the files walked are the pages, and
what is matched is the contents of their <% … %>, <%= … %> and <%! … %> blocks.

session.getAttribute($key$)
group $key$

Every key the pages read out of the session, one row per key — a question a JSP query cannot ask, since to the page grammar a scriptlet is a token. The
query language does not change: the same holes, constraints and clauses, use of included.

Each block is lifted out and wrapped in the smallest legal Java that makes its kind parse — a scriptlet is statements, a declaration is members, a
<%= %> is an expression — then matched and mapped back onto the page. A hit's line, its preview and where a click takes you are the code
as written, never the scaffolding.

Type constraints come back undecided: the resolver is asked about a file, and a wrapped scriptlet is in no file. And
group enclosing has nothing to name — the page is the method. Use group file.

title: Searching & replacing
text: Structural search

title: Searching & replacing
text: Where the results land, how a rewrite is applied, and what the panel says when the pattern is beyond what it can answer.

title: The panel
text:
The query runs across the top, the answer sits under it, and the selected match is shown in context beside it. A query is two or three
lines with holes — never a document — so it gets a band rather than a column, and no line numbers.

A query with group

A table

A row is a count, with no single place to show, so there is no context column. Undecided hits get a column of their own.

A query without

A list of places

↑/↓ read the file beside them; nothing opens until Enter.

The left column

Templates (each says what it is for and shows its query), the queries you ran lately (Recent) and the ones you named and kept
(Saved), with a filter. A click fills the field and nothing runs until Ctrl+Enter. The column can be dragged wider. The
templates are also offered by the query field's completion, next to the ones you saved.

Language

Java, JSP and Java in JSP are offered only when the project has pages; a Java-only project has no selector.

Where

The whole project, a module, the current directory or the current file. It is the language's own in clause, written for you — a query that
has its own in keeps it.

Holes

The holes the query binds are chips under the field: a click inserts one at the caret (in the replacement when that is where you were typing), and
hole adds a new one. A syntax error is underlined in the field with its message, and a replacement naming a hole the query does not bind is underlined too.

Export
CSV, JSON or a Markdown table, to the clipboard or a file — whichever shape is on screen, so a grouped query exports the table, not the places it summarised.
The line under the results
How long the scan took and how many files it parsed. Read them together: a query with a literal to grep for reads a tenth of the project, one made only of holes reads all of it.

title: The query field
Keyboard
text:
Key — Does

Ctrl+Shift+M — Opens it

Ctrl+Enter — Runs the query

Ctrl+Shift+Space, or Ctrl+Space — Completions

Ctrl+Shift+Enter — With Replace on, previews the changes

↑ / ↓, F3 / Shift+F3 — Walk the matches (F3 also from the query field); the file beside them follows

Space or F2 on a result — Shows its preview (again to hide it; Esc hides it too)

Enter on a result — Opens that place and closes the dialog

Esc — Stops a running search; otherwise closes

title: Replacing
text:
Turn on Replace and write the template — Java again, with the captures put back:

pattern: $a$ == null ? null : $a$.$m$()
replacement: Optional.ofNullable($a$).map(X::$m$)

• Preview changes lists every file the rewrite would touch with only the changed lines (and a little context), numbered, with how many lines come and go.

• Untick the files you do not want; Replace selected writes the ticked ones, and Replace all files from its menu writes every one.

Hover preview. Rest the pointer on a result for a moment (or press Space / F2 on the selected one) and a card shows the
code around the match, a few lines either side, the match itself marked. With Replace on and the changes previewed, it shows instead
what that match becomes — the changed lines with their neighbours, before and after. The file is read only when the card appears, and kept.

Results are grouped by file, collapsible, with the match underlined on its line. A running search can be stopped (Esc): what had arrived stays, marked partial.

A structural replace rewrites places you did not look at, and its whole advantage over a textual one is precision — worth something only if you can check.

A capture the pattern does not bind
Refused before any file is read, listing what the pattern does bind. Otherwise it would render as an empty string: valid Java, wrong code, no error anywhere.
A file changed since the preview
Every file is read again and compared before writing; one that changed is refused by name, since the rewrite in hand was computed from bytes that are no longer there.

title: What it says when it does not know
text:
A type constraint needs the classpath, and a legacy project's is often incomplete. When Bennu cannot decide whether a receiver is the type you named, the hit is
kept and marked undecided — never quietly dropped.

A filter silently excluding what it could not read would produce a table that looks complete and is short by however much failed to resolve: "this API
is used 12 times" instead of "12 I could confirm, and 380 I could not read". The table shows both — a row's undecided count in brackets beside its total — and
negating an unknown stays unknown.

title: Why it is fast, and when it is not
text:
A pattern over five thousand files would be five thousand parses. But every useful pattern holds literals that must appear —
log.debug, SimpleDateFormat, createStatement — so those are grepped for first and only files that could match are parsed:
on a typical query, a tenfold cut.

$o$::$m$ has nothing to grep for, so every file is parsed. The field says so as you type — whole-project scan — and the line under the
results says how many files were read: the honest way to explain why one query is instant and another takes seconds.

title: Worked examples
text:
The panel offers these to start from; each uses a different part of the language.

use of · group

The census before a refactor

use of $m$ on com.acme.OrderService
group $m$
Which methods are used, how often, across how many files.

A type constraint · group enclosing

Which of my methods touch a deprecated API

new $x: java.text.SimpleDateFormat$($p...$)
group enclosing

A text glob

Logging concatenated instead of parameterised

log.$lvl: ~debug|info|warn$("$s$" + $x$)
group $lvl$

or · group file

A call and its method reference, together

$o$.place($a...$)
or $o$::place
group file

title: Structure & trees
text: Editor

title: Structure & trees
text:
Two ways of looking at the file you have open rather than at the project: the members it declares, and the tree the parser
actually built out of it.

title: Structure
text:
The Structure tool, on the left rail, lists the open file's symbols — types, methods and fields — grouped by kind,
filterable, and sorted by position or by name. Click a symbol to jump to its declaration.

For Java the list is read from the parse tree, so every member the file declares is there — a signature wrapped over several lines, a return
type with nested generics such as Map<String, List<Foo>>, a brace on its own line, a text block. The same list
feeds File Structure, which also shows nested types indented under their owner. Members a framework generates, such as
Lombok's, have no declaration in the file and are not listed.

• A method with @Override carries an override marker, an up arrow, so the members that specialise a
supertype stand out.

• Collapse all and Expand all in the header fold or unfold the whole tree, as in the Project panel.

title: Trees
text:
Alt+9 opens Trees on the right: two readings of the file in front of you, on two tabs.

Why did it read it that way?

Syntax

What the parser actually built, anonymous nodes and all.

What does it mean?

Model

The same parse in the language's own vocabulary, with resolved types.

Syntax:

The anonymous nodes — commas, keywords — are shown by default: they are noisy, and very often the answer. The ⧩ button hides them for the
reading where they are not.

• Fieldthe part a node fills in its parent — the difference between "an identifier" and "the name of the method"

• inventeda node the parser had to make up to keep going

• truncateda subtree cut short, rather than pretending the file ends there

Model:

The AST: the same parse in Java's vocabulary, all the way down — types, members and bodies, every
statement and expression as if, for each, call, local variable, binary
rather than as the grammar's node names. Four things separate it from Syntax, and all four are the point:

Punctuation is gone

Commas, brackets and semicolons are not concepts.

Wrappers are unwrapped

A call statement is a call, not an expression_statement holding one; (a + b) is an addition.

Every child says its part

condition, then, receiver, argument, returns. A signature is rows — each parameter its own line, span and click — not a rendered string.

Resolved types are shown

conn : java.sql.Connection. A bare name that is a class reads Files → java.nio.file.Files, an arrow for a colon: static versus instance, visible.

Types, their annotations and modifiers each have a column, and a member nobody wrote is marked generated — a record's accessors
and canonical constructor. They are part of what Bennu understands, so leaving them out would make the tree disagree with completion;
selecting one takes you to the declaration that owes it.

A construct the model has no entry for keeps its grammar name and its children — the tree is never wrong, only occasionally less pretty.
Types need the classpath, so on a project still indexing the tree is complete and untyped, and fills in as the index lands.

title: Model — a JSP
text:
A page has its own vocabulary, and the tab reads it in that: the libraries the page declares and what each
uri resolved to, the tags with the library each came from, their attributes with the type
the TLD declares, the expressions, the scriptlets and the includes. Three things it shows that the parse cannot:

Nesting

The JSP grammar is deliberately flat — an opening and a closing tag are siblings, which keeps a page with unbalanced markup colouring
correctly. The model pairs them up, tolerantly: a close with no open, or a tag never closed, costs the rows below it nothing.

Which library a tag is from

<s:iterator> is a name until the page's own <%@ taglib %> says what s is. A prefix
nobody declared says so in that column — the most common reason a taglib "stops working".

What is an expression

value="%{codice}" and value="Codice" are one shape to a grammar and opposite things to a reader, so
the flavour — OGNL, EL — is a column rather than something to squint at the quotes for.

Page text is left out on purpose: a page is mostly prose and markup, and listing every run of it would bury the rows that carry meaning.
The Syntax tab has them all.

Both tabs:

• They follow the buffer, not the file on disk — the moment you want a tree is the moment you typed something that read
differently than you expected.

• Selection travels both ways: clicking a node selects its bytes in the editor, and moving the caret opens the tree down to what holds
it, scrolled into view.

• The filter matches kind, field and text at once, so "the method called place" is one query.

• Both read Java and JSP — pages, fragments and tag files. The page tree comes from the grammar colouring
the file, so panel and colours cannot disagree.

Each tab says so in its own words — "no grammar for XML yet", "no declaration model for XML yet" — rather than showing an empty panel, which
would read as a fact about your file instead of about the tool.

title: Struts navigation
text: Java & JSP

title: Struts navigation
text:
In a Struts application the behaviour is spread across XML rather than expressed in code. These are the jumps that put it back together: an action="…" string
on one side, a configuration entry, a class and a view on the other.

title: Actions, includes and page variables
text:
The caret on — Ctrl+B — Alt+F7

An action="…" reference — The <action> config, its view JSP, or the action class — Every JSP using it

A page variable's reference — from <c:set var>, <s:set var>, <c:forEach var>, <s:iterator var> — Where the variable is set — Every reference in the page — it is page-scoped

An include path — <%@ include file>, <jsp:include page>, <s:include value> — The referenced JSP — —

What is flagged, with a warning squiggle:

• An absolute action reference resolving to nothing — never a wildcard or a runtime ${…} / %{…} one.

• A static include whose file does not exist — <%@ include file>, <jsp:include page>, <s:include value>,
<c:import url> — never a computed or http(s):// one.

Inline <script> and <style> blocks are highlighted as JavaScript and CSS. And while editing a JSP, the toolbar's Insert
tag menu drops a ready-made snippet at the caret — <c:set>, <s:set>, <s:property>,
<s:iterator>, <c:forEach>, <s:if> / <c:if>, <s:url>,
<s:text>, <s:textfield> — with placeholder attributes to overtype.

title: Form fields are action properties
text:
The name="…" of an <s:textfield>, <input> or <s:select> inside a form is a property of the form's
action class:

• Ctrl+B jumps to its get, set or is accessor in the action.

• A name that is not a property gets a warning — a likely typo, "this parameter does not exist on the action".

• The same works from a <field name="…"> in a *-validation.xml.

• Properties inherited from a project BaseAction are found up the extends chain, and a public field counts as a property —
OGNL reads fields, and a legacy action's parameter bags are often a nested class of public fields with no accessor.

The check fires only when the action resolves to a project class whose properties are known.

Not every name= is a property. Struts spells several unrelated ideas the same way, and only form controls bind one:

Tag — What name= is

<s:textfield>, <s:select>, <s:hidden>, … — a property of the action

<s:text name="label.user"/> — a key in a resource bundle

<s:i18n name="…"> — the bundle itself

<s:action name="…"/> — an action to invoke

<s:bean name="com.acme.X"> — a class

<s:param name="…"/> — the parameter's own name — its value= is the expression

<s:form name="…"> — the HTML element's name

Struts 1 writes <html:text property="user"/>, a text input; Struts 2 writes <s:text name="label.user"/>, a lookup. So which prefix a page
bound to Struts is read from its own <%@ taglib %> lines, never assumed — and a tag from a library Bennu does not recognise is left alone.

title: A view JSP and its action
text:
A view with no form — just OGNL, %{customer}, <s:property value="…"/> — has its action worked out from the Struts result
mappings, the reverse of action → view. That action drives Ctrl+B on an OGNL reference and its "unknown property" warning.

One answer
Used automatically — one action, and also several actions sharing one class, which is a page reachable through three routes, not an ambiguity: the properties come from the class.
Disagreeing answers
An action picker in the toolbar pins one, remembered per file — one row per class, with the routes reaching it underneath. It also overrides a single answer.

Only plain %{…} value-stack roots are checked — EL ${…} scoped attributes and #-prefixed context or iterator
variables are left alone.

title: From struts.xml
text:
The config file points the other way: it names the class and the method an action runs. Ctrl+B on an <action> tag:

The caret on — Opens

class="…" — The action class — a fully qualified name, or a Spring bean id resolved to its class

method="…" — That method, on the action class or on a project superclass that declares it. A wildcard like method="{1}" is left alone

name="…" — The action class

title: Following the whole path
text:
Go-to and hover follow every segment, not only the head. On %{ordine.cliente.nome} — or a field named that way —
Ctrl+B on cliente opens it on Ordine, and on nome on Cliente:

• each segment is resolved on the class the one before it is declared as, with List<T> and other single-argument wrappers seen through;

• a type name resolves as Java does — the declaring file's nested classes first, then its imports, then its package — which tells one action's inner
JspParam from the nine others a legacy project declares;

• holding Ctrl underlines the segment under the pointer, so what a click opens is what is underlined.

At a property with no accessor, a type with no project source (a JDK or library class), a name meaning several things — a stopped walk does nothing, never a jump to the wrong
file. The "unknown property" warning still judges only the first segment: the rest depend on types a legacy tree often cannot resolve, and a warning answers to a
stricter standard than a jump you asked for.

From a page variable:

Inside <s:iterator value="%{elencoBandi}" var="bando"> — or a <c:forEach items var>, or a <c:set> — the
declaration is the only place saying what the variable holds, so it is read: the expression is resolved against the action, the container seen through (a
List<Bando> makes the variable a Bando), and %{bando.titolo} follows. A variable declared from anything but a plain
path — a call, a comparison — stays untyped.

Attributes that are OGNL without saying so:

<s:iterator value="comunicazioni.dati"> and <s:if test="showRiferimento"> carry no %{…} and are OGNL all the
same — the wrapper is needed only on attributes Struts declares as strings, backwards from what a reader expects. So go-to follows those too, for tags from a library bound to
Struts and only the attributes Struts evaluates. <c:if test="…"> is JSTL, another language, and is left alone. The warning stays on
%{…} only: a go-to resolving nothing does nothing, while a warning is a claim.

title: Inside a loop, the value stack is deeper
text:
<s:iterator value="comunicazioni.dati"> pushes the current element on top, so a bare name under it — %{codice} — is a property of
that element before it is anything of the action's. Go-to resolves top down: the innermost element, each enclosing one, then the action, stopping where the name is
declared. A nested iterator's own expression is read against its parent's element.

A name in a loop whose element type could not be resolved is one about which nothing is known, so nothing is said — "I cannot see that type" is no evidence a property
is missing. Where the element type resolves, the check judges the name against every level of the stack.

Included fragments:

A fragment (.jspf) a view pulls in has no action of its own, so it inherits the actions of the pages including it, transitively. The picker, go-to
and the warning all work there: its fields — even those belonging to a form declared in the parent — and its OGNL are checked against the parent view's action.

title: Struts validation files
text:
• On a Java action class in a Struts project, the toolbar's Validation button — also in the command palette — creates
<Class>-validation.xml beside it, from a DTD-headed skeleton following the Struts naming convention, and opens it. If it exists, it just opens it.

• On that file, Validators opens the chain builder.

• Pick a field — the action's writable properties are offered as chips — and stack an ordered chain: add, remove and reorder validators, each with its
parameters, message and short-circuit flag, stopping the chain on first failure. Types and parameters come from the built-in Struts catalogue, and a live
preview shows the XML.

• Add to file appends the chain — creating the <field> or growing an existing one — so you never place a caret by hand.

title: Tag libraries
text: Java & JSP

title: Tag libraries
text: The tags you write come from .tld files, and most of them live inside dependency jars. Bennu reads both, so a taglib tag stops being opaque text.

title: What a page gets
text:
Bennu reads the .tld files a page declares — the project's own, and the ones inside the dependency jars, which is where the tags you actually
write come from.

Typing

Completion

<s: lists that library's tags; inside a tag, its attributes minus those already written. A uri="…" in a directive completes from every library the project can resolve.

Resting the pointer

Hover

The TLD's own prose — the tag's description, an attribute's type, whether it is required, whether it accepts a runtime expression. On a legacy library, often the only documentation there is.

Ctrl+B

Go to the TLD

On the uri, the TLD — one inside a jar included; on a tag name, its <tag> declaration; on an attribute, its <attribute>.

Squiggles

Checks

A tag the library does not declare, an attribute it does not have, a required attribute missing, a uri nothing on the classpath ships.

title: Where it stays silent
text:
A project whose dependencies have not resolved reports nothing rather than everything. A prefix the page never declared is never flagged — it usually comes from an
included fragment, invisible from the page. And a tag declaring dynamic-attributes, or written as a .tag file, has an attribute list that is
unknown rather than empty.

title: Editing a .tld
text:
A .tld is itself edited with completion and checks, against a tag-library grammar that is built in. Both generations are covered — the JSP
1.1 spellings (tagclass, bodycontent) beside the modern ones.

A TLD names its schema at java.sun.com, and the only copy sits inside a servlet container's jars — provided scope, often absent. The file that
defines a project's whole tag vocabulary was the one XML file with no vocabulary of its own.

title: The template language
text: Code templates

title: The template language
Printing values
Filters
text:
A filter changes a value on its way out. It follows the value after a |, and
filters chain from left to right.

Template

}
{{ "product_name" | camel }}
{{ class.name | snake | upper }}`, 'jinja')}

Writes

{`order_line
productName
ORDER_LINE`}

Bennu adds four filters for writing Java:

• snakecustomerName → customer_name

• camelcustomer_name → customerName

• pascalcustomer_name → CustomerName

• java_stringany text as a Java string literal, quoted and escaped

• imported"java.time.LocalDate" | imported is LocalDate — and the file being written gets the import

• argumentsin validation tests, valid | arguments is every valid value as a constructor's arguments; arguments(field.name, case.value_java) changes that one field's

And these from Jinja itself come up the most:

Filter — Example — Writes

upper, lower, capitalize — {'{{'} "id" | upper {'}}'} — ID

replace — {'{{'} class.name | replace("Line", "Row") {'}}'} — OrderRow

length — {'{{'} class.fields | length {'}}'} — 3

join — {'{{'} class.fields | map(attribute="name") | join(", ") {'}}'} — id, productName, quantity

default — {'{{'} class.package | default("com.example") {'}}'} — the package, or com.example when there is none

first, last — {'{{'} (class.fields | last).name {'}}'} — quantity

selectattr, rejectattr — {'{%'} for f in class.fields | rejectattr("id") {'%}'} — every field but the @Id

indent — {'{{'} body | indent(4) {'}}'} — every line after the first moved in by four spaces

title: Conditions
Loops
Variables
Macros
Blank lines and indentation
text:
A line that holds nothing but a {'{%'} … {'%}'} tag leaves nothing behind — not even the line —
so a template can put every if and for on a line of its own and still write code
without gaps. That is why the examples above look the way they do.

The flip side: a line that ends in a tag after some text loses its line break with the tag. In the
constructor above, the blank line after {'{%'} endif {'%}'} is what puts each parameter on a line
of its own. And a - inside a tag removes the spaces and line breaks on that side of it:
{'{{'} value -{'}}'} swallows everything up to the next text, {'{%'}- if {'%}'} everything
before it.

{'{{'} class.nmae {'}}'} writes an empty string rather than failing, so a typo shows up as a gap in
the output. The preview beside the template is the quickest way to catch it — and the editor offers the real
names inside every tag.

title: Comments and directives
Template reference
text: Code templates

title: Template reference
text:
What a template can tell Bennu about itself, what it can read — about the project, your style and the thing
it is generated from — and a complete template for every kind to start from.

title: Directives
text:
A directive is a comment line starting with bennu., usually at the top of the template. The
- before {'#}'} keeps the line from leaving a blank one behind.

}Repository.java -#}
`, 'jinja-java')}

Directive — Kinds — What it says

bennu.description — All — What the template is for, shown next to its name in every list and in completion.

bennu.output — From a class — members — inserted into the class, the default; file — a new file beside it; text — to copy.

bennu.file — From a class, New file, Configuration class — The name of the file written, relative to the class's folder or the folder chosen. It is a template too: {'{{'} class.name {'}}'}Repository.java.

bennu.requires — All — What a project needs for the template to be offered — see below.

bennu.constants — Validation tests — Classes to look up the constants holding each expected message in — see DTO Lab.

bennu.abbrev — Abbreviations — The word that expands it, when that is not its file name — so the file can be called logger-for-this-class and the word stay logd.

bennu.stops — From a class — true reads the output as a snippet: $1, {'${'}1:name{'}'} and $0 become tab stops in the class. Off by default — generated code and snippets both use $.

title: When a template is offered
text:
bennu.requires lists what a project must have, separated by commas. A template whose requirements
the open project does not meet is left out wherever templates are offered — the New file dialog, the template
bars, Generate, the abbreviations in completion — and its row in Settings › Code Templates
says why, as in Needs Java 16 or later.

Requirement — Met when

java >= 16 — The project's Java level is 16 or later.

lombok — A dependency whose artifact is lombok is on the classpath.

org.projectlombok:lombok — The same, by group and artifact — for a name two groups share.

spring-boot >= 3 — Spring Boot is there, in version 3 or later.

!lombok — Lombok is not there.

A version can be bounded with >=, >, <=, <,
= and !=, and versions compare number by number: 1.18.30 is later than
1.18.4. Until the project's Java level and classpath are known, nothing is held back.

Until a project picks a template with Use for this project, it generates with the first one it
meets. The built-in configuration classes are listed record first (java >= 16), then Lombok
(lombok), then a plain class — so a project gets the one it can compile, and one of yours with
its own bennu.requires joins the same choice.

title: What every template reads
text:
Besides what its kind reads, every template has project, style and naming —
and every filter, among them imported, which adds what the code needs to the file's imports.

project — where it is generated:

• javathe Java level, 17; 0 while it is not known

• dependenciesevery dependency on the classpath, as group:artifact

• artifactsthe same dependencies by artifact alone: lombok, spring-boot

• versionsthe version of each, by group:artifact

• resolvedwhether the classpath has been read yet

style — how you write Java:

From Settings › Java › Code Style. Its methods write a declaration the way those settings say, so a
template does not spell the same {'{%'} if {'%}'} chain every time it declares something:

• local(type)what goes before a local's name. val when you use Lombok's and the project has Lombok; else var when you use it and the project is on Java 10 or later; else the type — with final in front of var or the type when locals are final. For a local with an initializer, which val and var both need

• param(type)a parameter's type, final when parameters are

• braces(body)a one-line body in its braces, with a space inside them or without

{{ style.local(field.type_simple) }} {{ field.name }} = source.{{ field.getter }}();
{% endfor %}

public void rename({{ style.param("String") }} name) {{ style.braces("this.name = name;") }}`, 'jinja-java')}
// final parameters, spaces in braces`, 'java')}
And the settings themselves, to test in an {'{%'} if {'%}'} of your own:

• final_paramsgenerated parameters and locals are final

• lombok_vallocals are Lombok's val — true only when you prefer it and the project has Lombok

• local_varlocals are var — true only when you prefer it and the project is on Java 10 or later

• switch_with_returna switch that yields a value is an arrow-style switch expression

• space_in_bracesa one-line body has a space inside its braces

• blank_line_between_membersmembers are separated by a blank line

title: style.rust — how you write Rust
Imports
text:
A template never has to write an import, or wonder whether the file already has it. A type put
through imported is written by its simple name, and the file gets the import:

} {{ field.name }}Date;
{{ style.local("java.util.List" | imported) }} names = new ArrayList<>();`, 'jinja-java')}

style.local(…) does the same for Lombok's val, which is a type like any other. Where the
imports go follows where the output goes:

A new file
Among its own imports, in order.
Members inserted into a class
Into that class's file, in the same undo step as the members.
An abbreviation
Into the file it is typed in, as it expands.
Text to copy
Nowhere — the preview says which imports it needs.

Nothing is added for a type in java.lang, in the file's own package, covered by a wildcard import, or
imported already.

title: New file
From a class
Configuration properties
Configuration class
Validation tests
text:
Rendered with the DTO Lab's cases: the class, a valid value for every field, and one case for every way each
constraint can fail, with the violations the project's validator reported. Every variable, with the built-in
template, is on the DTO Lab page.

title: Abbreviations
text:
Rendered in the file the abbreviation is typed in, whatever language that is; the template's name is the word
that triggers it — or its bennu.abbrev — and the language in its name says where it is offered.
class_name is the file's own name outside Java, where a file does not declare a type.

• class_name, package, file_namethe file it is typed in

• date, yeartoday and its year
