The result is a snippet: $1, $2 are the Tab stops, {'${'}1:name{'}'}
is one with a default, and $0 is where the caret ends.

private static final org.slf4j.Logger LOG = org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger({{ class_name }}.class);$0`, 'jinja-java')}

title: Postfix
text:
Typed after a value's dot, a postfix template replaces the value with its text: orders.logv. The template's name is what is typed.
bennu.applies says which values it is offered on — alternatives separated by commas, any of which will do:
any (the default), reference, primitive, boolean, number, string,
array, iterable, collection, map, optional, closeable,
throwable, or a class name with its package, meaning that class and its subtypes. A word that names nothing leaves the template out
rather than offering it everywhere. bennu.level offers it only on modules at that Java level or later.

• exprthe value's source text

• type, type_simpleits type as a declaration writes it, and the class name alone

• namea name for a variable holding it

• element_type, element_nameone element of an array, an Iterable or an Optional — empty otherwise

• level, varthe module's Java level, and whether it has var

• indentone indentation step, as the file writes it

• class_name, package, file_name, date, yearas for abbreviations

The result is a snippet, like an abbreviation's, and the classes its text names are imported. One of yours named like a built-in postfix template
replaces it on the values yours applies to.

for ({{ element_type }} \${1:{{ element_name }}} : {{ expr }}) {
{{ indent }}$0
}`, 'jinja-java')}

title: Preview and parameters
text:
The eye button in a template's toolbar renders it beside the source as you type. It renders with the first
class of the last Java file opened, or any class picked with Choose…; a New file template with
a name typed there; a Configuration class template with a configuration file and a prefix.

Parameters lay a JSON object over everything the template reads, to see a branch the data at
hand does not take. Objects merge key by key; a list or a value replaces what was there. Parameters are for
the preview only.

Parameters — Shows the template as if

{'{'} "class": {'{'} "name": "Invoice" {'}'} {'}'} — the class were called Invoice, with the same fields

{'{'} "style": {'{'} "lombok_val": true {'}'} {'}'} — you wrote locals with val

{'{'} "style": {'{'} "local_var": true {'}'} {'}'} — you wrote locals with var — what style.local(…) writes included

{'{'} "project": {'{'} "java": 11 {'}'} {'}'} — the project were on Java 11

title: Code templates
text: Editor

title: Code templates
Seven kinds of template
text:
Every template has a kind. The kind decides where you use the template, what it can read, and
where what it writes ends up.

New file dialog

New file

A whole file, named after what you type. Your templates are listed under the built-in shapes, as Your templates.

Right-click on a Java class

From a class

Code written from the class at the caret: members inserted into it — a builder — or a file beside it — a Spring Data repository for an entity.

Right-click on a @ConfigurationProperties class

Configuration properties

The keys the class binds, written out as YAML or .properties with a sample value for each, to copy or to append to a file.

The wand on application.yml

Configuration class

The other way round: a @ConfigurationProperties class written from the keys you select — a record, a Lombok class or a plain one.

DTO Lab › Tests

Validation tests

One test for every way a constraint can fail, expecting what the project's own validator reported.

Java completion

Abbreviations

A word you type that expands into a snippet, next to psf and sout, with Tab stops to fill in. In any language: the name says which.

Java completion, after a dot

Postfix

A name typed after a value — orders.logv — that replaces the value with a snippet built around it, offered only on the values it says it applies to.

title: Your first template, step by step
text:
The quickest way to a template of your own is to start from one that already works and change it while
looking at what it writes. Here is the builder again:

• Open Settings › Code Templates — or run Code templates… from the command palette. The
seven kinds are listed, and each has a page of its own: the templates of that kind on the left, and the one you pick
on the right — what it writes, what the project needs for it, and where its file is.

• Under From a class, press the copy button on builder and name the copy — team-builder. It opens in the editor.

• Open any Java class in another tab, go back to the template and press the eye button in its toolbar. The preview beside it renders the template against that class, and follows every key you type.

• Change something — the builder's methods, a comment on top, the order of the fields — and watch the preview change with it. A mistake shows as a message above the last output that worked.

• Put the caret on a line of the template: the lines it writes light up in the preview, scrolled into view. Select something in the preview and the template lines that wrote it light up in the editor.

• Save. In the class, right-click › Generate from a template… now offers team-builder, and Use for this project makes it the one this project generates with.

Its body is on that page beside the list, so most of the time there is nothing to open. When you want the whole
thing, a built-in opens in the editor like one of yours — read-only, with its preview — and Copy
makes it yours.

A template of yours can be renamed from the same list — the file moves, a tab open on it
follows, and a project generating with it keeps generating with it. For an abbreviation the name is the word
you type, so renaming one is how you change what expands it.

A postfix template can be started without opening Settings: New postfix template… in the command
palette opens the same dialog on the Postfix kind, and the copy opens in the editor.

title: Where templates live
text:
Yours

In your profile, one folder per kind: bennu/templates/<kind>/<name>.<extension>.jinja
— for instance bennu/templates/class/team-builder.java.jinja. They belong to you rather than to a
project, so every project sees them.

Built-in

Inside Bennu, and always there, so every kind has a template that works. They cannot be changed or deleted —
copy them instead. One badged Starter is there only to be copied: the New file dialog already
makes a class, and an abbreviation nobody chose is a word that would expand in every Java file. Bennu never
generates with a starter, and a starter abbreviation is not offered in the popup until you have made it yours.

A project's choice

Which template a project generates each kind with, kept in the project's .arbor/bennu/config.toml.
A single generation can still pick another. Until the project chooses, it uses the first template it can —
see Template reference › When a template is offered.

The extension before .jinja is the language the template writes. It is how the editor colours
the template — team-builder.java.jinja is Java with template tags on top — and how the preview
colours what it writes. New template… asks for it where the kind lets you choose, which is why the
starting point is a copy: what you copy already writes something.

Four of the six read a Java class, the Spring model or Bean Validation — From a class, the two
configuration ones and the validation tests — so on a Cargo workspace they are not listed: there is nothing for
them to run on. New file and abbreviations are about the file rather than the
language, and are there on every project.

title: Generating
text:
Kind — Where — What happens

New file — The New file dialog, under Your templates — The file is created in the chosen folder and opened.

From a class — Right-click on a Java class › Generate from a template…; the command palette; From a template… in the Generate dialog (Alt+Insert) — Members go into the class as one undo step; a file is created beside it; or text is copied.

Configuration properties — Right-click on a @ConfigurationProperties class › Generate configuration properties…; the command palette — YAML or .properties is copied, or appended to a file you pick.

Configuration class — The wand in the toolbar of application.yml and its profiles; the right-click menu; the command palette — The class is created in the chosen folder and opened.

Validation tests — DTO Lab › Tests — A test class is written, or tests are added to an existing one.

Abbreviations — Typing the abbreviation in a file of the language it writes — The snippet replaces the word, and Tab walks its stops.

Postfix — Typing the template's name after a value's dot, on the values it applies to — The snippet replaces the value, its imports are added, and Tab walks its stops.

Nothing is written before you have seen it. Members are inserted only while the class is still the text
they were computed against — a class edited in the meantime is generated again. Text appended to a file
goes into its buffer, so the file's own unsaved changes stay where they are.

title: A configuration class from YAML
text:
In application.yml — or .properties, or a profile file — select the lines
whose keys the class should bind and press the wand in the editor toolbar. The class binds the group of keys
your selection shares, and gets exactly those keys. With nothing selected, it starts from the group the caret
is in, and offers the groups around it instead.

Selecting the mail group and generating with the record template writes:

}`, 'java')}

Each key becomes a field typed by its value — 587 is an Integer, 30s a
Duration — and each group of keys a nested type. In the dialog every key has a box, so a key can
be left out; a group's box stands for everything below it. Groups that are the same thing under different
names — postgres1 and postgres2 with the same keys — become one type in a
Map<String, …>, and the Map switch on a group decides otherwise. The profile
files beside the one open (application-dev.yml) are read too, so a key only one profile sets still
gets a field.

title: Abbreviations
text:
An abbreviation template called logd.java.jinja is offered when you type logd in a
Java file, and dbg.rs.jinja when you type dbg in a Rust one: the language in the name
says where it belongs, and one written without a language — licence.jinja — is offered in every
file, which is what a header or a banner wants. That is why New template… asks abbreviations for an Abbreviation rather than a name.
One called like a built-in abbreviation — psf — replaces it.

The two can be told apart when the file name makes a poor trigger: Settings › Code Templates ›
Abbreviations shows the word beside each template and lets you change it, which writes a
bennu.abbrev line into the template. So the file can be logger-for-this-class and the
word stay logd.

What you type is matched whatever case it is in, as it is for psf and
sout: an abbreviation named Hget is offered on hget.

Its text is a snippet: $1, $2 are the places Tab walks through,
{'${'}1:name{'}'} is one with a default, and $0 is where the caret ends. The template
runs first, so it can use the file the abbreviation is typed in:

private static final Logger LOG = LoggerFactory.getLogger({{ class_name }}.class);$0`, 'jinja-java')}

Write the body at the left margin: what it writes is re-indented to the line it lands on, so a
method written flat in the template arrives lined up with the class it is typed into. A template with no stops at
all is indented the same way.

{'${'}1:name{'}'} written in two places is filled in both as you type, and Tab visits the
pair once — a field and the parameter it is assigned from stay the same word without you writing it twice. The
copies are drawn fainter than the one you are typing in.

title: Tab stops in generated members
Following the project and your style
text:
Every template can read the project it is generating for — its Java level and its
dependencies — and your style from Settings › Java › Code Style. And style writes
a declaration the way you do — val where you use Lombok's, var where you use that, the type
everywhere else — so one template fits every project:

} {{ field.name }} = source.{{ field.getter }}();`, 'jinja-java')}

And a template that only makes sense in some projects can say so in one line —
{' bennu.requires: java >= 16 {'#}'} — to be offered only where it applies. Both are in
Template reference.

title: For an AI client
text:
An AI client connected to Arbor can list your templates with bennu_list_templates and render one
with bennu_render_template — on a class, on the keys of a configuration file, or for a new file's
name — so the code it writes is shaped like yours. Both only read: what a template renders comes back with
where it would go, and nothing is written.

title: Testing
text: Build, run & test

title: Testing
What counts as a test
text:
Read from the sources, not file names

Java

A method with @Test — or JUnit 5's @ParameterizedTest, @RepeatedTest, @TestFactory, @TestTemplate — a public void testXxx() in a JUnit 3 TestCase, or, under TestNG, any public method of a class annotated @Test. Setup and teardown are never tests.

An attribute ending in test

Rust

#[test], and equally #[tokio::test], #[sqlx::test], #[actix_web::test] or the next runtime's — a closed list would miss the next. #[bench] counts; #[rstest] and #[test_case(…)] are marked cases, producing many.

• That is why a helper called OrderTestUtils does not appear, and a JUnit 3 class named anything at all does. An abstract base holding shared tests is shown but cannot run
alone — Surefire instantiates concrete classes.

• #[ignore] shows as skipped and runs only when asked: the eye toggle adds --include-ignored. #[should_panic] is badged — the one row that
passes by failing.

• Discovery reads the file on disk: both build systems compile from disk, so an unsaved test is one the runner could not run anyway.

title: Two places, and why
text:
The Tests tool window
Alt+5, right rail: the catalogue — everything the sources declare, with a filter and a ▷ on every row. On a Cargo workspace it also fills with verdicts as a run streams. Its header folds the whole tree either way, which on twenty crates is the view you can read.
A run
In the Run console (Alt+R), as a tab beside your launched programs, because a test run is a launch: a command, a live transcript, a Stop, an outcome. Its transcript is the console's own — interpreted, with clickable frames.

title: The tree
text:
Runner — Levels

Java — class → case

Rust — crate → target → module → test

The Rust levels are not decoration: tests::works means nothing in a workspace where twenty crates have one. Every level runs — the ▷ on a crate, a target or a module runs it and
everything under it.

• A target is what cargo builds and runs as one binary — the lib, each bin, each file under tests/, each bench — and the unit that reports a
duration, so timings sit on target rows. libtest does not time cases without an unstable flag, and a divided-out figure would be invented.

• Rust rows are there before anything runs, and turn green, red or grey as results arrive. A case no declaration matches is added, not dropped — how an
#[rstest]'s generated cases appear.

title: Starting a run
text:
From — Runs

The Tests window's ▷ — That row. An abstract or disabled Java class has no ▷: Surefire cannot instantiate the first, and the second would report skipped.

The ▶ in a Java file's gutter — Run or Debug for that class or case. A disabled test keeps its arrow and says so. A suite (@Suite, @RunWith(Suite.class)) and the outer class of @Nested tests have a class arrow too, even with no @Test of their own. Arrows come from the file on disk, so an unsaved @Test has none.

Ctrl+Shift+F10 in the editor — The test the caret is in; above the first test, the class (Java) or the file's target (Rust)

Run tests on a folder or file in the project tree — What is under it — offered only where there is something, with the count

Ctrl+Shift+F5 — Every test

Ctrl+F5 — What ran last

The ▷ menu, the command palette — Run all tests, Rerun tests, Rerun failed tests, Stop the test run

title: Debugging a test
text:
Every ▷ in the Tests panel has a bug icon beside it running the same thing under the debugger. Nothing to attach, no port: the forked test JVM dials back to Bennu and suspends
until it arrives, so the breakpoints in your buffer are hit on the first run.

When one is hit, the run's tab becomes the debugger — transport controls on its status row, frames and variables in the two columns left of the tree — and comes forward on its own.

The forked JVM is Maven's child, not Maven, so Stop takes the whole process group — otherwise a test suspended at a breakpoint would outlive its run, and the editor would keep a current line in a
program nothing could resume.

A project with <forkCount>0</forkCount> runs tests in Maven's own JVM, with no forked process to debug — that run is refused with the reason. A debug run is forced to a
single fork, since one listener accepts one connection.

title: Test classes that are never run
text:
The JUnit Platform runs engines, one per dialect: junit-jupiter-engine for JUnit 5, junit-vintage-engine for JUnit 4. A project migrated to Jupiter without
the vintage engine still compiles every JUnit 4 test, and Surefire simply never runs them.

Surefire reports on what it ran, so nothing says so — except the Tests panel, above the tree, with the count and a class name. The other way is just as quiet: only the vintage engine
means the JUnit 5 tests are the skipped ones.

Nothing is claimed before the classpath resolves — an empty jar list means not looked yet — and nothing at all on a plain JUnit 4 build, which never loads the Platform.

title: A pom that pins which tests run
text:
A Surefire plugin configured with a literal <test> makes a selection impossible: Maven gives the pom's value precedence over -Dtest, so running
one class is read and discarded. The Tests panel says so above the tree, before anything runs, and a run that went ahead is marked widened.

Written as a property, it works and keeps its default:

`, 'markup')}

A plain mvn test still runs the suite, while a run started here sets that property and gets the class or case you picked. Any property name does — Bennu reads the one your pom
uses; ${test} is the case where it is Surefire's own.

The button on that warning makes the change: the pinned value becomes a property and <test> a reference to it, named test whenever the pom leaves that name free —
steerable from a bare terminal and any tool. You see which pom will be written first, and only that line changes; comments, order and indentation stay.

title: Reading the results
text:
The tree fills as the run goes — class by class under Maven, test by test under cargo. Select a row and the right pane shows its failure message, exception type and stack trace (Java) or its
captured panic (Rust); select nothing and it shows the runner's output, interpreted like the Run console's.

Mark — Means

✓ — Passed

✗ — Failed — the test ran and disagreed with the code

⚠ — Errored — it threw before it could judge anything (Maven only; libtest has no such distinction)

– — Skipped

flaky — Failed, then passed on a rerun

Failed and errored are kept apart on purpose: they are debugged from opposite ends. The toolbar filters to failures, sorts by duration, and offers Rerun failed — a parameterized test reruns
as a whole declaration, since a failing invocation rarely fails alone. While cargo compiles, the panel names the crate it is on.

title: Things worth knowing
text:
• A test run and a build never overlap — two build processes on one tree fight over the output directory — and starting one during the other is refused.

• Stop really stops: the build tool and everything it started are killed.

• Java tests are selected by simple class name, which every Surefire understands — so two same-named classes in different packages both run.

• Rust tests are narrowed on both sides — cargo picks the binaries (-p, --lib, --test) and the binary filters by name — so one test means one test.

• A cargo run passes --no-fail-fast: otherwise the first failing crate ends the run and every later crate reports nothing.

• A selection too large for one command line is widened, not silently cut, and the panel says so.

• Neither runner is offline: a project only ever compiled may lack its test-only dependencies, and an offline failure there would read as a Bennu bug.

• Doc tests are run by cargo test itself, under a doc-tests target.

title: The index
text: Reference

title: The index
text: Nearly everything else in this manual is a question asked of the index. This is what it is, when it exists, and what an empty answer means while it is still building.

title: What it is
text:
Completion, go-to declaration, find usages, rename, hover and go to class all answer from a semantic index Bennu builds in the background when a Java
project opens. The footer shows its progress, and reads Indexed · N types once it is warm.

Means "not yet", not "nothing there". The footer says which state the index is in.

title: When there is no index to answer
text:
A file outside every project
A Java file that no open project contains gets syntax checks only. The footer reads Not indexed, and the file carries one informational line at the top saying semantic checks are off. When a folder above it holds a pom.xml, clicking Not indexed — or Open project … in the command palette — opens that project (the outermost pom.xml of the chain, so a module opens as part of its reactor), or switches to it when it is already in the workspace.
An index that failed to build
A notification says what failed, the footer reads Index failed, and the index inspector says build failed instead of building. Only syntax checks run until a rebuild succeeds.

title: The index inspector
text:
Index inspector… in the command palette browses what the index holds — types, members, jars, the JDK, beans, actions and relations — with a filter and jump-to.

Type names
How many distinct class names completion can offer, counting the JDK's, every resolved jar's and your own. It tells completion is not offering my library classes from the library classes were never loaded — the same from the popup. A few thousand means the JDK alone answered; a project with jars runs to tens of thousands.
Libraries
What Bennu reads of a dependency jar is kept in a file of its own, named after the jar (group, artifact, version) in Bennu's data folder, and shared by every project that depends on that jar: the second project to use a library finds it already decoded. A jar rebuilt in place (a SNAPSHOT) starts a new file. Deleting the jar-index folder is safe; the files are read again from the jars.
Rebuild
When something looks stale or a class you know exists does not turn up: Rebuild there, or Rebuild index in the palette, invalidates the index and recomputes it. It re-scans the sources on disk and reads the JDK level and source encoding from the poms again — it does not compile; that is Ctrl+F9. A rebuild of a project that is not open says so rather than doing nothing.

title: What it walks
text:
Every .java under the project root except what nothing should index: hidden directories, and Maven's target/ — apart from
target/generated-sources, where an annotation processor writes source that is yours to navigate.

Settings → Java → Excluded directories adds to that list. Entries are folder names matched at any depth, so build excludes every
build folder in a multi-module tree. A change applies to the next build of the index, which Rebuild index gives you at once.

title: It keeps up with your edits
text:
The index is not a snapshot of the project as opened. As you type, the file you edit is read into it again — so a method just written has its usages, and one you just
stopped calling loses them. Nothing has to be saved, rebuilt or reopened for find usages, rename and hover to agree with go-to about what the code says.

• When an edit changes what a file declares — a method added, renamed or removed, a signature or supertype changed — the files resolving against it are read
again too. Typing inside a method body changes nothing anyone else resolves, so it costs one file.

• Who extends whom keeps up the same way. A method rename carries its override family, so a class that has just started implementing an
interface must be known as one — or the rename would move the interface's method and strand the class on the old name. Changing an extends or
implements clause files the type again immediately.

The command palette (Ctrl+K) lists the editor and tool-window actions; Keyboard shortcuts has every binding.
In a Cargo project the Java-only tools are hidden, and Ctrl+F9 runs cargo check.

title: Tomcat
text: Java & JSP

title: Tomcat
text: Run a web module on a Tomcat Bennu starts and configures for you — or push the page you just changed into one that is already running.

title: Running on Tomcat
text:
Add a Tomcat Server to the run configurations (the + in Run Configurations). ▶ and Shift+F10 build the
module, generate a server for it and start it; Shift+F9 does the same under the debugger. The server's output is a console tab like any other —
Stop ends it, ⟳ starts it again — and the browser opens on the application when Tomcat says it has started.

Server:

• Tomcat — an installation Bennu downloaded, or any folder holding Tomcat 8.5, 9, 10.1 or 11. Download… lists the stable releases of a line
straight from Apache, checks the download against Apache's SHA-512 and unpacks it, by default into one folder in your Bennu profile shared by every project: a version is downloaded once,
and two projects — or two configurations of one — run on it side by side, each with its own ports and context.xml. Folders changes where.

• The servlet package decides what runs: Tomcat 9 and earlier speak javax.servlet, Tomcat 10 and later jakarta.servlet, and an
application written for one does not load on the other. Bennu reads which one the project imports and marks a mismatch before launch.

• Ports — HTTP and shutdown. A port something is already listening on is flagged as you type.

Deployment:

Live serves the module's src/main/webapp directly, with its compiled classes and runtime dependencies mounted underneath — nothing is packaged,
and a JSP saved in the editor is the JSP the next request runs. The dependency jars appear as a real /WEB-INF/lib folder (linked from the local repository, no copy
where the disk allows), so code that lists it at start-up finds the jars as it would in a packaged WAR. Only the module's own classes appear under /WEB-INF/classes; the sibling modules it is built from are loaded but not listed there, since a WAR would carry them as jars. Classes are searched before the jars, as in a WAR, so a class of the project that replaces one of a library wins. External serves a WAR or exploded folder built elsewhere. The context path decides where the
application is served.

Each configuration gets its own generated server folder (.arbor/bennu/tomcat/<configuration>, in the project), rewritten at every launch; logs and compiled JSPs are kept.
The installation itself is never touched — which is why one installation can serve any number of configurations, as long as their ports differ.

Server libraries are jars, and folders of jars, that Tomcat itself must load — a JDBC driver the project does not depend on, a logging binding. They are copied into the generated server's lib/ at every launch (a folder adds the .jar files directly in it, so one added later is there next time; paths are absolute or relative to the project). Two versions of one library are flagged in the console, because only one of them is used.

title: context.xml
text:
The data sources, environment entries and parameters Tomcat offers the application through JNDI. The generated file is written into the server folder, not into the
project, so development credentials never end up in a WAR or in the repository.

• Guided builds the file from a list of resources, with the result shown live. Raw XML is the text itself, in the code editor, for what the form
does not model (a Valve, a Manager). The two are one document seen twice: entering Raw starts from what Guided would write — unless the text was edited by hand,
when Regenerate from the form starts over — and going back reads the text into the form, so an <Environment> typed in Raw is a row of the list. Parts the form cannot show are named first, and
switching drops them from the file only on a yes.

• Add offers a data source, an environment entry or a parameter — and the two ways of not starting from nothing: Detect from the project
lists the JNDI names the project's own files ask for (web.xml, @Resource, lookup(), persistence.xml, Spring XML), each
with the line it came from, and adds the missing ones; Paste XML reads an existing context.xml or a <Resource> copied from
a server.xml.

• From a Picus connection is a picker in the Add menu: each connection is a row, and the one you pick is written as a data source — host, port, database and user, and the driver for its engine (PostgreSQL, Oracle).
It takes the first JNDI name the project asks for that the context lacks. Picus never hands out a password, so you type it once. On a data source,
Test connection reads the host, database and user out of the JDBC URL, takes the password typed in the form, and asks Picus to open that connection and close it again — it shows the database answers
with what the form says, not that the driver jar is the right one. A data source taken from a Picus connection and not changed since is tried with the password Picus holds.

• Each row of the list has a checkbox and its own trash, shown on hover. Tick several rows (or Ctrl/⌘-click, Shift-click, Ctrl+A):
with more than one data source selected the form becomes a bulk editor — pool sizes, driver, a find-and-replace across the URLs (swap a host everywhere), and
where the passwords live.

• The JDBC driver is looked for in three places, in this order: the server libraries of the Deployment tab, the project's runtime classpath, and — for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite — Maven Central, once, into the Tomcat folder of your Bennu profile, reused by every project, as long as automatic dependency downloads are on. A driver found in the first two is copied into the server's lib/ at launch. For any other driver (Oracle, DB2, SQL Server), add its jar to the server libraries.

By default a data source's password is kept outside the repository, in a file in your Bennu profile, and handed to Tomcat as a system property: the generated
context holds only ${jdbc.Gestionale.password}. It is a plain file in your profile, not the system keychain — it keeps the password out of anything that is
versioned, not out of reach of someone who can read your files. In the context file writes it as text instead.

title: Launch
text:
JVM options, the classpath scope, the environment (rows and an optional .env file, as for any configuration) and whether the debugger waits before starting.
The default scope, Runtime, leaves out what the project marks provided; an API that an application server would have supplied (JAX-RS, say) is supplied by nobody on Tomcat, so
add it as a runtime dependency or run with Every scope.

title: Linking a Tomcat that is already running
text:
• Open Tomcat hot-swap… from the command palette.

• Pick the Tomcat root — the folder holding webapps/, bin/ and conf/. Bennu validates it and lists the deployed web
applications.

• The one this project maps to is selected for you — by <finalName>, by artifactId or folder name, or as the only application deployed.
Pick another if that is not it.

The link is remembered per project.

title: Deploying pages
text:
Command — Does

Deploy current JSP Ctrl+Shift+F10 — Saves the open JSP and copies it into the deployed application, at the same path it has under the project's webapp source folder. Tomcat recompiles it on the next request.

Deploy all JSPs to Tomcat — command palette — Copies every page at once.

Files are copied as they are, so each JSP keeps its own page encoding.

A toast confirms what was deployed — or says why it could not be: no Tomcat linked, no webapp source folder, or an ambiguous target to pick in the settings.

title: Tool configuration files
text: Editor

title: Tool configuration files
text:
Three files in a JVM project look exactly like the hundred other .properties around them and are nothing like them. Their
keys are not names somebody chose — they are an API, published per release, with defaults and legal values written down. Bennu knows
that vocabulary, and which half of it your version understands.

Lombok

lombok.config

Properties syntax, plus +=, -= and clear.

JUnit

junit-platform.properties

Jupiter's and the Platform's keys, on one version line.

Struts

struts.properties

A legacy Struts application's constants — the security ones included.

title: What you get
text:
Completion

The documented keys, each with its type and default on the right. Past the =, the legal values — but only where the set is
genuinely closed: a duration, a class name or a field name has no candidates, because offering the default as the only entry would dress
a guess up as a choice.

Hover
On a key: what it changes, what it defaults to, what it accepts, and the release it arrived in.
Ghost text
Only where the answer is certain — the documented default for a value left empty, or the one continuation a key prefix admits. Anything less belongs in the popup, where the alternatives show.
Squiggles
For the three things that are true by construction — below.

title: The version is the interesting part
text:
Bennu reads the version out of your poms — the parent chain, the ${…} properties and
<dependencyManagement> folded in, so a version pinned in a parent or imported from a BOM counts — and offers only the
keys that version has:

• On Lombok 1.16 you are not shown lombok.addNullAnnotations.

• On JUnit 5.2 the whole junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.* block is absent, because it arrived in 5.3.

That is the common case on a real tree — Lombok through a starter, a Gradle build with no pom, a corporate parent this machine never
fetched — and the safe direction: a key too many, never a key missing from a project that has it. The tables follow the same rule: a key
is dated only where the release that introduced it is certain.

title: What is flagged, and what deliberately is not
text:
Flagged — Why

A key your version ignores — It is in the file and looks right, and the tool reads the line and does nothing with it — the failure that costs an afternoon, because nothing else says so.

A deprecated key — With the name of what replaced it.

A value outside a closed set — MAYBE where the key takes CALL, SKIP or WARN. A ${…} placeholder is left alone: what it expands to is somebody else's business.

A decision, not an omission. The tables are the keys worth documenting, not a transcription of every constant a tool defines — so a key
not in them means not written down here, never not understood. A warning under a correct line is the finding people
learn to ignore, and it takes the true ones with it.

title: Lombok
text:
lombok.config is properties syntax with two additions, both understood:

• += and -= add to and remove from a list key — the lombok.copyableAnnotations and
lombok.accessors.prefix shape.

• clear <key> is a statement whose second word is a key, so it completes there too.

The lombok.<feature>.flagUsage family is complete: every feature Lombok can report on, each taking
WARNING, ERROR or ALLOW — the lever for banning a feature a team has decided against. The file
means nothing before Lombok 1.14, which is where the version floor sits.

title: JUnit
text:
junit-platform.properties carries two namespaces on two version lines: junit.jupiter.* belongs to Jupiter
(5.x), junit.platform.* to the Platform (1.x). They are not independent — the release train
ships Platform 1.N with Jupiter 5.N, always — so every version Bennu reports is the Jupiter one,
even for a junit.platform.* key.

The file is found anywhere in the project, in practice src/test/resources. Each of these three files has an icon of its own
in the project tree, so it stands apart from the message bundle beside it.

title: Struts
text:
struts.properties is where a legacy Struts application is configured, and its keys are documented in a
default.properties inside struts2-core.jar that nobody opens. Completion, hover and the version gate work as
above, dated by the struts2-core version the project resolves.

The same constants can be written three ways — here, as <constant name="…"/> in struts.xml, or as an
<init-param> in web.xml. The .properties spelling is the one served, because the XML one
already has a DTD behind it.

Several are what an advisory was about. struts.enable.DynamicMethodInvocation chooses a method from the URL, and was on by
default before 2.5. struts.ognl.allowStaticFieldAccess is the half of static access that survived;
struts.ognl.allowStaticMethodAccess is the half that did not — a value for it does nothing from 2.5, and the hover says so
where it is written. The struts.excluded* deny lists are the ones every release extends, which is why
struts.additional.excludedPatterns exists: it adds to the built-in list where the others replace it.

title: Validation & problems
text: Editor

title: Validation & problems
text: The squiggles that appear while you type, before anything is compiled — what each check looks for, and what it deliberately stays quiet about.

title: Checked as you type
text:
Java files are checked as you type, without compiling: errors are red squiggles, warnings yellow — except a name that resolves to nothing (an unknown variable, method, class, field or import), which is painted red where it is written instead of underlined — and everything is listed in the
Problems panel.

Java, JSP and configuration XML are the files an analyzer understands; a .dig, TOML or SQL buffer is highlighted but not checked. A
language a server serves — Rust, TypeScript, Svelte — is checked by that server, and its results land in the same Problems panel.

It is a best-effort check that complements Build, which runs the real compiler. The compiler's own errors appear in the buffer too,
marked (build) with what javac said — the symbol it could not find, the type it required against the one it found. They describe the file as
the compiler read it, so editing it clears them and live validation covers the file until the next build.

title: The checks
text:
What the compiler would refuse:

• Syntax errorsa malformed statement, a missing ; or brace

• Not a statementlist.clear; — the call's () forgotten — or 1 + 1;

• Unknown method or fieldon the receiver's inferred type, so s.lenght() on a String is caught

• Wrong argument counta call or new matching no overload; varargs understood

• Wrong argument typefoo(1) where foo takes a String — only when a single overload is unambiguous. Generics are invariant: a Page<Dog> is not a Page<Cat> (nor a Page<Animal>), whether it is a variable, the result of a call to a method with no type variable of its own, or passed to a method of the same class

• Unresolved importa type that does not exist; needs the classpath complete

• Unresolved typein a declaration, extends, generics or catch — an annotation counts, and so does a nested type through its outer (below)

• Type incompatibilityan impossible cast, or a value of the wrong type assigned or returned — int x = "1";, int y = "1" + 1;

• Missing or wrong returna non-void method that can finish without returning, a value from a void method, a bare return; where a value is needed

• Inheritanceextending a final class, a record, an enum or an interface; implementing a non-interface; leaving an inherited abstract method unimplemented

• Constructorstwo with one signature, and a subclass constructor that must call super(…) because the superclass has no no-arg one

• Finalreassigning a final that already has a value, or overriding a final method; a final field assigned once across if/else is fine

• Duplicatestwo fields, parameters, locals in a block or types in a scope with one name — and a lambda parameter shadowing a name in scope (a field may be shadowed)

• Unreachable codeafter a line that always returns, throws, breaks or continues

• Switchon long, float, double or boolean, and a switch expression arm that yields nothing

• Case labelsa number or string for an enum selector, a name that is no constant of that enum, a literal of the wrong family on a String or boxed-integer selector

• Lambdasa parameter count not matching the functional interface, or a target that is not one; modifying a captured local inside

• Declarations and modifiersan abstract method in a concrete class, default outside an interface, illegal combinations, an abstract record or one with instance fields, an enum constant needing a constructor

• Misplaced annotations@Override on a field

• File name and packagea public class not matching its file, or a package not matching its folder — with Alt+Enter to set the package or move the file; package-info.java and module-info.java held to their shapes

• Java versiona feature newer than the target level — records, sealed types, var, text blocks, switch arrows, lambdas; a String selector needs 7, yield 14, type patterns, when guards and case null 21; a Lombok var is allowed below 10

• Genericsnew List<String>[], new T(), generics in instanceof or catch, this/super in a static context

• Type argumentsthe wrong count — List<String, Integer>, Map<String>; the diamond, wildcards and raw types are fine

• Erasure clashf(List<String>) beside f(List<Integer>)

• Duplicate interfacelisted twice, or twice with different type arguments

• Cyclic inheritancea type that extends or implements itself, transitively

• @Override overriding nothinga name found nowhere in a fully known hierarchy — usually a signature typo

• super.method()calling a method no superclass has

• Exceptionsan unreachable catch, a multi-catch listing a type with its supertype, a try-with-resources resource that is not AutoCloseable

• Enum switch exhaustivenessa switch expression over an enum missing constants and a default — naming the missing ones

title: Warnings
text:
• Importsunused or duplicate, and a redundant wildcard — import java.lang.*;, or one on the file's own package

• Constructor lookalikea method named like its class — a constructor written with a return type, which Java silently treats as a method

• Suspicious codea variable assigned to itself, a constant division or modulo by zero, strings compared with ==, switch fall-through, a return/break/continue in finally, a stray ;

Details worth knowing:

Static imports
A member brought in with import static and used unqualified — PI, max(a, b) — resolves to its type; a name no static import supplies is still caught.
An annotation's import
@SpringBootApplication with no import is the same "cannot find symbol" — the easiest to leave behind, since the code around it still reads correctly.
A name has to be in scope, not merely to exist

Four things put a simple name in scope: an import of it, a wildcard over its package, the file's own package, and
java.lang. So String and the throwables need no import, while Set, List and every other
java.util name do — and so does a class of this project that lives in another package, however findable it is elsewhere.
A name none of the four reaches reads as "cannot resolve", and Alt+Enter offers the import.

A class at the left of ::

.map(GComuni::getCodistat) with no such class in scope is "cannot resolve", on the name, like new GComuni(),
and Alt+Enter offers the import. Only a name written like a class is judged — an upper-case initial and a lower-case letter
somewhere — and never one the file also uses as a value, so list::add, this::run, LOGGER::info
and String[]::new stay silent.

A nested type through its outer
Cfg.MyProva where Cfg declares no MyProva is caught, judged only when the qualifier is a type this project declares — so com.acme.Foo and a library's Map.Entry are left as written. Alt+Enter offers the import.
Types
Reference types are compared only between concrete classes, never second-guessing interface or generic code; boxing and widening are allowed. A fluent chain is checked — Optional.ofNullable(repo.kind()).orElse(null) returned as an Integer is caught — unless it is handed a lambda or method reference, whose type Bennu does not infer.

The checks that lean on the standard library and the dependencies — unknown members, argument counts, unresolved types, compatibility, inheritance, lambda
targets — run once a JDK is available and stay silent about anything they cannot resolve with certainty. They never report a false error.

title: While a member does not parse
text:
A file being typed usually has one member that does not parse yet, and the rest is checked normally. The error is charged to the member it landed
in — method, constructor, field, initialiser — and everything outside it is validated as if the file were whole, nested classes below included.

Inside that member you get the syntax error and nothing else: recovery reads what it can as code, so a half-closed string literal would turn its own contents
into a page of undefined symbols. When no member can be blamed — an unbalanced brace at class level, changing what every member below is nested in — the
whole file falls back to its syntax error alone.

title: Data flow
text:
Three checks follow a value through a method rather than reading a declaration:

• a member reached on a local that is definitely null;

• a null check whose answer is already known;

• a value assigned to a local and overwritten before anything reads it.

It reads a method's statements in order and forgets everything at the first branch — an if, a loop, a try, a
switch — and tracks locals only, since another method could change a field between two lines. It misses more than it finds, and
that is the trade: a wrong flow analysis accuses working code of throwing, with no way for the reader to see why.

title: Broken characters
text:
Two encoding checks ride the ordinary validation, in any text file rather than only the ones an
analyzer understands — a message bundle, a code template, a .sql, a README — because they are about bytes
and not about a language. encoding.mojibake flags text that was UTF-8 and got read as Windows-1252, and
carries the correct character as a one-click fix. encoding.undecodable flags a byte that could not be read
at all, and has no fix by nature: the answer is to reload the file in the encoding it is written in. See
Encodings.

title: Turning a check down
text:
Under Project Configuration → Inspections every check has a severity — error, warning,
weak or off. That is a policy over kinds: "this project does not care about unused imports". For one place, the
source says so:

`, 'java')}

The annotation covers the declaration it sits on; the comment covers its own line, or the line below it. A comment naming no code silences
everything on the line it covers. Javac's vocabulary — unused,
fallthrough, all — is honoured where it overlaps, so a legacy file already carrying it need not say it twice.

title: Naming conventions
text:
Declarations can be checked against how they are meant to be spelled, and every name that breaks the rule is flagged. It is
off until you turn it on, per kind of declaration — nothing is assumed about a project that never asked.

It is set at two levels. Settings → Editor → Naming is your answer for every project: adopt a convention once instead of
retyping it into every checkout. Project Configuration → Naming is what one project spells differently — and each row there says whether the
value it shows is the project's or came from your profile, with Back to your profile to hand a language back. A project that must not be judged by your
conventions at all turns Start from your profile off and is read by itself alone.

The two are merged per target rather than per language, so pinning constant in one project keeps your type and method
answers. Never check globs add up — both levels are naming a place that should not be judged — and exceptions apply in order, the project's after yours.

Bennu's own parser

Java

Every declaration is seen, locals and parameters included.

The language server's outline

TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust

Types and their members only — locals and parameters are not in an outline, so those rows are greyed out. The server must be installed.

Pick a convention for each kind — types, methods, fields, constants, parameters, locals, type parameters, enum constants, package segments — or leave it at
any, which checks nothing. Use the standard convention fills in what the community uses — for Java PascalCase types,
camelCase members, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants. The conventions are a fixed list, not patterns you write, and that is what makes the
fix possible: a pattern can refuse a name, a convention can build the right one. Code templates build names with the same conventions — see
Template reference.

A violation is a weak warning — its own level, drawn faintly and grouped apart in Problems. A name breaking a house style is true, but it is not
a defect.

title: Fixing names
text:
Alt+Enter on a name offers Rename to theRightName. A Java local or parameter is renamed straight away, since nothing
outside its file can refer to it. Anything a caller could use — a method, a field, a type, and everything in a server-read language — opens the rename preview
with the name filled in. A rename does not rewrite JSP, OGNL or reflection strings, which is exactly why those fixes ask first.

For more than a couple, Fix naming in file and Fix naming in project in the command palette. They are always there — the
continuous check does not have to be switched on, and no convention has to be configured first.

• The rule. With a convention configured the fix uses it. Without one it uses what the project's code already does, kind by kind — a kind needs
at least eight names that only one spelling fits, and 60% of them agreeing — and the language's standard wherever the code is inconclusive. The review says which it
is (configured, detected or standard), lists the rules with where each came from, and lets you switch between them: choosing another
plans the fix again.

• The review opens at once and fills in as the plan is built, with progress — and a Stop that still hands you what it had.

• Argue with it: group by file, by kind or not at all; switch a kind off or pick it only; untick a group
or a single name; filter by name or file; select all, none or invert. Each row shows the old and the new name with the changed characters marked,
its kind, and how many places it rewrites. The pane under the list shows the declaration line, the files the rename reaches and an editor for the name — type
your own and it is written everywhere (a type's file is renamed to match). Go to declaration steps the review aside and a toast brings it back as it was.
The footer always counts what Apply will do — nothing out of sight is still applied — and the list is windowed, so thousands of names scroll like a handful.

• The Left alone tab lists what the fix will not touch, grouped by reason.

• Apply — a long list asks you to confirm the count first. Nothing was written before, and the whole fix is a single Undo after.

Keyboard: ↑ ↓ move, Space ticks, F2 edits the name, F filters, A / N / I
select all / none / invert, Ctrl+Enter applies, Esc closes.

Two names in a file becoming the same name; a spelling already used there — how a bulk fix turns compiling code into two members with one signature; a method
overriding something from a dependency, whose name a jar fixes; a field or getter whose @JsonProperty, @Column or similar annotation
has no explicit name, so renaming it would change the JSON, XML or column other systems read; a package, whose name is its directory; and a file whose bytes are
not valid in the project's declared encoding, where the editor and the index read it differently. Every refusal is listed with its reason. Names that JSP, OGNL
or reflection reach by string are not detected — that is the case the rename preview exists for.

Never reported: generated code — build output, @Generated, a "do not edit" banner — constructors (their type is reported instead),
@Override methods (the supertype's name), and platform names like serialVersionUID. Add your own path globs under Never check.

A project rarely has one convention, so a subtree can have its own. Under Exceptions, name one, give it path globs, and set the conventions that apply
inside — only those are replaced. Test sources are the usual case: test00_invalid_ragioneSociale mixes camelCase and snake_case on
purpose, and an exception setting method to any under **/src/test/** stops reporting it while keeping the type and constant rules
that Never check would drop. When two exceptions claim a file, the later one wins.

title: Validating the whole project
text:
The checks normally run on the file you are editing. To run them over every .java file at once, in a Maven project:

• Open the chevron of the Build split button.

• Pick Validate (no compile) — or make it the default, so Ctrl+F9 runs it.

• The Build window reports timing — total, average per file, the slowest file with a fast, normal or slow verdict — and every problem lands in
Problems, grouped by file.

Errors decide the verdict; warnings never do. A run with warnings only reads as passed, the counts coloured for what they are — red
errors, yellow warnings, grey when there are none. A build and a validation cannot run at the same time.

Cached
Each file's result is kept against the exact project types it depends on, so an unchanged project validates instantly again, and after an edit only the changed file — and whatever its types touched — is checked.
Warmed up
The cache fills in the background right after indexing, so the first validation is already instant. Settings → Java → Validate project on open turns that off.
It shows as Analyzing project in the Jobs panel, and Cancel there stops it for real — a build or a validation of the same project waits for it, so a pass that is too slow is not something to sit behind.
A validation that has waited more than five minutes for it gives up and says so, rather than staying on Compiling…. If one file stays in validation for more than twenty seconds, the job's output and a notification name it.
A background citizen
At most about half the cores by default, so the editor stays responsive. Settings → Java → Validation CPU threads caps it (1 for single-threaded); its sibling Indexing CPU threads caps the index build and the reference walk, serial by default. Cancel on the "Validating…" status stops a sweep.

title: The Problems panel
text:
A tree grouped by severity — Errors and Warnings at the top, then Weak warnings such as naming
and the informational levels — each split by source: a JDK node, an Encoding node, one node per file. A file with errors and warnings appears under both, with just
that severity's rows, and every node collapses.

• It follows the file you are editing live: a fixed problem disappears, a new one appears, and that file's entry stays right after you switch away.

• Once Validate (no compile) has run, saving refreshes the whole panel quietly — so a fix that resolves an error in a different
file clears there too.

Whatever a language server reports lands here too — rust-analyzer's cargo check, TypeScript's, Svelte's, Angular's on a template —
including for files you have never opened, arriving as each check finishes, with nothing to run or arm.

Only this project's files. A server reports on the whole crate graph it built, which for a path dependency means files of another
repository; those are real and not yours to fix from here, so they are left out — open that project to see them. The same rule drops a registry checkout and, when
a session sits on an outer workspace, that workspace's other members.

The sources are kept apart on purpose: a polyglot repository can have a Java half just validated and a Rust half being checked, and either replacing the other would
make a cargo check quietly erase a validation depending on which finished last.

Machine-generated expressions:

Everything that reasons about types — hover, the checks comparing types, completion after a dot — walks the expression it looks at, and nesting is that
walk's cost. A generated concatenation of thousands of pieces, an unrolled query builder or a generated messages class nests one level per piece.

Bennu stops descending and answers unknown for that expression: its hover says nothing and the type checks skip it — only there. Syntax
checks, the outline, find usages and go-to are unaffected, and hand-written code never reaches the limit: a long fluent chain is tens of levels, not hundreds.

title: Voice
text: Imber

title: Voice
text:
Talk to Imber instead of typing. Speech is turned into text by a model that runs on this computer: the audio is never
recorded to disk and never sent anywhere.

title: Three ways to speak
text:
How — What happens

Microphone button in the message box — Hold it to talk and release to finish, or tap it once to start and again to stop. The text is inserted where the caret is, and with a model that keeps up it appears while you are still talking (see below). Esc, or a click on the spinner, cancels a recording or a transcription in progress.

(hold) — Opens the voice overlay, records while the keys are down and sends the sentence to Imber when you let go. The file and the selected lines are attached exactly as they are when you type.

(tap) — A quick tap leaves the microphone open instead; tap again to stop. The microphone button works the same way.

Wake word — Say “Ehi Imber” or “Hey Imber”, then your request. See below.

title: The voice overlay
text:
The window dims and Imber appears in the middle as a glowing orb that swells and sends out ripples with your voice, above a thin
waveform. Listening… gives way to Transcribing… and Thinking…; what was understood is shown large as you
speak, the words that have just arrived a little dimmer until the next piece settles them, and the file and the selected lines
that go with the request appear as chips. When the sentence ends it is sent to Imber: the orb shrinks into a header and the answer
streams into a card below it, with code and diagrams rendered as in the panel. Typing a follow-up, or choosing
Continue in the panel, closes the overlay and opens the Imber panel on the same conversation. It can be turned off in
Settings › Voice; the answer then simply appears in the panel.

• Enter while listening stops the recording and sends what was said at once. Esc, a click on the dimmed area or the × cancels the recording or the transcription, and closes the overlay once there is an answer.

• Ctrl+Enter in the follow-up field sends it to the panel.

• When nothing was heard the overlay offers Try again; when there is no speech engine, no model or no microphone access it explains what is missing and offers Open Voice settings.

• With animations switched off, or reduced motion requested by the system, the orb, the ripples and the waveform stay still; only fades remain.

title: Choosing a speech model
text:
Settings › Voice lists the models with their size on disk, how fast each will feel on this machine, how accurate it is and which
languages it covers, and the seconds of work it needs per second of speech (estimated from your physical cores, memory and GPU,
and replaced by the real figure once Test it or a dictation has measured it). One is marked Recommended for your PC (hover the badge for the reason): the most accurate one that keeps up with speech, worked out from the cores, the memory and
whether a GPU is used, and from the language you chose: Italian and the other non-English languages never get the two smallest
models, which are poor there. Without a GPU that means Small (or Base for English on a small CPU): the Medium, Large and Turbo
models need many seconds of computing per phrase on a laptop CPU, so they are only recommended with GPU acceleration or when a measurement shows they keep up. The model in use is shown as In use; the first model you download is selected automatically, and choosing another with Use takes effect immediately.

• Download asks first, showing the name, the size, where it comes from and the free disk space. The file is checked against its published SHA-256 before it is used, and appears in the Jobs panel while it downloads.

• Test it records five seconds with that model (the button counts down, then shows Transcribing…; Stop cancels either phase), shows what it understood and the measured speed. The measurement is remembered and corrects the estimates for every model.

• Use my own model file… picks a ggml Whisper file you already have.

title: Text while you speak
text:
With Live text while you speak on (Settings › Voice), a pause of about half a second finishes a piece of speech, which is
transcribed in the background and inserted at once while you keep talking; when you stop, only the last piece is left to transcribe.
Each piece is given the previous text as context. A model that would fall behind your speech on this PC (more than 0.7 s of work per second of
speech) does not do this: the overlay says so and the text appears when you finish. Nothing can hang: every transcription has a time limit
derived from the length of the recording and can be cancelled.

title: Vocabulary hints
text:
With Vocabulary hints on, the project name, the class being edited, the files open next to it and the words in your
selection are given to the recogniser, so names come out spelled right.

title: Memory and CPU
text:
The speech engine is a separate process that starts the first time you use voice and exits after the idle time set in the settings
(five minutes by default); at rest it uses no memory and no CPU. It appears in the processes list with its memory, whether it is
idle or transcribing, and a way to stop it, and each download or transcription is listed as a job.

title: Wake word
text:
While the wake word is armed Arbor listens continuously and uses some CPU. Nothing is recorded to disk and no audio leaves your
computer. A microphone mark in the status bar is shown for as long as it is on; click it to turn it off.

• It is off by default and never arms by itself after a restart. Arm and disarm it from Settings › Voice or the command palette (Voice: arm wake word).

• It listens only while Arbor is the focused application, unless Also when the window is in the background is on, and disarms itself after the number of minutes you set without being used.

• Loudness is checked all the time, which is nearly free. Only when someone speaks does a small speech model look at the first seconds for the phrase, and no more than a few times a minute.

• The phrase is matched loosely, so “hey amber” or “ei imbar” work; it must open the sentence. The list of phrases is yours to change.

• A pause (1.2 seconds by default) ends the request, which then opens the voice overlay like the shortcut does.

title: If it does not work
text:
• No microphone / access denied: Windows — Settings › Privacy & security › Microphone; macOS — System Settings › Privacy & Security › Microphone; Linux — check that PulseAudio or PipeWire exposes an input device to your user.

• “No speech was heard”: nothing loud enough was said; check the microphone in Settings › Voice.

• Slow: choose a smaller model; Test it tells you what to expect. The model marked Live text keeps up with your speech.

• “No model selected” although one is installed: press Use on it; the notice disappears as soon as a model is in use.

title: XML schemas
text: Java & JSP

title: XML schemas
text:
An XML file in a Java project is a configuration language whose vocabulary is written down precisely — in the DTD or XSD the document names — and normally nothing reads
it. Bennu does: open a struts.xml, a web.xml, a pom.xml or a beans.xml, type <, and the elements that
may go there are listed, each with the schema's own description.

title: Where the schema comes from
text:
A document names its schema by URL, and Bennu never fetches it during a scan. It does not have to: frameworks ship their grammar inside their own jar.

Jar — Carries

struts2-core.jar — struts-2.5.dtd

spring-beans.jar — Every spring-beans.xsd ever published

So the file the URL names is already on the machine. Schemas kept in the project are found too, and win over a jar copy of the same name. The Maven POM is the one nobody
ships, so its vocabulary is built in.

title: What you get
text:
Typing

Completion

Elements filtered by what the parent may contain; attributes minus those written; attribute values where the schema closes the set.

When one thing can follow

Ghost text

Never where the rest of the name is already written — most carets, in a document whose closing tags the editor typed for you.

Resting the pointer

Hover

The schema's documentation, the required attributes, and which grammar answered.

Ctrl+B

Go to the declaration

On a tag or an attribute, its declaration in the schema — which turns <result type="…"> from a word into something you can read.

title: Following the schema itself
text:
Ctrl+B on the DOCTYPE or the xsi:schemaLocation opens the grammar the file is actually checked against — the copy out of the
jar, not the address it is written as.

When nobody ships one, Bennu downloads it once and caches it — and the cached copy joins the catalog, so a pom.xml stops being answered by the built-in table and
starts being answered by the real Maven schema. Nothing is ever fetched during a scan, only when you follow the link.

On a machine with no copy of the Struts DTD a struts.xml has no completion, no checks and no hover — and following the address in its DOCTYPE fixes
all three at once. Every other answer here needs a grammar first, so this one is offered with or without.

title: When only another version is on the machine
text:
A legacy struts.xml declares struts-2.1.dtd and the jar ships struts-2.5.dtd — the same schema, a different digit, and a strict name
match resolves nothing. The nearest version answers instead: the newest one at or below what the document asked for — an older schema can only offer less than the
project may write — and the oldest of the newer ones only when there is nothing below. The Schemas list marks it.

Completion and hover from a neighbouring version cost a keystroke when wrong; an underline read off the wrong schema is an accusation about a document that may be correct.

title: The elements a schema insists on
text:
A <servlet> with no <servlet-name>, a Spring <bean> missing what its schema demands, a Struts
<action> without its <result> — the schema already says these are errors, and Bennu reads it and says so.

• The demand must be unambiguous: where the grammar offers a choice — a servlet may name a class or a JSP — neither side is asked for.

• What the schema wraps in an optional group is not asked for either.

Logging configurations:

log4j2.xml and logback.xml are in the same position as the POM — no schema in any jar — so their vocabulary is built in too: the appenders, layouts, filters, policies and loggers
of Log4j2, and the appenders, encoders, rolling policies and loggers of Logback, with each element's attributes (the required ones marked) and the values the closed ones take — a level, ACCEPT /
DENY / NEUTRAL, true / false. Both are plugin systems, so a table of what ships can never be the whole vocabulary: these grammars complete and explain, and
never underline — an appender of your own is not an error.

The conversion patterns in these files are coloured as the small language they are — in a pattern="…", a filePattern, a Logback <pattern> or <fileNamePattern>, and Log4j 1.x's
ConversionPattern. Each % conversion takes the hue of what it prints (the date, the level, the logger, the thread, the message, an MDC value) — the same ones the console uses for those columns, so a pattern and
the line it produces read alike — its {options} are quieter, the newline and the exception are dimmed, and a ${property} is marked as the substitution it is. %highlight{…}, %style{…} and
Logback's %highlight(…) are looked through, so the conversion inside them keeps its own colour.

title: The POM's required fields
text:
A <dependency> with no <artifactId>, a <parent> without its version, a root POM that never says who it is — Maven
refuses to build them all, and being told at build time is what this is here to stop. The conditional ones are honoured:

• <groupId> and <version> are required only when the POM has no <parent>.

• A missing <version> on a dependency or a plugin is never reported — it may come from <dependencyManagement> or a parent this file cannot see.

title: What it will not do
text:
• Check how many of something is legal, or what belongs in an element's text.

• Say anything without a schema: no grammar means no completion, no ghost text, no warnings — a vocabulary guessed from the tags already there would propose whatever typo
is already there.

• Check inside content the schema leaves open — ANY, xs:any, a POM <configuration>.

A document mixing four namespaces usually has schemas for one of them, and the rest must be invisible rather than wrong. An element containing a prefixed child is left
alone too, since the namespace nobody can read here may supply exactly what looks missing.

page: Members that do not exist yet
title: Members that do not exist yet
text: Completion

page: Members that do not exist yet
title: Members that do not exist yet
text: Members written nowhere in the source: the ones you are about to create, and the ones the compiler or Lombok generate.

page: Members that do not exist yet
title: Members that do not exist yet
text:
Two families, one gesture: you are in a class body, you start typing a name, and the thing you mean has not been written.

The method this class calls and does not declare:

You wrote randomico() inside a method; now rand in the class body offers to declare it. The call site is the
specification: the arguments' types and names become the signature, what the result is used as becomes the return type, and a call from a
static method asks for a static one — the reading the Create method quick fix makes, so the popup and
Alt+Enter cannot describe one member two ways.

• It is read from the tree, not from the diagnostic — which is what survives typing. A half-written name in a class body is a syntax
error, and while it lasts its member is not validated, so the red mark under randomico() disappears exactly when the offer is wanted.
The call is still in the tree.

• It reads the calls made on this class from elsewhere in the file, which a nested class needs:
c.randomico("ciao") written in the outer class, on an instance of the inner one, makes ra in the inner class offer it — as
public, since another class calls it. Only a receiver whose type resolves to the class you are in counts.

• A method reference asks as surely as a call: after .map(this::toIdentity), toId in the class body offers
toIdentity with the signature of the functional interface it is passed as — and draws it as ghost text when it is the only
match.

• A method the class inherits is not missing: the supertypes are walked first, and an unreadable hierarchy means silence.

page: Members that do not exist yet
title: The accessors a field is missing
text:
Typing getCust in a class body offers getCustomer(), and accepting writes the whole method:

`, 'java')}

• getXor isX for a primitive boolean — what JavaBeans says and what reflecting frameworks look for

• setXwith this. on the assignment: the parameter shadows the field

• withXthe builder-style setter, assigning and returning the object so calls chain — the member Generate writes under "With"

A final field is offered a getter and nothing else; a static one no withX, with no this to return.
A field named isActive keeps its prefix and is set and chained by its property: setActive, withActive.

As ghost text
When exactly one candidate matches, the answer also appears ahead of the caret — → public String getCustomer() { … } — written with Tab. Two candidates produce nothing, however close the second: ghost text reads like text already there, so being wrong costs trust.
In the open popup
The grey text previews the highlighted row, following the arrows — on one line, since the popup opens right under the caret. It is the popup's selection drawn, not a second proposal: Tab still belongs to the popup.
With the popup closed
After Esc, or with the auto-popup off, the proposal is drawn in full, and Tab writes it.

Only at a member position — not in a method body, where getCustomer is a call, and not after a dot; only for a field
with no accessor already; and never on an empty prefix. Generate (Alt+Insert) is still the
place for the whole set, with the style options — fluent accessors, snake_case names, final parameters. A completion takes the
conventional form.

page: Members that do not exist yet
title: Arguments and the editor's closing parenthesis
text:
The closing ) the editor adds when you type ( does not silence the ghost text: @PostMapping(value = |)
and foo(a, |) are completed and the parenthesis stays where it is. Inside an annotation, value = is completed with the
value the project writes for that element. After you pick a method from the list, its arguments follow the overload you picked. list.toArray(
draws Item[]::new when the list's element type is known, and where the project passes several different lambdas or constants to
a method, the start they share (it -> , Boolean.) is drawn.

Where an argument or a declaration fixes a class, the ghost text writes how the code makes one: a method of the same file that returns it
(tabellato(), otherwise a static factory (Pair.of(, List.of(), otherwise new Foo(.
A generic parameter is settled from the arguments already written and from what the call around it wants: after
Collections.addAll(items, the ghost text draws the element type of items (Pair.of(), and inside that call
the type its second argument must have (List.of().

After a comma, if the element before it is a call, the same call is drawn again with its string literals emptied and a number held in a
string counted up: tabellato("1", "ITALIA"), → tabellato("2", "").

page: Members that do not exist yet
title: Generated members
text:
Plenty of Java members exist at compile time and nowhere in the source. Bennu models them, so completion, hover, find usages and the checks treat
them like any declaration.

From the language

Records

An accessor per component — p.x(), not getX() — the backing fields, the canonical constructor, and toString, equals, hashCode. A member the record writes itself always wins.

When the file imports Lombok

Lombok

@Getter, @Setter, @Data, @Value accessors, @With copies, the @Slf4j log, the @AllArgsConstructor and @RequiredArgsConstructor constructors — on an enum with valued constants too — and @UtilityClass, making every member static and the class final.

That is what makes the annotation mean anything — your own @Data in another package generates nothing. A record's members need no such gate.

@Accessors
At class or field level, the field's winning: fluent = true names both accessors after the field — o.customer() reads, o.customer("x") writes — and chain = true, which fluent turns on by itself, makes the setter return the object. The prefix element is not read yet.
AccessLevel
On @Getter and @Setter, at class or field level: @Setter(AccessLevel.PACKAGE) is a package-private setter; AccessLevel.NONE generates nothing. Generated constructors carry their access the same way, with the parameters Lombok gives them — @RequiredArgsConstructor takes the unassigned final fields and the @NonNull ones.
@Builder
The class it really generates: the static builder(), a setter per field returning the builder, build(), and with toBuilder = true the instance toBuilder(). @Singular adds the single-element adder — .tag("a"), named from the field or @Singular("tag") — and clearTags(). A @Builder.Default field is still a constructor parameter. On a constructor or a static factory, the builder takes that element's parameters, is named after what it builds, and build() returns that.
@Value, @FieldDefaults
@Value makes the fields private final and the class final, though the source writes none of it. @FieldDefaults(makeFinal = true, level = …) does the same, with @NonFinal and @PackagePrivate honoured.
@Delegate, @SuperBuilder
Their members depend on a type that cannot be read while indexing, so the type is marked as having more members than the list — nothing concludes "no such method" from their absence, and the rest of it is checked as before.

A primitive boolean field already starting with is keeps it, as Lombok does:

Field — Getter — Setter

boolean isRunning — isRunning() — setRunning(…)

boolean is_attivo — is_attivo() — —

boolean isattivo — isIsattivo() — what follows is is lowercase — —

Boolean active — getActive() — a wrapper is a plain getter — —

There is no name in the source to jump to, so it has nothing to open. Go-to on the backing field, or a record's component, works.

page: The order things are offered in
title: The order things are offered in
text: Completion

page: The order things are offered in
title: The order things are offered in
text:
What comes first, and why: eight signals, strongest first.

What comes first is worked out from what the engine already knows, and it decides most of what completion feels like. Strongest first:

• What the position wants. The only term about the hole rather than the candidate. In
String name = order. there are forty members on order and a handful that can be written there — and nothing
about order says which, because the constraint is left of the =. It is read from a declaration with a written
type, an assignment to something typed, a return — a lambda's too — and a condition, which wants a boolean and
turns a member list into its predicates. The exact type comes before a subtype, and the only exact match is preselected: return Ra
in a method returning RawIdentity opens on RawIdentity, return builder. on build(), a bare
return on the local or field of that type. With a generic return, Optional<RawIdentity>, the element type follows
the outer one. A void method sinks where a value is wanted. It ranks, never filters: hiding the misses would hide the
right answer whenever the type is not the one expected.

• Who declares it. After a dot, what the receiver's own type declares comes first, then what it inherits — the nearest
supertype first — then java.lang.Object's, last. A record's components come before the equals,
hashCode and toString the compiler writes for it. Only the position's type and how literally your letters match
come before this: route. opens on prefix(), preselected, while route.to still offers
toString above a declared targetOrigin.

• What you picked last time. A fact about you, not the code: on a List you reach for stream,
not listIterator. Kept per declaring type, so what is learned about java.util.List carries to every
receiver inheriting it. Frequency and recency both count, so a fresh choice can overtake an old habit and one stray pick cannot bury a
