name you use constantly. It lives for the session and is never written to disk — a persisted ranking that drifted would be invisible.

• What the receiver is. After a type — Color. — the statics are the answer and a constant goes to
the very top, instance members to the bottom. Through a value — color. — the other way round, more gently: a
static through an instance compiles, it is just rarely meant. After a type the popup also offers class — Order.class
— which no class declares but every type has; where a Class<…> is wanted it ranks first. The same goes for what the
language gives without declaring it: an array offers length and clone() (and the methods of Object,
not those of its element type); a class name you are inside of offers this and super
(Outer.this), and a direct superinterface offers super (Iface.super.run()); and
new Foo( on a class with no constructors shows the empty one. Inside a lambda, an argument that nothing of a known
type fits is drawn as the lambda's own parameter (x -> tag( → x); a parameter starting with
_ is never used.

• Deprecated. Still offered, since you may be reading old code, but last — on your own source, since library members
carry no annotations in compiled form.

• What this file already uses. A name already in the buffer is likely wanted again. It decides between otherwise-equal
candidates, and cannot do more.

• The name being filled. String customerName = c. has three String members and the alphabet puts
email first; the declaration says name. A candidate whose words echo the hole's rise — getName reads as
name, orders as order, a shared tail or head counts less than the whole name. In an argument slot the
hole is named by the callee: findByCustomerId( lifts customerId.

• What the project does. How often the project calls each method, and which method it calls after the previous one in
the chain — close() after open(), on the same variable even when the calls are statements apart. Counted while
the index builds, as a band (each step a doubling, a name used once counts for nothing), never written to disk.

The last two, and the shape of the code below, are Smart suggestions in Settings → Completion: each is a switch, and a
strength scales the learned ones. They only add to a score — nothing is hidden — and none can overrule the type the position wants.

At the start of a call argument the list is then reordered once more by a small model fitted offline on public code. It reads where the
list put each row, what kind of row it is, how recently this file used the name, how much the name echoes the parameter's own, and whether its
type is the parameter's. It only reorders: nothing is hidden or added, a habit that leads the list keeps its place, and it follows the same
switch as the learned picks. Nothing is learned on your machine by it.

title: Positions with their own rules
text: Completion

title: Positions with their own rules
text: After a dot, in arguments, in annotation values, in a declaration: what each position offers.

title: After a dot
text:
The list is the members of the value on the left, and its postfix templates — nothing else: no keywords, no words from the file, no local names. When
the value's type cannot be worked out, the popup says there are no suggestions rather than offering what cannot follow a dot.

title: Method references
text:
After Type:: or value:: the list is the methods a reference can name, and new for a class that can be
instantiated. The ones that fit the function expected there come first — in optional.map(ResolvedIdentity::|), the instance methods with
no parameters and the static methods taking a ResolvedIdentity — and accepting one writes only the name.

title: Functions passed as arguments
text:
Inside a call that takes a function, the type the function receives is offered first: in identity_resolver.resolve_identity().map(|) it
is ResolvedIdentity, the value inside the Optional. Ctrl+Space with nothing typed opens on it,
preselected, with its import.

title: A builder does not repeat itself
text:
After Device.builder().name("a"). the methods the chain has already called, and that return the same type (the fluent setters), move to the end of
the list: id, type and build come first. Nothing is removed, and with a prefix typed the order is the usual one.

title: Annotation values and configuration keys
text:
Inside an annotation's parentheses the list opens on the values the other files write for that element (produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,
"/orders"), most used first. Inside @Value("${…"), @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "…") and
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "…") it offers the keys of application*.properties|yml|yaml and bootstrap*, nested YAML
flattened with dots, the nearest module's first. The first request in a session may find nothing while the project is read once in the background.

title: Mapping two classes
text:
In a method that copies one object into another, the empty line after the construction or after a mapping line offers the next property of the target that no line
assigned yet, taken from the source by name and type (equal, equal ignoring case, _ and plurals, or id against customerId) and written in the
style the lines above use (d.setX(e.getX()); or .x(e.getX())). A type that would need a conversion, or two sources that fit equally, are left to you.

title: The class an argument takes
text:
In service.list(C|) the type names open on the class the parameter takes, preselected, with its import, ahead of names that merely start alike. When overloads
disagree about the slot, the usual order stands. After EnumType.TI| the constants that share a word with the names around the caret rise above the others.

title: The constants of the class a position wants
text:
Where the code wants a class — Money m = |, a parameter of that class — its constants and no-argument static factories (Money.ZERO, Money.zero(),
Optional.empty()) are offered first, with their import. Only members that return exactly that class; String, the boxed types and Object are left out, and an enum has its own list below.

title: An argument that takes an enum
text:
When the call has one overload at that position (a builder's type(|)), its parameter is the enum and the list opens on that enum's
constants, written DeviceType.PIN with their import. Each constant is split into words (TIPO_PIN → tipo,
pin, the enum's own name left out) and compared with the words around the caret: a field called pin in the file or
a method connectPin puts PIN first, preselected when it is the only best fit. Overloads that disagree offer no constants.
The same holds wherever the surrounding code fixes the enum: the other side of == / !=, a ternary branch, an array element, equals(…),
List.of(…), a declared variable's initializer and a constructor argument. In a case label the constants appear bare, without those an earlier label already names.

title: Keywords by position
text:
The language's keywords are offered by position: at the start of a statement the statement words (return first in a method that returns a value, after if/for/while
in one that does not), in a class body the member modifiers, at the top of the file package, import and the type declarations, and after = or ( only the words an
expression can start with. else, catch and finally appear only right after the block they continue.

title: Arguments by type and by name
text:
In transfer(|) the parameters, locals and fields of the class whose type fits the slot come first, those whose name looks like the
parameter's own name before the others (from leads the slot called from), and a clear winner is preselected. When
overloads disagree about the slot, or after a ., the list is the usual one.

title: A declaration's name
text:
After the type of a declaration — a field after its modifiers, a local variable, a method or constructor parameter, a for or
try resource — the name IntelliJ would suggest is drawn ahead of the caret, and Tab writes it:

Written — Suggested

private final OrderRepository — orderRepository

List<Order> , Order[] — orders

Optional<Order> — order

Class<?> — clazz

The name is spelled the project's way: with the convention its naming rules set for fields, local variables or parameters, and where they set none,
with the one the file's names already follow — among identity_resolver fields, private final FilterConfigurator suggests
filter_configurator.

A name already declared where Java would refuse a second one gets a digit (order1). Once you start typing the name, the suggestion stays
only while it continues what you typed. It never appears after return, new or an operator, inside arguments, strings or
comments, or in a class header.

title: Smart suggestions and ghost text
text: Completion

title: Smart suggestions and ghost text
text: The learned and project-aware signals, the rest of the line drawn in grey, and the type names that bring their import.

title: Smart suggestions
text:
Chains
When the position wants a type, members of members that produce it are offered below the direct fits: String name = order. also
lists getCustomer().getName(). Zero-argument calls only, one level deep, through your own classes; a member that already
fits is not chained through, and a call that is already written gets none.
Builders
A setter already called in the chain sinks: after Order.builder().customer(c). the next property or build() leads, not
customer again.
Unused locals
A local declared and not used yet rises: it is very probably what comes next.
catch (
The exceptions the try above can throw come first — from throw new and from the throws clause of each call it
makes (the first few calls; one that cannot be bound to a single overload says nothing). A multi-catch leaves out the alternatives it
already lists, and a second catch reads the same try.

Keywords come below anything the index resolved. Words scraped from the buffer are offered only when the index answered nothing —
before it finished building, or in a file no project owns: they are a regular expression over the text, and beside resolved names they bury
them under look-alikes. How well what you typed matches still decides between neighbours.

title: Finishing the line
text:
Beside the popup, Bennu can draw the rest of the line in grey after the caret: Tab writes it, Esc dismisses it.
It has several sources, and all but the last need no model.

A constructor
Type public Order( in a class with fields and the whole constructor is drawn: the parameters, the closing parenthesis and a body that assigns each
one. It takes the instance fields that have no value — not static ones, not a final field that already has one — and it is not offered when the class
already has a constructor with that many parameters or when the name is not the class's own. It is written from the class, not guessed, so it needs no model.
A block of several lines can be taken one line at a time: Ctrl+→ (Cmd+→ on macOS) writes the
first line and keeps the rest drawn; Tab writes what is left. The closing parenthesis the editor added with the ( is overwritten.
equals, hashCode, toString
Type public boolean equals(, public int hashCode( or public String toString( and the method is drawn from the instance fields: == for
primitives, Double.compare and Float.compare for floating point, Arrays.equals for arrays and Objects.equals for the rest, with
transient fields left out of the first two. A class that declares the method already gets nothing, and so does one without fields. Objects and
Arrays are written short when the file imports them, and as java.util.Objects when it does not, so the block compiles as it is. A long expression breaks between
fields, before an operator.
Methods the class owes its supertypes
Start the name of a method the class has to implement or may override — compa, int compareTo( — and the whole declaration is drawn, @Override
above and a body that compiles (return 0;, null, nothing for void). The list is the one behind Implement / override methods; abstract
methods come first, a method that is only overridable needs its full name, and one the class already declares is not offered again. A method whose types the file would need an
import for is left to that dialog.
A test for a method
In OrderTest, start total, testTotal or void total and a @Test method is drawn that builds an Order and calls
total() with the default of each parameter's type. The class under test is the one the file name points to under src/main/java; the assertions are yours. Private
methods and tests already written are not offered.
Lines copied from the project
Every line the project's files hold is counted at each word start, as the last few words before it and what followed them. When you reach the same words, the rest of the line most often written after them is drawn, with the share of the sightings as its confidence. It needs the words seen at least twice, and below half of the sightings nothing is drawn. A strong share (70% or more) goes before the model; a weak one is only used when the model has no answer. When no ending is sure but most sightings start alike, only the words they agree on are drawn (findBy and not the arguments), at least two of them and with at least 70% agreeing. Lines under 25 characters, imports and comments are not counted. Forget what Bennu learned empties it. Copy lines from the project in Settings › Completion › Ghost text switches it off.
Small layers you can switch off
Four layers have a switch each in Settings › Completion › Ghost text: Suggest variable names (on: after a type, Order ▌ becomes order), Suggest usual arguments (on), Suggest creation arguments and Repeat list items
(both off by default: measured on public projects, fewer than one suggestion in ten was useful to the person typing). Switch one to change it.
Getter and setter bodies
On the empty line under public String getName() { the body is drawn from the field of the same name and type — return name; — and under public void setName(String name) { it is this.name = name; (and return this; for a setter that returns the class). The style, this.x or x, is the one the file's other accessors use. Without such a field, or with a static one, a field of another type or an array, nothing is drawn.
The assignment a constructor is missing
Add a field and a parameter of the same name to a constructor and, on an empty line in its body, this.field = field; is drawn for the first field the body does not set yet. A field with a value, a static one and a parameter with no field by its name are left alone.
The function a call takes
At users.stream().map( the function the project usually passes to that call is drawn — User::getName, or u -> u.getName() if that is how it writes it — for the type the index knows the function receives. Both must agree: the method has to exist on that type, and the project has to have passed it to that call at least twice and in at least 40% of the cases among that type's methods.
What a test checks
In a test file, on the empty line under a local variable, the assertion the project's tests write under such a variable is drawn up to the value you have to supply: assertThat(total).isEqualTo(. It needs the same shape at least three times and at least half of the assertions that follow a declaration.
Handling an exception
On the empty line after catch (SQLException e) { the statement this project usually writes first for that exception is drawn, with the variable's name taken from the block in front of you:
throw new DataAccessException("failed", e);. It needs the same handling at least three times and at least 60% of the catches of that type. An empty catch teaches nothing, and a multi-catch has no one type, so neither is counted.
Log statements
The project's log calls are counted once, in the background, as a counter per pattern — never a list of the calls. A pattern is the level
plus a template in which the logger, the method's name and parameters, and the caught exception are slots, and a counter is kept for the three
places a log goes: the first statement of a method, inside a catch, anywhere else. Start a log call and, when one pattern clearly leads
its place, the rest of the statement is drawn with the slots filled from your method: log.debug("START - rename({}, {})", from, to);.
A project with no house style gets nothing. A saved file replaces its own contribution, so counters follow the code. The counters are saved in your Arbor data folder (templates and logger names only, never source) and updated when .java files change on disk while the project tree is open.
Lines the project repeats
Lines that at least two files write alike are remembered (the text of those only, in memory, never on disk). When the start of your line is
one that other files all finish the same way — at least two files, and four in five of the continuations agree — the rest is drawn from them,
ahead of the model: return repository.findOr ends the way the project always ends it. Your own file does not count in its own favour,
and a saved file replaces what it contributed. It is part of the same switches as the log statements and the model.
The body of a sibling method
After the { of a method (or on the empty line below it), if another method has a similar name and the same parameters, its body is drawn with the words that differ replaced
(findByCodiceCliente → findByCodiceFornitore, in names, parameters and types). It is held in memory only and never saved. If the new body would use a name that
exists nowhere in the project, it is not drawn.
The next statement of a method
On the empty line inside a method that already has a statement, the next one is drawn from the methods of the open project that begin the same way and have a similar signature — the same shape of statement, names and values aside —
with their names changed to yours: parameters by position, locals by order of declaration, the other names chosen among your parameters, locals and fields. It is drawn only when at least seven in ten of those methods agree on the shape of what comes next
(from the third statement on, the shape most often seen after the last three decides), and not when it would read a variable you do not have. It learns only from the project that is open, is held in memory and is never saved.
Annotations the project always writes
At the start of a member, after @PostMapping(, the arguments the project writes for that annotation are drawn (the text of the strings left empty), without the elements you already typed; on the empty line under an annotation, the annotation that usually comes next is drawn in the layout the project uses. Held in memory only, never saved, and only when at least three uses agree to the tune of 60%.
The usual argument
In a call's parentheses, when other files always pass the same argument at that place (at least three, and most of them), its text is drawn after the caret, or completes what you have typed
(filter(Boo → Boolean.FALSE::equals), and the completion list puts it first. A local variable or parameter inside the argument is not part of the habit: new Factory().create(v1) and new Factory().create(v2) are counted as one, new Factory().create($0:Order) (the slot is the variable's declared type), and drawn with the nearest variable in scope of that type; with none, nothing is drawn. The What Bennu has learned window shows the template, and hiding a row hides the template. Held in memory only, never saved. Where the parameter is a type variable (.field(helper( with <T> Matcher<T> helper(T value)), the call around it decides what T is: a usual argument of another type (a constant of the wrong enum) is not offered, and when nothing settles T it is drawn fainter and listed after the other rows.
What you pick
After a type (list.) or in an argument of a call, the entries you chose at least twice there are put first in the list, the one you chose most often preselected when it was at least three picks and half of them.
Only the names and the counts are kept, in your Arbor data folder; the switch is Count how often suggestions are taken, and Forget deletes them.
What Bennu remembers
Argument habits, annotation shapes and variable names are saved per project in your Arbor data folder (short pieces of code, never in a repository, never sent anywhere), and where a project has seen too little they
can be borrowed from your other projects. Two switches in Settings → Completion turn the two parts off, and Forget deletes everything. Where two variables fit an argument equally, the one your project usually passes
at that place is drawn.
One name, any case
The type a project creates under a variable name and the statement that follows another are counted by the words of the name, so jaxbProcessor,
jaxb_processor, JaxbProcessor and JAXB_PROCESSOR are one name: what is learned in a file written one way helps in another written the other way.
The page of what Bennu has learned lists such a name once, as its words joined by underscores.
Argument lists
Right after the ( of a call, the arguments are drawn all at once when each parameter has a clear match among the names in scope (same type, a name like the
parameter's, or the only name of that type) or a clear constant of its enum. A parameter nothing in scope fits gets a value that merely compiles (null, 0, false, "") as long as at least one other parameter has a real match. When several names fit a parameter equally (two variables of the same type, a parameter that resembles neither), the one declared first is drawn as a guess. With the editor's own ) already
there, only the arguments are drawn.
The local model
A small model that runs on your machine, in the background, and answers nothing while it is busy or still loading. After a . it is
constrained to the member names the index offers there, so it cannot invent one. It is a guess, so it is off until you turn it on.
It stays silent after a finished annotation, statement or block, and a line that is only a type (Order, final List<Item>)
gets a variable name (order, items) instead of a call. A line that names a type, method or variable the file and
project do not have, a ternary, or a continuation that is not a real word is thrown away, and a missing space after =, return or if is added.
The word you are typing is not shown to the model but forced as the start of its answer, so a half-typed word does not confuse it,
and a new line under an unfinished call chain (a builder) gets the next step without typing anything.
A declaration is never offered where an argument goes, and a member the receiver does not have (a builder method after
.build(), a method an && operand does not have) is checked against the index: the suggestion is cut before it, or dropped.
While the model writes a chain, the name after each dot is limited to what the receiver written so far has, so a method that does not exist is not written in the first place.
While the completion list is open, the selected row shows what it adds in grey, so a list with one obvious row still shows its outcome.

Settings → Completion → Model suggestions has the switch, the folder with the model files (a personal copy there gives you a model
adapted to your own code), how sure the model has to be before it is drawn, a switch for the log statements, Count how often suggestions are taken (only how many suggestions of each kind were shown, taken with Tab and dismissed, per confidence level, in your profile; no code is stored and nothing is sent: when the model's suggestions are taken at least half the time above some confidence, the page offers that value and changes it only when you press the button), What Bennu has learned… (command palette, or the Open… button in Settings › Completion › Learning) lists what the completion counted and lets you stop offering a row or forget a counter of your own. Where a parameter is a Class<T> the list opens on the usual classes already written as String.class, and on the project's implementors where T is bounded; after a comma, the remaining arguments are drawn by their types. Where a call always takes a call on some variable (new ByteArrayInputStream(bao.toByteArray())), the ghost text draws it with the nearest variable in scope that has that method. On an empty line, after a statement the project always follows the same way, the start of the usual next call is drawn (jaxb_processor.marshal(); only the start, since the arguments are filled by the other layers. Remember what Bennu learned in each project also lets suggestions follow how the project is laid out: the space after if/for, before a brace and after a comma are measured from its files and used where the project is consistent, never inside string literals. Ignore commented-out code (off by default: blocks of code in // lines are left out of what the model reads, so it does not copy a version you commented out; explanations in comments are still read), Where a project creates the same type under a name nearly every time (bao is always a ByteArrayOutputStream), writing val bao draws the rest of the statement, and the popup after new lists that type first; it is listed under Types by variable name in What Bennu has learned…. Learn from corrections (off by default: after you take a suggestion it notes whether you left it, cut its tail, wrote on, changed a part, only re-lay it out — spaces, line breaks, indentation, which is not a change of content — or took it back, once you have moved on; a part you change and put back as it was counts as left alone; counters per kind of suggestion, in your profile, nothing sent; a kind you rarely keep is drawn with up to a third less confidence, so it shows less often — a suggestion you take and then remove whole is not counted against it, since going another way is not the suggestion being wrong, while one you never take is; Keep the text too adds a log of the texts capped at 1 MB; Notify when it learns shows each counted correction as a notification, with the kind of suggestion, where, what happened and how many of that kind were seen — for checking what is learned; Forget deletes both), Check with Bennu (the model's line is run through the code checks of the method you are in and dropped when it calls a method the receiver does not have, passes the wrong arguments or uses a variable that does not exist; a class you have not imported yet does not count against it, nor does a statement that is not finished), and Try three candidates: the model
gives three answers and the first that passes the checks is drawn, instead of nothing when its only answer fails. It is several times slower (about 280 ms against 60 in the lab), so it is off by default. The palette has
Model suggestions: turn on / off.

title: Type names
text:
A simple name usually resolves to several types, so type names get two terms of their own:

What this file has said
Nothing outranks it: a type the file imports, then a package it wildcard-imports, then its own package, which needs no import.
Accepting a type name imports it

With Auto-import on accept on, the import is added when you accept a type name from the list — after new, in a
declaration, a generic, a cast, an annotation, a catch, a throws — and a single Ctrl+Z
takes back the name and the import together. A name several packages share is imported when the ranking above has a clear winner and the
file reaches none of them yet; on a tie nothing is imported and Alt+Enter asks which.

What the project imports
Every import in the codebase is somebody choosing a candidate, and the aggregate predicts the next choice. It is weighed against distance — the nearest package by shared prefix, so a sibling beats a cousin — with the JDK ahead of the rest of the classpath, because a name matching both a JDK type and something in a jar you never opened is almost always the JDK one.

The two are weighed, not ordered, and the balance is the point: java.util.List imported in four hundred files beats an
it.acme.model.List nobody imports, though the second is nearer. A type imported once beats nothing — that is a
coincidence, not evidence.

Settings → Completion → Order type names by what this project imports switches the second term off at once. What the file
itself imports still comes first — that was never a statistic.

title: Where the import counts come from
text:
They are counted while the index builds, in the pass that already parses every file — one lookup per import
line. Nothing is written to disk: a saved copy would go stale, and a project that dropped a library would go on recommending it with nothing
saying why. They are not updated as you type either — whether a codebase uses java.util.List does not change because you saved
a file, and an order shifting under you would be worse than one a rebuild behind. They refresh with the index.

A count is used as a band: each step a doubling, stopping at 128. Four imports against eight is real; four hundred against
eight hundred is not, and a ranking that pretended otherwise would pin one ubiquitous type to the top for ever. A wildcard counts for the whole
package, one band weaker.

title: Animated popup and ghost text
text:
Settings → Completion → Animate the popup and ghost text (off by default) fades the list in when it opens and uncovers ghost text
from left to right as it appears. The text is whole from the first instant, so Tab takes the entire line even halfway through.
Typing along a proposal shortens it without replaying the effect. It follows the app's animation setting and does nothing when animations are off.

title: Ghost text for certain continuations
text:
Beside the accessors above, two more continuations are drawn ahead of the caret, because each can only be one thing. Tab writes it;
anything else you type replaces it, and when there is any doubt nothing is drawn. Settings → Completion → Ghost text for certain
continuations turns both off.

A caught exception's name
catch (IOException draws e, spelled the project's way, and e1 when e is already in scope —
a catch parameter may not shadow a local. Qualified types, final and a multi-catch are read; nothing is drawn once a name is started.
The next case
On an empty line after the last arm of a switch over an enum, the first constant not yet covered, in declaration order, written in the
style of the arms already there (case X: or case X ->). Not drawn when there is a default, a pattern or
null label, an arm that falls through, or a selector whose enum cannot be read.

title: Annotations, abbreviations and postfix
text: Completion

title: Annotations, abbreviations and postfix
text: Names that expand into code: annotations, your own abbreviations, and postfix templates.

title: Annotations
text:
Typing @ opens the popup on its own, with annotation types only — from every type on the classpath to
the few hundred annotations on it, so the list is short and nearly always holds the answer.

• It narrows again from where the caret is: above a field, one whose @Target only allows a method sorts below the ones that belong
there. Ranked, not hidden — an annotation from unread bytes reports no target, and reading that as a refusal would hide it.

• The list is complete from the first letter: what is capped is how many annotations are offered, not how many names are looked
at, so @S reaches SuppressWarnings past the hundreds of classes also starting with S.

• Accepting one adds its import, and the ones you accept come first for as long as the project stays open — never written to disk, never above an
import the file already made.

title: Abbreviations
text:
Type psf and the list offers public static final, with psfi and psfs under it for
int and String. These are IntelliJ's own Java abbreviations, deliberately — fifteen years of psf should work
here without configuring anything.

Family — Abbreviations

Modifiers — pf, prf, psf, psfi,psfs, prsf, prsfi, prsfs, psvm for a main

Printing — sout, souf, serr

Statements — fori, ifn, inn, thr, iter

• Several blanks are walked with Tab, and the body is re-indented to where it lands — a psvm three levels
into a class arrives lined up.

• They are added to what the index found, never substituted: a field called psfCount still appears, under them.

• Offered only where a bare word is typed — after a . the list answers "what members does this have".

• Abbreviations of your own sit beside them, written as code templates — see Code templates.
Yours are not Java's: the language in a template's name says where it is offered, so a dbg.rs.jinja
expands in a Rust file, answered by rust-analyzer, and one written with no language expands in any file. The
built-in family above stays Java's.

iter is the one that reads the surrounding code: it loops over the nearest array or Iterable local or parameter
in scope, with the element type and a name spelled the project's way (var from Java 10). It is offered only where such a variable
exists, at the start of a statement, and its row says which variable it loops over.

Abbreviations that would have to guess — a version that guesses writes a name that is not there. iter is offered only when
there is something to iterate.

title: Postfix templates
text:
Write the expression first, then say what to do with it:

`, 'java')}

The point is not keystrokes: it lets you think in the order you think — the value, then the control flow around it — instead of committing to an
if ( before you know what goes in it. They appear in the completion list under the name you type, with IntelliJ's names on purpose.

What a template writes depends on the type of the expression, and a template is only listed where it applies:
.for on a collection or an array, .if on a boolean, .nn on a value that can be null,
.ifpe on an Optional. The names it proposes come from the code, spelled in the project's naming convention for local variables or, where none is set, in the one the
file's names follow — orders.for declares an order
of the element type — and the imports its text needs are added with it. Templates appear once the type is known and you have started typing a name
after the dot.

Family — Templates

Null checks — .nn / .notnull, .null, .reqnonnull

Conditions — .if, .else, .while, .not, .assert, .switch

Loops — .for / .iter, .fori, .forr, .forEach, .stream

Optional — .opt, .optof, .ifp, .ifpe, .ifget, .orThrow, .orGet

Statements — .var, .return, .throw, .try, .twr, .synchronized, .sout, .soutv, .souf, .serr

Expressions — .inst / .instanceof, .cast, .castvar, .par, .arg, .lambda, .format, .new on a class name

They follow the Java level of the file's module, and write what that level compiles rather than disappearing:

Template — Below — From

.var, .for, .twr — the declared type, Order order — Java 10: var order

.inst — instanceof and a cast into a local — Java 16: a type pattern

.ifpe — if (…isPresent()) … else … — Java 9: ifPresentOrElse

.stream on an Optional — map(Stream::of).orElseGet(Stream::empty) — Java 9: not listed, stream() is its member

An expression that does work is never written twice: where the older form needs the value in two places, repo.findById(id).ifget
declares a local for it first, and .fori, whose bound runs on every iteration, is not offered on a call. Templates with no equivalent
at the level — Optional before Java 8, .twr before 7 — are not listed. Rust gets its own postfix set from rust-analyzer, in
the same list.

Postfix templates of your own sit beside them — a template of the Postfix kind, offered on the values it says it applies to. See
Code templates.

title: Matching and writing
text: Completion

title: Matching and writing
text: How the letters you type are matched, what accepting a row writes, and how to read a row.

title: How a name is matched
text:
A name does not have to be spelled the way it is declared. What you type is matched three ways, best first, and which one
matched is part of the order:

Match — Typed — Reaches

An exact prefix — toLo — toLowerCase

A prefix ignoring case — TOLO — toLowerCase — a shift held one letter too long

The camel humps — tolc, aAE, SBA, MAXV — toLowerCase, addAllElements, SpringBootApplication, MAX_VALUE — an underscore starts a word too

It is one rule for every kind of candidate — a member, a local, a static import, a class name.

Settings → Completion → Popup decides when the popup arrives and how forgiving it is: whether it opens on its own while you
type, after how long a pause, or only on the chord; and case-sensitive matching. That last is about case, not humps — off, only the
first letter must agree, the one that carries information in Java since a capital means a type; on, every letter must, so aAE
still reaches addAllElements and aae no longer does.

title: A name with nothing to its left
text:
Java says exactly what a bare identifier can mean, and the popup offers those things nearest first:

• What the scope binds — locals, method and lambda parameters, the for variable, a try-with-resources, a
catch parameter, a pattern variable from o instanceof Foo f. A variable of this block beats a parameter of the
method; in one block, the line above beats twenty lines up. A shadowing name is offered once, as the inner one — what the name resolves to.

• The enclosing type's own members, and what it inherits, without this..

• What an import static brought in, with the type it came from on the row — the one case where nothing else
on screen says where a bare name is from.

• Class names, from the type-name index.

A local is not in scope inside its own declaration, so int counted = coun offers counter, not counted.
In a static method an instance member is not offered at all: it would not compile.

Str is a type being written and str a variable, and no score makes one the other. A capitalised name with a
lowercase letter leads with types; anything else leads with what is in scope, where a SCREAMING_CASE constant of your own class
lives. Both lists are always offered, so a prefix read the "wrong" way costs a scroll, not an answer.

title: What accepting one writes
text:
A method is a call: accepting size writes size(). When it takes arguments the caret lands between the
parentheses, where the parameter hints strip is about to describe them; when it takes none, after them.

• Parameter names are not written — tabbing through put(key, value) placeholders to delete them is slower than typing,
and a class file carries no names anyway.

• When the call is already written — t.si() with the caret after si, correcting a name — the
parentheses are left alone, not doubled.

• A class picked after new writes the call too: ArrayList becomes ArrayList<>() (the
diamond only for a generic class), with the caret after it when a constructor takes nothing and between the parentheses when every one
takes something. An interface or an abstract class writes Runnable() {} with the caret inside the braces — an anonymous class —
except an abstract class that can only be built with arguments, where the caret waits between the parentheses. A name that stands for
several classes (Shape, in java.awt and elsewhere) keeps just the name until you choose its import, and an enum is not a thing you create.

• An overloaded method is one row per overload, fewest parameters first — wait(),
wait(long timeoutMillis), wait(long timeoutMillis, int nanos) — since each leaves the caret in a different place.
After :: they are one row, because a method reference writes only the name. A method that merely overrides an
inherited one appears once.

• What could not be written there is not offered: a private member of another class, a package-private one from another package,
and a protected one through a receiver outside its package and your class — route.clone() and
route.finalize() are not Java, this.clone() is.

title: Reading a row
text:
The icon
What it is. A member is a circle — m method, c constructor, f field,
v variable, p parameter — and a type a rounded square — c class, i interface,
e enum, r record, @ annotation; a package is a folder, a template {'{}'}. A dot in the
corner marks static, a lock final, a dashed outline abstract, a diagonal stroke deprecated.
The name
What it is called, with the letters you typed marked. Bold when the receiver's own type declares it,
regular when inherited, dimmed when it is java.lang.Object's. A deprecated one is struck through.
The parameters
Beside the name, with their names where the member carries them: equals(Object obj). A library compiled without
parameter names shows the types alone.
The right edge
What a method returns or a field holds — getClass() as Class<? extends ServiceRoute>,
typed after the receiver — and, for an inherited member only, where it comes from: what tells List.of from
Set.of.

The documentation of the highlighted row appears beside the list — the card hover draws, from the same answer, so the two
cannot describe one member two ways. It is fetched only for the row you highlight: a library's documentation is read from its sources archive,
and doing it for four hundred rows would put an archive read per candidate on the keystroke that opened the popup.

title: Type names and their imports
text:
Typing a capitalised name (not after a dot) offers every class matching it across the JDK, your dependencies and your
project, each with its package — and (+N more) when several packages declare the name. Within each match tier your project's types
come before a jar's, and shorter names before longer.

• Accepting a name that maps to a single class adds its import — turn that off with Settings → Completion →
Auto-import on accept. An ambiguous name inserts just the name; Alt+Enter → Import '…'
picks the package.

• A qualified name completes one segment at a time: import org. offers springframework, and
import org.springframework.boot. offers its packages beside its classes.

• A receiver not imported yet still completes: Arrays. without the import offers its members, and accepting
one adds the import too — for an unambiguous name only.

• A type receiver offers its nested types beside the statics — Map. offers Entry.

A nested type completed by its simple name is written through its outer, since Inner alone is not a name Java resolves:

One import serves every nested type of that class, the form people write by hand. Where the simple name is already in scope nothing is added:
inside the outer class or a sibling nested in it, and in a file that imports the nested type outright.

Other languages:

In TypeScript and JavaScript — and in a .svelte file and an Angular project's templates — the popup
is the language server's: typescript-language-server, svelteserver, ngserver. Install it from Settings →
Language Servers; without one the file is still coloured, folded and edited, with nothing to suggest.

No language server will serve a JSP — a template that prints JavaScript, half of it <%= %> holes. The names the block
declares (var, function, foo: function (…) and their parameters) come first, then the browser globals.
After document., location., Math. and the rest of the platform, the members are read off the object
itself in the engine the page runs in — not a list that could be stale. Hover says the same. What it cannot know is jQuery:
$ is offered, $(…). has no object to read.
