title: Imber: Bevy games and the profiler
text: Imber can look into a running Bevy game over its Remote Protocol, change it only if you allow that, and read the newest profiler recording to propose a performance change.

page: Imber: Bevy games and the profiler
title: Looking into a running game
text:
The Look into a running Bevy game family (Settings › Imber › Tools it may use, for projects with a Cargo.toml) connects to a game over the Bevy Remote Protocol. The game needs RemotePlugin and RemoteHttpPlugin, and the connection is to this machine only.

• brp_connect: connects, and waits for the game to come up if it is still starting.

• brp_query: entities with their component values.

• brp_get: one entity in full.

• brp_resources and brp_get_resource: the resources and one resource's value.

• brp_types: the type registry, so it knows the shape of a component before it asks for it.

• brp_screenshot, brp_stats, brp_actions and brp_states: the game's window as an image (900 px wide unless asked otherwise), its frame time and diagnostics, and the actions it lets a remote client run. These need the arbor-bevy-remote plugin in the game (see Bevy Remote).

• brp_watch: one entity observed for a few seconds (5 by default, 30 at most), reporting which fields changed and their first and last value.

Reading never asks. The connection itself and the protocol are explained on the Bevy Remote page.

page: Imber: Bevy games and the profiler
title: Changing a running game
text: Let it change a running Bevy game in Settings is a separate switch, off by default, and it needs the Bevy family on. It adds brp_mutate, brp_insert, brp_remove, brp_spawn, brp_despawn, brp_set_resource, brp_reparent and brp_call, and, to play the game, brp_key, brp_type, brp_mouse, brp_gamepad, brp_action and brp_set_state (brp_action runs one of the game's own registered actions). brp_call calls any Remote Protocol method by name; a method that only reads (rpc.discover, anything named query, get or list) runs without the question, any other asks like the rest. These act on live state with no review and no undo. Imber asks once per conversation ("Let Imber change the running game?"), the yes covers every change in that conversation, and every change is listed in the run's summary. Autonomous mode does not skip the question.

page: Imber: Bevy games and the profiler
title: Reading a profiler recording
text: The project-intelligence family includes three read-only profiler tools. bennu_profile_recordings lists the recordings the Profiler tool window made. bennu_profile_diff compares two of them method by method (the share of the run each took before and after, biggest changes first), to check that a change made the code faster. bennu_profile_summary is a compact summary of one recording (the newest unless Imber names another): the hottest methods with their source lines, the biggest allocation sites and allocated types, lock contention and garbage-collection pauses. Imber uses it to find the method worth optimising and to propose a change. These three only read: with no recording they tell you to make one first. Recording by hand is described on the Profiler page; Imber recording for you is below.

page: Imber: Bevy games and the profiler
title: Recording a running JVM
text: The Profile family (profile_start, profile_stop) lets Imber record a JVM that is already running on this machine with Flight Recorder, through jcmd. Imber asks at every start, naming the JVM, because a recording samples a running program (nothing in it is changed, it runs a little slower). Imber names the JVM by process id or by part of its main class; with neither, it gets the list to choose from. One recording per conversation, started in one message and stopped in a later one. profile_stop ends the recording, waits until it has been read and saved, and returns its summary; the recording is then in the Profiler window like any other. A recording keeps sampling until it is stopped. Sub-agents never have these tools, and the family can be switched off like any other.

title: Imber: Conversations
text: Imber

title: Imber: Conversations
text: Every conversation with Imber is saved on disk, listed by the title in the panel header, and is either an agent conversation (works in the project) or a chat (talks only).

title: The conversation switcher
text:
The title in the header is a switcher. It lists your conversations, today's first, each with the model it used, when it was last touched and what it cost. The open one shows as saved. Choosing a row opens that conversation, with its thread and its context meter.

• New conversation: the pencil-and-square button in the header, or the command Imber: New conversation in an isolated copy for a conversation in a copy.

• Rename: the pencil next to the title.

• Delete: the trash next to the title, or Delete conversation in the … menu. It asks first. Deleting a conversation also removes its isolated copy, its index and the processes started in it. The money it cost stays counted against your limits: costs are kept in a ledger of their own.

Conversations are plain files in Bennu's data folder (arbor/data/bennu/assistant), one per conversation, holding both what the panel draws and what is sent to the model next time.

title: Agent or Chat
text:
The Agent / Chat switch in the header chooses between two kinds of conversation. Each has its own list and its own home screen, and a conversation is one or the other for good; opening a chat from the list switches the panel to Chat.

Agent — Chat

Works in the project — Yes: reads, searches, edits, builds, runs, debugs through Bennu's tools — No. It cannot read, search or change anything

What it sees — The project, the open file, the selection, the instruction files — Only what you type or select

Tools — All the families you left on — Four: the help about Bennu, opening a panel, drawing a diagram, showing a picture

Modes and reach — Mode menu and Reach apply — Not shown: nothing to ask

Good for — Anything about the project — A question unrelated to the project, or when you want to be sure nothing is touched

Chat only in Settings › Imber › New conversations makes new conversations chats by default. Git, skills and sub-agents are not available in a chat.

title: The home screen
text: With no conversation open the panel shows its home. An agent home offers six starters about the project (explain this file, explain the project, show me a panel, find why it fails, document it, review my changes); a chat home offers four that need no project (explain a concept, write a regex, rewrite a text, think it through). It also lists your four most recent conversations and the month's spending so far.

title: What is in the thread
text:
• Your messages on the right; Imber's as flowing Markdown (headings, lists, tables, quotes, highlighted code) that you can select. Hover an answer to copy it or open it as a document, a Markdown editor where you can edit and save it without changing the conversation. Hover your own message to copy it.

• Tools it used, folded into one line that opens on demand ("Read 2 files · Searched once").

• Cards for proposals (Imber › Reviewing changes), questions, access prompts, the step plan, sub-agents, live runs and debugger stops.

• Notices in the thread: a compaction, a limit reached, an access grant, a system note about another conversation.

title: The step plan
text: For work with several steps Imber writes a plan first and ticks the steps off. The card lists them (done, in progress, still to do) with a bar and "3 of 7 · 43%". The percentage is steps done over steps planned: it says how much of the list is done, not how long the rest will take, and it goes down if the plan grows. The plan costs a few hundred output tokens per update, a few cents for a task of several steps. Questions and small changes get no plan. Step plan in the composer's settings menu (and in Settings › Imber) switches it off; the tool and its instruction are then not sent at all.

title: Several conversations at once
text: Two conversations can run on the same project. A file one of them is changing is reserved to it until its run ends: the other is refused, naming the conversation, and can wait or work elsewhere (reading is never blocked). Services and debug sessions belong to the conversation that started them. Builds queue. See Imber › Running and observing.

title: Imber: Cost and context
text: Imber

title: Imber: Cost and context
text: Every request carries the whole conversation, so the cost depends less on how much Imber writes than on how much it re-reads; Bennu keeps that small, shows where tokens go, and stops a run at the limits you set.

title: The context meter
text:
Above the composer a bar shows how full the model's window is, split into tool definitions, Imber rules, project instructions, the skills index, files and search results, and the conversation. It stays calm until 75%, turns amber there and red past 90%. Open the line for the breakdown and for how much of the last request came from the provider's cache. Every figure is an estimate (about four characters to a token); the exact count comes back with each answer.

Show what would be sent… (the panel's … menu) lists the same parts for the next request, in the order the provider reads them, with the cost when the cache is cold and when it is warm.

title: Models, prices and the context window
text:
The model list and prices are a file, models.toml, built in. Settings › Imber › Models and prices › Create a price file creates your own copy (assistant-models.toml in Bennu's config folder): an entry with the same id replaces the built-in one and any other id is added, so a price change or a new model needs an edit and a Reload, not a new build. An entry gives [model.price] (input, output and optionally cache_read, cache_write_5m, cache_write_1h), the context_max window, the efforts it accepts and, for a model that charges more for long prompts, [model.long_prompt] with over_tokens and its own rates. Cost is worked out request by request, with cache reads and writes at their own rates.

The context window is the largest window Imber may use in a conversation, 50K up to 1M; a size the model cannot hold is listed but cannot be picked, and changing to a smaller model shrinks the window to fit.

title: How the cost is kept down
text:
• The provider's cache. Tool definitions, instructions and the conversation so far are cached, so a request pays full price only for what the previous one did not already send. Anything that changes the start of a request starts it over, which is why the open file travels with your message and not with the instructions.

• Long cache. By default the tools and instructions are kept in the one-hour cache (Settings › Imber › Keep instructions cached for an hour) instead of the five-minute one. It costs a little more the first time and pays off when you pause for more than five minutes between messages or open another conversation in the same project.

• Reading the same thing twice. A file already read comes back as one line when unchanged, and as the lines that differ when changed. file_outline and read_files help open big files by the part that matters.

• Big results are digests. Counts, grouped problems, the files most affected, and a statement of what was left out. expand_result gives the detail.

• Old results are stubbed in a batch. When many old file reads and search results have piled up they are replaced all at once by one-line stubs saying how to fetch them again, and the thread says so. In a batch, never one per message, because changing a message makes the cache start over from it.

title: Compacting
text:
Compact conversation… (offered by the context meter) first clears the output of older tool calls, then folds everything before your last message into a summary. What you type in the dialog is what the summary must not lose, as with /compact "…" in Claude Code.

• The summary is written by the cheaper side model (Settings › Imber › Cheaper model for side jobs; by default the cheapest Haiku in the price list), with fixed sections: goal, decisions, state, open questions and your preferences, followed by the files changed and the current plan taken from the record word for word.

• It happens when you ask, automatically when the conversation reaches 90% of the largest window you chose (clearing first, summarising only if that is not enough), and at the end of a run once the conversation is past 60% of the window.

• The thread says how many messages became how many tokens and which tool output was not kept. Compacting costs one request, added to the conversation's cost.

title: Changing model or window in a long conversation
text: A new model cannot reuse what the old one has cached, so a conversation of several thousand tokens sends all of it again at full price. Bennu asks first, with an estimate. A smaller context window asks only when the conversation already fills it (it would be compacted first); a larger one changes nothing. Turn the question off with Settings › Imber › Confirm costly changes.

title: When a request fails
text:
A failed request is told apart by what caused it, and only the causes that pass by themselves are tried again.

• Sent again, automatically: no connection or DNS failure, a connection that goes silent (no data for two minutes) or drops while the answer streams, rate limit (429), overloaded (529) and server errors (5xx).

• Never retried: a rejected key (401/403), no credit or an account usage limit, a conversation too long for the window, an unknown model, an invalid request, and your own Stop. These end the run at once with the reason and what to do.

• How long it waits: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and then 30 seconds, each spread a little at random so agents that fail together do not return together, never less than the provider's own retry-after. A network that stays down is waited out for about three minutes in total; a provider that keeps answering "not now" is asked five times. A retry-after longer than two minutes is reported rather than waited for.

• While it waits the thread shows one calm line with the attempt and the seconds left: Retry now skips the wait, Stop ends the run at once. There is no toast per attempt. When the connection returns the line goes and the answer continues; the text the broken attempt had already shown is taken back and written again.

• Money: an attempt that failed after the provider had started it can still have been billed; it is counted once, as a request of its own. Spending limits are checked before every retry exactly as before a first request.

• When it gives up the message says what happened and the next step; the provider's own words are under Details. Every turn that finished is saved. Retry under the message sends the same request again, with no new message from you.

• Compaction (manual, automatic and at the end of a run) waits only about twenty seconds, then stops with the reason; the conversation is left exactly as it was and the next run tries again.

• Sub-agents retry the same way; their card shows waiting to retry. A failed agent reports to the conversation what failed, whether starting it again can help, and whether it had already changed files.

title: Spending limits
text:
Settings › Imber › Spending limits holds limits in euros: per conversation (default €5), per day (from midnight, your time; €10), per week (from Monday; off), per month (from the first; €50). 0 switches one off.

• A conversation or a period at its limit does not start another request, and a run in progress stops before the request that would take it over; the thread says which limit.

• The composer flags a limit from 80% of it (Warn from, adjustable) and shows what the conversation has cost.

• Limits count what conversations still running have spent so far, so two at once cannot together pass a daily, weekly or monthly limit that neither passes alone.

• Costs are recorded per run in a ledger of their own (usage.jsonl in the data folder): deleting a conversation does not hand its money back.

• Prices are in dollars, so amounts are converted at the Exchange rate you keep by hand (default 0.92 euros per dollar); with no usable rate a dollar counts as a euro. The rate never moves on its own.

• Sub-agents count against the same limits and have a cap of their own (Imber › Sub-agents).

title: Imber: Debugging with Imber
text: Imber

title: Imber: Debugging with Imber
text:
With the Debugger family on, Imber can debug a Java program instead of guessing: it sets breakpoints and logpoints, runs the program under the debugger or attaches to one, waits for a stop, reads the stack and values and steps, on the very session the Debug panel shows.

The debugger itself is described on the Debugging and Frames, values and watches pages; this page covers what is specific to Imber.

title: What it can do
text:
Step — Tools — Asks?

Set, list, remove breakpoints and logpoints — debug_set_breakpoint, debug_list_breakpoints, debug_remove_breakpoint — No

Start a session — debug_launch (builds and runs a main class), debug_attach (to a JVM on 127.0.0.1) — Every time

Wait and look — debug_wait_stop, debug_stack, debug_variables, debug_evaluate, debug_output — No

Move — debug_step (several steps at once), debug_resume, debug_run_to (like Run to Cursor), debug_break_on_exception, debug_select_thread — No

Let go — debug_detach — No

title: Its breakpoints are visible and yours
text: Breakpoints Imber sets are saved in the project's breakpoints, drawn with a sparkle in the gutter and badged Imber in the Breakpoints list (Ctrl+Shift+F8). You can disable or delete them like any other. It never changes or removes one you set, and holds at most 20. A logpoint can say "only when total > 100" through a condition and a pass count, and can ask for values to be captured at the stop. A line that holds no code (a comment, a brace, an annotation, a declaration) is moved to the next line that does, and Imber is told which line it ended on.

title: Reading values cannot change anything
text:
Values are read as paths (order.customer.name, items[2].price) through fields and array slots. Method calls, constructors, assignments and ++ are refused before they reach the program, with or without approval. Variables named like secrets (password, token, secret, apiKey, credential…) are masked. Results are capped: frames, variables and long values are cut and say so.

Nothing is ever run in the program, so toString() is never called. Instead, the common JDK types are read from their fields: a BigDecimal reads as 123.45, dates and times (LocalDate, OffsetDateTime, Instant, java.util.Date…) as ISO text, enums as their name, boxes and Optional as their content, and lists, maps and sets as ArrayList(size=3). Any other object reads as Type@id and is opened with a longer path.

title: Several threads, and why a stop happened
text: Each stop says whether it is new (a breakpoint reached now), a step, or leftover (hit while another stop was still open), and which condition let it through with the values it read. A breakpoint Imber sets with suspend: "thread" stops only its own thread; when several threads are stopped the report lists the others, debug_select_thread switches between them, and debug_step and debug_resume accept a thread. Resuming moves on to the next waiting stop. debug_step skips a record's accessors, and with return_value it also reports what the method it left returned. Removing a breakpoint resumes the threads parked on it, never the stop in front of you.

title: Reading the program's output
text: Each launch keeps what the program prints under its session id, and debug_output reads it also after the program has exited. Without an id it reads the program this conversation launched last, so another conversation starting its own debug run never changes what Imber reads; the id that debug_launch printed selects a specific one. The last eight launches are kept.

title: The session belongs to the conversation
text: The session outlives one message: when a run ends the program stays alive (suspended, if it was stopped at a breakpoint, so you can inspect it) and the next message goes on from there. There is one debug session per conversation. It ends when Imber detaches (a program it launched is stopped, one it attached to is resumed and left running), when the program exits, after the idle time in Settings › Imber › Debug session idle time (30 minutes by default, counted from the last debug tool), when the project closes, or when you press Stop beside the debugger controls, where the line "Imber … ends in N min if unused" shows how long is left. Breakpoints it set without starting a session stay for you to use.

title: When the program stops while Imber is not waiting
text:
Bennu itself notices the stop and takes a snapshot while the program is still suspended: where it stopped, the top of the stack, the top frame's locals and the values the breakpoint asked to capture (capped and with secrets masked). What happens next follows the conversation:

• A run is active: the snapshot reaches Imber as a system note with its next tool result.

• No run is active: the note is queued for your next message, and the thread shows a card ("Stopped at Order.java:42 in OrderService.total") with Send to Imber now.

• Start a run by itself: off by default (Settings › Imber › Start a run when the program stops, or per conversation from the composer's menu › Decisions). At most three an hour per conversation. It spends money and counts toward your limits.

title: Changing the program: a separate switch
text:
Let it change the program it debugs (off by default) offers four tools: debug_throw creates an exception inside the program (its constructor runs there) and throws it from the line the stopped thread is on, debug_force_return makes the method on top of the stack return a literal value at once (finally blocks included), debug_drop_frame discards a frame so the call runs again, debug_set_value writes a number, boolean, character, String or null to a local, a field or a path such as order.total (final and static fields are refused). All need a stop; the last two need a VM that supports them. The program changes while it runs and there is no undo: side effects already produced stay. Imber asks once per conversation (Autonomous does not skip the question) and every change is listed in the thread and in the Debug panel as an Imber action.

The debugger tools target Java programs: a main class to launch, or a JVM listening on a local debug port.

title: Imber: Decisions and questions
text: Imber

title: Imber: Decisions and questions
text: The decision level sets how much Imber chooses alone when a choice is yours; when it does ask, it asks with a card of choices in the thread.

title: The decision level
text:
Level — Behaviour

Ask at forks (default) — It stops to ask when a choice is yours.

Only big decisions — It asks about architecture, new dependencies and anything hard to undo, and decides the rest.

Decide itself — It picks the best option, asks only when truly blocked (at most two questions a run) and lists its decisions at the end.

Set the default in Settings › Imber › New conversations › Decisions. A conversation can follow the setting or have its own level: composer settings menu › Decisions, or Imber: Decisions in this conversation… in the Command Palette. A change applies from the next message.

title: Your own words about decisions
text:
Under the level there is a free-text field ("Your instructions about decisions", up to 2,000 characters) for your own rules at any level, for example "always ask before touching public API" or "never add a dependency". A conversation can add its own text in the same window; it is appended to the global one.

The same window also holds the conversation's own switch for Start a run when the program stops (see Imber › Debugging with Imber).

title: Questions
text:
Where it would otherwise guess, Imber asks with ask_user. Each question is a column of choices, one per row: pick one, or tick several, and Other… is always there to type your own. When it asks several things at once, a strip of tabs names them (a tick once answered): jump to any, or use Back and Next; the last step sends all the answers together, so changing an earlier one costs nothing. Answered, the card shrinks to what you decided and stays in the thread.

Questions about access or confirmation ("Allow this?", "Start a process?") are not part of this: they follow the mode and reach, see Imber › Permissions and modes. Sub-agents cannot ask you questions.

title: Imber: Working from the editor
text: Imber

title: Imber: Working from the editor
text: Imber can be asked from the margin of the editor, from a doc comment, from a Markdown selection and from a stack trace, each with a ready-made request; pasted code is fenced automatically and the panel can take the room of the editor.

title: The sparkle in the margin
Doc comments
text: In a Java or Rust file a sparkle in the gutter sits on every doc comment, and under the caret on a declaration that has none. It offers Improve this comment, Check against the code (parameters, return value, exceptions, statements the code contradicts), Make it shorter, Translate to English / Italian and Write documentation. The request carries the file, the lines and the declaration, so there is nothing to type; the result comes back as a proposal like any other edit.

title: Markdown files
text: In a Markdown file, selecting a passage shows a small button at its end: Improve the writing, Make it shorter, Say more, Fix spelling and grammar, Translate.

title: Stack traces
text: In the Run and Build output, the line that starts a stack trace has a Fix with Imber button that sends the trace and asks for the cause in the project.

title: Pasting code into the composer
text:
Code pasted into the message box becomes a fenced block with its language (```java … ```), with a blank line either side, at the caret; one Ctrl+Z takes it back out. A paste counts as code when it spans several lines and looks like source (brackets, statements, indentation, a recognisable language such as Java, Kotlin, Rust, TypeScript, JSON, XML, SQL, YAML, properties or shell); prose, lists and single lines are left as they are. The language comes from the text, or from the open file when the text does not say. A paste made inside a fence does not open another one.

• Each block of the message being written is listed above the box with its language, line count and first line. Click a row to read the block highlighted, or the cross to remove it.

• In the thread your message shows its blocks highlighted, like Imber's own.

• Ctrl+Shift+V pastes exactly what is on the clipboard, with no fence. Settings › Imber › Wrap pasted code in a fenced block turns the wrapping off.

• A paste over 200 KB is cut at a line and a notice says so.

title: Expanding the panel
text: The button in the panel header (or a double-click on the header, Ctrl+Shift+U, or Imber: Expand panel) covers the editor area and the bottom dock; the title bar, the rails and the side panels stay. The same button, the same keys, Imber: Restore panel or Esc from inside the panel (when no menu or window is open over it) put it back at the width it had. The editors are only covered, not closed: their scroll, cursors and unsaved changes stay as they were. Expanded, the conversation is a centred column: prose keeps a comfortable line length, while code, diagrams, diffs and the cards for live runs use the full width. Closing the panel, or opening another one on the right, ends the expansion.

title: What travels with a message
text: The file you are in and the lines you selected travel with the message, shown as chips above the text; the selection is read when you click into the composer. Instruction files in play appear as chips too.

title: Imber: Troubleshooting
text: Imber

title: Imber: Troubleshooting
text: The messages Imber and Bennu show most often, what each one means, and what to do.

title: "No API key is set. Add one in Settings › Imber."
text: Open Settings › Imber › Connection, paste your Anthropic key and press Save. See Imber › Getting started.

title: "Open a project first — Imber works inside one"
text: Agent conversations need an open project. Open one, or switch to Chat for a question that has nothing to do with a project.

title: A run stopped with a limit message ("Raise the limit in Settings › Imber › Spending limits to go on")
text: A conversation, day, week or month reached its limit in euros. Raise the limit under Settings › Imber › Spending limits, or set it to 0 to switch it off. See Imber › Cost and context.

title: "… is outside what you allowed. Open it for reading, or for reading and writing?"
text: Imber reached for a file outside the reach. Choose Deny, Allow reading or Allow reading and writing; the answer covers that folder for the session. To avoid the question, widen the reach or add the folder under Settings › Imber › What it may reach. See Imber › Permissions and modes.

title: "The user has switched that kind of tool off" / "this is a chat"
text: The family is off in Settings › Imber › Tools it may use, or the conversation is a Chat. Turn the family on, or start an Agent conversation.

title: "Editing is switched off"
text: Edit files is off (Settings › Imber, or composer › Settings › Permissions). Imber is read-only until you turn it on.

title: "… holds secrets and is never written" / "the repository's own .git files are never changed here"
text: Hard limits. Edit the file yourself.

title: The status line says "No connection - retrying" (or "The API is overloaded", "Rate limit reached")
text: A request failed for a reason that usually passes, and Imber is waiting to send it again. The line shows the attempt and the seconds left; Retry now skips the wait and Stop ends the run. When the connection comes back the line disappears and the answer continues; nothing you did in between is lost. See Imber › Cost and context › When a request fails.

title: A run ended with "You are offline", "The API stopped answering" or "The connection dropped"
text: Imber waited for the connection for about three minutes and it did not come back. Everything that had finished is saved. Fix the connection (or the VPN/proxy), then press Retry under the message: the same request is sent again, with no new message from you.

title: "The API key was rejected"
text: The key is invalid, revoked, or may not use that model. Open Settings › Imber › Connection, save a valid key, then press Retry. Nothing is retried automatically: waiting would not help.

title: "The account has no credit left or reached a usage limit"
text: The provider refused because of the account, not Imber's own spending limits. Check the plan and billing of the provider account, then press Retry.

title: "The conversation no longer fits the model's window"
text: Compact the conversation (the panel's … menu › Compact), or start a new one, then press Retry. See Imber › Cost and context.

title: "The rate limit was reached" / "The API is overloaded"
text: Imber already tried five times, waiting at least as long as the provider asked. Wait a minute and press Retry, or use a lighter model or effort.

title: A sub-agent failed with a connection error
text: The agent's card says what failed; the conversation that started it is told the same, including whether the agent had already changed files. Ask for the agent again; its earlier changes stay.

title: The proposal card says Outdated
text: A file changed after Imber read it. Nothing was written. Use Re-apply on current file, Ask to redo, or Discard. See Imber › Reviewing changes.

title: "Wait for Imber to finish, or stop it first"
text: The action (deleting a conversation, applying or discarding an isolated copy) needs the run to be over. Press Stop, or wait.

title: Another conversation is changing this file
text: A file is reserved by the conversation that is changing it until its run ends. Wait for that run, work on another file, or stop the other conversation. Reading is never blocked.

title: A build waits behind another
text: Builds from every conversation and the Build button share one queue per project. Open the Live panel to see it. For Cargo projects, composer › Build isolation › Separate target avoids the wait at the cost of disk space.

title: "A git worktree needs git access, which is off"
text: Turn on Settings › Imber › Git, or use the text-only copy.

title: "The project is too large for a plain copy"
text: A plain isolated copy is capped at 512 MB or 40,000 files. In a git repository use the worktree kind (git access must be on).

title: The conversation got expensive
text: Check the context meter's breakdown. Compact the conversation, start a new one, lower the effort, switch off families you do not need (screenshots are costly), or use a cheaper model. See Imber › Cost and context.

title: Answers ignore a project rule
text: Check that Settings › Imber › Project instructions is on and that the file is among the chips above the composer. Files are cut at 16 KB each and 40 KB together.

title: A skill is not used
text: A skill is invisible until enabled in the skills manager. Check Imber › Skills for the folders, the format, and the size limits.

title: "Imber could not write a diagram that parses"
text: After three tries the source is shown as text. Copy it from the notice, or ask Imber to simplify the diagram.

title: A debug session ended by itself
text: An unused session ends after the idle time in Settings › Imber (30 minutes by default), when the program exits, or when the project closes. See Imber › Debugging with Imber.

title: Imber says it cannot do something Bennu can
text: It acts only through its tools: no shell, no push, nothing outside the reach. Check Imber › Tools it can use for the tool, and the family switch.

title: Imber: Getting started
text: Imber

title: Imber: Getting started
text: Open the panel with Alt+A, store your Anthropic API key once in Settings, pick a model, and send a request.

title: Open the panel
text: The panel sits on the right of the editor. Open it with Alt+A, the sparkle on the right rail, or Toggle Imber in the Command Palette. With no conversation open it shows its home: the mode you are in, the project, the file and the instruction files it would work with, a few starters (an agent card sends a request at once; a chat card leaves the start of a sentence in the composer) and your recent conversations. The panel opens on it.

title: Set the API key
text:
Imber is billed to your own Anthropic account. Every message costs money, and the conversation shows what it has cost.

• Open Settings › Imber (the … menu of the panel has Imber settings…).

• Paste the key under Connection › API key and press Save. The page then shows Set; it never shows the key again.

• Remove deletes it from the vault.

The key is kept in a credential vault of its own, apart from the one that holds your git tokens, is never written to a config file, and is sent only to Anthropic with each request. Without a key a request fails with "No API key is set. Add one in Settings › Imber."

title: Choose a model, effort and window
text:
The composer has one quiet line under the text box:

• Model: each entry shows what it is for, the size of its window and its price per million tokens (input / output). The list and the prices come from a file; see Imber › Cost and context.

• Settings (the sliders icon): Effort (how hard it thinks: Low, Medium, High, Extra high, Max; a model without such a setting ignores it), Context window (the largest window Imber may use, 50K up to 1M, limited by the model), Reach, Permissions, Decisions, Skills…, Step plan, Sub-agents, Isolated copy and Build isolation. Each shows its current value.

• Mode (agent conversations only): Manual, Accept edits or Autonomous. See Imber › Permissions and modes.

The defaults for a new conversation are set in Settings › Imber › New conversations: Opus 5.5 at High effort with a 200K window, in Manual mode with the reach "this project". The composer changes them for the conversation you are in. The full list is in Imber › Settings reference.

title: Send a first request
text:
• Open a project (Imber works inside one) and the file you care about. The file you are in and the lines you selected travel with the message, shown as chips above the text.

• Type a request, for example "Explain what this class does" or "Rename total to amountDue everywhere".

• Press Ctrl+Enter to send; Enter is a new line.

• Stop (the square where Send was) ends a run; what it had written stays.

In Manual mode a change arrives as a proposal card; open Review to read the diff and Apply all (Ctrl+Enter in the review window) or Reject all. See Imber › Reviewing changes.

title: See the request before it is sent
text: The … menu has Show what would be sent…, which opens the exact request for the next message without sending it, and Dry run, which makes Send show the request instead of making it. Both list where the size comes from and a rough cost. The key is masked.

title: Project instructions are read automatically
text: The project's CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, and your own assistant-instructions.md in Bennu's config folder, are added to Imber's instructions, so it follows the build command, conventions and no-go areas a team has written down. Each file is cut at 16 KB and all together at 40 KB, and a file whose text repeats another is sent once. They appear as chips above the text. They never override the access prompts or the ban on a shell. The switch is Settings › Imber › New conversations › Project instructions.

title: Imber: the assistant in Bennu
text: Imber

title: Imber: the assistant in Bennu
text: Imber is the AI assistant built into Bennu: a chat and agent panel on the right of the editor that reads, searches, edits, builds, runs and debugs your project through Bennu's own tools, and asks before anything that matters.

title: What Imber is
text:
Imber runs on Claude, a model made by Anthropic, and talks to it with your own Anthropic API key. It is not a separate product: it lives in the Bennu window (Alt+A, or the sparkle on the right rail) and works on the project that is open. The name is Latin for rain: the thing the whole forest of Arbor runs on.

There are two kinds of conversation, kept apart by the Agent / Chat switch in the panel header. An agent conversation works inside the project with Bennu's tools. A chat conversation has no tools on the project at all: it only sees what you type or select, and can look up Bennu's own documentation, open a panel and draw a diagram.

title: The ideas behind it
text:
• Bennu's tools, never a shell. Imber reads and changes the project through the same engine you use: the index, usages, rename, structural replace, build, tests, Local History. It cannot type arbitrary commands.

• You decide how much it decides. Three modes (Manual, Accept edits, Autonomous), four reaches (this file, this project, all open projects, anywhere on disk) and a matrix of what asks when. See Imber › Permissions and modes.

• Everything it changes can be reviewed and undone. Proposals, a diff window, Undo on applied changes, Local History, and an isolated copy for risky work. See Imber › Reviewing changes.

• The cost is visible and capped. Every conversation shows what it cost, and limits in euros stop a runaway run. See Imber › Cost and context.

• Your key stays on your machine. It lives in a credential vault of its own and goes only to Anthropic. See Imber › Privacy and safety.

title: Where to read next
text:

Imber › Reviewing changes — Proposals, outdated proposals, Undo, Local History, the isolated copy.

Imber › Tools it can use — Every family of tools, how to switch one off, git, several projects.

Imber › Running and observing — Processes, recipes, scenarios, logs, the build queue and who broke the build.

Imber › Debugging with Imber — Breakpoints, stops, snapshots and the tools that change a running program.

Imber › Bevy games and the profiler — Looking into a running Bevy game and reading a profiler recording.

Imber › Screenshots and diagrams — Seeing a front end on localhost, and drawing Mermaid diagrams.

Imber › Skills — Teaching Imber how you want a kind of task done.

Imber › Sub-agents — Helpers with a clean context for side tasks.

Imber › Decisions and questions — How much it decides alone and how it asks you.

Imber › Cost and context — Tokens, the cache, compaction, limits in euros.
